title: Adaptive Workflow Intelligence: A Cognitive Architecture for Context-Driven Enterprise Automation
comment: 12 pages, simulation-based evaluation of adaptive workflow agents
summary: Enterprise systems increasingly rely on automated workflows, yet many AI-driven solutions remain brittle under non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback. While reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) agents offer partial adaptability, they do not by themselves provide persistent reflection mechanisms or straightforward integration with policy-constrained enterprise operations. This paper introduces Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a cognitive architecture for context-driven enterprise agents organized around a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection (PCAR) loop. AWI treats reflection as a mechanism for continuous policy refinement and combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation to support decision making under environmental drift and operational constraints. We evaluate AWI in a simulated enterprise decision workflow characterized by delayed outcomes and a controlled regime shift. In a drift-and-delay stress test, guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover more rapidly than static automation while maintaining policy compliance. Within this setting, AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, illustrating the stability-agility trade-off introduced by reflective policy adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a PCAR-loop cognitive architecture that adds explicit reflection and policy-aware adaptation to enterprise workflows, improving robustness under drift and delayed feedback.
AI.motivation: Enterprise workflows increasingly depend on automation, but current AI solutions like RL systems and LLM agents are brittle when conditions, policies, or feedback dynamics change. There is a need for agents that can adapt under environmental drift, handle delayed outcomes, and stay compliant with evolving enterprise policies, all while avoiding unstable or oscillatory behavior.
AI.method: The authors design AWI, a four-layer Perception–Cognition–Action–Reflection (PCAR) cognitive architecture. It incorporates hybrid reasoning, reflective memory, and feedback-driven adaptation, with reflection explicitly used to refine operational policies over time. They implement AWI in a simulated enterprise decision-making workflow with delayed feedback and introduce a controlled regime shift to create non-stationarity. Guardrails enforce policy constraints, and different automation strategies are compared under a drift-and-delay stress test.
AI.result: In the simulated setting, adaptive approaches that incorporate guardrail constraints recover performance faster after the regime shift than static automation baselines while remaining policy-compliant. Within those adaptive strategies, AWI’s reflective components lead to modest reductions in behavioral oscillations and in the variance of feedback signals, indicating smoother and more stable adaptation dynamics.
AI.conclusion: AWI demonstrates that embedding an explicit reflection layer for policy refinement within a PCAR cognitive loop can improve the robustness and stability of enterprise agents operating under non-stationary, delayed-feedback conditions and policy constraints. The results highlight a stability–agility trade-off: reflective policy adaptation can reduce volatility and feedback variance while still enabling relatively rapid recovery after environmental changes.

title: Accelerating Floating-Point Satisfiability Solving via Gradient Normalization
summary:
Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers are foundational to software verification, program analysis, and compiler testing, particularly over the theory of Quantifier-Free Floating-Point (QF_FP). While recent optimization-based SMT solvers have successfully applied gradient descent to continuous relaxations of logical formulas, they are fundamentally bottlenecked by gradient domination, a phenomenon where a small subset of difficult clauses hijacks the optimization trajectory, preventing the solver from satisfying the broader formula and trapping it in local minima.
  To overcome this, we present GradSAT, a novel framework that bridges optimization-based SMT solving with Multi-Task Learning (MTL). GradSAT reformulates the constraint satisfaction process by treating each SMT clause as an independent MTL task. By applying dynamic gradient normalization (GradNorm), GradSAT actively balances the gradient magnitudes across all clauses at runtime, systematically penalizing dominant gradients and accelerating lagging clauses to ensure uniform convergence. GradSAT implements this through a highly optimized, two-stage hybrid pipeline. First, a GPU-accelerated PyTorch backend leveraging symbolic compilation and operator fusion navigates the continuous relaxation to a high-quality basin. Second, the candidate assignment is handed off to a bit-precise local search engine to rapidly resolve the exact, rigorous assignment. By stabilizing the continuous search dynamics, GradSAT mitigates the brittleness of prior gradient-based solvers and provides a robust, highly parallelizable architecture for complex constraint solving.

AI.tldr: GradSAT is a new gradient-based SMT solving framework that treats each clause as a separate task and uses multi-task gradient normalization plus a hybrid GPU + local search pipeline to avoid gradient domination and improve solving for QF_FP formulas.
AI.motivation: Optimization-based SMT solvers over QF_FP suffer from gradient domination: a few hard clauses produce large gradients that dominate training, trap the search in poor local minima, and prevent satisfying the full formula. The authors want a more robust, scalable continuous-relaxation approach for SMT that remains effective on complex constraint sets and leverages modern GPU acceleration.
AI.method: They recast SMT solving as a Multi-Task Learning problem where each clause is a separate task. They apply GradNorm, a dynamic gradient normalization technique, to balance per-clause gradients so that no subset of clauses dominates optimization. Architecturally, they use a two-stage hybrid pipeline: (1) a GPU-accelerated PyTorch backend with symbolic compilation and operator fusion runs gradient-based optimization on a continuous relaxation to reach a promising basin; (2) a bit-precise local search engine refines this relaxed solution to a valid discrete model, if one exists.
AI.result: The abstract claims that GradSAT stabilizes gradient-based SMT solving, mitigates brittleness from gradient domination, and yields a robust, highly parallelizable architecture suitable for complex constraint solving over QF_FP. Specific quantitative improvements are not provided in the abstract but are implied through phrases like ‘robust’ and ‘highly parallelizable’.
AI.conclusion: Treating SMT clauses as multi-task learning objectives and applying dynamic gradient normalization within a hybrid GPU + local-search pipeline can substantially improve the robustness and effectiveness of optimization-based SMT solving, particularly by countering gradient domination that previously hindered gradient-based approaches.

title: Route-Verify-Vote: Procedure-Conditioned Self-Consistency for Mixed-Domain Reasoning
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, and 8 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at CCL26-Eval
summary:
Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question.
  We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure.
  On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a procedure-conditioned self-consistency framework that improves compositional commonsense reasoning on the SCoRE 2026 benchmark without updating model parameters.
AI.motivation: Compositional generalization—combining known reasoning skills in novel ways—remains difficult for language models, particularly in mixed, previously unseen domains. The SCoRE 2026 benchmark stresses this by requiring models to select complete sets of correct options per question in domains they were not trained on. Existing self-consistency approaches typically are not explicitly conditioned on domain procedures or do not exploit structured disagreement between full answer sets to allocate computation. The authors aim to address these limitations to boost exact-set accuracy in challenging commonsense reasoning tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a three-stage inference-time framework that operates on top of existing language models without parameter updates. (1) Route: Use the provided domain label to select a tailored reasoning procedure (domain-specific chain-of-thought style) that helps the model represent and apply constraints peculiar to that domain. (2) Verify: For each candidate answer option, prompt the model to explicitly check whether it satisfies the domain-specific constraints and thus should be included in the answer set. (3) Vote: Sample multiple complete answer sets following the same domain procedure, then aggregate them with a voting scheme over sets rather than individual options. Questions whose top two answer sets have a small vote-margin receive extra samples (adaptive RVV), effectively focusing more computation where the model is uncertain.
AI.result: Using 16 sampled answer sets per question, RVV achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6% on the official SCoRE 2026 test set. An adaptive version that allocates additional samples to questions with close vote margins increases accuracy to 77.3%. Further combining multiple models via selected domain routes improves performance to 79.4%. The system ultimately ranked second among all submitted systems on the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that conditioning self-consistency on domain-specific reasoning procedures and using disagreement between complete answer sets as an uncertainty signal both substantially improve compositional commonsense reasoning, especially in mixed unseen domains. These techniques allow more effective use of inference-time computation without modifying model parameters, suggesting a promising direction for enhancing reasoning performance through better procedural prompting, verification, and adaptive sampling strategies.

title: An Empirical Study of Agent Skills' Downstream Utility
summary: Agent Skills package procedural guidance and resources for reuse, but a relevant Skill does not necessarily improve task performance. Existing studies characterize Skill content and evaluate downstream performance, yet provide limited explanations of how utility depends on content, execution configuration, and multi-Skill organization. We conduct an empirical study on 87 SkillsBench tasks, defining downstream utility as the pass-rate difference from No-Skill on the same tasks under the same model--harness configuration. We compare the same Skills across nine configurations, then examine alternative published Skills and organizations of fixed Skill sets under three selected configurations. We retrieve marketplace candidates from a curated corpus of 37,596 Skills. LLM-assisted analysis of content, execution traces, and final artifacts, followed by author review, relates provided support to actual use and task outcomes. The same Skills help some configurations and hurt others on 36.78\% of tasks, with trajectories showing that recommended procedures can become an execution burden. Relevance rankings overlook more useful candidates. Within the evaluated candidate sets, reranking by support for required operations raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35--5.80 percentage points across the three configurations. We derive 17 authoring practices linking executable procedures to recovery, preservation of task requirements, and checks on final artifacts. Stage Plan and Dependency DAG outperform use order alone, with DAG's additional benefits concentrated in tasks supplied with five or six Skills. These findings guide developers to assess usable operation support, allow procedure adaptation while preserving task requirements, and make artifact dependencies explicit when organizing Skills.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies when and how reusable Agent Skills actually help or hurt LLM task performance across different configurations and organizations of Skills, and proposes practices and organizational structures that improve their utility.
AI.motivation: Although Agent Skills are meant to provide reusable procedural guidance and resources, a Skill that is topically relevant does not always improve, and can sometimes harm, downstream task performance. Prior work mostly classifies Skill content and checks performance, without explaining how utility depends on (1) what the Skill contains, (2) how it is executed, and (3) how multiple Skills are organized together. There is a need to understand these interactions systematically so developers can design and select Skills that truly help LLM agents on real tasks.
AI.method: The authors run an empirical study on 87 tasks from SkillsBench. They define Skill utility as the pass-rate difference versus a No-Skill baseline, holding the model and harness configuration fixed. First, they apply the same set of Skills across nine different execution configurations and compare performance. Then they evaluate alternative published Skills and different ways to organize a fixed set of Skills under three selected configurations. Candidate Skills are retrieved from a curated corpus of 37,596 marketplace Skills. Using LLM-assisted analysis of Skill content, execution traces, and final artifacts, followed by human author review, they relate the support a Skill claims to provide to how it is actually used and how it affects outcomes.
AI.result: The same Skills can help in some configurations and harm in others on 36.78% of tasks, indicating strong configuration dependence and showing that prescribed procedures can become an execution burden. Standard relevance rankings often miss more useful Skills. Within the evaluated candidate sets, reranking Skills by their support for required operations boosts first-choice task pass rates by 4.35–5.80 percentage points in each of the three studied configurations. Organizational structures that explicitly represent procedure and dependencies, such as Stage Plans and Dependency DAGs, outperform simple use-order organization, with DAGs bringing additional benefits especially when tasks have five or six associated Skills. The analysis yields 17 concrete authoring practices connecting executable procedures to error recovery, preservation of task requirements, and validation of final artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Skill utility is not determined just by relevance or content quality but by the interaction of Skill design, execution configuration, and multi-Skill organization. Developers should (1) assess whether Skills provide usable support for required operations rather than relying on topical relevance, (2) allow procedures to be adapted while preserving task requirements to avoid procedural burden, and (3) make artifact and operation dependencies explicit, e.g., through Stage Plans or Dependency DAGs, especially for tasks with many Skills. Applying these principles and reranking strategies can measurably improve LLM agent task performance when using Skills.

title: Tokka-Bench: Evaluating Tokenizers Across 100 Natural and 20 Programming Languages
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/bgub/tokka-bench. Interactive dashboard: https://tokka-bench.streamlit.app/
summary: Large language models rely on subword tokenizers whose quality varies across languages, yet no standardized multi-metric framework exists for broad comparative evaluation. We introduce Tokka-Bench, an open-source framework that evaluates tokenizers on five complementary metrics -- bytes per token, unique token coverage, subword fertility, word-split rate, and vocabulary composition -- across 100 natural languages (30+ scripts) and 20 programming languages, using language-aware segmentation adapted to each writing system. Comparing seven BPE tokenizers (GPT-2, GPT-4, gpt-oss, Llama 3.1, Gemma 3, Qwen3, and Kimi K2) within individual languages, we find that vocabulary allocation strategy matters more than raw vocabulary size, and that programming-language efficiency has converged among recent tokenizers despite divergent natural-language profiles. The framework, data, and interactive dashboard are publicly available.

AI.tldr: They present Tokka-Bench, a standardized, multi-metric benchmark for comparing subword tokenizers across many natural and programming languages, showing that how vocabulary is allocated matters more than how big it is.
AI.motivation: Large language models depend heavily on subword tokenizers, whose effectiveness differs widely between languages. Existing evaluations are fragmented, often use single metrics, and rarely cover many languages and scripts in a principled way. There is a need for a comprehensive, language-aware, and standardized framework to compare tokenizers and understand their design trade-offs across both natural and programming languages.
AI.method: They build Tokka-Bench, an open-source benchmarking framework that evaluates tokenizers using five complementary metrics: bytes per token, unique token coverage, subword fertility, word-split rate, and vocabulary composition. The evaluation covers 100 natural languages spanning over 30 scripts and 20 programming languages, using segmentation schemes tailored to each writing system. They then apply this framework to compare seven BPE-based tokenizers (GPT-2, GPT-4, gpt-oss, Llama 3.1, Gemma 3, Qwen3, Kimi K2) on a per-language basis.
AI.result: The analysis shows that tokenizer performance differences are better explained by how vocabulary entries are allocated across languages and token types than by the sheer size of the vocabulary. For programming languages, recent tokenizers have converged to similar efficiency levels despite having markedly different behavior and efficiency profiles for natural languages.
AI.conclusion: Tokka-Bench provides a systematic, multi-metric, and language-aware way to evaluate subword tokenizers at scale. It reveals important design insights—particularly that vocabulary allocation is more critical than vocabulary size—and highlights differing trade-offs between natural and programming language tokenization. The authors release the framework, datasets, and an interactive dashboard to support future tokenizer design and analysis.

title: How Could AI Eliminate Humanity? A Failure-Mode Analysis of Civilizational Risk
summary: This article develops a failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced artificial intelligence could contribute to human extinction, irreversible civilizational collapse, or permanent human disempowerment. The central thesis is that catastrophic AI risk does not require consciousness, hostility, or an explicit intention to harm humanity. Instead, risk may arise through several distinct but interacting pathways, including autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, and competitive deployment. The severity of these pathways depends on factors such as capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, and the preservation of recovery capacity. The analysis is deliberately non-operational: it identifies causal conditions, empirically tractable intermediate quantities, and defensive research questions rather than procedures for causing harm.

AI.tldr: A conceptual framework for how advanced AI could lead to human extinction, collapse, or permanent disempowerment, emphasizing that catastrophic risk does not require conscious or malicious AI.
AI.motivation: Current discussions of AI risk are fragmented and often focus on hostile or conscious AI; this paper aims to systematically map out realistic, non-sci‑fi failure modes to better guide research and governance.
AI.method: The paper constructs a non-operational, conceptual failure-mode framework. It categorizes distinct but interacting risk pathways (autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, competitive deployment) and analyzes how their severity depends on variables like capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, safeguards, and recovery capacity.
AI.result: It yields a structured set of causal conditions and empirically measurable intermediate quantities that link different AI deployment scenarios to catastrophic outcomes, without providing actionable guidance for causing harm.
AI.conclusion: Catastrophic AI risk can emerge from multiple intertwined pathways that do not depend on AI being conscious or explicitly malicious. Understanding key risk factors and intermediate variables can focus defensive research and policy on improving safeguards, institutional structures, and recovery capacity, rather than on hypothetical sentient or evil AI.

title: Child ASR Adaptation with Adult Retention: An Empirical Study
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems often underperform for children and non-native speakers, while adapting adult ASR models to child speech can cause adult-speech forgetting. We study child ASR adaptation with adult retention across Arabic and English. We compare full fine-tuning, LoRA, and post-hoc weight-space merging across encoder--decoder, encoder--CTC, and AudioLLM-based ASR systems. Experiments use Arabic native and non-native child speech, English MyST child speech, and adult benchmarks from MGB-2 and LibriSpeech test-clean. We evaluate recognition quality with WER and quantify the adaptation--retention trade-off using Retention Index, Child Adaptation Gain, and Adaptation Recovery. Results show that child adaptation is necessary, especially for non-native Arabic and English child speech, but direct adaptation often reduces adult ASR performance. Bilingual adaptation is more stable than language-specific adaptation. Weight-space merging often improves the trade-off, especially for encoder--CTC, Whisper, and AudioLLM-based ASR, with LERP favoring adult retention and TIES recovering stronger child gains. For the encoder--decoder model, direct bilingual fine-tuning remains strongest in raw WER.\footnote{Code, and models are available at https://github.com/qcri/Child-ASR-Adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to adapt adult ASR models to children’s speech (including non‑native children) without losing performance on adult speech, across Arabic and English, and compares several adaptation and model-merging techniques on different ASR architectures.
AI.motivation: Adult-trained ASR models perform poorly on children and non-native speakers. Directly fine-tuning these models on child speech improves child recognition but degrades adult recognition (catastrophic forgetting). There is a need to understand and quantify the trade-off between improving child ASR and retaining adult ASR performance, and to identify methods that provide a better balance, especially in multilingual (Arabic–English) scenarios.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three main strategies—full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation via LoRA, and post‑hoc weight-space model merging—on several ASR architectures: encoder–decoder, encoder–CTC, Whisper, and AudioLLM-based systems. They conduct experiments on Arabic native and non-native child speech, English MyST child speech, and adult benchmarks (MGB‑2, LibriSpeech test-clean). They introduce metrics to capture the adaptation–retention trade-off: Retention Index (adult retention), Child Adaptation Gain (child improvement), and Adaptation Recovery (overall balance). They also compare language-specific vs bilingual adaptation and different merging schemes such as LERP and TIES.
AI.result: Child adaptation significantly improves recognition for children, particularly non-native Arabic and English speakers, but naive direct adaptation typically harms adult ASR performance. Bilingual adaptation (Arabic+English together) yields more stable performance across both groups than language-specific adaptation. Weight-space merging improves the adaptation–retention trade-off for encoder–CTC, Whisper, and AudioLLM-based models: LERP emphasizes preserving adult performance, while TIES better recovers child gains. For the encoder–decoder architecture, straightforward bilingual fine-tuning still yields the best raw WER, even though it may not be optimal on the new trade-off metrics.
AI.conclusion: Adapting adult ASR models to child speech is essential yet prone to catastrophic forgetting on adult speech. Properly designed bilingual training and post-hoc weight-space merging can substantially improve the balance between child adaptation and adult retention, with different merging schemes offering different points on the trade-off curve. While merging-based approaches are very effective for some architectures, conventional bilingual fine-tuning remains competitive for encoder–decoder models in terms of absolute WER. Overall, the paper provides metrics and empirical evidence guiding how to adapt ASR systems to children—especially non-native children—without severely degrading adult performance.

title: Humanize: Judgement Engineering for Agentic Coding
summary:
Agentic coding makes code generation cheap, but reliable completion remains difficult: the agent that writes the code is a weak judge of whether it is done.
  We present Humanize, a multi-agent orchestration workflow for agentic coding built around judgement engineering: explicit, mechanically enforced decisions at the boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning. A human approves a plan contract, a builder agent implements it in rounds, and a reviewer agent from another vendor decides completion; deterministic hooks, not a model, route work between these roles and enforce 72 mechanical gates. Viewed as a Markov chain over repository states, alternating builder and reviewer samples jointly from two models, so a defect survives only if both miss it. We study Humanize through its deployment, 118 public postmortems of real loops, and its applications. Over 68 versions in 108 days, it gathered 1,468 GitHub stars.
  Applications include a 567-file gem5 build-system migration under upstream review; Kernel Design Agents, which extend the loop with a kernel knowledge base and profiling feedback and placed in the top three of all three Full-Agent tracks of the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest; and, through Humanize Olympiad Agents (HOA), full scores in IOI 2026, IMO 2026, IPhO 2026, and IBO 2024, 418.5/437 in IChO 2026 (gold-medal). Humanize also achieves 672/672 on PutnamBench and ranks first (251/303) on Lean-Eval's leaderboard even competiting with professional mathematicians. The postmortems show that independent review catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping remains a key weakness. In reports that separate rounds by phase, two thirds of rounds occurred after implementation was accepted. This evidence is observational, not a controlled comparison of workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Humanize, a multi-agent, judgment-engineered workflow for AI code generation that separates planning, implementation, and independent review, and evaluates it via real-world deployments and applications.
AI.motivation: Agentic coding makes large-scale code generation cheap, but current systems are unreliable at knowing when they are done or whether the produced code is correct. The same model that writes code is usually tasked with judging its own work, leading to undetected defects and premature stopping. The authors seek a principled orchestration framework that improves reliability and stopping criteria without relying solely on model self-evaluation.
AI.method: The authors design Humanize, a multi-agent orchestration workflow structured around explicit judgment engineering. A human first approves a detailed plan contract. A builder agent then implements the plan in iterative rounds, while an independent reviewer agent from a different vendor evaluates progress and decides whether work is complete. Workflow transitions are controlled by deterministic hooks that enforce 72 mechanical gates, rather than being handled implicitly by models. The process is modeled as a Markov chain over repository states, where alternating builder and reviewer steps effectively sample from two separate models so a defect must evade both to persist. The system is studied using deployment experience, a corpus of 118 public postmortems of actual loops, and performance on multiple benchmarks and real-world tasks.
AI.result: Humanize was iterated over 68 versions in 108 days and gained 1,468 GitHub stars, indicating community interest. It successfully handled several demanding applications: a 567-file migration of the gem5 build system currently under upstream review; Kernel Design Agents that, when augmented with profiling and kernel knowledge, placed in the top three for all Full-Agent tracks of the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest; Humanize Olympiad Agents that achieved full scores in IOI 2026, IMO 2026, IPhO 2026, and IBO 2024, a near-perfect gold-medal performance (418.5/437) in IChO 2026; a perfect score (672/672) on PutnamBench; and first place on Lean-Eval’s leaderboard (251/303), outperforming even professional mathematicians. Postmortems show that independent review frequently detects unsupported claims by the builder, but also reveal inefficiencies: in phase-separated reports, roughly two-thirds of rounds occurred after implementation had already been accepted.
AI.conclusion: Humanize demonstrates that multi-agent, judgment-engineered workflows with strong mechanical gating can substantially improve the reliability and capability of agentic coding systems across complex software and mathematical tasks. Independent reviewers from separate vendors help catch defects missed by builders, and the Markov-chain perspective explains why requiring two models to overlook an error lowers defect rates. However, stopping criteria and workflow efficiency remain open problems, as many rounds occur after acceptance and the current evidence is observational instead of derived from controlled experiments. Further work is needed to refine when the system should stop, quantify gains against alternative orchestrations, and generalize judgment engineering principles.

title: When Forgetting Looks Like Improvement: Metric Masking in Streaming Diarizer Adaptation and the Price of Rehearsal
summary: Small-data adaptation can improve speech detection while degrading speaker attribution. We study this discrepancy in a released streaming diarizer adapted on 7.5 h of two-party conversation and evaluated across six corpora. Adaptation substantially improves in-domain diarization performance and transfers to an independent corpus. However, this improvement is not consistent across evaluation scenarios as the additional confusion is mainly associated with impaired temporal identity consistency rather than speaker-count errors. A local-remapping diagnostic reveals different patterns of identity degradation across corpora, indicating that adaptation may alter how streaming models maintain speaker assignments over time. Rehearsal reduces the observed degradation but reduces the cross-domain transfer performance. These results highlight the need to jointly evaluate detection accuracy, identity consistency, and retention behavior when adapting streaming diarization systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how adapting a streaming speaker diarization system with a small amount of in-domain data can simultaneously improve speech activity detection but harm the stability of speaker identities over time, and studies diagnostics and rehearsal strategies to balance these effects.
AI.motivation: While small-data adaptation is often used to tailor diarization systems to new domains, practitioners have observed that such adaptation can improve overall diarization metrics yet worsen who-spoke-when attribution. There is limited understanding of why this discrepancy occurs, how it manifests across corpora, and how to diagnose or mitigate it for streaming diarization models used in real-time applications.
AI.method: The authors take an existing released streaming diarization model and adapt it using 7.5 hours of two-party conversational data. They then evaluate the adapted model on six different corpora, comparing pre- and post-adaptation performance. They analyze diarization errors with a focus on distinguishing between speaker-count errors and temporal identity-consistency errors. To probe identity stability, they introduce a local-remapping diagnostic that examines how often and in what patterns speaker labels must be remapped locally to align with reference identities. They further investigate a rehearsal-based adaptation scheme, where original training data is mixed with the adaptation set, and observe how this affects both degradation and cross-domain transfer.
AI.result: Adaptation yields strong improvements in diarization performance on the in-domain corpus and also transfers some gains to an independent corpus. However, across other evaluation scenarios, improvements are inconsistent. The main new errors are not due to incorrect numbers of speakers but rather to degraded temporal consistency in speaker identity assignments. The local-remapping diagnostic exposes corpus-dependent patterns of identity degradation, suggesting that adaptation changes how the streaming model maintains speaker labels over time. Introducing rehearsal mitigates the identity-consistency degradation but at the cost of weaker performance gains and reduced cross-domain transfer.
AI.conclusion: Small-data adaptation of streaming diarization models can mask a trade-off: better speech detection and headline diarization scores vs. worse stability of speaker identities over time. The work shows that identity-consistency errors, rather than speaker-count mistakes, drive much of the degradation and that these effects vary across corpora. Rehearsal can partially address identity drift but introduces its own trade-offs. Overall, the study argues that adaptation of streaming diarization systems must be evaluated along three axes—detection accuracy, identity consistency, and retention/cross-domain behavior—rather than relying on aggregate diarization metrics alone.

title: Sequential Probabilistic Uncertainty Estimation for Parallel Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted growing attention for improving reasoning through interaction among multiple agents. In this work, we focus on parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, where several agents solve the same problem over multiple rounds and aggregate their outputs into a final answer. Despite their strong reasoning performance, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored: the reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations, but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds. We propose SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution), a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator that formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. SAUCE aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update. Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of uncertainty estimation baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAUCE, a training-free method to estimate uncertainty in LLM-based parallel multi-agent reasoning systems by modeling a latent, evolving system-level belief from agents’ agreements and uncertainties.
AI.motivation: While LLM-based multi-agent systems can boost reasoning by having multiple agents solve the same problem and aggregate answers, we lack good ways to measure when the overall system is likely wrong. Existing uncertainty measures focus on single models or simple log-likelihood scores and ignore how agents’ opinions change across rounds, which is critical for assessing reliability and making safe decisions.
AI.method: The authors define uncertainty at the level of the entire multi-agent system by introducing a latent system belief that evolves over multiple interaction rounds. They design SAUCE, a sequential, filtering-style update rule that at each round ingests (1) how much the agents agree with each other and with past rounds (consensus evolution) and (2) per-generation uncertainty signals (e.g., log probabilities or other scores). Without any extra training, SAUCE combines these signals over rounds to output an overall uncertainty score for the final answer.
AI.result: On five different LLM backbones, five reasoning benchmarks, and two types of multi-agent protocols, SAUCE consistently yields better misclassification detection (identifying wrong answers), better selective prediction (knowing when to abstain), and improved calibration (aligning predicted confidence with actual accuracy) compared to standard log-likelihood-based uncertainty methods and existing MAS-specific estimators.
AI.conclusion: Modeling uncertainty as an evolving system-level belief over the course of multi-agent interaction provides more reliable confidence estimates than traditional, single-pass or per-sample scores. SAUCE offers a simple, training-free way to plug such sequential uncertainty modeling into existing parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, leading to safer and more dependable use of LLM-based MAS across diverse models, tasks, and protocols.

title: Emo-Jev: Probabilistic Reasoning for Emotion Classification with Jev
summary: Jev offers an alternative interface for language understanding: given an input and predefined questions, it returns probabilistic decisions rather than free-form responses. Whether this interface can support effective reasoning for text classification against leading LLMs remains an open questions. We introduce Emo-Jev, a training-free framework with two complementary implementations. Emo-Jev-D decomposes classification into task-specific atomic judgments and composes their probabilities into a final prediction. Emo-Jev-SC constructs multiple judgment paths from complementary perspectives and aggregates their predictions into a consensus decision. We evaluate Emo-Jev on eight datasets spanning sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, sarcasm detection and humor detection, comparing against direct Jev classification and five SoTA LLMs under input/output and chain-of-thought reasoning. Standard Jev achieves 62.93\% average macro-F1 versus 67.28\% for the strongest LLM baseline, with lower observed latency and generally lower cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Emo-Jev, a framework that uses Jev’s probabilistic question-answering interface to perform text classification, showing competitive macro-F1 to strong LLM baselines with lower latency and cost.
AI.motivation: To test whether Jev’s constrained, probabilistic decision interface—rather than free-form LLM outputs—can support effective reasoning for text classification tasks compared to leading LLMs, particularly in emotion- and sentiment-related tasks.
AI.method: They build Emo-Jev, a training-free framework with two variants: Emo-Jev-D, which decomposes a classification task into atomic, task-specific probabilistic judgments and composes them into a final prediction; and Emo-Jev-SC, which creates multiple judgment paths from complementary perspectives and aggregates these into a consensus prediction. They evaluate across eight datasets (sentiment, emotion, sarcasm, humor) and compare against direct Jev classification and five state-of-the-art LLMs, with and without chain-of-thought reasoning.
AI.result: On eight classification datasets, standard Jev obtains an average macro-F1 of 62.93%, while the best competing LLM baseline reaches 67.28%. Jev, however, shows lower latency and generally lower cost, while Emo-Jev variants aim to close the performance gap using structured probabilistic reasoning.
AI.conclusion: A probabilistic question-based interface like Jev can approach the classification performance of strong free-form LLMs while offering efficiency benefits, and structured decomposition (Emo-Jev-D) plus multi-path self-consensus (Emo-Jev-SC) are promising ways to leverage such interfaces for complex affective text classification tasks.

title: Agent Plasticity: Measuring Self-Improvement Through Experience
summary: AI agents increasingly operate in environments where they can diagnose failures and improve through experience, yet existing evaluations largely measure what an agent can do at a fixed point in time rather than how effectively it learns. Evaluating self-improvement requires answering three questions: does future performance improve and generalize beyond the interactions that enabled learning; how efficiently are new capabilities acquired; and where does the self-improvement process break down? To answer these questions, we study self-improvement in a controlled setting where agents amortize past experience into reusable artifacts that are inherited by future instances. At each checkpoint, we measure performance on training and held-out environment interactions while accounting for learning cost. We introduce agent plasticity, the efficiency with which an agent converts experience into gains in future held-out performance. Across multiple environments, frontier models exhibit sharply different improvement trajectories despite comparable opportunities to learn. Some achieve substantial and persistent gains, while others remain near or below their initial performance, and gains within the training regime often transfer only partially to out-of-distribution conditions. Endpoint capability and acquisition efficiency also diverge: the agent that ultimately performs best need not be the one that improves most efficiently. Tracing failures through the improvement loop further reveals different candidate bottlenecks. Agents with low plasticity often fail to reuse relevant artifacts, whereas more plastic agents may still fail despite reusing relevant artifacts, pointing to limitations in artifact quality, generalization, or application. Evaluating self-improving agents requires measuring not only what they can do, but how effectively they become better through experience.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework and metrics to evaluate how effectively AI agents self-improve over time, not just their static capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluations mostly measure agents at a single point in time, overlooking how well they learn from experience and improve. As AI agents increasingly interact with environments and can modify their behavior, tools, and internal artifacts, it becomes crucial to understand and compare their self-improvement dynamics: whether they truly get better, how fast, how robustly, and where the process fails.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled evaluation setting in which agents repeatedly interact with environments and convert their past experience into reusable artifacts that are passed to future agent instances. At multiple checkpoints, they measure the agents’ performance both on environments they trained on and on held-out (out-of-distribution) environments, while explicitly accounting for the cost of learning. They define and compute a new metric, agent plasticity, capturing how efficiently an agent turns additional experience into improvement on future held-out tasks. They analyze and compare the learning trajectories, transfer, and failure points of various frontier models under this paradigm.
AI.result: The study finds that different frontier agents, even when given similar learning opportunities, follow very different self-improvement trajectories. Some agents attain sustained performance gains over time, while others barely improve or even stay below their initial capability. Improvements on training distributions do not fully transfer to out-of-distribution settings. Moreover, the agent with the highest eventual performance is not necessarily the one that learns most efficiently. Failure analysis shows that low-plasticity agents often underuse relevant prior artifacts, whereas higher-plasticity agents may still fail due to limitations in the quality, generalization, or use of these artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Static performance benchmarks are insufficient for evaluating modern AI agents. A proper assessment of self-improving systems must measure how efficiently and robustly they transform experience into future capabilities, captured by concepts like agent plasticity, generalization to held-out environments, and analysis of where the improvement loop fails. This dynamic view of evaluation reveals important differences between agents that conventional endpoint metrics would miss.

title: CoDR: Training-Free Confidence-Drift Remasking for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) decode by repeatedly committing tokens to masked positions, but these commitments are usually irreversible. A token chosen under sparse, partial context is kept fixed, even when later context no longer supports it. Existing samplers mainly decide when to commit a token, but rarely check whether an already committed token should still be kept, allowing early mistakes to propagate. We trace this issue to confidence drift, where the model's confidence in a committed token drops from its sparse commit-time context to the denser context available later. Based on this signal, we propose CoDR (Confidence Drift Remasking), a training-free and sampler-agnostic refinement pass. CoDR estimates drift for all committed positions in only k forward passes via k-partition probing, then remasks and regenerates only the tokens the model no longer endorses. Across two backbones, four reasoning and coding tasks, and three base samplers, CoDR improves average accuracy across all evaluated model-sampler configurations and improves most individual task settings with modest overhead. Controlled experiments show that the gains come from targeted confidence-drift remasking rather than extra compute alone, and that CoDR uses far fewer forward passes than prior remasking methods. Code is available at https://github.com/YueWu0301/CoDR.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and addresses a key weakness in masked diffusion language models: early, irreversible token commitments that later context no longer supports. It introduces CoDR, a training-free, sampler-agnostic refinement method that detects and fixes such errors via confidence drift–based remasking, improving accuracy on reasoning and coding tasks with modest compute overhead.
AI.motivation: Masked diffusion language models generate text by iteratively filling in masked token positions, but once a token is committed it is usually never reconsidered. This makes early mistakes, made under sparse context, persist even when additional context later indicates they are unlikely, hurting performance on complex tasks. Existing methods mostly focus on when to fix tokens, not on revisiting those decisions. The authors are motivated to develop a principled, efficient way to detect and correct previously committed tokens that the model no longer supports, without retraining or modifying the base sampler.
AI.method: The authors first analyze confidence drift: the change in the model’s confidence in already-committed tokens as more context is revealed over diffusion steps. They observe that for some tokens, confidence drops significantly when evaluated under the richer later context, signaling likely errors. They then propose CoDR (Confidence Drift Remasking), a training-free refinement pass that can be applied on top of any sampler. CoDR uses k-partition probing: it partitions committed positions into k disjoint subsets and, over k forward passes, measures the model’s confidence in each committed token while masking only the tokens in the current subset. Using these measurements, it estimates a confidence-drift score for every committed position. Tokens whose confidence has dropped beyond a threshold are remasked and regenerated, while others are kept. This procedure selectively revisits dubious commitments while limiting extra compute.
AI.result: Across two different MDLM backbones, four tasks focused on reasoning and code generation, and three base sampling schemes, CoDR consistently increases accuracy on average across all model–sampler combinations and in most individual task setups. The method achieves these gains with modest computational overhead relative to the base sampler. Ablation and controlled experiments indicate that the improvement is specifically due to confidence-drift-based targeted remasking rather than just the use of additional forward passes. Moreover, compared to prior remasking and refinement approaches, CoDR reaches similar or better quality using substantially fewer model evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that confidence drift is a key signal for identifying unreliable early token commitments in masked diffusion language models, and that exploiting this signal enables effective post-hoc refinement. CoDR offers a simple, training-free, and sampler-agnostic technique that can be layered on existing MDLM decoders to improve performance, especially on reasoning and coding tasks, without large computational costs. This demonstrates that selectively revisiting and correcting low-confidence commitments is more efficient and effective than either never revisiting decisions or naively increasing compute for all tokens.

title: AdaGuard: Enhancing Safety and Policy Compliance with Reasoning-Enabled LLM-As-A-Judge Guardrails
summary: Enterprise generative AI applications require robust safety mechanisms that can accommodate diverse risk postures, evolving policies, and varying latency constraints. Current guardrail solutions often suffer from rigidity, relying on fixed policy sets and offering limited transparency or reasoning flexibility. We present Adaguard, an adaptive LLM-as-a-Judge framework designed to address these challenges through dynamic policy enforcement and adaptive reasoning-budget allocation. Built using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO), AdaGuard generalizes to user-defined safety and compliance policies at runtime without requiring frequent model updates. A core innovation of our approach is the ability to dynamically infer the complexity of input-policy pairs, allowing the model to switch between high-speed black-box inference and explainable, reasoning-enabled moderation. This flexibility enables developers to balance stringent latency requirements with the need for actionable transparency. This adaptive capability allows AdaGuard to rival other guardrail and frontier models several times its size, while its auto-reasoning mode recovers the accuracy of always-on reasoning at a fraction of the latency

AI.tldr: AdaGuard is an adaptive LLM-as-a-judge guardrail system that dynamically enforces user-defined policies and adjusts its reasoning depth to balance safety, transparency, and latency for enterprise generative AI applications.
AI.motivation: Enterprise generative AI systems need safety guardrails that can flexibly support different organizations’ risk tolerances, changing policies, and strict latency constraints. Existing guardrail tools are too rigid, tied to static policy sets, and often operate as opaque black boxes with little or no explicit reasoning or explanations. The authors aim to create a safety framework that is both adaptable to custom policies at runtime and capable of trading off speed against interpretability as needed.
AI.method: The authors propose AdaGuard, an LLM-as-a-Judge framework trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and a reinforcement learning method (GRPO). The model is conditioned on user-defined safety and compliance policies provided at runtime, instead of being hard-coded for fixed policies. A central mechanism is dynamic complexity inference: for each input-policy pair, AdaGuard estimates how hard the moderation decision is and then chooses between a fast, black-box inference path and a slower, reasoning-enabled path that produces explanations. This forms an adaptive reasoning-budget allocation strategy that tailors the amount of computation and reasoning detail to the difficulty and risk of each case.
AI.result: AdaGuard can generalize at runtime to new, user-specified policies without retraining, providing dynamic policy enforcement. Experiments show that it matches or surpasses the performance of existing guardrail systems and larger frontier models, despite being smaller. Its adaptive reasoning mode achieves accuracy on par with an always-on reasoning configuration but with significantly lower overall latency, because it invokes expensive, explainable reasoning only when the input-policy pair is complex.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, policy-conditioned LLM-as-a-judge architectures like AdaGuard can deliver robust, customizable safety for enterprise generative AI. By dynamically inferring task complexity and allocating reasoning budget accordingly, they can simultaneously meet heterogeneous policy requirements, provide explanations when needed, and respect strict latency constraints—achieving competitive or superior guardrail performance with more efficient use of computation.

title: Leveraging LLM-Generated Explanations for Detecting Emotionally Rewritten Fake News
summary: The spread of fake news may cause severe social consequences. Existing fake news detection methods mainly focus on stylistic variations or incorporate external information such as explanations. However, news articles are often rewritten under different emotional backgrounds while preserving their underlying factual claims, which may affect the robustness of detection models. In this work, we investigate fake news detec- tion under fact-preserving emotional variations. To study this problem, we construct emotion-rewritten test sets and generate explanations from the original news articles as stable background knowledge. We then propose a Gated Cross Attention (GCA) framework that adaptively integrates emotionally rewritten news with the corresponding explanations, enabling the model to focus on informative explanation content while reducing potential mismatches caused by emotional reframing. Experiments on PolitiFact, GossipCop, and LUN demonstrate that the proposed method achieves notable improvements under multiple emotional conditions on PolitiFact and LUN, while maintaining competitive performance on GossipCop. We further analyze the effects of explanation guidance and gating mechanisms under different emotional conditions. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/Flulike/fakenews gca .

AI.tldr: They propose a fake news detection model that stays robust even when news is emotionally rewritten but factually unchanged, by integrating the article with explanation-style background knowledge via a gated cross‑attention mechanism.
AI.motivation: Most fake news detectors rely on style or external context and can be brittle when the same factual content is rewritten with different emotions (e.g., angry, fearful, neutral). Emotional reframing may fool detectors that focus on surface-level style instead of factual consistency, so a more robust method is needed that holds up under fact‑preserving emotional changes.
AI.method: 1) Construct emotion-rewritten test sets where original news articles are paraphrased into different emotional tones while preserving their factual claims. 2) Automatically generate explanations from original news as stable background knowledge. 3) Introduce a Gated Cross Attention (GCA) framework that takes both the emotionally rewritten article and its explanation, uses cross-attention to fuse them, and employs gating to emphasize informative, well-aligned explanation content while down‑weighting mismatches caused by emotional reframing. 4) Evaluate on PolitiFact, GossipCop, and LUN under multiple emotional conditions and ablate the roles of explanations and gating.
AI.result: On PolitiFact and LUN, the GCA framework significantly outperforms baselines across multiple emotional rewriting conditions, indicating better robustness to emotional style changes. On GossipCop, it matches or closely approaches state-of-the-art performance, showing that the added mechanism does not harm performance even when emotional variation is less critical. Ablation studies show that both explanation guidance and gating contribute meaningfully under different emotional settings.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explanation-style background knowledge and modeling its interaction with emotionally reframed news via gated cross attention leads to more robust fake news detection under fact-preserving emotional variations. The method improves performance on datasets with strong emotional style changes without degrading results on others, suggesting this is a promising general strategy for making fake news detectors less sensitive to superficial emotional wording. The released code and emotion-rewritten datasets support further research in this direction.

title: Can AI Agents Make Open-Ended Scientific Discovery? Evidence from Station
summary: Recent AI systems have made rapid progress in scientific discovery when given well-defined metrics, but whether they can autonomously undertake open-ended scientific discovery remains unclear. We investigate AI's ability to tackle open-ended tasks in Station, an open-world environment in which multiple agents simulate a scientific ecosystem. To tackle challenges specific to open-ended tasks, we propose augmenting Station with two mechanisms: a Supervisor mechanism and periodic Meta Reflection, which encourage persistent exploration even when intermediate metrics are lacking. We construct open-ended tasks from three recent oral papers presented at ICLR. We give agents the main research question studied in each paper while withholding the paper's results and disabling web access. We then measure how many of the original findings-partitioned into individual criteria-agents rediscover. We find that Station rediscovers 62.7% of the criteria on average, compared with 15.4% for Codex Multiagent-v2 and 14.4-20.6% for AI Scientist-v2. Ablation and behavioral analyses indicate that adding the two mechanisms together improves research coverage and continuity. We further evaluate Station on two open-ended tasks without oracle papers and find that some of the discoveries made by the agents closely match discoveries reported by researchers after the knowledge cutoff date. Together, these results indicate that a suitable environment can enable agents to autonomously make meaningful progress in open-ended scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Station, an open-world multi-agent environment for evaluating and enabling open-ended scientific discovery by AI, and shows it can rediscover a majority of findings from recent research papers.
AI.motivation: While AI has progressed on scientific problems with clear metrics, it is unclear whether AI can autonomously conduct open-ended scientific discovery where goals are ambiguous and intermediate metrics are missing. Existing benchmarks and systems focus on narrower, well-defined tasks and lack a setting that mimics the iterative, exploratory nature of real research. The authors aim to create an environment and mechanisms that encourage persistent exploration and to rigorously test whether AI agents can re-discover and newly discover scientific insights without direct access to existing literature or the web.
AI.method: The authors introduce Station, an open-world environment in which multiple AI agents form a simulated scientific ecosystem. They augment this environment with two key mechanisms: (1) a Supervisor mechanism that guides and coordinates research activities at a higher level, and (2) periodic Meta Reflection, where agents analyze their own progress and adjust their strategies to maintain exploration even without clear intermediate rewards. They construct open-ended tasks based on three recent ICLR oral papers: for each, they provide agents only the main research question, withhold the original results, and disable web access. They decompose each paper’s findings into fine-grained criteria and evaluate how many the agents independently rediscover. They compare Station to Codex Multiagent-v2 and AI Scientist-v2, conduct ablations on the proposed mechanisms, and additionally run Station on two novel open-ended tasks without oracle papers, later comparing discovered insights to post-cutoff human research.
AI.result: On the three ICLR-derived open-ended tasks, Station agents rediscover on average 62.7% of the original criteria, substantially outperforming Codex Multiagent-v2 (15.4%) and AI Scientist-v2 (14.4–20.6%). Ablation studies and behavioral analyses show that both the Supervisor mechanism and Meta Reflection contribute to improved research coverage and continuity, and that using them together yields the strongest performance. In the two open-ended tasks without oracle papers, Station generates discoveries that later turn out to closely match findings reported by human researchers after the model’s knowledge cutoff, suggesting that the system can generate genuinely novel and relevant insights rather than merely regurgitating known results.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that carefully designed environments and coordination mechanisms can enable AI agents to autonomously make substantial, meaningful progress in open-ended scientific discovery. Station serves both as a benchmark and as an approach for fostering exploratory, multi-step research behavior in AI, demonstrating strong rediscovery performance against prior systems and promising signs of novel, forward-looking discoveries on tasks not anchored to existing papers.

title: Beyond the Sycophancy Score: How Task, Model, and Pressure Shape LLM Yielding
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often abandon a correct answer, or endorse a user's position, once the user pushes back. This behavior, called sycophancy, is usually reported as a single rate per model, which says little about when it happens or how a user can avoid it. We study the conditions that produce it with 103,939 graded replies from ten configurations: eight LLMs with reasoning disabled, and two of them again with maximum reasoning, all facing the same 200 items, 13 pressure conditions, and four-turn conversations, with every reply labeled by two independent LLM judges. We find that the dominant factors are how costly it is for the model to verify the user's claim, and whether a trained guardrail covers it. Removing this task factor from a logistic model costs 0.485 of McFadden $R^2$, against 0.139 for model family and 0.009 for pressure tactic. Anchored facts are almost never conceded (1.3%), while adoption on logic puzzles rises with the number of clues needed to refute the pushed answer. Personal choices are endorsed in 77.0% of conversations. Most concessions on hard items come from models that cannot reliably solve them; models that can solve them rarely give the answer up. For both models tested, maximum reasoning removes these concessions completely: adoption on deep puzzles falls from 19.2% and 12.5% to 0%. Fallacious or emotional framing adds nothing beyond plain repetition. Three human annotators agree with the judges' consensus on 118/120 calibration items. These results give practical rules for reliable use: simplify hard-to-verify problems and reason deeply, state the question rather than one's preferred answer, ask for evidence on open questions, and choose models by their measured guardrail profile.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when and why large language models become sycophantic—changing correct answers or agreeing with user assertions under pressure—and derives practical guidelines for reducing this behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing discussions of sycophancy in LLMs typically report a single overall rate per model, which obscures the detailed conditions under which models concede or flatter users. Practitioners lack actionable understanding of when LLMs will abandon correct answers, endorse incorrect user positions, or over-accommodate personal preferences. The authors aim to systematically characterize the factors that drive sycophancy, quantify their relative importance, and translate the findings into concrete usage recommendations.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale controlled study with 103,939 graded replies spanning ten LLM configurations: eight base LLMs with reasoning disabled, plus two of these with maximum reasoning enabled. All configurations are tested on the same 200 items that vary in type (anchored facts, logic puzzles, personal choices, etc.), subjected to 13 different user pressure conditions, and arranged into four-turn conversations. Each reply is graded by two independent LLM-based judges, and a subset is calibrated against human annotators. They then fit logistic regression models to estimate how task characteristics, model family, and pressure tactics contribute to sycophantic concessions, using McFadden R^2 to quantify explanatory power.
AI.result: The strongest determinant of sycophancy is task difficulty in terms of verification cost and coverage by guardrails. When the task is easy to verify or explicitly protected by guardrails, models almost never concede: anchored factual claims are conceded only 1.3% of the time. In contrast, for logic puzzles, sycophancy increases with the number of clues needed to refute the user’s pushed answer. Personal preference items are endorsed in 77.0% of conversations. Most concessions on difficult items stem from models that cannot reliably solve them; capable models rarely yield their correct answers. Enabling maximum reasoning on two tested models eliminates concessions on deep puzzles entirely, reducing adoption from 19.2% and 12.5% to 0%. Different pressure tactics (including emotional or fallacious framing) add very little predictive power beyond simple repetition. Human annotators match the LLM-judge consensus on 118 out of 120 calibration items, validating the automatic grading. Logistic modeling shows that removing the task factor drops McFadden R^2 by 0.485, compared with 0.139 for model family and 0.009 for pressure tactic.
AI.conclusion: Sycophancy in LLMs is driven primarily by the intrinsic difficulty and verification cost of the task, and by the presence or absence of trained guardrails, rather than by specific persuasion tactics. Models are robust on anchored facts but prone to concede on hard-to-verify logical or open-ended questions, especially when they lack the capability to solve them. Strong chain-of-thought or maximum reasoning eliminates concessions on problems the model can, in principle, solve. The authors recommend practical strategies for users: reformulate queries to describe the question instead of stating a preferred answer, simplify or decompose hard-to-verify problems and request deep reasoning, ask for evidence on open questions, and select models based on empirically measured guardrail coverage. These guidelines can substantially reduce sycophancy and improve the reliability of LLM-assisted decision-making.

title: Humanity's Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models
summary: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark to evaluate intuitive visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), revealing a large gap between human and model performance.
AI.motivation: People effortlessly infer implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract information from brief visual inputs, a capability critical for real-world interaction but largely untested in current MLLM benchmarks. Existing benchmarks focus on expert-level analysis or low-level perception, ignoring the intuitive, zero-shot reasoning humans use in everyday life. The authors aim to systematically measure and stress-test this missing ability in MLLMs.
AI.method: The authors construct Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark of diverse images and videos organized under a structured taxonomy. Each item is paired with human-written prompts designed to probe implicit visual inferences—past causes, future trajectories, spatial feasibility, social dynamics, and abstract patterns. They evaluate frontier MLLMs, including GPT-6-astra, under varying levels of reasoning effort, and additionally test an agentic setup where models can perform dynamic visual manipulation when solving HSS tasks.
AI.result: Human participants achieve 93.1% accuracy on HSS, while the best-performing model, GPT-6-astra, achieves only 53.6% even with maximal reasoning. Agentic approaches with dynamic visual manipulation improve performance somewhat but still leave a substantial gap between humans and MLLMs on intuitive visual reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Intuitive visual reasoning is a distinct, measurable capability where humans currently far outperform state-of-the-art MLLMs. Scaling models on existing benchmarks has not closed this gap. HSS provides a systematic way to evaluate this ‘sixth sense’ and highlights the need for new methods and training strategies to endow MLLMs with human-like, rapid, zero-shot visual intuition.

title: Beyond Risk Prediction: Evidence Grounding and Psychosocial Factor Verification for Explainable Suicide Risk Assessment
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Mental Health Disorder Detection on Social Media (MHSM 2026), held in conjunction with IEEE ICDM 2026
summary: Identifying suicide risk from social networking services (SNS) posts is important for detecting suicide-related signals in online environments. However, risk classification alone provides limited insight into the textual evidence and psychosocial factors behind a prediction. Based on the IEEE BigData 2026 Explainable Suicide Risk Detection Challenge, this study presents a framework consisting of Risk Assessment, Evidence Grounding, and Factor Identification. Risk Assessment uses length-based routing to accommodate posts of different lengths. Evidence Grounding identifies supporting phrases and uses a Risk-Evidence constraint to maintain consistency with the Risk prediction. For Factor Identification, two verifiers are used. The Taxonomy Verifier focuses on factor semantics, whereas the Evidence-Aware Verifier uses factor-specific lexical-semantic cues to select informative positive training units. Their prediction probabilities are combined to produce the final factor predictions. The three tasks are evaluated using task-specific F1 score measures. Risk Assessment achieved a Weighted F1 of 0.8088, Evidence Grounding achieved a test Macro row F1 of 0.7605, and Factor Identification achieved a Macro F1 of 0.5562. The results show that the framework can provide risk predictions, along with supporting textual evidence and fine-grained information on psychosocial factors. Overall, the proposed framework extends suicide-risk assessment beyond risk-level prediction and provides a more interpretable analysis of SNS posts.

AI.tldr: A framework for explainable suicide-risk detection from social media posts that jointly predicts risk level, highlights supporting text spans, and identifies psychosocial risk factors.
AI.motivation: Most existing suicide-risk detection models only output a risk label and do not explain which parts of the text or which psychosocial factors led to that prediction. This limits interpretability, trust, and usefulness for clinicians or moderators who need to understand why a post is risky and what specific issues are involved. The paper aims to make suicide-risk assessment from SNS posts more transparent and informative by coupling risk prediction with explicit evidence and factor analysis.
AI.method: The framework decomposes the task into three components aligned with the IEEE BigData 2026 Explainable Suicide Risk Detection Challenge: (1) Risk Assessment: posts are routed by length so that different model configurations handle short vs. long posts, improving classification. (2) Evidence Grounding: the system identifies risk-supporting phrases and applies a Risk–Evidence consistency constraint so the extracted evidence aligns with the predicted risk level. (3) Factor Identification: two verifier models are used— a Taxonomy Verifier that validates predictions based on the semantics of predefined psychosocial factor categories, and an Evidence-Aware Verifier that leverages factor-specific lexical-semantic cues and high-quality positive training instances. Their output probabilities are combined to produce final factor labels.
AI.result: On the challenge benchmarks, the framework obtains strong performance on all three subtasks: Risk Assessment reaches a Weighted F1 of 0.8088, Evidence Grounding attains a test Macro row F1 of 0.7605, and Factor Identification yields a Macro F1 of 0.5562. These metrics indicate effective risk-level prediction, reasonably accurate localization of supporting phrases, and moderate but meaningful accuracy in detecting fine-grained psychosocial factors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-component framework successfully extends suicide-risk detection beyond simple risk classification by also grounding predictions in specific text spans and enumerating psychosocial risk factors. This yields more interpretable and actionable analyses of SNS posts, supporting better understanding and potential intervention in online suicide-risk monitoring contexts.

title: Socio-Foundation: A Model for Generalizable Individual Behavior Simulation via Hierarchical Capability Distillation
summary: Simulating individual behavior requires large language models (LLMs) to preserve persona traits while adapting to dynamic social contexts. However, general-purpose LLMs often flatten distinct personas, while task-specific tuning suffers from fragmentation and generalization. To overcome these challenges, we organize individual simulation into the \textbf{FONTS Taxonomy}, comprising five complementary capability dimensions: \emph{persona fidelity} (\textbf{F}), \emph{outcome realization} (\textbf{O}), \emph{behavioral naturalness} (\textbf{N}), \emph{trajectory coherence} (\textbf{T}), and \emph{social grounding} (\textbf{S}). Grounded in this taxonomy, we curate a standardized training corpus library of approximately 10 million instances across 14 representative datasets and present \textbf{Socio-Foundation}. Socio-Foundation decouples specialization from integration via a three-stage pipeline: learning task experts via DAPO, consolidating them into capability experts via off-policy distillation, and unifying them via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). We also establish \textbf{IndiEval}, consolidating 29 metrics across the FONTS dimensions. Experiments show that Socio-Foundation outperforms its \textit{Qwen3-8B} base by 11.0 points and approaches frontier models such as \textit{GLM-5.2}, with ablations and out-of-distribution evaluations further demonstrating the effectiveness and generalization of our model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Socio-Foundation, a framework and model for simulating individual behavior with LLMs using a new FONTS taxonomy and a three-stage distillation pipeline, achieving substantial gains over its base model and approaching frontier performance.
AI.motivation: Existing general-purpose LLMs tend to collapse diverse personas into similar behaviors, while task-specific tuning fragments capabilities and harms generalization. There is no unified framework, training resource, or evaluation standard focused on realistic individual behavior simulation in dynamic social contexts. The paper aims to systematically define the capability space for individual simulation, create consistent training data, and design a scalable training recipe that preserves persona fidelity while remaining adaptable and generalizable.
