BEACON-SP performs ontology-guided graph retrieval and multi-hop reasoning for clinician-facing QA, and is evaluated against a vector-based RAG baseline on 1,500 queries across 15 clinical categories for 100 patients under a corrected evaluation protocol.
AI.result: On the 1,500-query benchmark, BEACON-SP outperforms a vector-based RAG baseline in completeness, clinical relevance, and evidence grounding, with modest gains in factual accuracy. In paired criterion-level comparisons, clinicians (or evaluators) prefer GraphRAG responses in 76.4% of cases, indicating that ontology-guided graph retrieval better supports clinical decision needs than standard vector RAG.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-guided GraphRAG using patient knowledge graphs and a unifying suicide-prevention ontology can substantially improve the structure, contextualization, and grounding of patient-specific evidence for clinician-facing QA. This suggests that ontology-grounded graph-based retrieval is a promising approach for clinical decision support in behavioral health and suicide prevention, beyond what conventional vector-based RAG can provide.

title: ToolRACER: A Robust Agentic Conversation Emulation Resource for Agent Training and Evaluation
summary: Task-oriented conversational agents remain fragile under real world conversation scenarios as they rarely follow a predictable script, especially when users exhibit non-cooperative behavior. Existing function-calling benchmarks often emphasize successful, cooperative interactions and underrepresent adversarial conversation trajectories, thereby limiting the training resources available for developing robust agents. We present ToolRACER, a synthetic data generation pipeline that coordinates user, assistant and tool emulation models to generate and validated multi-turn interactions between a user and an agent. Using \sysn, we construct ToolRACERBench a robust multi-turn conversation benchmark spanning six domains, ranging over 55 varied personas, generating a validated corpus of 5.6K conversation trajectories, with approximately 66\% of conversations containing failure-prone conversation scenarios. We inject adversarial behaviors, producing validated conversational interaction trajectories that capture realistic, robust scenarios. We evaluate models trained on ToolRACERBench against internal benchmarks, as well as on function calling benchmarks such as $τ^2$-bench, BFCLv3 and ACEBench to evaluate agentic accuracy and robustness. Models trained on ToolRACERBench improve end to end agentic accuracy across $τ^2$-bench and ACEBench, demonstrating significant gains when mixed with in-domain dataset in small language models for agent capability tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ToolRACER, a synthetic data generation pipeline and benchmark (ToolRACERBench) for building more robust, tool-using conversational agents that can handle adversarial and failure-prone multi-turn dialogues.
AI.motivation: Most task-oriented conversational agents and existing function-calling benchmarks assume cooperative users and predictable dialogue flows, which makes agents fragile in realistic, messy, or adversarial conversations. There is a lack of high-quality, validated training data and benchmarks that systematically capture non-cooperative and failure-prone interactions, limiting progress on robust tool-using agents.
AI.method: The authors build ToolRACER, a synthetic generation pipeline that coordinates three components—user simulator, assistant/agent simulator, and tool emulation models—to automatically generate and then validate multi-turn conversations involving tool calls. Using this pipeline, they create ToolRACERBench: a benchmark covering six domains and over 55 user personas, producing 5.6K validated interaction trajectories. About two-thirds of these trajectories intentionally include adversarial or failure-prone conversational scenarios, achieved by injecting adversarial behaviors into the simulated users and interactions. They then train models on this dataset and test them on multiple external function-calling benchmarks.
AI.result: ToolRACERBench contains 5.6K validated multi-turn conversations, with roughly 66% involving challenging, failure-prone scenarios across six domains and 55+ personas. Models trained on ToolRACERBench, especially when combined with in-domain data for small language models, achieve higher end-to-end agentic accuracy on τ^2-bench and ACEBench, and show improved robustness on internal benchmarks and BFCLv3, compared to models trained without this data.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic but carefully validated adversarial and failure-prone dialog data, generated via a coordinated multi-agent simulation pipeline, can substantially improve the robustness and tool-usage accuracy of conversational agents. ToolRACER and ToolRACERBench offer a practical way to stress-test and strengthen function-calling agents beyond cooperative, scripted scenarios, especially benefiting smaller models when mixed with domain data.

title: Shared-Roadmap Generation and Evaluator for Multi-Agent Path Planning Using Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
summary: Multi-agent path planning (MAPP) in continuous environments often relies on roadmaps to balance safety and search efficiency. However, traditional roadmap generation methods, such as lattice grids or standard sampling-based approaches, frequently face a trade-off between graph density and the likelihood of finding feasible, high-quality solutions. In this paper, we propose a scalable heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for the automated generation and evaluation of shared multi-agent roadmaps. Our model covers the representation of waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as distinct nodes in a heterogeneous graph, allowing it to reason over global connectivity and inter-agent interactions. By training on occupation density maps aggregated and collected from expert solver trajectories, the GNN learns to identify critical points of interest and prune redundant nodes and edges. This process produces a compact, coordination-aware roadmap that is invariant to task permutations and is reusable for multi-agent pick and delivery tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework can reduce planning effort and can potentially find better solutions, reaching at least 40% reduction in runtime and in graph size for dense roadmaps.

AI.tldr: They use a heterogeneous graph neural network to automatically generate compact, reusable multi-agent roadmaps that speed up continuous multi-agent path planning while preserving solution quality.
AI.motivation: Classical multi-agent path planning in continuous spaces depends on pre-built roadmaps. Existing roadmap construction techniques (e.g., lattices, PRM-style sampling) must choose between sparse graphs that miss good solutions and dense graphs that are expensive to search. This trade-off becomes acute for many agents and tasks, where coordination, safety, and search efficiency are all critical. There is a need for an automated way to build smaller, coordination-aware roadmaps that still capture high-quality paths and can be reused across tasks.
AI.method: The paper introduces a scalable heterogeneous Graph Neural Network framework that constructs and prunes multi-agent roadmaps. It models waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as different node types in a heterogeneous graph, enabling reasoning about their distinct roles and interactions. The GNN is trained using occupation density maps derived from expert solver trajectories, which encode which regions and connections are important for good multi-agent solutions. During inference, the network evaluates roadmap nodes and edges, identifying critical points and removing redundant ones to produce a smaller yet expressive roadmap. The design ensures permutation invariance with respect to task ordering so the same roadmap generalizes across task permutations.
AI.result: Experiments on multi-agent pick-and-delivery tasks with dense initial roadmaps show the learned GNN-based roadmap construction can significantly shrink the graph while maintaining or improving solution quality. In particular, the approach achieves at least a 40% reduction in both runtime and graph size for dense roadmaps, indicating improved planning efficiency and scalability.
AI.conclusion: A heterogeneous GNN can effectively learn from expert trajectories to generate compact, coordination-aware roadmaps for continuous multi-agent path planning. By modeling different entities as distinct node types and leveraging occupation density maps, the framework yields reusable roadmaps that reduce graph size and planning time without sacrificing solution quality, alleviating the traditional density-versus-efficiency trade-off in roadmap-based MAPP.

title: Multi-Objective Aligned Small Language Model Framework for SUD Patient Dialogue Generation
summary: Substance Use Disorder (SUD) counseling requires patient responses that reflect underlying cognitive states such as beliefs, coping strategies, and readiness for change. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent text, they often fail to produce cognitively coherent and clinically realistic patient behavior, especially under ethical and data-scarce clinical settings. Moreover, deploying frontier-scale LLMs in healthcare applications presents practical challenges including high computational cost, latency, privacy concerns, and limited deployability in resource-constrained environments, motivating the need for cognitively aligned small language models (SLMs). We propose a cognitively grounded framework for SUD patient dialogue generation that explicitly models and aligns latent cognitive components with patient histories and counselor questions. Our pipeline consists of two stages: cognitive component detection and cognitive component-aligned dialogue generation. To enable effective learning with smaller models, we combine knowledge distillation from high-capacity teacher models, preference optimization from human-annotations, and attention-guided reward shaping. Extensive evaluations using automatic scores like BERTScore, ROUGE, METEOR and BLEU, and LLM-as-judge hit-metrics against both human and teacher-model references show that cognitively informed fine-tuning substantially improves cognitive realization and alignment over a generic instruction-tuned baselines and mental health domain specific SLMs, with particularly strong gains for open-ended cognitive components.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework to generate cognitively coherent, clinically realistic small‑model patient dialogues for substance use disorder counseling by explicitly modeling latent cognitive components and aligning them via knowledge distillation, preference optimization, and reward shaping, achieving better cognitive alignment than generic and domain SLM baselines.
AI.motivation: Substance Use Disorder counseling relies on patient utterances that faithfully reflect internal cognitive states (e.g., beliefs, coping strategies, readiness to change), but off‑the‑shelf LLMs—especially when constrained by ethics and limited clinical data—often produce text that is fluent yet cognitively incoherent or clinically unrealistic. At the same time, frontier LLMs are hard to deploy in healthcare due to computational cost, latency, privacy, and resource constraints, creating a need for smaller models that remain cognitively and clinically aligned. The authors aim to bridge this gap by explicitly modeling cognition in SUD dialogues and making such modeling feasible with small language models.
AI.method: The authors design a two‑stage, cognitively grounded dialogue generation pipeline for SUD counseling. Stage 1 detects latent cognitive components (e.g., beliefs, coping strategies, readiness levels) from patient history and counselor queries. Stage 2 conditions a small language model on these detected components to generate patient responses that are cognitively aligned with the inferred internal state. To compensate for limited data and model capacity, they integrate three training strategies: (1) knowledge distillation from high‑capacity teacher LLMs to transfer richer cognitive patterns, (2) preference optimization using human annotations to align responses with clinical expectations, and (3) attention‑guided reward shaping to nudge the model toward correctly realizing targeted cognitive components. The resulting SLM is then evaluated both with standard text similarity metrics and with LLM‑as‑judge comparisons to human and teacher outputs.
AI.result: Across automatic similarity metrics (BERTScore, ROUGE, METEOR, BLEU) and LLM‑as‑judge evaluation, the cognitively informed SLM outperforms generic instruction‑tuned baselines and other mental‑health‑oriented SLMs in generating SUD counseling dialogues. Improvements are especially notable for responses involving open‑ended cognitive components, where the model must demonstrate nuanced internal states rather than simple surface matching. The enhanced model shows better realization and alignment of latent cognitive factors relative to reference human and teacher outputs.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling latent cognitive components and aligning dialogue generation to them enables small language models to produce more cognitively coherent and clinically realistic SUD patient responses, even under data and resource constraints. A combination of knowledge distillation, preference optimization, and attention‑guided reward shaping effectively compensates for smaller model capacity, yielding significant gains over strong baselines. The work suggests that cognitively grounded training pipelines can make deployable, privacy‑preserving SLMs viable for sensitive healthcare dialogue applications where frontier LLMs are impractical.

title: When the Governor Becomes the Disturbance: Control-Generated Disturbance and Cost-Aware Backoff in Governed Tool-Using Agents
comment: Includes ancillary experimental data and a Python script for reproducing numerical summaries. Code: https://github.com/CriticalAttentionSystems/CASAgentGovernor
summary: Supervisory governors can interfere with the tool-using agents they regulate. We study this possibility in a controlled file-recovery environment where increases in regulatory intensity trigger experimentally imposed tool failures. A cost-blind governor can turn these failures into persistent blocking that prevents task completion. We compare this governor with a backoff rule that reduces intervention probability using a moving average of known induced events. On a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent, the failure pattern appears under both result replacement and execution of corrupted tool arguments. For the persistent policy, adaptive backoff improves completion relative to a fixed weak governor with approximately matched intervention frequency. A Gemini 2.5 Flash experiment comprising 576 episodes across 6 tasks also shows reduced blocking and improved completion under backoff; among the tested settings, intermediate backoff strength achieves the highest observed aggregate success. These results identify an interaction between intervention cost and persistent action blocking, together with a possible mitigation. The cost mechanisms are imposed and their induced events are directly observable to the backoff rule; applicability beyond this controlled environment remains an empirical question.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how supervisory governors that interfere with tool-using agents can inadvertently cause persistent task blocking, and evaluates an adaptive backoff rule as a mitigation in a controlled file-recovery setting.
AI.motivation: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools and are subject to safety governors or regulatory interventions, there is a risk that overly aggressive or cost-blind intervention policies will repeatedly disrupt tool calls and prevent agents from completing tasks. Understanding when such persistent blocking arises and how to mitigate it is important for designing safe yet effective oversight mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled file-recovery environment in which increases in regulatory intensity are experimentally linked to induced tool failures. They implement supervisory governors that probabilistically interfere with the agent's tool calls. They compare a simple, cost-blind governor to an adaptive backoff governor that lowers its intervention probability based on a moving average of observed induced events. Experiments are performed with a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent under two failure injection modes (result replacement and execution with corrupted arguments) and with Gemini 2.5 Flash across 576 episodes and 6 tasks. They tune backoff strength and compare completion rates and blocking patterns across conditions.
AI.result: The cost-blind governor can convert intermittent tool failures into persistent blocking, effectively preventing task completion. This pattern appears across different failure injection modes. Introducing adaptive backoff substantially reduces persistent blocking and improves task completion relative to a fixed weak governor with a similar overall intervention frequency. In the Gemini 2.5 Flash experiments, backoff also reduces blocking and improves completion, with intermediate backoff strength achieving the best aggregate task success among the tested configurations.
AI.conclusion: Supervisory intervention policies that ignore the cost of interference can unintentionally create persistent action blocking in tool-using agents. An adaptive backoff strategy that modulates intervention probability based on observed induced events can mitigate this effect, improving task completion without necessarily reducing total oversight frequency. However, because the experiments rely on imposed cost mechanisms and directly observable induced events, it remains unclear how well these findings generalize beyond the controlled file-recovery environment, and further empirical work is needed to validate the approach in more realistic settings.

title: Dialect-Robust Speech Language Models with Synthetic Pseudo-Dialect Augmentation
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Accepted to IEEE SLT 2026
summary: Speech Language Model (SLM) performance often degrades on dialects due to data scarcity. Conventional text-to-speech (TTS) augmentation struggles to cover diverse dialects as it requires a certain amount of real dialect speech. We propose synthesizing pseudo-dialect speech by converting LLM-generated dialect text via a standard-language TTS model, requiring zero real dialect speech. Additionally, we introduce intermediate standard-text prediction during training, acting as semantic normalization for downstream tasks. We evaluate dialect understanding via dialect-to-English speech translation across Japanese, German, and Chinese dialects. Compared to synthetic standard speech baselines, pseudo-dialect augmentation improves scores for Japanese (from 25.38 to 26.24) and German (from 31.57 to 32.47). Furthermore, the intermediate standard-text prediction effectively bridges the semantic gap, boosting performance to 28.26 for Japanese and from 11.67 to 16.37 for Chinese. These results suggest that our approach scales to various languages without requiring speech resources specific to each dialect.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a way to improve speech language model performance on dialects using only standard-language TTS and LLM-generated dialect text, plus an intermediate standard-text prediction step, achieving better dialect-to-English translation across Japanese, German, and Chinese dialects.
AI.motivation: Speech language models often perform poorly on dialects because there is very little real dialect speech data available. Traditional TTS-based data augmentation still needs some real dialect speech to cover prosody, pronunciation, and variation, making it hard to scale to many dialects and languages. The authors want a method that can improve dialect understanding without requiring any dialect-specific speech resources.
AI.method: 1) Use a large language model to generate dialectal text for several dialects. 2) Convert this dialect text into audio using an off-the-shelf standard-language TTS model, even though the TTS is not dialect-specific, thereby creating "pseudo-dialect" speech. 3) Train speech models for dialect-to-English translation using this synthetic data. 4) Introduce an auxiliary intermediate prediction task during training where the model first predicts normalized standard-language text before producing the final translation, serving as a semantic normalization layer that helps bridge dialect-standard variation. 5) Evaluate on dialect-to-English speech translation benchmarks for Japanese, German, and Chinese dialects, comparing to baselines that only use synthetic standard-language speech.
AI.result: Pseudo-dialect augmentation yields improvements over synthetic standard-speech baselines in dialect-to-English translation quality: Japanese scores increase from 25.38 to 26.24 and German from 31.57 to 32.47. Adding the intermediate standard-text prediction further improves performance: Japanese rises to 28.26, and Chinese improves substantially from 11.67 to 16.37. These gains suggest that synthetic pseudo-dialect data and semantic normalization are effective for multiple languages and dialects, even without using any real dialect speech in training.
AI.conclusion: Creating pseudo-dialect speech by passing LLM-generated dialect text through a standard-language TTS model can effectively augment training data for dialect understanding without any dialect-specific speech resources. When combined with an intermediate standard-text prediction objective, this approach helps normalize dialectal variation and significantly improves dialect-to-English speech translation for Japanese, German, and Chinese dialects. The results indicate that the method is scalable across languages and dialects, offering a practical path to better dialect support in speech language models where real dialect audio is scarce.

title: From High Recall to High Utility: Dataset-Adaptive Post-Processing of LLM-Generated Customer Intents
summary: Large language models can extract useful signals from heterogeneous enterprise data, but high-recall extraction often produces outputs that are duplicated, uneven in granularity, semantically overlapping, or too numerous for downstream systems and human reviewers to use effectively. We present a dataset-adaptive post-processing architecture developed for Customer Intent Extraction (CIE), where unstructured customer language is transformed into stable, traceable intent units. The approach separates recall-oriented extraction from utility-oriented reduction. Source-specific preprocessing first isolates evidence from multimodal plans, sparse operational records, and structured opportunity data. Candidate intents are then standardized and deduplicated, optionally enriched with metadata for embedding computation, represented in a shared semantic vector space, and grouped using a clustering strategy selected according to the candidate set's characteristics. Cluster-level keywords provide an explainability layer, while singleton reassignment requires agreement between embedding and keyword similarity. Finally, constrained language-model aggregation produces one concise intent per cluster without introducing unsupported concepts, and the resulting unit retains provenance, clustering, embedding, and generation metadata. This treats post-processing not as cosmetic cleanup, but as a semantic reduction layer converting high-recall LLM outputs into reusable enterprise intelligence. We also describe two downstream applications: Machine-Generated Intents, which infer likely objectives for customers lacking direct evidence from peer customers with similar profiles, and intent-guided semantic retrieval and mapping, which uses the stable intent as a query against a downstream decision space, illustrated here by mapping customer intents to business outcomes.

AI.tldr: They propose a post-processing architecture that turns noisy, high-recall LLM-extracted customer intents into concise, stable, and reusable intent units for enterprise use.
AI.motivation: High-recall extraction from large language models over messy enterprise data yields many redundant, overlapping, and inconsistently granular intent statements that are hard for systems and humans to use. The authors want a principled way to distill this noisy output into compact, traceable, and semantically meaningful units that downstream applications can reliably consume.
AI.method: They design a dataset-adaptive post-processing pipeline for Customer Intent Extraction. First, they do source-specific preprocessing to pull evidence from multimodal plans, sparse records, and structured data. Then they generate many candidate intents with high recall. These candidates are standardized, deduplicated, optionally enriched with metadata, embedded into a shared vector space, and clustered using strategies selected based on the candidate set. Clusters are given keywords as an explanation layer. Singletons are re-assigned only when both embedding and keyword similarity agree. Finally, a constrained LLM aggregates each cluster into one concise intent without adding unsupported content, while preserving metadata about provenance, clustering, embeddings, and generation.
AI.result: The architecture converts scattered, overlapping candidate intents into a smaller set of concise, stable intent units that retain traceability and rich metadata. It enables two concrete applications: (1) Machine-Generated Intents, where intents are inferred for customers with little direct evidence using peers with similar profiles, and (2) intent-guided semantic retrieval and mapping, where stable intents are used as queries to map customer goals onto business outcomes or other decision spaces.
AI.conclusion: Treating LLM post-processing as a semantic reduction layer, rather than superficial cleanup, makes high-recall extractions practically useful in enterprise settings. The proposed architecture systematically reduces noisy candidate intents into stable, explainable, metadata-rich intent units that can power downstream analytics, inference over sparse customers, and semantic retrieval/mapping tasks.

title: OnlineQAT: On-Policy Distillation for Ultra-Low-Bit Large Language Models
summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) can recover much of the accuracy lost when large language models are compressed below four bits. Existing re- covery stages, however, are commonly optimized on fixed completions or teacher-generated answers, whereas the deployed quantized model condi- tions on prefixes generated by itself. Quantization errors can therefore move the model into states that are absent from offline recovery data. We introduce OnlineQAT, a two-stage framework that first obtains a usable low-bit initialization through block-wise QAT and then performs on-policy distillation (OPD) on student-generated responses. At each visited pre- fix, a frozen full-precision teacher provides a sampled reverse-KL training signal. On Qwen3-1.7B, OnlineQAT obtains the best average among the compared quantized methods: 57.28 at W3A16 and 32.52 at W2A16, im- proving over ReasoningQAT by 2.90 and 0.44 points, respectively. The results suggest that student-visited states provide a useful recovery signal beyond fixed-completion training, particularly at three bits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OnlineQAT, a two-stage quantization-aware training framework that combines block-wise QAT with on-policy distillation from a full-precision teacher to better recover accuracy for sub-4-bit LLMs, particularly at 3 bits.
AI.motivation: Standard quantization-aware training for large language models usually optimizes on fixed completions or teacher-generated answers, but deployed quantized models generate their own prefixes, leading to quantization-induced states that are not seen during offline recovery. This mismatch can limit how well QAT recovers accuracy, especially at very low bit-widths (≤4 bits).
AI.method: OnlineQAT first obtains a strong low-bit initialization via block-wise QAT, then applies on-policy distillation (OPD) where the quantized student model generates its own prefixes and responses. For each visited prefix, a frozen full-precision teacher model provides a training signal via sampled reverse-KL divergence, aligning the student’s distribution with the teacher specifically on student-visited states.
AI.result: On the Qwen3-1.7B model, OnlineQAT achieves state-of-the-art average performance among compared quantization methods: 57.28 at W3A16 and 32.52 at W2A16, outperforming ReasoningQAT by 2.90 and 0.44 points, respectively. These metrics demonstrate improved accuracy recovery for low-bit quantized models, particularly at 3 bits.
AI.conclusion: Training on student-generated trajectories via on-policy distillation, guided by a frozen full-precision teacher with a reverse-KL objective, effectively recovers performance lost due to aggressive quantization. The approach leverages the actual states encountered by the deployed quantized model, providing a stronger recovery signal than traditional fixed-completion QAT, with especially notable gains at 3-bit weight precision.

title: Justice After Identity: Large Language Models and the View from Everywhere
summary: The search for a common view of justice and fairness has challenged human collective activity, as our diverging judgments are unavoidably shaped by the self-interests of social position, personal benefit, cultural inheritance, and historical circumstance. John Rawls famously attempted to overcome this limitation through popularizing a philosophical tradition known by the phrase "the original position" - a thought experiment by which people select principles of justice without knowing the identities or advantages they will possess. Critics, however, have long questioned whether people can meaningfully suspend their social identities and suppress morally relevant forms of lived experience. Artificial intelligence engaged to calculate algorithmic and agentic fairness introduces a novel possibility. LLMs have no singular class, race, gender, nationality, or biography, yet their parameters encode linguistic representations of a vast range of human identities and moral traditions. Perhaps the ethical judgments of LLMs could approximate an integrative original position - a "view from everywhere" generated not by excluding social identities but by computationally incorporating their diversity.It is unlikely that humankind will "hand over the keys" to computational systems by simply delegating complete agentic control of distributive and procedural collective processes. But AI may play a role, perhaps a positive one, interacting with individual and collective human judgment as we often confront increasingly polarized views on what is fair and just. We present data comparing human, base model, and frontier/fine-tuned model judgments about classic moral dilemmas while systematically varying identity relationships and Rawlsian constraints on identity. We conclude by speculating whether, if advanced AI systems provide humans with thoughtful advice, humans would actually be likely to accept it.

AI.tldr: The paper explores whether large language models (LLMs) can approximate a Rawlsian “original position” by offering fairness judgments that integrate diverse social identities, and compares human and AI responses to moral dilemmas under varying identity and information constraints.
AI.motivation: Human judgments of justice and fairness are heavily influenced by self-interest and social identity, making it difficult to reach shared principles of justice. Rawls’ original position was proposed as a way to abstract away from these biases, but critics argue people cannot truly suspend their identities or ignore lived experience. With LLMs now capable of representing many perspectives without having a fixed identity themselves, the authors are motivated to investigate whether AI can contribute to or approximate an impartial standpoint on fairness and help in contexts of growing polarization.
AI.method: The authors design experiments involving classic moral dilemmas in which both human participants and different types of AI models (base models and more advanced frontier/fine‑tuned models) are asked to make ethical or fairness-related judgments. They systematically manipulate identity relationships in the scenarios (e.g., who is affected, their social roles) and apply Rawlsian-style constraints on identity information to simulate versions of the original position. They then compare the judgment patterns across humans and the models.
AI.result: The data show systematic differences and similarities between human judgments and those of base versus frontier/fine‑tuned LLMs across the constructed moral dilemmas. While the abstract does not provide numerical outcomes, it implies that advanced models can generate comparatively integrated, identity-sensitive yet less identity-bound judgments, illustrating how they might approximate a “view from everywhere” under certain conditions.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that advanced AI systems, particularly LLMs, have the potential to approximate an integrative Rawlsian original position by computationally incorporating diverse social identities rather than abstracting away from them. They suggest that AI might positively augment human deliberation on fairness and justice but emphasize that humans are unlikely to fully delegate decision-making authority. The paper ends by raising the open question of whether people would actually follow AI’s ethical advice, even if it is thoughtful and seemingly impartial.

title: Expert Coupling in MoE Pretraining: Reducing All-to-All Overhead with Correlated Placement and Token Shuffling
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers replace the feed-forward block of a Transformer with E expert networks, and each token is routed to k of these experts. Under expert parallelism (EP) the experts are distributed across GPUs, and every MoE layer runs all-to-all collectives in the forward and backward passes to dispatch tokens to their experts and then combine the results. On a cluster with 8 AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs per node, these collectives can take 45% of the training step at EP32 with top-2 routing and 60% with top-6 routing. We find that early in pretraining routers have already learned to assign tokens to experts in correlated patterns, both within a layer and across layers. At top-2, 0.8% of the expert pairs in a layer are selected together by 42% of tokens, and the experts a token selects at one layer predict the experts it selects at the next layer. We use these correlations to keep more token--expert assignments on the token's own GPU, which reduces communication across GPUs and across nodes. Correlated expert placement puts experts that are often selected together on the same GPU. Combined with a dispatcher that sends each token to each GPU once, it removes up to 58% of dispatched rows. Token shuffling applies when sequence parallelism shards tokens across the EP group. It moves each token to the GPU predicted to hold its next-layer experts during the reduce-scatter that follows attention. On one node this raises the share of token--expert assignments served on the token's GPU from 12.5% to 59%. In Megatron-LM, across EP degrees from 8 to 64 with top-2 and top-6 routing, the two methods reduce all-to-all time by 1.16-2.63X and end-to-end step time by up to 1.41X. Neither method changes the models' underlying routing decisions or expert parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper optimizes Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training by exploiting correlations in token–expert routing to reduce inter-GPU communication, significantly speeding up all-to-all collectives and overall training without changing the model’s routing or expert parameters.
AI.motivation: MoE Transformers scale model capacity by using many expert networks but require expensive all-to-all communication under expert parallelism, which can dominate training time (up to 60% in their setting). The authors observe that token-to-expert routing is not random: tokens repeatedly choose similar expert combinations within and across layers. They aim to exploit these structural correlations to keep more computation local to each GPU, thereby reducing communication overhead while preserving model quality and routing behavior.
AI.method: 1) Analyze routing patterns during pretraining and quantify correlations in expert usage within and across layers (e.g., a small fraction of expert pairs accounts for a large fraction of jointly selected experts; experts chosen at one layer are predictive of choices at the next). 2) Correlated expert placement: place experts that are frequently co-selected by tokens on the same GPU and use a dispatcher that sends each token at most once to each GPU, thereby reducing the number of rows (token–expert assignments) that must be dispatched across GPUs. 3) Token shuffling under sequence parallelism: during the reduce-scatter after attention, move each token to the GPU predicted to hold the token’s next-layer experts, so that subsequent token–expert assignments are more often served locally. Implement and evaluate these techniques in Megatron-LM across different expert-parallelism degrees and routing configurations (top-2, top-6).
AI.result: Empirically, early in pretraining they find strong correlations: at top-2 routing, only 0.8% of expert pairs account for 42% of jointly selected pairs, and expert selections are predictive across consecutive layers. Using correlated expert placement plus the modified dispatcher removes up to 58% of token–expert dispatch rows. With token shuffling, the share of token–expert assignments served on the token’s own GPU increases from 12.5% to 59% on a single node. Across expert-parallelism sizes from 8 to 64 and routing choices (top-2 and top-6), these methods reduce all-to-all communication time by 1.16–2.63× and cut end-to-end training step time by up to 1.41× on clusters with AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs.
AI.conclusion: MoE routing in large Transformer models exhibits strong, exploitable correlation patterns across experts and layers. By co-locating frequently co-selected experts on the same GPU and proactively shuffling tokens to GPUs that will host their next-layer experts, the authors substantially reduce all-to-all communication under expert parallelism. These techniques accelerate training (notably communication-bound MoE layers) without changing the model architecture, router decisions, or expert parameters, making them attractive, non-intrusive systems-level optimizations for large-scale MoE training frameworks like Megatron-LM.

title: Epistemic Uncertainty-Aware Defect Detection for Quality Control in Medical Device Manufacturing
summary: Objective: We investigate whether accounting for epistemic uncertainty can improve the reliability of automated defect detection in medical device manufacturing. Methods: We consider a machine learning framework that operates on heterogeneous manufacturing and device-report data represented with Knowledge Graphs. To mitigate errors arising from uncertainty in the decision model, we analyze a principled rejection strategy to abstain from predictions whose estimated epistemic uncertainty exceeds a specified threshold. We evaluate the approach using standard synthetic benchmarks and real-world medical device report data. Results: The theoretical results establish the validity of the method characterizing the regimes under which it is expected to be effective. Empirically, the rejection strategy enables explicit control of coverage, that is, the proportion of samples for which the model issues predictions, while improving performance on the retained samples. On 266,170 real-world FDA MAUDE device reports, a 10% abstention rate reduces classification error by 48%, and more aggressive rejection (approximately 70% coverage) yields near-perfect accuracy on the retained samples. On standard synthetic manufacturing benchmarks, abstaining on 9% of the decisions, our approach reduces the risk up to 63% compared with the standard no-abstention approach. Conclusions: Abstaining from predictions with high epistemic uncertainty can provide a practical tool for controlling the reliability of machine learning-based defect detection, especially in high-stakes medical device manufacturing applications. Significance: Uncertainty-aware defect detection may support safer and more reliable quality assurance in medical device manufacturing by identifying cases that require additional inspection rather than issuing potentially harmful predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that using epistemic‑uncertainty‑based abstention in a knowledge‑graph ML framework can greatly reduce error and risk in automated defect detection for medical devices, by not predicting on the most uncertain cases and thus improving reliability on the remaining ones.
AI.motivation: Automated defect detection in medical device manufacturing is high‑stakes: incorrect defect/non‑defect classifications can lead to unsafe products or unnecessary waste. Existing machine‑learning systems typically output a label for every sample, even when the model is highly uncertain, which undermines trust and safety. There is growing interest in uncertainty‑aware ML, but it is unclear, in this domain, how principled handling of epistemic uncertainty and selective abstention affects reliability, especially when using rich, heterogeneous data such as that encoded in knowledge graphs.
AI.method: The authors use a machine‑learning framework that operates on heterogeneous manufacturing and device‑report data encoded as Knowledge Graphs. They introduce and analyze a principled rejection (selective prediction) strategy that estimates epistemic uncertainty for each prediction and abstains when this uncertainty exceeds a chosen threshold. They provide theoretical analysis to characterize the conditions under which this abstention scheme is valid and beneficial. Empirically, they evaluate the method on standard synthetic manufacturing benchmarks and on a large real‑world dataset of FDA MAUDE medical device reports, comparing error and risk with and without abstention at different coverage levels.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that the proposed uncertainty‑based rejection rule is well‑founded and identifies regimes where it should improve performance. Empirically, the strategy provides explicit control over coverage (fraction of samples the model predicts on) and consistently improves accuracy on the retained subset. On 266,170 real FDA MAUDE device reports, abstaining on 10% of the most epistemically uncertain cases reduces classification error by 48%, and at about 70% coverage the retained predictions achieve nearly perfect accuracy. On synthetic manufacturing benchmarks, abstaining on 9% of decisions reduces risk by up to 63% compared with always predicting.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating epistemic uncertainty and allowing the model to abstain on highly uncertain cases can substantially enhance the reliability of automated defect detection, particularly in safety‑critical medical device manufacturing. Selective abstention offers a practical mechanism to trade off coverage against accuracy, routing ambiguous or high‑risk cases to additional human or procedural inspection instead of forcing potentially harmful automated decisions.

title: The Persona Hierarchy Model: Understanding Contextual Generalization in Fine-Tuning LLMs
summary: Language models are routinely fine-tuned under a fixed context, such as a generic system prompt, persona or domain-specific instruction, yet the learned behavior sometimes stays confined to that context and sometimes broadly generalizes to unseen contexts. We propose the Persona Hierarchy Model to explain this: a shared default persona influences behavior across contexts. Under this model, fine-tuning that modifies the shared persona promotes broader transfer, whereas changes to local personas remain more context-specific. Across 120 fine-tuned models spanning four behaviors and 15 training contexts, generalization narrowness positively correlates with the similarity between the training context's persona and the default persona (Pearson's r = 0.72 for Qwen3-4B). Prior fine-tuning under the default context can broaden generalization in subsequent training under other contexts. Aligning contextual responses with default-persona responses produces stronger effects. Finally, we propose persona-preserving regularization (PPR) to confine undesired contextual generalization. In RL, PPR cuts reward hacking from 42-55% to at most 0.2% under every evaluated prompt while retaining accuracy gains. These results support the Persona Hierarchy Model as an explanation for contextual generalization and can motivate future controls on unintended generalization for better alignment of LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Persona Hierarchy Model to explain when fine-tuned behaviors in language models stay context-specific versus generalize to new contexts, and introduces a regularization method to control unintended generalization.
AI.motivation: Language models are often fine-tuned under specific prompts or personas, but the resulting behavior sometimes overgeneralizes beyond the intended context or remains too narrow. There is a lack of clear explanation and control over this contextual generalization, which poses challenges for alignment and safety.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Persona Hierarchy Model, where a shared default persona underlies all contexts and local personas are context-specific variations. They empirically study 120 fine-tuned models (four behaviors, 15 training contexts) to measure how much behaviors generalize and how this relates to persona similarity with the default persona. They run interventions such as pre-finetuning on the default context, aligning contextual responses with default-persona responses, and propose persona-preserving regularization (PPR) in RL training to constrain changes to the default persona.
AI.result: They find that generalization narrowness is strongly correlated with the similarity between the training-context persona and the default persona (e.g., Pearson’s r = 0.72 for Qwen3-4B). Prior fine-tuning in the default context increases subsequent generalization, and explicitly aligning contextual outputs to default-persona outputs strengthens this effect. Using PPR in RL dramatically reduces reward hacking from 42–55% to at most 0.2% across prompts while preserving accuracy improvements.
AI.conclusion: The empirical evidence supports the Persona Hierarchy Model as a useful explanation for contextual generalization in LLMs: changes to the shared default persona drive broad transfer, whereas local persona changes remain narrow. By leveraging this structure, techniques like persona-preserving regularization can reduce unintended generalization and reward hacking while keeping performance gains, offering a promising direction for improving alignment controls in fine-tuned language models.

title: RippleCP: Measuring Counterfactual Checkpoint Advantage in Coding Agents
summary: Agent checkpoint systems decide what state is recovery-relevant, how to snapshot it, and whether rollback is admissible. None decides which of the safe boundaries they expose are worth materializing. We formulate this as counterfactual checkpoint advantage, the reduction in future recovery cost obtained by checkpointing a candidate rather than skipping it, and measure it by driving a CP branch and a SKIP branch to the same logical failure and recovering both under matched model, tool, verifier, and stopping conditions. On a frozen pilot of 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 106 real recovery branches, checkpointing saves 49.4 s per task, and that figure resolves into two regimes two orders of magnitude apart. The first checkpoint returns 100.0 s on 156.5 s of protected work, a conversion of 0.64; a second one step later returns-1.1 s on 41.8 s, a conversion of -0.03. Recovery is a re-derivation rather than a replay, so preserved work is a poor guide to saved work, and the classical elapsed-work rule misprices the second checkpoint by its full nominal cost. We identify where placement can pay, and set the bar a placement policy must clear.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and where it is actually worth taking checkpoints for autonomous agent systems, introducing a metric called counterfactual checkpoint advantage and empirically showing that naive checkpoint placement based on elapsed work can badly misprice checkpoints.
AI.motivation: Existing agent checkpoint systems decide what and how to checkpoint, and when rollback is allowed, but they do not decide which among the many safe potential checkpoints are economically worth materializing. This leads to over-checkpointing or misplaced checkpoints that may cost more than they save. The authors want a principled way to quantify the benefit of a checkpoint decision so that checkpoint placement policies can be evaluated and optimized.
AI.method: They define “counterfactual checkpoint advantage” as the reduction in future recovery cost when checkpointing at a candidate point compared to skipping it. To measure it, they run two parallel branches from the same agent state: one that checkpoints (CP) and one that skips (SKIP). Both are then driven to the same logical failure and recovered under identical models, tools, verifiers, and stopping conditions. Using a frozen pilot of 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 106 real recovery branches, they empirically estimate the time saved by different checkpoint placements and compare it to traditional elapsed-work-based pricing rules.
AI.result: On their benchmark, checkpointing saves an average of 49.4 seconds per task. However, the benefit is highly uneven: the first checkpoint on a branch protects 156.5 seconds of work and returns 100.0 seconds of recovery savings (conversion 0.64), while a second checkpoint taken just one step later protects 41.8 seconds but yields -1.1 seconds of net savings (conversion -0.03). Thus, many candidate checkpoints are actually net losses once recovery is modeled realistically as re-derivation instead of replay. Classical heuristics that price checkpoints purely by protected elapsed work substantially overvalue such low-yield checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Preserved work (how much effort is checkpointed) is a poor proxy for actual saved work under realistic recovery dynamics, where agents re-derive rather than replay prior reasoning. Classical elapsed-work rules can dramatically misprice additional checkpoints, especially closely spaced ones. The authors identify the conditions and regions where checkpoint placement can deliver meaningful benefit and establish a quantitative bar that any placement policy must exceed, enabling more rational and selective checkpointing strategies for agent systems.

title: ARCS: Towards Precise Text-to-SQL via Structured Disambiguation
summary: As text-to-SQL systems move beyond demonstrations toward real-world deployment, ambiguity in user questions becomes a primary source of errors. Such ambiguities are often subtle, domain- or data-specific, and can silently cause system outputs to deviate from the user's true intent. Ambiguity is traditionally addressed through conversational clarification, which is often inefficient, cognitively demanding, and poorly aligned with real-world user workflows. We propose structured disambiguation, a new paradigm in which ambiguity is resolved through explicit, constrained interactions rather than free-form dialogue. We construct ARCS (Ambiguity Resolution Corpus for SQL), the first text-to-SQL benchmark featuring naturally occurring, unconstrained ambiguities over real-world databases, with complete annotations of all valid ambiguity points, interpretations, and SQL queries. Experimental results show that text-to-SQL remains challenging in the presence of ambiguity: gpt-6-sol achieves only 51% end-to-end execution accuracy, and no open-source model exceeds 27%.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles ambiguity in text-to-SQL by introducing a new interaction paradigm, structured disambiguation, and a benchmark dataset (ARCS) of naturally ambiguous questions over real databases, showing current models still struggle heavily under ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-SQL systems fail in realistic settings because user questions are often ambiguous in subtle, domain- or data-specific ways. Traditional solutions rely on conversational clarification, which is inefficient, mentally taxing, and does not fit typical user workflows. There is also a lack of benchmarks that focus on naturally occurring ambiguities and their multiple valid interpretations, making it hard to study and improve models in these conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose structured disambiguation, where the system resolves ambiguity via explicit, constrained interactions (e.g., targeted choices or prompts) instead of open-ended dialogue. They create ARCS (Ambiguity Resolution Corpus for SQL), a new benchmark built from real-world databases and naturally ambiguous user questions. ARCS is carefully annotated with all valid ambiguity points, the set of plausible interpretations, and the corresponding SQL queries for each interpretation. They then evaluate state-of-the-art closed- and open-source text-to-SQL models on this benchmark to measure performance under ambiguity.
AI.result: Experiments on the ARCS benchmark show that ambiguity significantly degrades text-to-SQL performance. Even a strong proprietary model (gpt-6-sol) reaches only 51% end-to-end execution accuracy when ambiguities are present, while all tested open-source models perform substantially worse, with accuracies below 27%. This indicates that current systems are far from robust in realistic ambiguous scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Ambiguity is a critical and under-addressed problem for deploying text-to-SQL systems in real-world environments. The proposed structured disambiguation paradigm offers a more practical way to resolve ambiguity than free-form clarification dialogue, and the ARCS benchmark provides a foundation for systematically studying and improving model behavior under ambiguity. The low accuracies of current models highlight a large remaining gap and the need for new methods specifically designed to handle ambiguous user inputs in text-to-SQL.

title: Constraint Tree Exploration for Learning from Language Feedback
summary: Natural-language feedback in interactive learning often explains why an action failed by pointing to violated requirements. Misinterpreting this feedback can lead an agent to rule out valid solutions. We study this setting by modeling user intent as latent constraints over an action space and formulating learning from language feedback as pure exploration over feasible regions. We introduce TRACE, an algorithm that organizes candidate constraints in a tree and tests each proposed refinement by generating actions that satisfy it. TRACE commits to the refinement only if the resulting feedback does not contradict it over repeated tests. We distinguish two ways of using the same feedback: (i) falsification, which detects contradictions to the constraint set currently being tested, and (ii) identification, which may additionally name a violated constraint. We prove high-probability coverage bounds with dependence on the candidate class size $H$ for TRACE-Falsification. With reliable identification, TRACE-Identification can replace this dependence by $K/p_{\mathrm{ext}}$, where $K$ is the number of latent constraints and $p_{\mathrm{ext}}$ lower-bounds the probability of extracting a missing true constraint from informative feedback. We evaluate TRACE across six language-feedback tasks. On RecMovie, TRACE-Identification achieves 73% and 86% final-output success under caps of 20 and 60 evaluated outputs, compared with at most 42% and 48% for the evaluated prompting baselines given the same feedback and output caps. Controlled identity-corruption experiments further show greater robustness than direct accumulation when the falsification detector remains reliable.

AI.tldr: They propose TRACE, an algorithm that learns hidden user constraints from natural-language feedback by treating learning as pure exploration over feasible regions, and show it is more robust and sample-efficient than prompting baselines.
AI.motivation: In interactive learning with natural-language feedback, users usually describe why an action failed by referencing violated requirements. If an agent misinterprets such feedback, it may wrongly eliminate good solutions. There is a need for a principled way to model user intent as constraints and to learn safely and efficiently from potentially noisy language feedback without discarding valid options.
AI.method: They model user intent as a set of latent constraints over an action space and cast learning from language feedback as pure exploration over feasible regions. They introduce TRACE, which maintains a tree of candidate constraint sets. TRACE repeatedly (1) proposes a refinement (candidate constraint set), (2) generates actions that satisfy this refinement, and (3) tests it using feedback. It only commits to a refinement if repeated testing shows no contradictions. They formalize two feedback usage modes: TRACE-Falsification, which only detects contradictions with the current constraint set, and TRACE-Identification, which additionally extracts explicit violated constraints from feedback. They prove high-probability coverage bounds: for TRACE-Falsification these depend on hypothesis class size H; for TRACE-Identification, with reliable extraction, the dependence becomes K/p_ext, where K is the true number of constraints and p_ext is a lower bound on the probability of extracting a missing true constraint from informative feedback. They empirically evaluate TRACE on six language-feedback tasks including RecMovie and controlled identity-corruption settings.
AI.result: Theoretically, they derive high-probability coverage guarantees for both variants of TRACE, with improved dependence on problem parameters when reliable identification is available. Empirically, on the RecMovie task, TRACE-Identification attains 73% and 86% success on final outputs under caps of 20 and 60 evaluated outputs, respectively, versus at most 42% and 48% for prompting-based baselines with the same feedback and output limits. In controlled identity-corruption experiments, TRACE demonstrates higher robustness than directly accumulating constraints, provided the falsification detector remains reliable.
AI.conclusion: TRACE provides a principled algorithm for learning from natural-language feedback by modeling it as constraints and doing pure exploration over feasible regions. Its tree-structured hypothesis management and careful use of falsification vs. identification allow it to achieve provable coverage guarantees and better empirical performance and robustness than prompting baselines. When feedback reliably identifies violated constraints, TRACE scales with the number of true constraints rather than the full candidate class size, making it more sample-efficient in realistic interactive learning settings.

title: Arctic Questions, Missing Answers: A Dataset and Benchmark for LLM Abstention in Arctic Science
summary: Large language models (LLMs) should abstain from scientific multiple-choice questions when no option is valid, but frequent abstention alone does not demonstrate sensitivity to answer availability. We introduce ArcticQA, a dataset of 194 questions derived from primary Arctic research, with automated checks of answer support and distractor contradiction against source evidence. We further develop ArcticAbstain, a paired benchmark comparing answer-present and answer-absent conditions, with the correct answer replaced by a distractor in the latter and an explicit abstention option in both. We evaluate eight models from the Gemini, Claude, and ChatGPT families at high reasoning effort, with three trials per condition, yielding 9,312 recorded responses. Answer-present abstention rates range from 0.0% to 63.0%, whereas replacing the correct answer increases abstention by 5.05 percentage points on average. These findings highlight substantial baseline differences and the need to evaluate abstention frequency and responsiveness jointly. The dataset and benchmark are available at https://github.com/BenWilcox8/arctic-qa.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ArcticQA and ArcticAbstain, resources to evaluate when LLMs should abstain from answering scientific multiple-choice questions, and shows current models have inconsistent and often insensitive abstention behavior.
AI.motivation: Large language models are increasingly used for scientific Q&A, where answering incorrectly can be harmful. Existing evaluations often look only at accuracy on questions with a guaranteed correct option and sometimes celebrate frequent abstention as a positive safety signal. However, frequent abstention alone does not show that models can discern when a valid answer is actually available versus when no option is supported by evidence. The authors want to rigorously test whether models can condition their abstention behavior on the true availability of a correct answer, especially in a specialized scientific domain (Arctic research).
AI.method: The authors construct ArcticQA, a set of 194 multiple-choice questions based directly on primary Arctic research articles. They implement automated checks ensuring that the keyed correct option is textually supported by source evidence and that the distractor options are contradicted by that evidence. On top of this, they build ArcticAbstain, a paired benchmark where each question appears in two conditions: (1) answer-present, with the true correct option available; and (2) answer-absent, where the correct option is replaced by a distractor, so no listed option is actually correct. In both conditions, an explicit “abstain” choice is added. They then evaluate eight LLMs from the Gemini, Claude, and ChatGPT families, running them at high reasoning effort, with three trials per model per condition, resulting in 9,312 responses. They measure abstention rates and how these change between answer-present and answer-absent conditions.
AI.result: Across models, abstention in the answer-present condition varies widely, from 0.0% to 63.0%, revealing large baseline differences in how often models decline to answer even when a correct choice is available. When the correct option is removed (answer-absent condition), abstention increases, but only modestly: on average by 5.05 percentage points. This indicates that many models do not strongly adjust their abstention behavior in response to the true availability of a correct answer, and some may either over-abstain or over-guess regardless of evidence. The results also show heterogeneity between different model families in both baseline abstention and responsiveness to the answer-absent manipulation.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that evaluating abstention behavior in LLMs requires looking at both how often they abstain and how sensitively this behavior responds to the actual presence or absence of a correct answer. Simply observing high or low abstention rates is insufficient to judge safety or epistemic calibration. ArcticQA and ArcticAbstain provide a controlled, evidence-grounded framework to study these properties in a realistic scientific domain, revealing current LLMs’ limitations in discerning when they truly know enough to answer. The authors make these resources publicly available to support future research on calibrated abstention and safer deployment of LLMs in scientific and high-stakes settings.

title: GeoNatureAgent (GNA): A Framework and Benchmark for Pre-Production Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents on Geospatial and Environmental Tasks
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Extended version of arXiv:2606.12821 (ACM SIGSPATIAL 2026 poster paper). Published at GeoIndustry '26 (ACM SIGSPATIAL Workshop)
summary: Before tool-using LLM agents are deployed in environmental and geospatial workflows, teams need evidence that an agent reliably selects the right operations against real APIs. We introduce GeoNatureAgent (GNA), a framework for pre-production evaluation of tool-using agents: a fixed sixteen-tool geospatial interface published as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so the agent under test is the only variable, scored against an identical tool layer, task suite, and deterministic scorer. Its flagship instance is a 103-task benchmark (a 93-task main suite across 18 categories plus a ten-task comparison expansion) evaluated against an open, self-hostable geospatial API serving three environmental indicators across Spain and Portugal. We evaluate nine LLMs under three temperature-1.0 seeds, reporting capability and per-case cost as orthogonal axes. (1) Claude Sonnet 4 achieves the highest capability (61.7% +/- 0.7% on all 103 tasks; 60.8% on the main suite), followed closely by DeepSeek V3.2 (57.9%), while no other model exceeds 53%; (2) the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier is mostly open-weight, with DeepSeek V3.2 offering 93% of Claude's capability at 11.3x lower list-price cost; (3) under strict all-checks scoring the best model sits 24-36 points below the 85-97% reported on general-purpose GIS benchmarks, whereas per-check partial credit for the top four models (86-90%) is comparable, so much of that gap reflects scoring strictness rather than task difficulty alone. The MCP server, evaluation harness, benchmark, and API are publicly available; swapping the tool executors and task suite instantiates an equivalent benchmark for any geospatial domain.

AI.tldr: They present GeoNatureAgent, a standardized pre-production evaluation framework and benchmark to test how reliably LLM agents use real geospatial tools/APIs.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents are starting to be deployed in environmental and geospatial workflows, but teams lack rigorous, realistic, and comparable evidence that agents can correctly select and use real tools/APIs before deployment.
AI.method: They build GeoNatureAgent (GNA), a fixed 16-tool geospatial interface exposed via MCP so that only the agent model varies. They create a 103-task benchmark (93-task core + 10 extra tasks) over an open, self-hosted geospatial API for three environmental indicators in Spain and Portugal, and an automatic deterministic scoring harness. They then evaluate nine LLMs (three seeds each, temperature 1.0), computing accuracies and per-case costs and analyzing the capability–cost tradeoff under both strict (all-checks) and partial (per-check) scoring schemes.
AI.result: Claude Sonnet 4 attains the highest capability at 61.7% ± 0.7% over all 103 tasks (60.8% on the main suite), narrowly ahead of DeepSeek V3.2 at 57.9%, with no other model surpassing 53%. The cost–accuracy Pareto frontier is largely dominated by open-weight models; DeepSeek V3.2 reaches about 93% of Claude’s capability at 11.3× lower list-price cost. Under strict all-checks scoring, the best model’s scores are 24–36 points below accuracies reported on general GIS benchmarks, but when using per-check partial credit, the top four models reach 86–90%, indicating much of the apparent gap is due to scoring strictness instead of purely higher task difficulty.
AI.conclusion: GeoNatureAgent provides a realistic, reproducible, and model-agnostic way to evaluate tool-using LLM agents for geospatial workflows, revealing substantial differences in both capability and cost across models and clarifying how scoring definitions affect reported performance. Because the MCP tooling and benchmark are modular, the same framework can be adapted to other geospatial domains by swapping tools and tasks.

title: Right Number, Wrong State? Measuring Cross-Jurisdiction Substitution in LLM Recall of State Policy
summary: When an LLM answers a state-specific policy question wrongly, it may be hallucinating, or it may be returning a real value that holds in another state. We test this with a minimal-set design: the question wording is fixed and only the jurisdiction varies, across the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia (51 jurisdictions) and three exactly defined Medicaid income-eligibility quantities. Gold values come from an official data book and agree with an independent source in 101 of 102 checked cells. Under a pre-registered protocol, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol reproducibly give another state's current value, identical across two independent repeats, for 10 and 25 of 153 items. Attribution is fragile, however. Crediting any wrong answer that equals another state's value yields 3-5x more reproducible substitutions than checking every number in the asked state's own records, because many apparent cross-state answers are the asked state's own values under another convention or from an earlier year. Claims about cross-jurisdiction error need a complete same-state reference set. We will release the protocol, gold table, and all model outputs.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether wrong answers by LLMs to state-specific Medicaid eligibility questions are true values for other states, using a tightly controlled 51-jurisdiction test, and finds that apparent cross-state substitutions are common but fragile to how “correctness” is defined.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently err on localized policy questions, but it is unclear whether these errors are pure hallucinations or accurate facts about different jurisdictions. Understanding this distinction matters for evaluating LLM reliability in legal and policy contexts, where jurisdiction-specific accuracy is critical and misattributed cross-state information can be harmful.
AI.method: The authors design a minimal-variation experiment where the text of each Medicaid eligibility question is held constant and only the jurisdiction (50 states plus DC) is varied, for three clearly defined income-eligibility quantities. They compile a gold-standard table from an official data book, cross-validating 101 of 102 checked entries against an independent source. Using a preregistered evaluation protocol, they query two LLMs (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol) and check, for 153 question–model–quantity combinations, whether wrong answers match any other state’s true value, and how sensitive those matches are to attribution rules, time conventions, and alternative representations of the same state’s numbers.
AI.result: Claude and GPT each give reproducible answers (identical across two runs) where a wrong value is exactly equal to another state’s current true value in 10 and 25 of the 153 evaluated items, respectively. However, when the authors broaden the matching to credit any wrong answer that equals another state’s value, they observe 3–5 times more reproducible cross-state substitutions than when they restrict checks to the asked state’s own official records, because many “foreign” values are actually the asked state’s figures under different conventions or from a different year.
AI.conclusion: Many LLM errors on state-specific Medicaid eligibility questions look like cross-state substitutions, but this interpretation is fragile: a substantial share of apparent cross-jurisdiction errors are better explained as mismatches in conventions or time points for the same state’s data. Therefore, robust claims about cross-jurisdiction hallucinations require a complete, carefully specified reference set for each jurisdiction and quantity. The authors commit to releasing their protocol, gold-standard table, and model outputs to support further evaluation.

title: From Uncertainty to Action: Learning to Steer LLM Agents
summary: Steering an LLM agent means deciding whether to correct it, at which step, and with which mechanism. Uncertainty is often used to decide when to correct an agent, but whether it can guide these decisions remains unclear. We steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step with each of four mechanisms and run each continuation to completion. The resulting stepwise outcome table (SOT) holds about 82,000 counterfactual continuations of 1,864 trajectories from three benchmarks and two agents. It shows that uncertainty can identify failing trajectories, but that no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps. We therefore propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor, offline or online, that learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer by it. A harm-budgeted trigger decides whether to steer, limiting the fraction of successful trajectories that VoS disturbs. VoS improves on unmodified execution in all 12 settings of benchmark, agent, and offline or online use, by 7.8 points on average, and outperforms the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11, by 2.9 points on average. Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to better decide when and how to intervene in an LLM agent’s multi-step trajectory, proposes a learned trajectory-level monitor called Value of Steering (VoS), and shows it improves performance over uncertainty-based triggers across multiple benchmarks and agents.
AI.motivation: Existing work often uses uncertainty signals to decide when to correct or steer LLM agents, but it is unclear if these signals can reliably determine at which step and with which mechanism to intervene. There is a need to systematically understand stepwise interventions and to develop a principled way to decide where and whether to steer an agent trajectory, especially to avoid unnecessary disruption of already successful trajectories.
AI.method: The authors construct a large stepwise outcome table (SOT) of about 82,000 counterfactual continuations derived from 1,864 agent trajectories across three benchmarks, two agents, and four distinct steering mechanisms. At each non-terminal step, they apply each steering mechanism separately, roll out the continuation to completion, and record the outcome. Using this SOT, they analyze the relationship between uncertainty signals and the effectiveness of steering, and then introduce VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor that learns, from SOT data, the expected benefit of steering at each step. VoS can be used offline or online to decide at which steps to intervene. A harm-budgeted trigger is used to control how often VoS is allowed to intervene so as to cap the proportion of already successful trajectories that are disturbed.
AI.result: The analysis confirms that while uncertainty is useful for detecting failing trajectories, no single uncertainty signal reliably pinpoints the best step for intervention. VoS, trained on SOT-derived outcomes, consistently improves over unmodified execution across all 12 combinations of benchmark, agent, and online/offline setup, yielding an average improvement of 7.8 points. Compared to five existing uncertainty-triggered steering methods, VoS performs best in 11 out of 12 settings, with an average margin of 2.9 points. Ablation studies show that using ground-truth measured outcomes for training and enforcing a strict harm budget are both critical to achieving these gains.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty alone is insufficient to decide when and where to steer LLM agents along their trajectories. By systematically exploring counterfactual stepwise interventions, the paper demonstrates that learning a trajectory-level value-of-steering function enables more effective and targeted interventions. The proposed VoS monitor, coupled with a harm-budgeted trigger, offers a practical and robust steering strategy that improves agent performance while limiting disruption to successful runs.

title: BanglaRhet: Benchmarking Classical and Transformer Models for Rhetorical and Persuasion Detection in Bangla Political Speech
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the 2026 2nd International Conference on Advances in Computing, Communication, Electrical, and Smart Systems (iCACCESS), Dhaka, Bangladesh. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23162113. Code: https://github.com/TSRohit99/banglarhet. Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/tsrohit99/banglarhet
summary: Political discourse often uses rhetorical and persuasive language to frame narratives, influence public opinion, and mobilize audiences. While Bangla natural language processing has made progress in sentiment analysis and opinion mining, systematic benchmarking of transformer models for fine-grained rhetorical and persuasion technique detection in Bangla political speech remains largely underexplored. This paper presents a benchmark study of transformer-based models for detecting rhetorical form and persuasive intent in Bangla political discourse. Using BanglaRhet, a manually annotated corpus of 30,289 Bangla political speech segments collected from publicly available political news sources, we formulate two supervised single-label classification tasks: rhetorical technique detection (contrast, repetition, exaggeration, metaphor, rhetorical questions) and persuasion technique detection (blame assignment, call to action, unity call, moral, emotional, and logical appeals). We evaluate four transformer-based models, BanglaBERT, BanglaBERT-Base, SahajBERT, and XLM-RoBERTa-Base, against classical TF-IDF baselines. BanglaBERT achieves the highest performance, with 65.40% macro-F1 for rhetorical technique detection and 66.46% for persuasion technique detection, outperforming the best tuned classical baseline by 19.2 and 13.8 macro-F1 points, respectively. Class-level analysis indicates that errors are mainly associated with semantic overlap among labels, figurative language, and class imbalance. The results provide initial benchmark baselines for Bangla rhetorical and persuasion-aware political discourse analysis and highlight the need for context-aware and multi-label modeling.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking transformer models for detecting rhetorical forms and persuasion techniques in Bangla political speech using a new annotated corpus, showing BanglaBERT performs best and establishing baselines for future work.
AI.motivation: Political discourse heavily relies on rhetorical and persuasive strategies, but in Bangla NLP, existing work has mainly focused on coarse-grained sentiment and opinion mining. There is no systematic benchmark for fine-grained detection of rhetorical and persuasion techniques in Bangla political texts, limiting automated analysis of such discourse.
AI.method: The authors construct BanglaRhet, a manually annotated corpus of 30,289 Bangla political speech segments sourced from public political news. They define two supervised single-label classification tasks: (1) rhetorical technique detection with labels like contrast, repetition, exaggeration, metaphor, rhetorical questions; and (2) persuasion technique detection with labels like blame assignment, call to action, unity call, moral, emotional, and logical appeals. They benchmark four transformer-based models (BanglaBERT, BanglaBERT-Base, SahajBERT, XLM-RoBERTa-Base) against classical TF-IDF-based baselines, evaluating performance with macro-F1 and conducting class-level error analysis.
