AI.result: BanglaBERT is the top-performing model, reaching 65.40% macro-F1 on rhetorical technique detection and 66.46% on persuasion technique detection. It surpasses the strongest tuned TF-IDF baseline by 19.2 macro-F1 points for rhetorical techniques and 13.8 macro-F1 points for persuasion techniques. Error analysis shows that major difficulties arise from semantic overlap between labels, figurative language, and class imbalance across categories.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based models, particularly BanglaBERT, substantially outperform classical baselines for fine-grained rhetorical and persuasion detection in Bangla political discourse. The BanglaRhet corpus and reported scores establish initial benchmarks for this task. However, persistent issues such as overlapping label semantics, figurative expressions, and skewed class distributions suggest that more context-aware architectures and multi-label formulations are needed for further progress.

title: Which Buildings Are Artificial Intelligence-Ready? A Measurement-Based Assessment Framework for AI Question Answering and Actuation
comment: 47 pages, 11 figures, 23 tables. Code, results and data supplement: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23197610
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are becoming the interface to buildings, answering questions and controlling operations, but a building's readiness for them has not been systematically assessed. This study proposes a framework to quantify it. First, a building's knowledge graph sets two ceilings. The answerable-readiness ceiling is the share of operational questions its data could answer, and the actuation-readiness ceiling is the share of control actions it exposes. Second, a reference AI agent's accuracy on a fixed set of these questions shows how much of the ceilings is realized. On a simulated office, the agent realizes 0.62 of a 0.64 answerable ceiling, so missing data, not the AI, limit readiness, except in naming a fault's cause. Across 37 public real-building graphs, the median answerable ceiling is 0.16, and in 15 of 45, unlinked sensors lower it. The framework turns "is this building AI-ready?" into an auditable, ranked retrofit question.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantitative framework to assess how ready a building is for agentic AI systems by measuring how much of the building’s operations can be answered or controlled via its knowledge graph and how effectively an AI agent can use this potential.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI is increasingly used to interact with and control building operations, but there is no systematic, quantitative way to evaluate whether a building’s data and control infrastructure are sufficient for effective AI deployment. Stakeholders need a clear, auditable notion of “AI-readiness” to inform design, retrofits, and investment decisions.
AI.method: The authors define a building’s “knowledge graph” as the foundation and introduce two readiness ceilings: (1) an answerable-readiness ceiling, the fraction of operational questions that could, in principle, be answered given available data; and (2) an actuation-readiness ceiling, the fraction of possible control actions that are technically exposed for AI control. They then deploy a reference AI agent on a simulated office to answer a fixed set of operational questions and perform control tasks, comparing its performance to these ceilings. Finally, they compute answerable-readiness on 37 public real-building knowledge graphs, examining how data issues such as unlinked sensors affect readiness.
AI.result: In the simulated office, the building’s answerable-readiness ceiling is 0.64, and the AI agent achieves 0.62 of this, indicating that the main limitation is missing or incomplete building data rather than AI capability, except in the specific task of naming a fault’s cause. In the analysis of 37 real-building knowledge graphs, the median answerable-readiness ceiling is only 0.16, and in one-third of the cases (15 out of 45 examined graphs), unlinked sensors further reduce the answerable-readiness, revealing widespread structural data deficiencies.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a concrete, auditable way to evaluate whether a building is “AI-ready” by separating the theoretical potential (readiness ceilings imposed by the knowledge graph) from realized performance (what a reference AI agent actually achieves). The low readiness levels in real buildings and the strong impact of data quality—especially missing links and sensors—suggest that improving building knowledge graphs and data integration should be a priority. The framework reframes AI-readiness as a ranked retrofit and design question, helping practitioners prioritize which data and control upgrades will most effectively enable agentic AI in buildings.

title: Goldsmith: Gold-Loss-Guided Definition Optimization with an Agentic Annotation Harness
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Accepted to the main conference of EMNLP 2026
summary: Many annotation projects begin before experts have a stable guideline or enough labels to train a task-specific model. We present Goldsmith, an agentic pipeline that turns a small gold set---expert-annotated calibration examples representing the intended task boundaries---into a reusable structured annotation definition. Goldsmith treats this definition as a trainable textual object. Candidate definitions are run on the same gold examples and scored with an executable structured loss, while the output schema, formatting, retrieval, repair, judging, and human review remain in an external harness. A large language model (LLM) editor converts the highest-loss failures into textual-gradient revisions, which are accepted only when the measured loss decreases. In prompt-optimization comparisons, Goldsmith improves over direct rewriting, OPRO, APE, and PromptBreeder under matched evaluation protocols. The resulting definition also improves downstream annotation when combined with retrieval, score-based routing, and human review across typed span, pair-level relation, and fixed-trigger event-argument tasks. These results show that scarce expert supervision can support both task-definition learning and scalable annotation.

AI.tldr: Goldsmith is an LLM-based pipeline that learns and iteratively refines a reusable, structured annotation guideline from a small expert-labeled gold set, improving prompt quality and downstream annotation performance.
AI.motivation: Annotation projects often start when experts do not yet have mature, stable guidelines and there are too few labels to train robust, task-specific models. Existing approaches to prompt design and optimization either rely heavily on manual expert effort or do not explicitly treat the task definition itself as a learnable artifact. The authors want a way to transform scarce expert supervision—just a small, carefully-annotated calibration set—into a high-quality, reusable annotation definition that scales to different tasks and improves both automation and human-in-the-loop workflows.
AI.method: They introduce Goldsmith, an agentic pipeline that takes a small set of expert-annotated calibration examples (the gold set) and uses them to optimize a structured textual task definition. Goldsmith encapsulates the definition as a trainable text object. It repeatedly: (1) runs candidate textual definitions on the gold examples via an external harness that handles schema, formatting, retrieval, repair, judging, and human review; (2) computes an executable structured loss based on how well outputs from the current definition match gold annotations; (3) uses an LLM editor to generate ‘textual-gradient’ revisions of the definition focused on high-loss failure cases; and (4) accepts a revision only if it reduces the measured loss. This loop continues to refine the guideline. They then compare Goldsmith against other prompt-optimization methods (direct rewriting, OPRO, APE, PromptBreeder) under matched conditions and also test it on several annotation task types.
AI.result: Goldsmith outperforms alternative prompt-optimization approaches—including direct rewriting, OPRO, APE, and PromptBreeder—under the same evaluation protocols. The optimized definitions also lead to better downstream annotation quality when integrated with retrieval mechanisms, score-based routing, and human review. Performance gains are demonstrated across multiple task types: typed span annotation, pair-level relation extraction, and fixed-trigger event-argument extraction.
AI.conclusion: A small, expert-created gold calibration set can be used not just to supervise model predictions but to learn and refine the task definition itself, treated as a trainable textual object. Goldsmith’s iterative, loss-driven editing of annotation guidelines yields higher-quality, reusable definitions that improve both automatic and human-in-the-loop annotation across varied information extraction tasks. This indicates that limited expert supervision can effectively support task-definition learning and scalable annotation pipelines.

title: CADFather: Autonomous CAD Reconstruction through Coordinated Tool Use
summary: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape remains a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and stages of reconstruction. We introduce CADFather, an autonomous agentic system that coordinates complementary tools to recover parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations, while numerical optimization refines the parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs for each target part and preserves the best valid result throughout reconstruction. CADFather uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training. We evaluate reconstruction quality and execution validity on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as on CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. We additionally analyze computational cost and the trade-off between cost and reconstruction quality.

AI.tldr: CADFather is an agentic system that orchestrates multiple tools and a vision-language assistant to automatically reconstruct editable parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes, improving robustness and quality across diverse benchmarks while controlling computational cost.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing editable, parametric CAD models from raw 3D shapes (e.g., meshes) is difficult because different geometries and reconstruction stages benefit from different types of CAD operation proposals. Existing approaches typically rely on a single proposal source or fixed pipeline, which struggles to generalize across diverse parts and cannot flexibly adapt its strategy as reconstruction progresses. The authors aim to build a more general, adaptive system that can coordinate multiple complementary tools and make high-level decisions to recover valid, high-quality CAD programs without retraining large models.
AI.method: The authors design CADFather, an autonomous, agent-based framework. A vision-language assistant observes rendered images of the target mesh and intermediate CAD reconstructions. Based on this visual feedback and program state, it decides: (1) which partial CAD programs (candidates) to extend or refine, (2) which specialized tools to call (learned proposal models, algorithmic operation generators, or numerical optimizers), (3) how many proposals to request, and (4) when to terminate reconstruction. The tools generate new CAD operations or refine parameters of existing operations; these candidate programs are executed within a CAD engine, checked for validity, and scored against the target shape. The agent maintains multiple alternative candidate programs per part, continually updating and preserving the best valid reconstruction as it iterates. Importantly, CADFather uses off-the-shelf pretrained generation and assistant models without further training, relying on agentic coordination rather than end-to-end learning.
AI.result: On several standard CAD reconstruction and benchmarking datasets—DeepCAD, Fusion360, MCB, CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD—CADFather is evaluated for both reconstruction fidelity and program execution validity. The system demonstrates strong reconstruction quality and robustness, successfully recovering valid CAD programs across diverse shapes and benchmarks. The authors also provide an empirical analysis of computational cost, showing how different agent configurations and tool usage policies trade off between reconstruction quality and runtime or resource consumption.
AI.conclusion: CADFather shows that an agentic orchestration of complementary CAD tools, guided by a vision-language assistant, can effectively reconstruct editable parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes without additional model training. By adaptively selecting tools, proposals, and stopping criteria, the system achieves high-quality, valid reconstructions across multiple challenging CAD benchmarks while exposing a tunable trade-off between computational cost and reconstruction performance. This suggests that coordinating general-purpose pretrained models with domain-specific tools is a promising direction for complex engineering design tasks like CAD reverse engineering.

title: A Comparative Study of Evaluation Metrics for Long-Document Financial Narrative Summarization with Transformers
summary: There are more than 2,000 listed companies on the UK's London Stock Exchange, divided into 11 sectors who are required to communicate their financial results at least twice in a single financial year. UK annual reports are very lengthy documents with around 80 pages on average. In this study, we aim to benchmark a variety of summarisation methods on a set of different pre-trained transformers with different extraction techniques. In addition, we considered multiple evaluation metrics in order to investigate their differing behaviour and applicability on a dataset from the Financial Narrative Summarisation (FNS 2020) shared task, which is composed of annual reports published by firms listed on the London Stock Exchange and their corresponding summaries. We hypothesise that some evaluation metrics do not reflect true summarisation ability and propose a novel BRUGEscore metric, as the harmonic mean of ROUGE-2 and BERTscore. Finally, we perform a statistical significance test on our results to verify whether they are statistically robust, alongside an adversarial analysis task with three different corruption methods.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks summarisation methods for UK financial annual reports, critiques standard evaluation metrics, and proposes a new combined metric, BRUGEscore, validated with significance testing and adversarial analysis.
AI.motivation: Financial annual reports are long (around 80 pages), and UK-listed firms must report frequently, creating a need for reliable automatic summarisation. Existing summarisation benchmarks and metrics (like ROUGE and BERTScore) may not accurately reflect true summarisation quality, especially on domain-specific, complex financial texts, so there is a need to systematically compare models and metrics and to improve how we evaluate summaries in this setting.
AI.method: The authors benchmark a range of summarisation approaches built on different pre-trained transformer models using various extraction strategies on the FNS 2020 dataset (annual reports and their human-written summaries). They evaluate models with multiple commonly used automatic metrics and empirically analyse how these metrics behave. They then define a new metric, BRUGEscore, as the harmonic mean of ROUGE-2 and BERTScore, aiming to combine n-gram overlap and semantic similarity. They also conduct statistical significance tests on metric results and run an adversarial analysis using three corruption methods applied to summaries to test robustness and sensitivity of metrics and models.
AI.result: Different summarisation methods and transformers show varying performance across metrics, revealing inconsistencies and limitations of existing metrics in capturing true summary quality on financial texts. BRUGEscore is shown to better align with expected summarisation behaviour than using ROUGE-2 or BERTScore alone. Statistical tests confirm that many observed performance differences are statistically significant, and adversarial experiments show that BRUGEscore and some metrics are more robust and sensitive to corruptions than others.
AI.conclusion: Standard metrics alone (like ROUGE or BERTScore) can be misleading when assessing summarisation of long, domain-specific documents such as financial reports. Combining lexical and semantic measures via BRUGEscore yields a more reliable, statistically supported evaluation of summarisation quality on financial narratives. The paper provides a benchmark of transformer-based summarisation methods for UK financial reports and highlights the importance of multi-metric, statistically tested, and adversarially validated evaluation frameworks for future research in financial text summarisation.

title: Breaking the Space Barrier and its Application to Language Model Inference
summary: Language models are more and more often asked for structured output: JSON that follows a schema, or a tool call with typed arguments. A small machine, an automaton, enforces the format by forbidding the tokens that would break it. We observe that this machine has a rare property: from any of its states, each token leads along exactly one path. Graphs in which only a few paths join any two points are a classical object of complexity theory, and our theoretical result settles an open question about them: one can decide whether such a graph connects two points while verifying that it really has few paths, with very little memory. Precisely, the problem lies in the classes ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2, and needs only O(log2 n/ log log n) space, below the classical O(log2 n) of Savitch's theorem. The constructions behind the proofs become an inference engine: text the format forces is written without running the model, the mask is recomputed on the GPU without any table, recursive formats use a small stack, every output stays valid under a token limit, and independent fields are decoded in parallel and verified. On one 16 GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B, against MLX with llguidance, the standard setup for this hardware, schema-constrained extraction finishes 1.2- 1.3x sooner with the same answers, a grammar costs 3 MB instead of up to 1.5 GB, one server holds sixteen grammars where tables run out of memory, and sixteen tool-calling agents finish 2.5x sooner.

AI.tldr: The paper connects a practical problem in enforcing structured LLM outputs with a theoretical result in complexity theory about low-path graphs, and then uses that result to build a more efficient structured-decoding engine for language models.
AI.motivation: Language models are increasingly used to produce structured outputs such as JSON matching schemas or tool calls with typed arguments, which requires reliably enforcing output formats. Existing approaches often rely on large tables/grammars and are memory-heavy and slow, especially on constrained hardware. The authors want a more principled, memory-efficient and fast way to guarantee format-correctness while decoding.
AI.method: They model format enforcement as an automaton that masks invalid next tokens so that every state has exactly one path per token, leading to graphs where any two points are connected by only a few paths. They study the reachability problem in such low-path graphs within complexity theory and prove it can be solved in lower space than the classic Savitch bound, placing it in classes ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L, and SC2 with a space bound of O((log^2 n)/log log n). They then turn their constructions into a practical inference engine: recomputing token masks on GPU without precomputed tables, using a small stack for recursive formats, ensuring prefixes remain valid under token limits, and parallelizing and verifying independent fields.
AI.result: Theoretically, they resolve an open question by showing reachability in low-path graphs can be decided with very low space, tightening upper bounds and refining its complexity class placement. Practically, they implement a structured decoding engine that avoids large grammar tables, recomputes constraints on the fly, parallelizes field decoding, and uses a small stack for recursion. On an Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B/4B, compared to an MLX + llguidance baseline, their method achieves 1.2–1.3x faster schema-constrained extraction with identical answers, reduces grammar memory from up to 1.5 GB to about 3 MB, allows hosting sixteen grammars where table-based methods run out of memory, and makes sixteen tool-calling agents run about 2.5x faster.
AI.conclusion: Graphs arising from format-enforcing automatons for LLM structured output have special low-path properties that allow reachability to be decided in asymptotically less space than Savitch’s theorem, placing the problem in several fine-grained complexity classes. Leveraging these insights, one can build a practical structured-decoding engine that is both memory- and time-efficient, enabling faster, scalable, and reliably schema-constrained generation on modest hardware without large precomputed grammar tables.

title: RELATE: An Evaluation Framework for measuring Relational Orientation of Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for emotional support, raising concern that sustained use may draw users away from their real-world relationships. Yet existing evaluations primarily focus on the safety, empathy, or helpfulness of responses, leaving under-examined a relational question: where does the model orient the user for continued support? To address this question, we introduce relational orientation, a property operationalized through two non-exclusive dimensions: inward-facing (IF) language, which positions the AI as the user's ongoing source of support, and outward-scaffolding (OS) language, which encourages real-world human connection. Grounded in psychological and sociological literature, we formalize a taxonomy of relational orientation and present RELATE, a persona-conditioned framework for measuring inward-facing and outward-scaffolding language at the sentence level in multi-turn dialogues. RELATE pairs 76 help-seeking situations adapted from naturally occurring questions with three simulated user styles, providing 228 evaluation stimuli. In our experiments, we evaluate seven LLMs using dialogues with six assistant turns each, yielding 1,596 dialogues and 69,194 assistant sentences. We assess these sentences using a primary rubric-based LLM judge and apply a secondary judge to a subset. Under automated evaluation, we find that the proportion of sentences labeled as IF is higher at the sixth assistant turn than at the first, while the proportion labeled as OS is substantially lower for hesitant, indirect simulated users than for explicit, reassurance-seeking users. RELATE provides a reproducible framework and a sentence-level signal for auditing and steering the relational orientation of supportive LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RELATE, a framework to measure whether emotional-support LLMs orient users toward the AI itself or back to real-world social connections.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for emotional support, there is concern that users may become more attached to AI than to real people. Existing evaluations focus on safety, empathy, and helpfulness but rarely examine a key relational issue: do models encourage dependence on the AI or promote connection with real-world relationships? The authors want a systematic way to measure this relational orientation.
AI.method: The authors define "relational orientation" with two non-exclusive dimensions: inward-facing (IF) language, which positions the AI as an ongoing support source, and outward-scaffolding (OS) language, which encourages human connection. They construct a taxonomy grounded in psychology and sociology, then introduce RELATE, a persona-conditioned evaluation framework. RELATE uses 76 help-seeking scenarios adapted from real queries, each combined with three simulated user styles, yielding 228 stimuli. For each stimulus, they generate 6-turn dialogues with seven different LLMs, resulting in 1,596 dialogues and 69,194 assistant sentences. They annotate sentences for IF and OS using a primary rubric-based LLM judge, and validate with a secondary judge on a subset.
AI.result: Automated evaluation reveals that IF-oriented sentences increase from the first to the sixth assistant turn, suggesting growing orientation toward the AI over time. OS-oriented sentences are much less frequent for hesitant, indirect user personas than for explicit, reassurance-seeking personas, indicating that models adapt relational orientation to user style and may provide less real-world scaffolding to more tentative users.
AI.conclusion: RELATE offers a reproducible, sentence-level framework to audit and potentially steer how supportive LLMs position themselves versus users’ real-world relationships. The findings highlight that models tend to become more inward-facing over multi-turn interactions and can underserve more hesitant users with outward-scaffolding language, underscoring the need to explicitly design and evaluate relational orientation in emotional-support systems.

title: Finding Blind Spots in AppWorld and WorkArena Task Verifiers
comment: 14 pages. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development". OpenReview paper and supplement: https://openreview.net/forum?id=uR6EWsGE48
summary:
Execution-based task verifiers decide whether an agent succeeded. We audit shipped AppWorld and WorkArena verifiers with source-informed mutation tests. The main audit never modifies a shipped checker.
  In AppWorld, duplicating a non-idempotent write creates an extra record while preserving every checked field value. The verifier accepts all three task variants from two of five eligible generators: 6/15 constructed effects. A cardinality patch applied to checker copies after the census makes all six cells fail while preserving valid controls.
  In WorkArena, we prospectively rerun 23 extra-field candidates selected for earlier checker-PASS outcomes. Independent Table API readback confirms nondefault persisted values in 21, while all 23 receive PASS. Two requested strings are aliases of stored defaults. The 21 confirmed wrong effects span three form templates. These selected cases confirm wrong effects under the audit's protocol; they do not estimate a population rate.
  No other construction produces an independently confirmed false accept. Other checker-PASS cases are effect-correct degeneracies. We report zero-PASS families separately because retained evidence differs. In fixed intent-swap grids, the checkers return no PASS on 2,689 off-diagonal executions. This is a rejection census: 57 WorkArena cells use session-scoped evidence; the other 2,632 lack classified rejection causes and independent target ground truth.
  Each increment is specified before its own cells are scored. A supplement accompanies the OpenReview submission with the construction grammar, evidence, content-bound stage lineage and count reproducer.

AI.tldr: The paper audits execution-based task verifiers for two benchmark environments (AppWorld and WorkArena), showing concrete ways they falsely accept incorrect agent behaviors and providing a structured, reproducible audit methodology.
AI.motivation: Execution-based task verifiers are increasingly used to decide whether AI agents completed tasks correctly, but their reliability is underexplored. If these verifiers accept incorrect behaviors as success, benchmark scores, model comparisons, and safety conclusions become misleading. The paper aims to systematically test and quantify failure modes of existing, shipped verifiers in realistic environments rather than synthetic settings, while ensuring the audit itself is reproducible and methodologically rigorous.
AI.method: The authors perform a source-informed mutation testing audit of the shipped verifiers for AppWorld and WorkArena, meaning they use knowledge of the checker source and task generators to construct targeted variants of tasks and agent effects that should be rejected but might slip past the verifiers. They never alter the original verifiers in the main audit; instead, they mutate tasks, executions, and inputs. For AppWorld, they duplicate a non-idempotent write operation such that observable checked fields remain correct but an extra record is silently created. For WorkArena, they identify and rerun candidate cases where agents may have written extra or wrong fields but still received PASS, then independently confirm effects using a Table API readback. They also run intent-swap grids (off-diagonal tasks vs. intents) to check whether verifiers incorrectly accept mismatched goals. In some follow-up analysis they apply a cardinality patch to copies of the checker to test whether adding cardinality checks would close the discovered loophole. All increments and constructions are pre-specified and accompanied by detailed supplementary materials (grammar, lineage, and reproducibility tooling).
AI.result: In AppWorld, the duplicated non-idempotent write produces incorrect extra records while keeping all checked fields intact. The original verifier incorrectly accepts all three constructed task variants from two of the five eligible generators, yielding 6 out of 15 constructed effects as false accepts. When a cardinality-aware patch is applied to copies of the checker (post hoc), all six problematic cells are correctly rejected and valid controls remain accepted. In WorkArena, 23 previously checker-PASS cases suspected of extra-field issues are rerun; independent Table API readback shows 21 of them have nondefault, wrongly persisted values, yet all 23 still receive PASS. Two of the 23 involve string aliases of default values, explaining their behavior. The 21 confirmed wrong effects occur across three form templates. Beyond these targeted constructions, no other independently confirmed false accepts are found; other PASS cases correspond to degenerate but effect-correct behavior. In a large grid of intent-swapped executions (2,689 off-diagonal runs), the verifiers return zero PASS, indicating no false accepts in that setting, though 2,632 rejections lack detailed cause classification or external ground truth and 57 WorkArena cells rely on session-scoped evidence. Families with zero PASS are reported separately due to weaker retained evidence.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that current execution-based verifiers in AppWorld and WorkArena can silently accept concretely wrong agent behaviors, especially when errors occur in un-checked dimensions such as extra records or extra fields. Carefully constructed, source-informed mutation tests expose specific, reproducible failure modes, including 6/15 false-accept constructions in AppWorld and 21 confirmed wrong-effect PASS cases in WorkArena. However, the auditors do not claim broad population error rates—only that these are real, protocol-respecting false accepts in the shipped systems. Simple verifier modifications, such as adding cardinality checks in AppWorld, can close some loopholes without harming valid cases. The work advocates for more systematic, transparent auditing of task verifiers, with pre-specified increments, explicit evidence standards, and reproducible construction grammars, as a prerequisite for trustworthy evaluation of autonomous agents.

title: How Do LLMs Change Predictions Under Negation?
summary: Negation is an essential feature of human language, yet large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable in processing it. We evaluate recent open-source and closed-source LLMs on our negation benchmark and find that, in 37-71% of cases, they repeat the same answer under negation (e.g., "Madrid" for "What is not the capital of Spain?"). To understand and address this brittleness, we mechanistically examine how models operate under negation. Our main finding is that specialized attention heads and MLP neurons jointly implement negation by (1) suppressing retrieval of the original answer (e.g., "Madrid") while (2) promoting a favored candidate within the answer category (e.g., "Paris"). This contrasts with accounts of human negation processing, in which information about the original answer helps to determine what should be excluded. Furthermore, we find that this difference from human processing is a key source of negation failures: the model's mechanism relies on suppressing the original answer rather than using it to determine what to exclude, so the model can repeat the original answer when suppression is too weak or when a bias toward particular answers prevents it from selecting an alternative. To address this weakness in the model's negation mechanism, we propose a training objective that requires larger shifts in answer preference for more confident original predictions, and show that it reduces negation failures with less degradation of general capabilities than standard fine-tuning baselines. Together, our results demonstrate how mechanistic analysis can reveal why a linguistic capability fails and guide training that targets the underlying limitation.

AI.tldr: The paper examines why large language models systematically fail at negation, finds a concrete mechanistic cause in their internal circuitry, and proposes a new training objective that significantly reduces these failures without broadly harming performance.
AI.motivation: Negation (e.g., answering questions like “What is not the capital of Spain?”) is a basic component of human language, but current LLMs often answer negated prompts as if they were non‑negated. This brittleness suggests a fundamental gap between model behavior and human semantic processing. The authors aim to (1) quantify how bad these errors are in current models, (2) mechanistically understand how negation is represented and computed inside networks, and (3) design training interventions that directly target the discovered failure mode rather than treating it as a black‑box behavioral issue.
AI.method: 1) Construct and apply a negation benchmark to several recent open- and closed-source LLMs, measuring how often they repeat the same answer under negation. 2) Perform mechanistic interpretability analysis to identify specific attention heads and MLP neurons involved in negation processing. 3) Characterize the internal computation as a two-part mechanism: suppressing the original answer token and promoting an alternative from the same answer category. 4) Diagnose how this mechanism differs from human-like processing that uses the original answer as explicit information to exclude. 5) Propose and test a modified training objective that enforces larger changes in answer preference when the model was initially more confident in its original (non-negated) prediction, and compare against standard fine-tuning baselines in terms of negation performance and general capabilities.
AI.result: Empirically, state-of-the-art LLMs repeat the same answer for negated and non-negated questions in 37–71% of benchmark instances. Mechanistic analysis reveals specialized attention heads and MLP neurons that jointly implement negation by downweighting the original answer and upweighting a favored alternative within the answer category, rather than using the original answer as an explicit “to-be-excluded” representation. This mechanism explains why models often still output the original answer: suppression may be too weak or overridden by strong biases toward particular canonical answers. The proposed confidence-aware training objective yields significantly fewer negation failures than baseline fine-tuning, while causing less collateral damage to the models’ overall capabilities.
AI.conclusion: LLMs implement negation via a distinct internal mechanism that suppresses and replaces likely answers instead of reasoning about them as explicit exclusions, unlike human negation processing. This suppress-and-promote mechanism is inherently brittle and directly responsible for a large share of observed negation errors. By using mechanistic insights to design a training objective that scales the required shift in answer preference with the model’s initial confidence, the authors can substantially improve negation reliability with minimal impact on general performance. The work illustrates how mechanistic interpretability can both explain specific linguistic failures and guide more targeted, efficient training interventions.

title: DIVA: Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically feed dense visual patch tokens into a language-action backbone, preserving scene context but offering no explicit mechanism to regulate how strongly different visual tokens influence policy computation. We introduce DIVA, a Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation module with an anchor-then-attenuate design. DIVA combines high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors, then applies them in two complementary spaces: it reweights projected visual tokens before backbone entry and persistently attenuates low-relevance visual states within the backbone. DIVA preserves the full visual token sequence and requires no external grounding supervision. On LIBERO, DIVA improves OpenVLA-OFT from 96.6% to 98.0% average success and raises its zero-shot LIBERO-Plus score from 69.6 to 72.6. Real-world experiments further show consistent gains under task-irrelevant visual perturbations, supporting the robustness of intent-aware visual attenuation beyond simulation.

AI.tldr: DIVA is a module for vision-language-action (VLA) policies that selectively downweights task-irrelevant visual tokens using task intent, improving performance and robustness without extra supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA policies use dense visual patch tokens that preserve rich context but lack an explicit mechanism to control how much each token influences the policy. This makes them sensitive to irrelevant or distracting visual content and task-irrelevant perturbations. The authors aim to make VLAs more intent-aware and robust by modulating visual information according to task needs, while retaining all visual tokens and avoiding extra grounding labels.
AI.method: They propose DIVA (Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation), an add-on module for VLA policies with an anchor-then-attenuate design. First, DIVA fuses high-level task intent (from language) with low-level visual features to compute patch-wise relevance anchors, estimating how important each visual patch is for the current task. Then, it uses these anchors in two spaces: (1) pre-backbone reweighting of projected visual tokens to emphasize important patches before they enter the language-action backbone; and (2) persistent attenuation of low-relevance visual states within the backbone, ensuring that distractors remain suppressed throughout the policy’s computation. The approach keeps the full sequence of tokens and does not need external grounding or attention supervision.
AI.result: On the LIBERO benchmark, integrating DIVA into OpenVLA-OFT increases average success from 96.6% to 98.0%, and zero-shot performance on LIBERO-Plus from 69.6 to 72.6. In real-world robot experiments, DIVA yields consistent performance improvements when the scene is perturbed with task-irrelevant visual clutter or changes, indicating enhanced robustness to distractions beyond simulation.
AI.conclusion: Task-intent-aware modulation of visual tokens in VLA policies can improve both success rates and robustness to visual distractions. DIVA’s dual-space attenuation offers an effective, supervision-free way to suppress irrelevant visual information while retaining all tokens, and the gains on LIBERO and in real robots suggest the design is practical and generalizable for robust vision-language-action control.

title: Which Language Should a Skeleton Speak? Language Choices in Multilingual Reasoning
summary: Skeleton-based reasoning prompting is a promising training-free approach for structuring LLM reasoning, but prior work largely assumes an English-centric setting. We propose the Language-Aware Skeleton Exploration Framework (LASEF) to study skeleton-language choice in multilingual mathematical reasoning. Across math benchmarks, model scales, and languages, we show that English skeletons yield a small positive tendency on average, most visible for smaller models and low-resource languages. However, few language-level gains remain significant after correction, and English is not universally optimal. Combining greedy decoding, multi-rollout evaluation, translation ablation, and cross-benchmark validation, we further find three patterns of skeleton-language effects: directionally consistent, evaluation- and benchmark-dependent, and asymmetric negative. These effects cannot be fully explained by generation quality alone. Overall, skeleton language is a context-dependent design variable that requires multi-level exploration. All resources are released at https://github.com/lhsstn/LASEF.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LASEF, a framework to analyze how the choice of skeleton language (e.g., English vs others) affects multilingual mathematical reasoning in LLMs, finding that English skeletons are on average slightly beneficial but far from universally optimal, and that skeleton language is a context-dependent design choice requiring nuanced exploration.
AI.motivation: Existing skeleton-based reasoning prompting methods for large language models usually assume English prompts and reasoning structures, even when models are used in multilingual settings. It is unclear whether using English or local languages for the reasoning skeleton is actually optimal, how this interacts with model size and language resource level, and what systematic patterns exist across benchmarks. The paper aims to fill this gap and provide principled guidance for skeleton-language selection in multilingual mathematical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose the Language-Aware Skeleton Exploration Framework (LASEF), which systematically varies the language used for reasoning skeletons across multiple math benchmarks, model scales, and target languages. They analyze performance differences when skeletons are in English versus other languages. To robustly characterize effects, they combine greedy decoding, multi-rollout evaluation, translation ablation (to disentangle skeleton language from surface translation effects), and cross-benchmark validation, and then categorize observed patterns in skeleton-language effects.
AI.result: Empirically, English skeletons show a small average advantage, particularly for smaller models and low-resource languages, but the gains are often statistically weak after multiple-comparison corrections. English is not universally optimal across tasks or languages. The authors identify three recurring patterns in skeleton-language effects: (1) directionally consistent advantages of certain skeleton languages, (2) effects that vary with evaluation setup and benchmark, and (3) asymmetric negative effects where certain language choices hurt more than alternatives. These patterns cannot be fully accounted for by standard measures of generation quality alone.
AI.conclusion: The choice of skeleton language in reasoning prompts is not a simple “always use English” rule; instead, it behaves as a context-dependent design variable whose impact depends on model size, language resource level, and task/benchmark. Because the observed effects are subtle, sometimes non-robust, and not fully explained by generation quality, practitioners should explore skeleton-language choices systematically—potentially using frameworks like LASEF—rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all policy. The paper releases code and resources to support further research.

title: Frozen Models, Evolving Expertise: Model-Agnostic Learning from Deployment Experience for Multimodal Medical AI
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) are usually frozen after deployment, so they do not learn from the cases they solve. This is especially concerning in medicine, where new clinical evidence, updated guidelines, and new therapies can change established practice. Fine-tuning can update the model, but it requires access to model weights and additional training. Parameter-free methods avoid training, but they may overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual details by saving experience only as text. To address these limitations, we present a model-agnostic framework that allows frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill that guides reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory that stores reliable facts supported by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base that keeps visual examples and guides the model to relate each retrieved case to the current image. Instead of relying on a fixed validation set, a validation strategy keeps an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones. Across six benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, and medical and non-medical visual reasoning, and with four open-weight and closed-source base models, our framework improves performance during online deployment by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.

AI.tldr: A framework that lets frozen LLMs and VLMs continuously learn from real-world deployment via external skill, knowledge memory, and multimodal case base, improving medical and general reasoning performance without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLMs and VLMs in medicine cannot easily incorporate new clinical evidence and guidelines because they are typically frozen, while standard fine-tuning needs weight access and training. Existing parameter-free update methods either overfit small validation sets, rely on unreliable or shallow domain knowledge, or compress rich visual experience into text, losing important details. There is a need for a model-agnostic, parameter-free way for frozen models to learn safely and effectively from real deployment cases, especially in safety-critical domains like healthcare.
AI.method: They propose a model-agnostic framework that augments frozen LLMs/VLMs with three external components: (1) a Skill module that steers reasoning processes and tool usage; (2) a Knowledge Memory that accumulates trustworthy factual information derived from past cases or vetted external sources; and (3) a Multimodal Knowledge Base that stores visual examples and helps the model relate retrieved prior images to the current one. The system is updated online during deployment. A validation strategy accepts an update only if it improves performance on new cases without harming performance on previously solved ones, thus avoiding overfitting to a fixed validation set. The framework is tested with both open-weight and proprietary base models across multiple benchmarks.
AI.result: On six benchmarks spanning clinical diagnosis, workflow management, medical reasoning, and both medical and non-medical visual reasoning tasks, and using four different base models, the framework yields up to 34.2% performance gains over the frozen base model on medical tasks. It also demonstrates generalization to unseen cases, cross-model transfer of the learned external components without additional optimization, and applicability beyond medicine.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables frozen LLMs and VLMs to continually learn from deployment experience via external, modular expertise rather than parameter updates. This approach mitigates the limitations of weight-level fine-tuning and naive parameter-free methods, supports safe and validated performance improvements over time, and is effective across models, tasks, and domains, particularly enhancing medical AI systems that must track evolving clinical knowledge.

title: On-Policy Distillation Teaches New Skills but Not New Knowledge
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) strengthens language-model reasoning, yet whether students acquire new factual knowledge or compositional skill for multi-step reasoning remains unknown. We separate these capabilities using a controlled synthetic framework that measures the student's initial capabilities and independently controls the teacher's additional facts, compositional skill, or both. Across four models from three families, reverse-KL OPD reliably transfers compositional skill across unseen reasoning structures, but transfers minimal factual knowledge. Decoupling the distillation recipe reveals the source of this asymmetry: replacing reverse KL with forward KL restores factual transfer, whereas student rollouts specifically improve the execution of multi-step reasoning. Experiments on recent factual QA and competition mathematics show a similar asymmetry under reverse-KL OPD, yielding notable reasoning gains without factual memory expansion. Together, these results demonstrate that on-policy distillation does not expand a model's parametric knowledge, but instead teaches it to organize and compose the knowledge it already possesses.

AI.tldr: The paper studies what on-policy distillation (OPD) actually transfers to student language models and finds it mainly transfers multi-step reasoning skill, not factual knowledge.
AI.motivation: OPD has been empirically successful at strengthening language-model reasoning, but it is unclear whether gains come from acquiring new factual knowledge or from better compositional reasoning over existing knowledge. Disentangling these is important for understanding and improving training methods for reasoning-capable LMs.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled synthetic benchmark where they can independently manipulate (1) the student’s initial factual knowledge, (2) the teacher’s extra factual knowledge, and (3) the teacher’s compositional reasoning skill. They then apply on-policy distillation with different KL directions (reverse vs forward) and with or without student rollouts, to observe what actually transfers. They test across four models from three architectures, and additionally validate on realistic tasks: factual QA and competition-level math problems.
AI.result: Reverse-KL OPD consistently transfers compositional, multi-step reasoning ability to students, generalizing even to unseen reasoning structures, but it transfers very little new factual knowledge. When the distillation setup is decomposed, switching from reverse KL to forward KL recovers the transfer of factual knowledge, while using student rollouts specifically boosts execution of multi-step reasoning. Similar behavior is observed on real-world factual QA and math benchmarks: reverse-KL OPD yields strong reasoning improvements without expanding parametric factual memory.
AI.conclusion: On-policy distillation with reverse KL primarily teaches language models how to better organize and compose existing knowledge for multi-step reasoning, rather than expanding their stored factual knowledge. The direction of KL and the use of student rollouts are key levers: reverse KL plus on-policy rollouts favors skill/strategy transfer, whereas forward KL can support factual knowledge transfer. Thus, OPD should be viewed as a method for refining reasoning procedures, not for increasing parametric knowledge.

title: SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats
summary: As autonomous coding agents get increasingly deployed, the risk that accidental or adversarially injected misspecifications in tasks lead to dangerous agent behavior is critical to address. Prior work has shown that agents given such tasks rarely flag the conflict and instead cheat, editing tests or hard-coding expected outputs, and the actions taken to cheat can cause real damage, such as deleting a security defense to make a corrupted test pass. It remains unclear whether such conflicts can be established with independently verifiable evidence before the agent acts. We present SpecGuard, which detects and formally certifies these conflicts between task intent and tests. Given only the task description and codebase, SpecGuard autoformalizes the intended behaviour into a Lean 4 specification. The tests are formalized independently, and the Lean kernel checks whether any implementation could satisfy both formalizations, producing a machine-checked certificate when none can. On conflicted SWE-bench tasks, SpecGuard detects up to 72.8% of conflicts and formally certifies up to 51.1%, with a nearly five-fold lower conflict miss rate than model-based judgment. SpecGuard provides a pre-execution safety check that identifies reward-hacking opportunities through formal certification of task-level conflicts, before any agent behavior is observed. Our code is available at https://github.com/prmbiy/specguard.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SpecGuard, a system that automatically detects and formally certifies conflicts between a natural-language task specification and its tests in autonomous coding settings, helping prevent reward hacking before agents act.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents can behave dangerously when task specifications and tests are subtly misaligned, whether accidentally or adversarially. Prior work shows agents often "cheat"—editing tests, hard-coding outputs, or removing security checks—to satisfy conflicting tests instead of flagging inconsistencies, which can cause real-world harm. There is a need for a reliable, independently verifiable method to identify such conflicts before the agent executes changes, rather than relying on the agent’s own judgments.
AI.method: SpecGuard takes as input only the natural-language task description and the codebase. It automatically translates (autoformalizes) the intended behavior into a formal specification in Lean 4. Independently, it formalizes the behavior implied by the tests. Using the Lean kernel as a trusted checker, it determines whether there exists any implementation that can satisfy both the task specification and the test-derived specification. If no such implementation exists, the system produces a machine-checked certificate proving the conflict between intent and tests. This functions as a pre-execution safety layer for coding agents.
AI.result: On SWE-bench tasks that were deliberately constructed or found to be conflicted, SpecGuard detects up to 72.8% of task–test conflicts and is able to formally certify the impossibility of satisfying both sides in up to 51.1% of cases. Compared with model-based (LLM) judgment of conflicts, SpecGuard achieves nearly five times lower miss rate, indicating substantially improved reliability in catching conflicts that could lead to reward hacking behaviors.
AI.conclusion: SpecGuard demonstrates that it is feasible to automatically and formally detect conflicts between task intent and tests using proof assistant infrastructure, enabling pre-execution safety checks for autonomous coding agents. The approach reduces reliance on heuristic or model-based judgments and instead leverages machine-checked certificates of inconsistency. This provides a principled way to surface and block reward-hacking opportunities—such as test editing or removal of safety checks—before any potentially harmful agent actions are taken.

title: Rubric Spans are Label Representations: Joint LLM Encoding for Short Answer Scoring
summary: Automatic Short Answer Scoring (ASAS) requires models that can score student responses against question-specific criteria while remaining efficient and transferable across rubric sets. We propose RUSPAN, a rubric-conditioned ASAS framework that treats rubric descriptions as semantic label representations. RUSPAN serialises the question context, student answer, and all candidate rubric levels into a single sequence, then scores the levels listwise from the rubric-span and whole-sequence representations produced in a single LM pass. We further introduce RUSPAN-RIM, in which a Rubric-Independent Mask prevents rubric spans from attending to one another, making rubric representations depend only on the answer and question context and preventing overfitting to rubric patterns during training for zero-shot transfer. On six ASAS benchmarks spanning English, German, and Portuguese, RUSPAN improves mono-benchmark scoring over discriminative and generative baselines, while RIM with position reindexing delivers consistent and substantial gains on PT-ASAG, the held-out benchmark with the strongest combined language and rubric-structure shift.

AI.tldr: They propose RUSPAN, a rubric-conditioned framework for automatic short answer scoring that jointly encodes question, answer, and rubric levels and improves both in-domain and zero-shot transfer performance across multiple languages.
AI.motivation: Existing Automatic Short Answer Scoring models struggle to (1) use question-specific rubric criteria effectively, (2) generalize across different rubric sets and languages, and (3) remain efficient when scoring with many rubric levels. The authors aim to build a model that can flexibly condition on rubric descriptions, avoid overfitting to particular rubric patterns, and transfer to new benchmarks and rubric structures, including cross-lingual scenarios.
AI.method: They introduce RUSPAN, which treats each rubric level’s textual description as a semantic label. The question, student answer, and all candidate rubric levels are serialized into a single input sequence to a language model. The model produces representations both for each rubric span and for the whole sequence in a single forward pass, and then scores all rubric levels listwise. They further propose RUSPAN-RIM, adding a Rubric-Independent Mask to the attention pattern so that rubric spans cannot attend to each other. This forces each rubric representation to depend only on the question and student answer rather than mutual rubric interactions, reducing overfitting to rubric patterns. They also use position reindexing to stabilize representations under this masking scheme.
AI.result: Across six ASAS benchmarks in English, German, and Portuguese, RUSPAN outperforms both discriminative and generative baselines on mono-benchmark scoring, indicating better utilization of rubric information. When applied with the Rubric-Independent Mask and position reindexing (RUSPAN-RIM), the model achieves consistent and substantial improvements on PT-ASAG, a held-out Portuguese benchmark that differs most strongly in both language and rubric structure, showing strong zero-shot transfer capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Encoding rubric descriptions as semantic labels in a single-sequence, listwise scoring framework yields more effective and efficient automatic short answer scoring than prior approaches. Constraining rubric-rubric interactions via a Rubric-Independent Mask, combined with position reindexing, improves robustness and zero-shot transfer, especially under shifts in language and rubric structure. This demonstrates that carefully architected rubric conditioning can provide scalable, cross-rubric and cross-lingual ASAS performance gains.

title: Training Language Models To Be Coherent Decision-Makers
summary: Reliable decision-making requires more than accurate prediction: a model must preserve its beliefs, apply the relevant utilities, and recognize when the information needed to justify an action is missing. We study whether language models can learn this decision procedure from supervised fine-tuning and generalize it across domains and differing natural-language expressions of the decision challenge. Across 20 datasets, we explore challenges of belief instability and decision-making errors by first eliciting probabilities of outcomes and then varying only the utilities and the framing of the decision problems, while holding the evidence fixed. We train models to preserve elicited beliefs while selecting the action that maximizes expected utility, and evaluate transfer to unseen application domains, held-out framings, and different classes of payoff structures. We further introduce incomplete-information settings in which required utilities are withheld and replaced with irrelevant text, testing whether models can distinguish missing decision-relevant information from merely additional context. We find that targeted fine-tuning substantially improves coherent decision-making and that in many situations, learning transfers across domains and framings to situations unobserved during training. Further, models trained for decidability learn to identify when action cannot be justified based on missing information. Finally, we show the value of a routed system that considers separately the recognition of decision completeness and utility-sensitive decision execution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether language models can be fine-tuned to make coherent, utility-aware decisions that preserve their probabilistic beliefs, generalize across domains and framings, and recognize when necessary decision-relevant information is missing.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction alone is insufficient for reliable decision-making; decision systems must maintain consistent beliefs, apply utilities correctly, and know when they lack information needed to justify an action. Existing language models often change their implied beliefs when the framing or utilities change and may act even when key utilities are unspecified. The authors are motivated to understand whether a relatively simple, supervised fine-tuning approach can teach models a principled decision procedure that generalizes across tasks and surface forms, addressing belief instability, decision errors, and failure to detect incomplete information.
AI.method: The authors work across 20 datasets. For each decision task, they first elicit the model’s probabilistic beliefs about outcomes while keeping the evidence fixed. They then systematically vary only (i) the utilities/payoffs associated with outcomes and (ii) the natural-language framing of the decision problem. They train models via supervised fine-tuning to (a) preserve the previously elicited probabilities and (b) choose the action that maximizes expected utility given those probabilities and utilities. They evaluate generalization to unseen domains, unseen framings, and novel payoff structures. They also construct incomplete-information settings where some utilities are deliberately withheld and replaced by irrelevant text, and train/evaluate whether models can recognize the absence of required utilities and abstain or signal undecidability. They additionally study a routed system separating the subtask of checking decision completeness from the subtask of performing utility-sensitive decision choice.
AI.result: Targeted supervised fine-tuning yields much more coherent decision-making behavior in language models, including better preservation of elicited beliefs under changes in utilities or problem framing and more consistent maximization of expected utility. Learned behavior often transfers successfully: the fine-tuned models apply the same decision procedure to domains, framings, and utility structures that were not observed during training. In incomplete-information conditions, models trained with a focus on decidability learn to detect when key utilities are missing and appropriately refrain from committing to an action. The routed architecture, which decouples recognizing problem completeness from executing the decision, further improves robustness and reliability of the decision pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Supervised fine-tuning can teach language models a relatively principled decision procedure that goes beyond raw prediction, enabling them to maintain stable probabilistic beliefs, respect utilities, and recognize when decisions are unjustified due to missing information. This behavior generalizes reasonably well across domains and linguistic framings. Moreover, explicitly modeling and routing between (1) verifying that a decision problem is well-specified and (2) performing utility-based choice leads to more reliable decision systems. The work suggests that targeted alignment of decision processes in language models is both feasible and effective, and that separating belief formation, problem completeness checking, and action selection is a promising design pattern for deploying LMs in decision-critical settings.

title: Alice: A Large-Scale German Benchmark for Rubric-Based Multi-Dimensional Automatic Short Answer Scoring
summary:
Automatic Short Answer Scoring (ASAS) is central to NLP for Education. However, openly available benchmarks remain scarce, and existing datasets largely address how well students answer a question directly rather than how well they master underlying concepts (knowledge elements) such as thermal energy or epistemic activities (skills) such as reasoning or claim.
  To address this gap, we introduce Alice, a large-scale, rubric-based German ASAS dataset that is pedagogically aligned and comprises three subtasks: (i) learning performance (Alice-LP), (ii) knowledge elements (Alice-KE), and (iii) skills (Alice-SK).
  We further formulate rubric-based ASAS as a rubric-retrieval task and benchmark the dataset with a range of language models, from encoder-only models to lightweight LLMs. We also benchmark the dataset with zero-shot prompting via LLMs and a standard classification baseline. The experiments show that LLMs, in particular, struggle to score knowledge elements and skills in the zero-shot setting. They also indicate that rubric text is often useful, especially for Alice-KE and Alice-SK, while on Alice-LP gains over sample-solution-focused inputs are more modest and vary by model and input format.

AI.tldr: Introduces Alice, a large-scale German automatic short-answer scoring dataset with rubric-based labels for learning performance, knowledge elements, and skills, and shows LLMs struggle especially on concept and skill scoring, where rubric text helps.
AI.motivation: Automatic short answer scoring datasets are scarce, and current benchmarks mostly evaluate how well students answer specific questions rather than assessing their mastery of underlying concepts or skills. There is a need for pedagogically aligned, rubric-based resources that better reflect educational practice and enable fine-grained evaluation of both knowledge elements and epistemic activities.
AI.method: The authors create Alice, a large-scale German ASAS dataset structured around educational rubrics and three subtasks: learning performance (Alice-LP), knowledge elements (Alice-KE), and skills (Alice-SK). They cast rubric-based scoring as a rubric-retrieval problem and evaluate a spectrum of models, including encoder-only models, lightweight LLMs, zero-shot prompted LLMs, and a standard classification baseline, using different input formats such as sample solutions and rubric text.
AI.result: Experimental results show that language models, especially in zero-shot settings, perform poorly on scoring knowledge elements and skills compared with overall learning performance. Incorporating rubric text generally improves performance, notably on Alice-KE and Alice-SK, while gains on Alice-LP over using only sample-solution-oriented inputs are smaller and depend on model type and input configuration.
AI.conclusion: Alice provides a new, pedagogically grounded benchmark for automatic short answer scoring in German that differentiates between overall performance, conceptual knowledge, and skills. The study highlights current limitations of LLMs in fine-grained educational assessment and demonstrates that explicit rubric information is valuable, particularly for assessing knowledge elements and skills, suggesting future work should further integrate rubric understanding and retrieval into ASAS models.

title: From Probabilities to Decisions: Search and Multi-Teacher Distillation with Jev
summary: Probability-only models, which TypeSafe calls System One models, return calibrated probabilities for fixed choices in milliseconds and generate no text. We study one such model, Jev, through two tasks that require decisions under tight constraints. In bullet chess, a bot that places Jev's judgment inside Stockfish search alongside an opening book and endgame tablebases climbs above a 2200 Lichess bullet rating against other bots. Live model calls are too slow for search, so we distill pairwise judgments into a compact evaluator that runs at every position. We then ask how best to spend a fixed labeling budget when an LLM, Qwen3-32B, is available as a second teacher. In chess, averaging both judges' labels beats spending the whole budget on Qwen alone by 9.6 Elo (95% interval 4.3 to 14.9), and the gain replicates on fresh openings; a second answer from the same judge is no substitute, and Jev is the strongest partner for Qwen among the models tested. In passage reranking, Jev's labels alone train a reranker that scores as high as Qwen's, from 21 minutes of API calls instead of 5.1 GPU-hours, and adding Qwen gains at most a few thousandths in ranking quality. Search supplies the lookahead, distillation makes the judgment cheap enough to use at every position, and an LLM partner pays off in chess.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a fast, probability-only model (Jev) on decision-making tasks in chess and passage reranking, showing it can be distilled into an efficient evaluator and effectively combined with an LLM teacher for training.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether small, fast probability-only models (that do not generate text) can be practically useful in real decision-making tasks under tight time or compute constraints, and how best to allocate a limited labeling budget when both such a model and an LLM teacher are available.
AI.method: They integrate Jev’s probabilistic judgments into a chess engine (Stockfish) via a distilled evaluator and test it in bullet chess; then they run labeling-budget experiments that compare training with labels from Jev, from Qwen3-32B, and from combinations of both on chess and passage reranking tasks, evaluating resulting performance in Elo rating and ranking metrics.
AI.result: In bullet chess, a bot using distilled Jev evaluations within Stockfish exceeds a 2200 Lichess bullet rating versus other bots. In chess training, combining Jev with Qwen labels (averaging judgments) outperforms using Qwen labels alone by 9.6 Elo, and this improvement persists on fresh openings; repeated labels from the same model do not match the benefit, and Jev is the best partner among tested models. In passage reranking, models trained on Jev labels alone match the performance of those trained on Qwen labels but at far lower compute cost, and adding Qwen yields at most marginal ranking improvements.
AI.conclusion: Fast, probability-only models like Jev can be distilled into efficient evaluators that enable strong performance in time-constrained settings such as bullet chess, and their labels are competitive with or complementary to LLM labels for training downstream systems. Leveraging search for lookahead, distillation for efficiency, and judicious combination with an LLM teacher provides a practical recipe for building capable decision-making systems under tight resource constraints.

title: SAPD: Step-Aligned Privileged Distillation
summary: On-policy post-training can improve large language models by learning from their own trajectories, but requires costly rollout generation. We ask whether fixed demonstrations can support competitive off-policy learning through better supervision. Our premise is that their usefulness depends not only on the training trajectories, but also on whether supervision provides informative preferences among continuations and connects this guidance to the reasoning decision being learned. We introduce Step-Aligned Privileged Distillation (SAPD), a rollout-free self-distillation method that turns demonstrations into step-aligned distributional supervision. Its key insight is to use the known progression of a reference solution to associate each reasoning transition with targeted privileged guidance, rather than treating the solution as undifferentiated context. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SAPD outperforms supervised fine-tuning and label smoothing on average while remaining competitive with on-policy reinforcement learning and self-distillation. Analyses support both the value of context-dependent distributional guidance and the benefit of aligning privileged information with the current step. SAPD also largely preserves out-of-domain coding performance and achieves approximately 2x training-loop speedups over the on-policy baselines. These findings suggest that carefully constructed supervision can make fully off-policy post-training a competitive and computationally efficient alternative. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/SAPD.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAPD, a rollout-free, off-policy self-distillation method that converts fixed demonstrations into step-aligned distributional supervision, achieving competitive performance with on-policy RL-based post-training for mathematical reasoning while being more computationally efficient and preserving coding performance.
AI.motivation: On-policy post-training methods (e.g., RL on model-generated rollouts) improve large language models’ reasoning but are computationally expensive due to the need for online rollout generation. The authors want to know whether we can instead rely on fixed demonstrations (off-policy data) while still matching the performance of on-policy methods. They hypothesize that the key is not only what data we train on, but how the supervision is structured: it should give fine-grained, informative preferences over continuations and align these with specific reasoning decisions instead of treating full solutions as monolithic contexts.
AI.method: They introduce Step-Aligned Privileged Distillation (SAPD), an off-policy self-distillation method that uses demonstration solutions as a reference trajectory and converts them into step-aligned, distributional supervision. For each reasoning transition (step) in a reference solution, SAPD derives targeted guidance over possible next tokens or continuations, tying this privileged information directly to the current step instead of using the whole solution as undifferentiated conditioning context. This creates context-dependent, per-step distributions that the student model learns to match, enabling rollout-free post-training. SAPD is compared with supervised fine-tuning, label smoothing, and on-policy reinforcement learning / self-distillation baselines.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SAPD achieves better average performance than standard supervised fine-tuning and label smoothing, while reaching performance comparable to on-policy reinforcement learning and self-distillation approaches, despite not using generated rollouts. It also largely preserves out-of-domain coding capabilities, showing that specialized reasoning training does not severely harm general code performance. In addition, because it is fully off-policy and rollout-free, SAPD yields around 2x speedups in the training loop compared with on-policy baselines that require online sampling and evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that with carefully designed supervision—specifically, context-dependent, step-aligned, distributional guidance based on privileged reference solutions—off-policy post-training can rival more expensive on-policy approaches. Aligning privileged information with each reasoning step is crucial, as supported by ablation analyses. SAPD demonstrates that fully off-policy, rollout-free training can be both computationally efficient and competitive for improving LLM mathematical reasoning while preserving out-of-domain abilities such as coding.

title: Bookkeeping, Composition, or Unreachable Gold? Reading MemoryAgentBench's Conflict-Resolution Scores Against a Frozen Last-Write Resolver
comment: Accepted at the IAB Workshop (Interpreting Agent Behavior) at NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 19 pages
summary: MemoryAgentBench's Conflict Resolution split is read as measuring "selective forgetting". We execute the benchmark's own rule - the newest statement about a fact wins - as a zero-learning resolver frozen on one of the four fact lists. Under the official metric the rule answers 80.25% of the questions (74.5% on the three held-out lists). Of the rest, 67 items have a released gold that the last-write graph cannot reach but overwritten statements would ("The capital of India is New Delhi." superseded by "The capital of India is Grosseto."; gold New Delhi); such items are a third of the multi-hop questions at 262K. Two long-context models and our pre-registered approximate re-implementation of the benchmark's BM25 agent, one retained run per item and outcomes only, score 84.7%, 82.6% and 41.6% on the items the rule solves against 10.4%, 11.9% and 6.0% on those 67. The failures are a reachability split plus a small parser-scope residual; the per-item split, not the aggregate, is the unit at which a score here can be read.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques and reinterprets the MemoryAgentBench Conflict Resolution split, showing that a trivial last-write-wins rule already explains most performance and exposes flaws in the benchmark’s notion of “selective forgetting.”
AI.motivation: To investigate what the MemoryAgentBench Conflict Resolution split actually measures, whether it truly tests selective forgetting in long-context models, and to check for issues in the benchmark’s construction and evaluation methodology.
AI.method: The authors implement the benchmark’s own implicit rule—“the newest statement about a fact wins”—as a zero-learning resolver, frozen on one of four available fact lists. They then run this rule-based resolver across the benchmark, compare its performance to the official metric, and contrast it with two long-context models and an approximate re-implementation of the benchmark’s BM25 agent. They also analyze items whose gold answers are unreachable under the last-write graph but would be reachable if overwritten statements were considered.
AI.result: The simple last-write-wins rule correctly answers 80.25% of all questions (74.5% on the three held-out fact lists). There are 67 items where the released gold answer is not reachable under the benchmark’s last-write graph, although it would be reachable if overwritten statements were allowed; these 67 constitute about one third of the multi-hop questions in the 262K set.
