On the subset of items solved by the rule, the two long-context models and the BM25-like agent achieve 84.7%, 82.6%, and 41.6% accuracy, respectively, but only 10.4%, 11.9%, and 6.0% on the 67 inconsistent items.
AI.conclusion: Most of the benchmark’s Conflict Resolution performance can be reproduced by a trivial, frozen last-write-wins rule, and a nontrivial portion of items has unreachable or inconsistent gold labels. The main source of failures is structural reachability plus a small parsing residual, implying that per-item reachability, not aggregate scores, is the meaningful unit of analysis. Consequently, the benchmark as used does not cleanly measure “selective forgetting” in long-context models and must be interpreted with care.

title: InsClaimBench: Benchmarking Insurance Claim Adjudication Across the Decision Chain
summary: Recent advances in reasoning-oriented large language models (LLMs) have motivated increasing evaluation of their ability to perform professional decision tasks. Insurance claim adjudication is one such task, requiring models to connect case evidence, insurance rules, intermediate judgments, and payout calculations across a structured decision process. We introduce InsClaimBench, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating insurance claim adjudication across the decision chain. Grounded in real claim materials and structured insurance rules, InsClaimBench contains 3,780 cases in 375 case families across auto, property, and health insurance, comprising 86,656 atomic rule judgments. It evaluates each claim from atomic rules through adjudication modules to payout decisions and amounts, with controlled factual variants testing whether required changes are correctly propagated across levels. Evaluation of six LLMs reveals a progressive loss of reliability along the decision chain. Payout-decision accuracy ranges from 74.23--80.19%, while joint decision--amount accuracy drops to 47.54--73.15%. Strong local performance also fails to ensure case-level correctness: atomic-rule accuracy reaches 95.48%, whereas rule-vector exact match peaks at only 36.90%, and the most frequent module errors are not necessarily those most associated with final-decision failure. Under factual changes, these inconsistencies further become propagation failures: module updates are less reliable than rule updates, correct local judgments can still yield incorrect payouts, and correct payouts can conceal intermediate errors. These results show that reliable claim adjudication requires consistent composition and propagation across the decision chain.

AI.tldr: The paper presents InsClaimBench, a benchmark to evaluate how well reasoning-oriented LLMs can handle end-to-end insurance claim adjudication, showing that current models struggle with consistent, multi-step decision chains and propagation of factual changes.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly applied to professional domains, there is a need to rigorously test their ability to perform complex, structured decision-making tasks like insurance claim adjudication. Existing evaluations often focus on isolated reasoning steps or simple QA, not on full decision pipelines where local judgments must be correctly combined, updated, and propagated. The authors aim to address this gap by providing a realistic, rule-grounded, end-to-end benchmark that exposes where and how LLMs fail in such decision chains.
AI.method: The authors construct InsClaimBench, an insurance claim adjudication benchmark grounded in real claim materials and structured insurance rules, spanning auto, property, and health insurance. It includes 3,780 cases organized into 375 case families, with 86,656 atomic rule judgments and controlled factual variants. The benchmark evaluates performance at multiple levels: (1) atomic rule judgments, (2) adjudication modules that aggregate rules, and (3) final payout decisions and amounts. Factual variants are used to assess whether models correctly propagate required changes through the decision chain. Six LLMs are systematically evaluated on all levels using metrics such as payout-decision accuracy, joint decision-and-amount accuracy, rule-vector exact match, and error propagation under factual changes.
AI.result: Across six LLMs, performance degrades as decisions move up the chain from local judgments to final payouts. Payout-decision accuracy ranges from 74.23–80.19%, but joint decision-and-amount accuracy is much lower at 47.54–73.15%. While atomic rule accuracy can be as high as 95.48%, the exact match of the full rule vector for a case is only 36.90%. Error analysis shows that modules that frequently err are not always those most responsible for final decision failures. Under factual changes, models exhibit propagation failures: updating module-level decisions is less reliable than updating rule-level decisions, correct local judgments sometimes still lead to incorrect payouts, and accurate payouts can mask mistakes in intermediate reasoning steps.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that current reasoning-oriented LLMs are not reliably capable of end-to-end insurance claim adjudication because they lack robust compositionality and error-free propagation across decision stages. Strong performance on individual, local judgments does not translate into globally correct case outcomes, particularly when factual conditions change. Reliable deployment of LLMs in this domain therefore requires methods and systems that ensure consistent composition of intermediate decisions, accurate propagation of updates, and better alignment between local reasoning quality and final adjudication correctness.

title: FreeEvolve: Learning to Evolve Beyond Fixed Loops
summary: Agent evolvers automate the design of the prompts, skills and workflows around language model agents, yet the optimization process they follow is still designed by hand: a fixed search loop decides how candidates are evaluated, which are kept and when the search stops. We propose FREEEVOLVE, which automates this process as well. An environment specifies the goal, target agent, evaluator, data and resource limits; within these limits, the evolver itself decides what to test, how much evidence to collect, which candidates to pursue and when to stop. These decisions follow an editable evolution skill, which we improve through meta-evolution by scoring each candidate skill on the fresh target agent it produces. The optimization process thus becomes a capability learned from experience rather than a loop engineered in advance. On tau3-bench, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3 and Terminal-Bench 2.1, FREEEVOLVE controls the evolution campaign by itself, yet improves the primary held-out metric by 13.6 points on average and matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers. The learned process keeps improving with experience: meta-evolved skills add 6.9 points over the seed skill on fresh target agents, demonstrating transferability across environments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FREEEVOLVE, a system that not only evolves language model agents (their prompts, skills, and workflows) but also learns how to optimize the evolution process itself, replacing hand-designed search loops with a learned, adaptive optimization skill.
AI.motivation: Existing agent evolvers can improve language model agents, but their optimization processes are rigid and manually engineered: a fixed loop defines how candidates are generated, evaluated, selected, and when to stop. This manual design may be suboptimal, hard to generalize across tasks, and unable to adapt as more experience is collected. The authors aim to make the optimization process itself learnable and adaptive, turning it into a capability that improves with experience and transfers across environments.
AI.method: The authors propose FREEEVOLVE, which operates in a specified environment that defines the goal, target agent type, evaluator, data, and resource limits. Within these constraints, the evolver autonomously decides which candidate agents to test, how much evaluation evidence to collect, which candidates to continue exploring, and when to terminate the search. These control decisions are parameterized as an "evolution skill"—an editable policy governing the evolution campaign. FREEEVOLVE applies meta-evolution over these skills: each candidate evolution skill is evaluated by running it to produce a "fresh" target agent and then scoring that agent on the task metrics. Skills that lead to better target agents are favored, thereby learning better optimization strategies over time.
AI.result: On benchmarks including tau3-bench, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, FREEEVOLVE autonomously manages the evolution process and achieves on average a 13.6-point improvement in the main held-out performance metric, matching or surpassing manually designed evolvers. Furthermore, when the evolution skill itself is meta-evolved using experience across environments, the resulting skills provide an additional 6.9-point improvement over the initial seed skill on new, previously unseen target agents, indicating that the learned optimization strategies generalize and continue to improve with further experience.
AI.conclusion: FREEEVOLVE demonstrates that the optimization loop around language model agents—the process that decides what to try, how to evaluate, and when to stop—can itself be learned rather than hand-engineered. By representing this loop as an editable evolution skill and improving it via meta-evolution, the system autonomously controls evolution campaigns, achieves strong performance across several benchmarks, and exhibits transferability of learned optimization strategies to new environments and target agents. This suggests a path toward increasingly automated, experience-driven design of both agents and their training algorithms.

title: From Pareto to Preference: Personalized Test-Time Scaling via Amortized Agentic Policy Discovery
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models by allocating additional inference computation. Existing approaches to improving TTS efficiency largely optimize accuracy against one resource dimension at a time, advancing either the accuracy--cost or accuracy--latency Pareto frontier. Yet user requirements are multidimensional: users may specify accuracy, latency, and inference-cost requirements jointly, and different requirements can favor different controllers. We formulate Personalized Test-Time Scaling as discovering executable controllers that maximize the joint satisfaction rate of user-specific requirements. To reduce the overhead of repeated policy discovery for new user profiles, we propose PersonTTS, an amortized agentic policy-discovery framework that reuses prior search experience through requirement-matched controller initialization and source-distilled procedural guidance, while retaining target-profile evaluation for every candidate. Experiments on AIME and HMMT show that PersonTTS substantially outperforms strong TTS baselines in joint requirement satisfaction on unseen user profiles and held-out problems. Under the same candidate-evaluation budget, cross-user experience reuse further improves policy quality while substantially reducing discovery-agent time and cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PersonTTS, an amortized framework for test-time scaling that discovers personalized inference controllers to better satisfy each user’s joint accuracy, latency, and cost requirements, reusing experience across users to improve efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time scaling methods mostly optimize along a single resource dimension (e.g., accuracy vs. cost or accuracy vs. latency), but real users have heterogeneous, multidimensional preferences over accuracy, latency, and inference cost. Different requirement profiles can favor very different test-time controllers, and repeatedly discovering new controllers for each user profile is expensive. There is a need for a principled way to personalize test-time computation while keeping the policy-discovery overhead manageable.
AI.method: The authors define Personalized Test-Time Scaling as the problem of discovering executable controllers that, for a given user requirement profile, maximize the probability that accuracy, latency, and cost constraints are jointly satisfied. They introduce PersonTTS, an amortized, agentic policy-discovery framework that (1) initializes controllers using prior search experience matched to the new profile’s requirements and (2) provides source-distilled procedural guidance during search, while (3) still evaluating all candidate controllers on the target profile. In essence, PersonTTS reuses solutions and search traces from earlier users to warm-start and guide controller search for new users, under a fixed evaluation budget.
AI.result: On math reasoning benchmarks (AIME and HMMT), PersonTTS achieves substantially higher joint satisfaction of accuracy, latency, and cost constraints on unseen user profiles and held-out problems than strong TTS baselines. Given the same candidate-evaluation budget, the cross-user experience reuse in PersonTTS yields both higher-quality controllers and significantly lower time and monetary cost for the discovery agent compared to non-amortized approaches.
AI.conclusion: Personalizing test-time scaling to user-specific multi-objective requirements and amortizing policy discovery across users leads to better alignment with user constraints and more efficient use of compute. PersonTTS demonstrates that reusing past search experience—via requirement-matched initialization and distilled guidance—can substantially improve the practicality of deploying adaptive test-time computation in large language models.

title: Few Bits, One Law: Toward W2A4KV2
summary: Extreme low-bit LLM compression is most challenging when weights, activations, and KV caches are quantized together: their distributions differ, and quantization errors interact throughout the network. We introduce CanonQ, a unified quantization-aware training framework that addresses these challenges by separating source canonicalization from task-aware adaptation. Fixed rotations and energy normalization map heterogeneous tensor sources to canonical coordinates, enabling frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks to be reused across layers and models. Joint training then adapts the network to the coupled errors of weight, activation, and cache quantization within a common scalar/vector interface. We bound frozen-codebook transfer error and local task loss, and derive an exact normalization-aware straight-through Jacobian that links quantization distortion to gradient bias. The strongest gains arise under joint W2A4KV2 compression: across LLaMA3-1B/3B/8B, CanonQ-Omni achieves up to 14.28x lower WikiText-2 perplexity and up to 57.9% higher mean zero-shot accuracy than prior state-of-the-art and representative quantization baselines. The benefits extend to Qwen3-1.7B, code generation, and mathematical reasoning: on instruction-tuned MobileLLM-Pro-1B at W2A16KV16, CanonQ achieves relative improvements of 41.7% in HumanEval pass@1 and 39.1% in GSM8K exact match over the strongest evaluated quantization baseline.

AI.tldr: CanonQ is a unified quantization‑aware training framework that enables very aggressive, low‑bit compression of LLMs (including weights, activations, and KV cache) while preserving performance, by canonicalizing tensor distributions and jointly adapting to quantization errors.
AI.motivation: Pushing large language models to extreme low-bit settings (e.g., 2-bit weights, 4-bit activations, 2-bit KV cache) is crucial for deployment on resource-limited hardware, but existing methods struggle when all these components are quantized together. Their distributions differ significantly, quantization errors interact across layers, and per-layer or per-tensor codebook design becomes complex and brittle. The authors want a single, principled framework that can reuse codebooks across layers/models and explicitly account for the coupled quantization errors during training, enabling strong compression without catastrophic loss in perplexity or downstream accuracy.
AI.method: CanonQ separates the problem into (1) source canonicalization and (2) task-aware adaptation. First, fixed rotations and energy normalization transform heterogeneous tensors (weights, activations, KV caches) into a common canonical coordinate system. In this canonical space, the method uses frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks—shared across layers and models—so quantization uses a unified scalar/vector interface. Second, they perform joint quantization-aware training where the network is optimized while quantized weights, activations, and caches are all active, adapting the model to the coupled errors introduced by the common codebooks. The paper provides theory: bounds on the error from using frozen codebooks, bounds on local task loss under this quantization, and an exact normalization-aware straight-through estimator Jacobian that connects quantization distortion to gradient bias during training.
AI.result: Under very aggressive compression regimes, especially W2A4KV2 (2-bit weights, 4-bit activations, 2-bit KV cache), CanonQ-Omni significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art and strong baselines. For LLaMA3 models at 1B, 3B, and 8B scales, it yields up to 14.28x lower perplexity on WikiText-2 and up to 57.9% higher mean zero-shot accuracy compared with these baselines. The framework generalizes across architectures and tasks, also improving Qwen3-1.7B, code generation benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval), and mathematical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K). On MobileLLM-Pro-1B with W2A16KV16 compression, CanonQ achieves relative gains of 41.7% in HumanEval pass@1 and 39.1% in GSM8K exact match versus the strongest competing quantization method.
AI.conclusion: CanonQ provides a unified, theory-grounded framework for extreme low-bit quantization of LLMs by decoupling distribution canonicalization from task-specific adaptation and reusing frozen Gaussian codebooks across layers and models. This design allows effective joint quantization of weights, activations, and KV caches, substantially improving perplexity and downstream accuracy over leading low-bit baselines, and demonstrating robustness across model families and tasks (including instruction following, code generation, and math reasoning).

title: SpikingVLA: Asynchronous Spiking Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: ANN-to-SNN conversion offers a practical route toward energy-efficient spiking Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by bypassing the substantial cost of training large-scale SNNs from scratch. However, existing methods often require many timesteps to maintain competitive performance, resulting in substantial inference latency for real-time VLA deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce SpikingVLA, an ANN-to-SNN conversion framework that enables accurate and low-latency spiking VLA inference. Specifically, we propose a Dendritic Integrate-and-Fire (DIF) neuron that alleviates channel-wise activation outliers through dendritic mixing and adaptive somatic firing, enabling accurate ANN-to-SNN conversion with fewer timesteps. Building on DIF neurons, we further introduce an asynchronous execution mechanism that overlaps temporal computation across VLA components, reducing synchronization overhead and latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpikingVLA achieves competitive navigation performance with substantially improved inference efficiency. Compared with existing spiking VLA methods, SpikingVLA improves SR and SPL by 11.9\% and 12.6\%, respectively, while reducing first-action latency by 11.2$\times$. These results establish SpikingVLA as a practical framework for deploying pretrained VLA models with high-performance and low-latency spiking inference.

AI.tldr: Proposes SpikingVLA, an ANN-to-SNN conversion framework for vision-language-action models that achieves accurate, low-latency spiking inference using a new neuron model and asynchronous execution.
AI.motivation: Training large-scale spiking neural networks for vision-language-action tasks from scratch is computationally expensive. Existing ANN-to-SNN conversion methods mitigate this but require many timesteps to match ANN performance, leading to high latency that is problematic for real-time navigation and control. The paper aims to make spiking VLA models both energy-efficient and fast enough for practical deployment.
AI.method: Introduce SpikingVLA, an ANN-to-SNN conversion pipeline tailored to vision-language-action models. The key technical component is the Dendritic Integrate-and-Fire (DIF) neuron, which uses dendritic mixing and adaptive somatic firing to reduce channel-wise activation outliers and support accurate conversion with fewer timesteps. On top of the DIF-based architecture, the authors design an asynchronous execution mechanism that overlaps temporal computation across the vision, language, and action modules to reduce synchronization overhead and overall latency.
AI.result: On navigation benchmarks, SpikingVLA attains navigation performance comparable to or better than existing spiking VLA approaches while being more efficient. Quantitatively, it improves Success Rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) by 11.9% and 12.6%, respectively, and reduces first-action latency by a factor of 11.2× relative to prior spiking VLA methods.
AI.conclusion: SpikingVLA demonstrates that carefully designed neuron models and asynchronous execution can significantly lower the timestep requirements and latency of converted SNN-based VLA systems without sacrificing performance. This positions ANN-to-SNN conversion as a practical strategy for deploying pretrained VLA models in real-time, energy-efficient spiking implementations.

title: AGAR: a reinforcement learning substrate for LLM program evolution
summary: Given a task and an evaluator, a language model can rewrite a candidate program while a search loop decides which rewrites survive, offering a practical route to algorithm discovery. But that loop is governed by five constants set by hand: which parent to select, how hard to mutate, how to keep diversity, what to remember, and a scalar score that never says which part of the program earned it. Reinforcement learning already has an estimator for each. The obstacle is that program evolution is not usually written down as a decision process. We formalize it as a Markov decision process whose action is the modular prefix the model is conditioned on, rather than the program it emits. Credit assignment, value estimation, adaptive exploration, and experience memory can then attach to distinct components. AGAR (Algorithm Generation As RL) provides the resulting substrate: any estimator can be replaced or switched off without changing the controller, making the transfer auditable one mechanism at a time, with no gradient training of the backend model. Across 19 tasks, two backends, and three seeds under one harness, AGAR improves on the stronger of two published baselines on most tasks, with gains concentrated in the competitive-programming family. The formalization also yields a checkable reading of prior work: these systems are implicitly zero-discount, not by choice, but because fitness is exogenous to an individual rather than a return over successors, leaving a discount factor nothing to act on.

AI.tldr: This paper recasts program-evolving language-model systems as a reinforcement-learning (RL) Markov decision process, enabling principled, modular replacements for the heuristic components of current algorithm-discovery loops.
AI.motivation: Existing systems that use language models to iteratively rewrite and search over programs rely on hand-tuned heuristics: how to pick parent programs, how much to mutate them, how to encourage diversity, what to cache or remember, and how to score candidates using a single scalar signal. These choices are brittle, hard to audit, and do not exploit the extensive theory and tools of RL for credit assignment, exploration, value estimation, and replay. Moreover, the field lacks a clear decision-theoretic formalization of program evolution, limiting principled improvement and comparison of methods.
AI.method: The authors formalize the iterative program-rewriting process as a Markov decision process in which the action is not the entire generated program, but the modular prefix (conditioning context) used by the language model to produce code. This abstraction allows standard RL components—credit assignment, value function estimation, adaptive exploration, and experience replay—to attach to distinct, well-defined parts of the search process. They implement AGAR (Algorithm Generation As RL), a substrate in which each heuristic estimator in the program search loop can be cleanly swapped with RL-based alternatives without changing the main controller and without training the underlying language model with gradients. They then run systematic experiments across 19 algorithmic tasks, two language-model backends, and three random seeds, under a unified evaluation harness, comparing against two strong published baselines.
AI.result: AGAR consistently outperforms the stronger of two prior baselines on a majority of the 19 evaluated tasks, with particularly notable gains on competitive-programming-style problems. The framework successfully demonstrates that modular RL components can improve program search performance without modifying or fine-tuning the underlying language model. Additionally, the formal MDP view clarifies that many prior systems effectively correspond to zero-discount RL setups, because their fitness signals are exogenous to each candidate and not modeled as a return over future successors, leaving no meaningful role for a temporal discount factor.
AI.conclusion: By viewing language-model-driven program evolution as a Markov decision process over conditioning prefixes, the paper provides a principled RL substrate—AGAR—that replaces ad-hoc search heuristics with modular, auditable estimators. This leads to empirical performance gains on a broad suite of algorithmic tasks and supplies a unifying lens on previous work, explaining why they implicitly behave like zero-discount RL. The approach suggests a path toward more systematic, RL-grounded design of algorithm-discovery systems without requiring gradient-based training of the base language model.

title: Bridge Routing Heads: Where Multilingual Multi-hop Reasoning Lives in LLMs
summary: Multilingual LLMs answer the same multi-hop reasoning question across languages, but we lack a mechanistic account of whether they share an internal circuit. We identify Bridge Routing Heads (BRH) in two large multilingual LLMs through a three-stage pipeline. The resulting language-specific head sets exhibit near-complete mutual exclusivity across the five languages, with a mean Jaccard similarity of only 0.017 for Llama 3.1 70B and 0.057 for Qwen 2.5 72B, revealing language-idiosyncratic circuits. Ablating general BRH increases two-hop Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) by 39-89x the random-head baseline, providing direct causal evidence of their role. Amplifying these heads in a failing target-language pass rescues up to 51.7% of cross-lingual failures, with no training. The two models share this dual-circuit pattern but allocate heads differently: Llama concentrates chaining in a large general pool, while Qwen leans on larger language-specific pools. Together these results show that activation-level intervention alone can recover correct answers from cross-lingual reasoning failures.

AI.tldr: The paper uncovers how multilingual LLMs internally route multi-hop reasoning across languages by discovering and intervening on specialized attention heads called Bridge Routing Heads (BRH).
AI.motivation: Although multilingual LLMs can answer the same multi-hop reasoning questions in different languages, it is unclear whether they use a shared internal reasoning circuit or language-specific ones. Understanding this mechanistically can clarify how cross-lingual generalization works and how to fix cross-lingual failures without retraining.
AI.method: The authors apply a three-stage mechanistic interpretability pipeline to two large multilingual LLMs (Llama 3.1 70B and Qwen 2.5 72B) to identify Bridge Routing Heads involved in multi-hop reasoning. They then analyze overlap of identified heads across five languages using Jaccard similarity, perform ablation experiments to measure causal impact on Negative Log-Likelihood, and run amplification interventions by boosting activation of selected heads in failing target-language passes.
AI.result: They find that the head sets associated with each language are almost mutually exclusive, with extremely low Jaccard similarity across five languages, implying language-idiosyncratic reasoning circuits. Ablating general BRH causes two-hop NLL to increase by 39–89 times compared to random-head ablation, demonstrating strong causal importance. Amplifying these heads in failing target-language runs recovers up to 51.7% of cross-lingual failures without any additional training. They also observe a systematic architectural difference: Llama 3.1 70B relies more on a shared general pool of heads, whereas Qwen 2.5 72B uses larger language-specific pools.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs implement multi-hop reasoning via largely language-specific attention-head circuits, rather than a single shared mechanism. Specific “Bridge Routing Heads” play a central, causally important role in chaining steps of reasoning. Targeted activation-level interventions on these heads can substantially repair cross-lingual reasoning failures without model retraining, and different models distribute this circuitry between shared and language-specific pools in systematically different ways.

title: RLDISCOVER: LLM-driven co-evolution of reinforcement learning algorithms
summary: LLM-guided program evolution has enabled discoveries in mathematics and computational optimization, raising the prospect of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms that self-evolve to improve how agents learn. However, realizing this prospect faces two obstacles. Joint search over coupled algorithmic components is difficult to scale: simultaneous changes can disrupt learning, while isolated changes overlook their dependencies. Evaluating candidate algorithms also requires costly training, with fitness remaining uncertain across random seeds. We introduce RLDiscover, a framework for the self-evolution of model-free deep RL algorithms. Progressive Co-Evolution advances from targeted component edits to joint evolution, while Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation balances search breadth and evaluation fidelity through staged training and repeated evaluation. Experiments across SAC, PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites show substantial improvements in mean return, with per-family median gains of 32%-84% and a peak return ratio of approximately 363x over a near-zero baseline. These gains include transitions from failed learning to successful task completion, and improvements persist when evolution starts from stronger open-source implementations. On measured SAC locomotion runs, evaluation uses approximately one-fifteenth the estimated compute required to fully evaluate the same candidate pool. Remarkably, independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations of adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and running statistics, with selected programs transferring to unseen tasks. These findings point toward a broader role for self-evolution in AI: discovering interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn.

AI.tldr: RLDiscover is a framework where LLM-guided program evolution automatically improves deep RL algorithms by progressively co-evolving their components and using probabilistic, staged evaluation to keep compute low, yielding large performance gains that transfer to new tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-guided program evolution has shown promise in math and optimization but applying it to RL algorithms is hard: jointly searching over interacting algorithmic components is unstable and expensive, and evaluating each candidate algorithm requires costly, noisy training over multiple seeds. The authors want a scalable way for RL algorithms themselves to self-evolve into better learning procedures.
AI.method: They propose RLDiscover, a self-evolution framework for model-free deep RL. It has two main techniques: (1) Progressive Co-Evolution, which starts with targeted edits to specific algorithm components and gradually moves to joint evolution of multiple components to respect dependencies; and (2) Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation, which uses staged, partial training and repeated evaluations across seeds to estimate candidate quality while limiting compute, adaptively trading off search breadth vs. evaluation fidelity. They run automated searches starting from standard RL algorithms like SAC, PPO, and DQN as well as stronger open-source baselines.
AI.result: On four benchmark suites, the evolved algorithms achieve substantial improvements in mean return, with median gains per algorithm family of 32%–84%, and in some cases a peak return ratio of ~363x compared to a near-zero baseline (turning failed learning into successful task completion). These improvements remain even when starting from strong open-source implementations. For SAC locomotion tasks, the evaluation scheme uses about 1/15 of the compute that would be needed to fully train and evaluate all candidates. Independent runs converge on similar, interpretable design motifs such as adaptive robust loss functions, progress-dependent value targets, and the use of running statistics, and these discovered programs transfer to unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: RLDiscover demonstrates that self-evolving, LLM-guided program search can reliably improve deep RL algorithms while keeping compute manageable, and that the evolved algorithms are interpretable and transferable. This suggests a broader future role for automated self-evolution in AI: not just tuning hyperparameters, but discovering new, human-understandable learning rules that make RL agents learn more effectively.

title: Shaer: Controlled Arabic Poetry Generation with Meter Subform and Semantic Conditioning
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. Code: https://github.com/AhmaddAbbass/Shaer ; models and datasets: https://huggingface.co/Shaer-AI
summary: Classical Arabic poetry generation requires simultaneously satisfying semantic, linguistic, and fine-grained prosodic constraints. Existing systems typically control broad poetic attributes but do not jointly model semantic intent, meter subform, and poem length. We present Shaer, a controllable Classical Arabic poetry generation framework jointly conditioned on natural-language descriptions, meter subforms, and target hemistich counts. To support this task, we construct an enriched corpus of 116,032 classical Arabic poems derived from Ashaar, containing normalized meter-subform labels and automatically generated, validated semantic descriptions. We then adapt Yehia-7B using QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning with a completion-only objective. Our evaluation combines automatic assessment of base-meter conformity, requested-subform adherence, and length control with three LLM judges, blinded human evaluation, and memorization analysis. Shaer achieves 95.17% base-meter accuracy, 91.75% poem-level meter-subform accuracy, and 83.40% exact count accuracy. Relative to its untuned foundation model, these results represent gains of 68.68, 57.77, and 38.93 percentage points, respectively; Shaer also attains the highest base-meter accuracy among all evaluated systems. Multi-LLM evaluation and a blinded human assessment of top-ranked outputs further indicate competitive semantic and literary quality. Finally, analysis of all 3,481 test generations finds no exact copies from the training corpus or paired source poems. Code, models, and datasets are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Shaer is a controllable framework for generating Classical Arabic poetry that jointly obeys semantic prompts, precise meter subforms, and target length, significantly outperforming its base model while avoiding memorization.
AI.motivation: Classical Arabic poetry generation must satisfy strict and intertwined constraints: meaning (semantic intent), language quality, and detailed prosodic structure such as specific meter subforms and poem length. Existing systems usually handle only coarse poetic attributes and fail to jointly control fine-grained meter variants and hemistich counts. There was also a lack of a large, well-annotated corpus that combines normalized meter-subform labels with semantic descriptions, limiting progress on fully controllable Arabic poetry generation and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors build an enriched corpus of 116,032 Classical Arabic poems from the Ashaar collection, adding normalized meter-subform annotations and automatically generated semantic descriptions that are then validated. They adapt the Yehia-7B language model using QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning with a completion-only objective, conditioning the model on three inputs: natural-language description (semantic intent), meter subform, and target number of hemistichs. For evaluation, they combine automatic metrics—base-meter conformity, requested subform adherence, and exact hemistich-count control—with multi-LLM judging, blinded human evaluation focusing on semantic and literary quality, and memorization checks against the training data and source poems.
AI.result: Shaer achieves 95.17% accuracy on base-meter conformity, 91.75% poem-level accuracy on the requested meter subform, and 83.40% exact match on target hemistich counts. Compared to the untuned Yehia-7B foundation model, these correspond to improvements of 68.68, 57.77, and 38.93 percentage points, respectively. Shaer attains the best base-meter accuracy among all evaluated systems. Multi-LLM and blinded human evaluations indicate that its semantic alignment and literary quality are competitive with other approaches. Memorization analysis over 3,481 test generations finds no exact copies from the training corpus or paired source poems.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that jointly conditioning on semantic descriptions, fine-grained meter subforms, and poem length enables precise, controllable generation of Classical Arabic poetry, significantly improving prosodic and structural accuracy over a strong base model while maintaining competitive semantic and literary quality. The absence of detected memorization suggests that Shaer generalizes rather than copying training data. By releasing code, models, and the enriched corpus, the work provides infrastructure for further research on controllable poetry generation and Classical Arabic NLP.

title: CM-DPO: Constraint-Margin Direct Preference Optimization for LLM Planning
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats all constraint violations equally: a $1 budget overshoot and a $1,000 overshoot induce the same training signal. It is also susceptible to length and style bias when preference pairs come from different model families. We introduce Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO), which replaces DPO's binary preference signal with a continuous margin derived from a deterministic symbolic verifier and scaled by violation severity. Hard and soft constraints are separated through a lexicographic objective, ensuring hard constraints are never traded off against preferences. To supply CM-DPO with bias-reduced training pairs, we generate preference data through procedurally generated constraint profiles (DCCG) and minimal-edit distillation from a reasoning teacher (RT-MED), within a framework we call SynPlan-R. On TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and out-of-distribution PlanBench, an 8B model fine-tuned with CM-DPO achieves 89.2% pass rate and 93.4% solve rate, matching multi-agent systems at 13x lower latency while outperforming GPT-4o on unseen Blocksworld by 9.2 points.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO), a safer and more precise preference-optimization method for constrained reasoning/planning LMs, plus a synthetic data framework (SynPlan-R) to reduce bias, achieving strong results on planning benchmarks at low latency.
AI.motivation: Standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has two main issues for constrained planning and reasoning: (1) it treats all constraint violations the same, so small and large violations produce identical learning signals, which is ill-suited when some violations (e.g., large budget overshoot) are far worse; (2) it is prone to length and style biases when preference pairs are collected from different model families, which distorts learning. There is also a need to strictly enforce hard constraints (safety, feasibility) without trading them off against soft preferences, and to train efficient models that can match or beat large multi-agent or proprietary systems on planning tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO), which generalizes DPO by replacing the binary win/lose signal with a continuous margin. This margin is computed by a deterministic symbolic verifier that evaluates constraint satisfaction and scales the signal based on the severity of constraint violations. They separate hard and soft constraints using a lexicographic objective: hard constraints must be satisfied first and are never traded against preferences (soft goals). To reduce bias in preference pairs, they propose SynPlan-R, a synthetic data framework combining: (1) DCCG (procedurally generated constraint profiles) to generate diverse, structured constraint scenarios; and (2) RT-MED (Reasoning Teacher Minimal-Edit Distillation), where a strong reasoning teacher’s outputs are minimally edited to produce preferred/non-preferred pairs with reduced length/style artifacts. They fine-tune an 8B model with CM-DPO on planning tasks using these curated pairs.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and the out-of-distribution PlanBench—the 8B CM-DPO model achieves an 89.2% pass rate and a 93.4% solve rate. It matches the performance of more complex multi-agent systems while running at 13x lower latency. On an unseen Blocksworld domain, the model outperforms GPT-4o by 9.2 percentage points, indicating strong generalization to new planning environments.
AI.conclusion: CM-DPO provides a more nuanced and constraint-aware preference optimization scheme by encoding violation severity via continuous margins and strictly separating hard from soft constraints. Coupled with the SynPlan-R data generation framework (DCCG + RT-MED), it yields an 8B model that achieves high pass and solve rates on multiple planning benchmarks, with strong out-of-distribution performance and significantly lower latency than multi-agent or large proprietary systems. This suggests that careful design of constraint-aware objectives and debiased preference data can make mid-sized models highly competitive for structured planning tasks.

title: Decoupling Logic from Persona: Structural Immunity of Edge LLM Agents to Context Pollution
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures. Experiment code, scoring rubric, pollution fixtures, adapters and run logs are released (see Appendix G)
summary: Small language-model agents on edge devices must hold a persona and reason correctly at once, inside one context window that fills with conversational history and persona instructions. We study what happens to the logical part of such an agent when that history is long, misleading and persona-heavy (persona-logic interference), and present a Decoupling Architecture (AO-DA) that separates logical inference ("What") from persona expression ("How") into two inference paths on one INT4 base model with hot-swappable LoRA adapters. The logic path receives only the core turn and emits a verifiable structured state (Micro-State); the persona path renders it in character with the full history. In same-base-model ablations on an Apple M2 laptop (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-3-4B-it, 4-bit; 480 runs over 4 pollution levels x 3 arms x 2 tasks x 2 personas x 5 seeds) we find: (i) the decoupled logic path is structurally invariant to pollution: its prompt stays at 180 (Llama) or 167 (Gemma) tokens while the mixed single-pass prompt grows from 242 to 1,203, and its outputs are byte-identical across levels (40/40); (ii) the mixed single pass degrades monotonically (composite logic score 0.669 to 0.150 on Llama, 0.487 to 0.150 on Gemma), mostly by failing to emit the required structured output (80-95% of runs on Llama, 100% on Gemma at the two highest levels); (iii) with the same pollution fed into the decoupled logic path, the dedicated-adapter, dedicated-format path is still more robust than the single pass on the 8B model (failure 0-20% vs 80-95%; paired $Δ$ +0.30 to +0.50, Cliff's $δ$ 0.50-0.85, Holm-adjusted $p \le 0.03$) but not on the 4B model, where both collapse. Separation costs one extra decode on a topic's first turn (28.2 s vs 18.2 s on Llama) and buys persona hot-swapping in 1.7 ms without re-running the logic path. Code, rubric, fixtures, adapters and logs are released.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how combining persona and reasoning in a single context harms logical reliability in small LMs on edge devices, and proposes a decoupled architecture that separates logic inference from persona rendering using the same quantized base model with LoRA adapters.
AI.motivation: On-device small LMs must both reason accurately and speak in a rich persona, but they are constrained by small context windows that quickly fill with history and persona instructions. This long, persona-heavy context can interfere with the model’s ability to perform correct logical inference, especially when history is noisy or misleading. The authors want to understand and mitigate this persona-logic interference while staying within strict compute and memory limits typical for edge devices.
AI.method: They design AO-DA, a Decoupling Architecture that runs two inference paths on the same 4-bit-quantized base model augmented with hot-swappable LoRA adapters. The logic path receives only the minimal current turn, produces a structured, verifiable Micro-State, and uses a dedicated adapter and format. The persona path, using another adapter, takes this Micro-State plus the full conversational and persona history to render the final response in-character. They experimentally compare AO-DA against a standard single-pass mixed prompt (persona + history + task) using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-3-4B-it on an Apple M2 laptop, under different levels of prompt “pollution” (irrelevant or misleading, persona-heavy history). They run 480 evaluations across 4 pollution levels, 3 experimental arms, 2 tasks, 2 personas, and 5 random seeds, and measure structural invariance, logic accuracy, and failure rates to emit required structured outputs, using statistical tests such as Cliff’s δ and Holm-adjusted p-values.
AI.result: (i) The decoupled logic path is structurally invariant to pollution: its prompt length is held nearly constant (≈180 tokens for Llama, ≈167 for Gemma), while the single mixed prompt grows from 242 to 1,203 tokens as pollution increases, and the logic path’s outputs remain byte-identical across all pollution levels. (ii) The single-pass mixed setup degrades monotonically in composite logic scores as pollution rises (from 0.669 to 0.150 on Llama; from 0.487 to 0.150 on Gemma), predominantly by failing to produce the required structured format (80–95% failure on Llama and 100% on Gemma at the highest pollution levels). (iii) Even when the same polluted content is fed to the logic path, AO-DA’s dedicated logic adapter/format is substantially more robust than the single pass on the 8B model (0–20% vs 80–95% failure, with paired score improvements Δ≈+0.30 to +0.50, Cliff’s δ 0.50–0.85, Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.03). On the 4B Gemma model, both approaches collapse under heavy pollution. AO-DA imposes an extra decode on the first turn of a topic (28.2 s vs 18.2 s on Llama) but enables persona hot-swapping in about 1.7 ms without recomputing logic.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling logical inference from persona rendering in small, quantized language models can significantly improve robustness to long, noisy, persona-heavy histories, at least for moderately sized models like Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. By constraining the logic path’s prompt and output structure and isolating it with dedicated adapters, AO-DA preserves logical consistency and structured output even as the conversational context becomes heavily polluted. While this benefit does not extend to a smaller 4B model under the same conditions, the architecture offers practical advantages—such as cheap persona switching—at the cost of one additional decode per topic. The work suggests that architectural separation, not just prompt engineering, is key to reliable reasoning in on-device, persona-rich conversational agents.

title: Trajectory Abstraction for the Science of Language Agent Behavior
summary: Scientific studies of language agents need behavioral variables that support hypotheses across tasks and models. We formulate this research problem as learning and testing a hierarchy of trajectory abstractions. A concrete recursive procedure first measures role- and phase-indexed events, proposes temporally constrained relations, and tests their stability across conditions. It then constructs episode-level motif variables from selected relations and repeats the analysis on those variables. Explicit measurement functions connect every abstraction level to the original trajectories. Observations and randomized protocol experiments assess the resulting hypotheses, while comparisons between intervention realizations determine whether an abstraction should be retained, refined, or restricted. We derive a finite-depth bound for accepted reductions, identify protocol effects on fixed abstractions, and characterize realization disagreement and composition of abstraction error. A finite-sample test makes projected intervention consistency operational, and constructed examples illustrate motif construction and abstraction refinement. The formulation distinguishes this experimental approach from semantic taxonomies, qualitative theory induction, and behavior-model recovery. It specifies a proposed research procedure for discovering generalizable behavioral hypotheses, with literature-relative novelty assessed separately from model-relative surprise.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a systematic, hierarchical method to define and test behavioral abstractions from language-agent trajectories, enabling stable, generalizable variables for scientific study of such agents.
AI.motivation: To do cumulative, scientific research on language agents, we need behavioral variables and constructs that are stable across tasks, models, and experimental conditions. Existing approaches either rely on ad hoc semantic labels, qualitative theorizing, or attempt to fully recover internal models, none of which provide a principled, experimentally grounded way to construct and validate reusable behavioral abstractions from raw interaction trajectories.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem as learning and testing a hierarchy of trajectory abstractions from agent interaction logs. Their recursive procedure: (1) defines role- and phase-indexed events along trajectories, (2) proposes temporally constrained relations among these events, (3) tests the stability of these relations across conditions and randomized protocols, and (4) promotes sufficiently stable relations to episode-level motif variables. These motif variables become the input for the next abstraction layer, with explicit measurement functions linking all layers back to raw trajectories. They introduce criteria and tests for when to retain, refine, or restrict abstractions based on intervention realizations, and provide a finite-depth bound on acceptable reductions, along with formal characterizations of protocol effects, realization disagreement, and composition of abstraction errors. A finite-sample statistical test is given for projected intervention consistency, and constructed examples illustrate the procedure in practice.
AI.result: The approach yields a structured framework for constructing, testing, and refining a hierarchy of behavioral abstractions (motifs) from language-agent trajectories. It delivers a finite-depth guarantee for accepted abstraction chains, formal tools to understand how experimental protocols affect fixed abstractions, and analyses of how disagreements between different realizations and compounded abstraction errors behave. The finite-sample test operationalizes when an abstraction’s projected responses to interventions are empirically consistent. Example constructions demonstrate how to build motif variables and update them when inconsistencies or protocol effects are detected.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a formal experimental methodology for discovering generalizable behavioral hypotheses about language agents via hierarchical trajectory abstractions. This distinguishes it from semantic taxonomies, qualitative theory induction, and behavior-model recovery by anchoring abstractions in explicit measurements and intervention-based tests. It offers a concrete research program where novelty is evaluated relative to existing literature and surprise relative to specific models, enabling more systematic and comparable behavioral science of language models and agents.

title: Judging in Latent Space: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Semantics-Preserving Compression
summary: Reward modeling often requires jointly representing and reasoning over multiple evaluation criteria, yet verbalizing this process token by token can incur substantial inference cost. Recent work on latent reasoning suggests that continuous states may support this computation more compactly. We introduce LatentGRM, a latent evaluation framework built on semantic chunking, compression, and reconstruction. By using the structure of rubric-guided evaluations to guide compression, LatentGRM learns compact continuous trajectories that support autonomous pairwise judgments without generating textual assessments. A separate interpreter reconstructs evaluation text from these trajectories, providing an offline view of the information retained under compression. Under matched training data and backbones, LatentGRM achieves competitive aggregate preference accuracy relative to explicit Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) judges at both 4B and 8B scales. Across four benchmark domains, LatentGRM-8B compresses evaluation trajectories by 8.9--9.2x and reduces total judge inference time by 6.1--7.0x at vote@5. Controlled rubric interventions show that criterion-dependent preference information is carried through the latent sequence. Together, these results demonstrate that continuous latent evaluation can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving competitive judgment quality.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LatentGRM, a framework that replaces explicit token-by-token rubric-based judging with compact continuous latent trajectories to cut inference cost while keeping judgment quality competitive.
AI.motivation: Traditional reward modeling and rubric-based evaluation require generating long textual reasoning for multiple criteria, which is computationally expensive at inference time. The authors are motivated by recent latent reasoning work suggesting that continuous hidden states could do this reasoning more compactly, enabling cheaper and faster evaluators that still capture rich, criterion-structured judgments.
AI.method: They build LatentGRM, which uses semantic chunking of inputs and rubric-guided evaluation steps, then trains a compressor to map these structured evaluation traces into compact continuous latent trajectories. A latent judge performs pairwise preference decisions directly in this latent space, without emitting text. Separately, an interpreter model is trained to reconstruct textual evaluations from the latent trajectories, allowing offline inspection of what information is preserved. They evaluate LatentGRM on multiple benchmark domains with 4B and 8B model backbones, comparing to standard supervised fine-tuned (SFT) rubric judges under matched training data and architecture.
AI.result: LatentGRM attains aggregate preference accuracy comparable to explicit SFT rubric judges at both 4B and 8B scales. In four benchmark domains, the 8B LatentGRM achieves about 8.9–9.2x compression of evaluation trajectories and yields 6.1–7.0x reduction in total judge inference time at a vote@5 setting. Controlled interventions on the rubric criteria indicate that criterion-specific preference signals are preserved and propagated through the latent sequence, confirming that the compressed representations still encode fine-grained evaluation information.
AI.conclusion: Continuous latent evaluation via LatentGRM can substantially cut the computational cost of reward modeling and rubric-based judging without sacrificing much in terms of judgment quality. The structure of rubric-guided evaluations provides a useful scaffold for learning compact latent trajectories that support accurate pairwise preferences, and the ability to reconstruct evaluations shows that key criterion-dependent information survives compression. This supports latent reasoning as a practical path toward scalable, efficient reward models and evaluators.

title: The Winner's Curse in LLM Self-Improvement Loops: Selection Noise, Lock-in, and Acceptance Rules
comment: 34 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables; code and saved experimental records included as ancillary files
summary: Self-improving LLM systems propose changes to themselves and keep those that score better on a small evaluation set. We treat this keep-if-better step as selection under measurement noise, model the correlated errors of the candidates in a single decision, and study empirically what happens when the evaluation set is reused. In runs where Qwen models rewrite their own instructions and every candidate is also scored on 600 held-out items, most proposals after the first are harmful, and the model gives the size of the winner's curse of a generation's best candidate. With a prior from a separate pilot, it matches the average overstatement of first-generation commits in native loops, though not setting by setting. In a pre-registered study, the final selection-set score of greedy loops exceeded held-out accuracy by 13 to 20 points with 16 selection items and by 1 to 5 points with 256. Held-out gains grew with the selection set on TREC but not on GSM8K, and the tested acceptance rules did not beat greedy acceptance over whole runs. Gains measured on the selection set also exceeded held-out gains when a current model refined a competent instruction, and in the validation scores of GEPA and MIPROv2. Scoring the starting and the current instruction on 64 items never used for selection removes the average bias of a loop's reported gain, but single estimates remain off by about 6 points. Self-improvement studies should report held-out gains with their uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how self-improving LLM loops that repeatedly "keep-if-better" on a small evaluation set systematically overestimate their true performance gains due to selection under noisy measurement, and shows how big this bias is and how to better report results.
AI.motivation: Self-improving LLM workflows increasingly let models rewrite their own instructions or components and accept a change when it scores better on a small validation set. However, repeated selection on the same small set, under noisy and correlated evaluation scores, can create an overly optimistic picture of progress (winner’s curse), but this effect is poorly quantified and often unreported. The authors want to formally model and empirically measure how much of the apparent improvement in such loops is real vs. noise, and to provide guidance for more reliable evaluation practices.
AI.method: The authors (1) conceptually frame the "keep-if-better" step in self-improvement loops as selection under measurement noise with correlated errors across candidates; (2) run empirical experiments where Qwen models rewrite their own instructions, evaluating each candidate on a small selection set as in normal loops, but also on a large held-out set (600 items) per generation; (3) use a prior derived from a pilot study to quantify the magnitude of the winner’s curse for the best candidate per generation and compare this to real self-improvement runs; (4) conduct a pre-registered study varying the size of the selection set (e.g., 16 vs 256 items), measuring the gap between selection-set scores and held-out accuracy on benchmarks such as TREC and GSM8K, and testing different acceptance rules (greedy vs alternatives); (5) examine other self-improvement settings (e.g., refining already competent instructions, GEPA, MIPROv2) and test a correction method based on scoring both the starting and current instructions on an extra small held-out set never used for selection.
AI.result: Empirically, after the first generation, most self-proposed instruction changes are actually harmful when judged by a large held-out set, even if they appear beneficial on the small selection set. The best candidate in each generation exhibits a sizeable winner’s curse: its apparent gain on the selection set overstates its true held-out gain, and a model-based prior from a pilot predicts the average overstatement for first-generation commits reasonably well. In a pre-registered experiment, loops using greedy acceptance showed selection-set scores that were 13–20 points higher than true held-out accuracy when using only 16 selection items, and still 1–5 points higher with 256 items. On TREC, actual held-out gains increased with larger selection sets, but this trend did not hold for GSM8K. Alternative acceptance rules did not outperform simple greedy acceptance over entire runs. Across several scenarios, including refining already strong instructions and in GEPA and MIPROv2 validations, improvements measured on the selection set systematically exceeded gains on held-out data. Using an additional 64-item evaluation set that is never used for selection to score both the initial and current instructions removed, on average, the bias in the reported gain, though individual run estimates still had about ±6 points error.
AI.conclusion: Self-improving LLM loops that repeatedly select "best" candidates using the same small evaluation set suffer from a substantial and systematic optimism bias: apparent gains on the selection set are often much larger than true improvements on fresh data, and many accepted changes after the first generation are actually detrimental. This is a classic winner’s curse effect amplified by reuse of a limited evaluation set. Larger selection sets reduce, but do not eliminate, the bias, and more complex acceptance rules do not clearly help. A practical mitigation is to maintain a separate small held-out set, never used for selection, and evaluate both the starting and current versions on it to debias average reported gains, while still acknowledging considerable uncertainty for individual runs. The authors recommend that self-improvement studies always report held-out performance gains along with their uncertainty estimates, rather than relying solely on selection-set improvements.

title: MIRROR: From Imitation to Internalization in LLM Personalization
summary: The demand for personalized LLMs is shifting from style imitation toward content quality. We investigate whether self-distillation can bridge this gap in existing fine-tuning paradigm. To address this limitation, we introduce MIRROR(Meta- personalization by Internalizing Reference-Revealed On-policy Reflections), a novel self-distillation framework that shifts LLM personalization from imitation toward preference internalization. First, we replace reference-token imitation with reference-revealed on-policy self-distillation, aligning the model's next-token distributions along its own generation trajectories with those of its reference-conditioned self, thereby internalizing user preferences rather than reproducing reference wording.Second, we introduce MIRROR-F, a focal plug-in that augments on-policy distributional alignment with selective supervision over informative reference tokens, thereby strengthening content generation while preserving user-specific expression. Across three personalized generation benchmarks, two model scales, and complementary reference-based and LLM-based evaluations, MIRROR and MIRROR-F achieve leading overall personalization performance and superior text quality, while exhibiting less catastrophic forgetting than SFT-based baselines on three unseen personalized generation tasks. The gains are consistent across model scales and application scenarios, translating to improved performance in LLM personalization tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MIRROR, a self-distillation framework to personalize LLMs by internalizing user preferences instead of imitating reference text, plus MIRROR-F which selectively supervises informative reference tokens to enhance content quality while preserving style, achieving better personalization, quality, and less forgetting than SFT baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized LLMs focus mainly on imitating the style or wording of user references via supervised fine-tuning, which does not fully capture or internalize users' underlying preferences and can hurt base model capabilities due to catastrophic forgetting. The authors want a personalization method that improves content quality and robust preference alignment while avoiding these drawbacks.
AI.method: They introduce MIRROR, a self-distillation framework where the model learns from its own reference-conditioned outputs ("reference-revealed on-policy self-distillation"). Instead of imitating reference tokens directly, they align the model’s next-token distributions along its own free-generation trajectories with those of a variant of itself that has access to reference information. This encourages internalization of user preferences. They also propose MIRROR-F, a focal plug-in that adds selective supervision over a subset of informative reference tokens to strengthen content generation without overwriting user-specific expression. The approach is evaluated across multiple personalized generation benchmarks, model sizes, and evaluation protocols.
AI.result: On three personalized generation benchmarks and two model scales, MIRROR and MIRROR-F achieve state-of-the-art or leading performance in personalization and text quality, outperforming supervised fine-tuning-based baselines. They also show reduced catastrophic forgetting on three unseen personalized generation tasks, with improvements consistent across different application settings and model sizes.
AI.conclusion: Self-distillation via MIRROR effectively shifts LLM personalization from shallow reference imitation to deeper internalization of user preferences, improving both personalization quality and overall text quality. The focal extension MIRROR-F further enhances content generation while maintaining user-specific style, and the approach scales well and generalizes better than traditional SFT-based personalization methods.

title: We Query, Therefore We Compute: On Oracle Computation beyond the Machine, with an Application to Agents
summary:
Agentic systems use large language models (LLMs) to carry out concrete tasks. Prior work often borrows abstractions such as scheduling, caching or isolation piecemeal from operating systems, so the mechanisms it builds share little common ground, and the shared view of the two forms of agentic system, Workflows and Agents, is limited. We construct an abstract machine that provides both.
  We treat the LLM as an Oracle and extend a two-stack pushdown automaton with one instruction, which hands the Oracle a whole stack as its query and appends the answer to that same stack. The machine thus performs two computations, the Oracle's and a Turing-complete one that we call the Priestess. A stack that the program only appends to grows autoregressively, as an agent's context does. Two symmetry breakings, S in storage and T in transitions, make a Priestess program the operating system of the programs the Oracle runs, and produce the Agent and the Workflow as the two placements of a task's program.
  For internally autoregressive Oracles, the two computations synchronize at the end of every answer under certain conditions, and through that synchronization we model caching and analyse scheduling. No guarantee that holds for every Oracle can fix which content crosses between the two computations, but such a guarantee does fix the boundary itself.
  The construction V fits the machine to a von Neumann computer. To show that it is realizable, we propose ArchNights, an extended RISC-V ISA and a Linux-style operating system implementing the machine by design. ArchNights-SE runs on gem5 as a computer system, becomes an agentic system when it runs an LLM as the Oracle, and will be open source.
  Agentic systems can then be designed as computer systems are. With a foundation built and a unified view, future work can share invariants and bounds, each with its conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a unified, OS-like abstract machine for LLM-based agentic systems (Agents and Workflows), treating the LLM as an oracle and the surrounding logic as a Turing-complete controller, and shows how to realize it on real hardware/OS (ArchNights).
AI.motivation: Current agentic systems using LLMs (Agents, Workflows) borrow concepts like scheduling, caching, and isolation from operating systems in an ad hoc, piecemeal way. There is no common formal foundation to describe both styles uniformly or to reason about system-level properties such as scheduling, caching, boundaries between the LLM and its controller, and correctness. The authors aim to provide a rigorous abstract machine that captures both forms, enabling principled design and analysis like in traditional computer systems.
AI.method: The authors construct an abstract machine by extending a two-stack pushdown automaton with a single new instruction that queries an Oracle (the LLM) using an entire stack and appends the Oracle’s answer back to that stack. The resulting system performs two coupled computations: a Turing-complete controller, dubbed the Priestess, and the Oracle. They analyze how a write-only (append-only) stack models autoregressive growth of an agent’s context, introduce two symmetry breakings—S (in storage) and T (in transitions)—to express operating-system-like control, and show how different placements of the task program correspond to Agents and Workflows. For internally autoregressive Oracles, they characterize when the two computations synchronize at oracle-response boundaries and use this to model caching and scheduling. Finally, they provide a construction V that maps the abstract machine to a von Neumann architecture, and propose ArchNights: an extended RISC-V ISA and Linux-style OS that implement the machine, validated via an ArchNights-SE system running on gem5 with an LLM as the Oracle.
AI.result: They obtain a formal abstract machine where an LLM is an Oracle and the surrounding Priestess controller is Turing-complete, together capturing both Agent and Workflow paradigms via different program placements. They show that under certain conditions on autoregressive Oracles, the Priestess and Oracle computations synchronize at each answer boundary, enabling formal modeling of caching and scheduling within the framework. They identify that no Oracle-agnostic guarantee can control the detailed content flow between the two computations, but such guarantees can rigorously define the boundary between them. They provide a concrete mapping (construction V) to von Neumann hardware and a designed system, ArchNights, including an extended RISC-V ISA and OS that realize the model. ArchNights-SE runs under gem5 and can function as an agentic system when coupled with an LLM Oracle, with plans to release it as open source.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a unified, OS-inspired theoretical and practical foundation for LLM-based agentic systems, showing that Agents and Workflows are two instantiations of the same underlying abstract machine. By treating the LLM as an Oracle controlled by a Turing-complete Priestess program, and by grounding this in a realizable hardware/OS stack (ArchNights), the paper enables agentic systems to be designed, reasoned about, and engineered with the same rigor as traditional computer systems, supporting shared invariants, bounds, and analyses across future work.

title: A Deafening Silence: Catastrophic Forgetting Lives in the Output Embeddings of Tokens the Data Never Speaks
summary: Continual pre-training and fine-tuning in Large Language Models (LLMs) inevitably induce catastrophic forgetting, typically mitigated by replay using often-inaccessible original data. In this data-free regime, we analyze where forgetting occurs and why. Systematic parameter freezing across five settings up to 1.4B reveals that forgetting concentrates selectively in the output embeddings of tokens rarely seen in the new corpus, whereas the same sqrt(v-hat) band of the body is inert and new learning resides elsewhere. This localization is governed by the vocabulary deficiency of the corpus rather than the training mode, allowing pre-retraining risk ranking from token counts alone within a fixed base model. Mechanistically, absent tokens receive persistent one-sided softmax gradients that Adam's second-moment (sqrt(v-hat)) normalization amplifies into full-sized updates. We therefore propose an intervention: raising Adam's epsilon exclusively for the output projection during training. Across eight settings spanning 160M to 12B parameters and four model families, this removes 39.4% to 67.9% of forgetting across all seven stable configurations without degrading target learning or requiring per-model tuning. The defense combines additively or better with replay (79.8% on Qwen/Korean) and rescues released-head LoRA from a 23-fold forgetting surge. Because post-hoc editing of the drifted rows recovers under 5% of forgetting, the intervention must operate during training. Our findings indicate that a single-line optimizer adjustment may serve as the primary defense against catastrophic forgetting where the corpus starves the vocabulary.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that catastrophic forgetting in continual pre-training/fine-tuning of LLMs is highly localized in output embeddings of underrepresented tokens, and shows that a simple optimizer tweak (raising Adam’s epsilon only for the output projection) substantially reduces forgetting without harming new learning.
AI.motivation: Continual pre-training and fine-tuning of LLMs often cause catastrophic forgetting of prior knowledge, and standard mitigation via data replay is impractical when original training data is inaccessible. The authors are motivated to understand precisely where and why forgetting happens in a data-free setting, and to design a simple, general, training-time intervention that can be applied without extra data, heavy computation, or per-model tuning.
AI.method: The authors run systematic parameter-freezing experiments across five continual training settings and models up to 1.4B parameters to localize where forgetting occurs. They analyze gradient and Adam optimizer statistics, focusing on output embeddings and the Adam sqrt(v-hat) term, in relation to token frequencies in the new corpus. Based on their mechanistic findings, they modify the Adam optimizer by increasing its epsilon only for the output projection layer and then evaluate this intervention across eight setups (160M–12B parameters, four model families), with and without replay, and with LoRA configurations, measuring reduction in catastrophic forgetting and impact on target-task learning.
AI.result: They find that catastrophic forgetting is concentrated in the output embeddings of tokens that are rarely or never present in the new corpus, while the corresponding band of the model body parameters remains stable, and that this behavior is driven mainly by vocabulary deficiency rather than specific training modes. They show that absent tokens accumulate one-sided softmax gradients that, after Adam’s sqrt(v-hat) normalization, lead to disproportionately large parameter updates. Their proposed intervention—raising Adam’s epsilon only on the output projection—reduces forgetting by 39.4%–67.9% across seven stable configurations without hurting target performance, combines additively or better with replay (achieving up to 79.8% forgetting reduction in a Qwen/Korean setup), and prevents a dramatic 23× forgetting increase in released-head LoRA. Post-hoc editing of drifted rows recovers less than 5% of forgetting, confirming the need for a training-time fix.
AI.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in data-free continual training of LLMs is structurally localized to the output embeddings of vocabulary-starved tokens and is exacerbated by the interaction of one-sided gradients with Adam’s second-moment normalization. Because this phenomenon is largely determined by vocabulary coverage, risk can be predicted from token counts in the new corpus for a fixed base model. A simple, training-time modification—raising Adam’s epsilon only for the output projection—acts as an effective, general, and tuning-free defense against such forgetting, works well with replay when data is available, and cannot be replaced by post-hoc parameter editing.

title: RT-Safe: Benchmarking Agent Safety in Real-Time Embodied Environment
summary: Rapid progress in AI agents has brought growing attention to agent safety, with extensive evaluation focused on digital environments. As agents move into the physical world, embodied safety becomes increasingly important: failures can cause human injury and costly hardware damage. Beyond selecting safe actions, embodied agents must also operate under real-time constraints: the physical world does not pause while an agent reasons. As pedestrians move and vehicles approach during inference, an action that appears safe at observation time may become unsafe before execution. Real-time embodied safety therefore depends on both decision quality and decision latency. We introduce RT-SAFE, a simulated urban benchmark for evaluating embodied-agent safety under real-time constraints. RT-SAFE combines navigation tasks with moving actors, environmental hazards, and traffic rules, while allowing the world to evolve throughout inference and action execution. Across eight VLMs, agents achieve high task completion yet almost never complete safely: in the hardest setting, only 0.7% of episodes finish without a safety event. More strikingly, matched static and real-time evaluations yield task completion rates of 91.3% and 94.1%, respectively, while real-time execution increases collisions by $12.3\times$. These results reveal that standard task success can mask substantial safety failures, and that decision latency itself can become a source of physical risk. Finally, we show that RT-SAFE can support offline RL training and substantially reduce collision rates while achieving strong task completion.
