AI.tldr: The paper introduces RT-SAFE, a simulated urban benchmark to evaluate the safety of embodied AI agents under real-time constraints, showing that agents can appear successful on tasks while still being highly unsafe due to decision latency, and demonstrating that offline RL on this benchmark can significantly reduce collisions.
AI.motivation: Existing safety evaluations for AI agents focus mainly on digital, static, or turn-based settings, where the environment effectively pauses while the agent reasons. As AI agents are deployed in the physical world (e.g., robots, autonomous systems), safety requires not just choosing safe actions but doing so fast enough that those actions remain safe by the time they are executed. There was a gap in benchmarks that explicitly test this interplay between decision quality and decision latency in dynamic, physically grounded scenarios. The authors aim to expose and quantify how real-time constraints can turn otherwise competent agents into unsafe ones, and to provide a platform for developing safer real-time embodied agents.
AI.method: The authors design RT-SAFE, a simulated urban environment benchmark for embodied agents. In RT-SAFE, agents perform navigation tasks in the presence of moving actors (such as pedestrians and vehicles), environmental hazards, and traffic rules, with the key feature that the environment continues to evolve during both inference and action execution. They evaluate eight vision-language model (VLM)-based agents in both a static setting (environment frozen during reasoning) and a real-time setting (environment evolving continuously), comparing task completion and safety metrics such as collisions and other safety events. They also use RT-SAFE as a platform for offline reinforcement learning, training policies based on logged trajectories to improve safety while monitoring task performance.
AI.result: Across the eight tested VLM agents, task completion remains high in both static and real-time settings (around 91–94%), but safe completion is extremely low: in the most challenging configuration, only 0.7% of episodes end without any safety event. When comparing static vs. real-time execution with matched conditions, overall task success is similar (91.3% vs. 94.1%), yet real-time execution leads to a 12.3× increase in collisions, indicating that time pressure and environmental evolution drastically worsen safety despite preserved competence on the nominal task metric. Offline RL training on RT-SAFE significantly reduces collision rates while still maintaining strong task completion, suggesting that the benchmark can support the development of safer real-time agents.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that conventional task success metrics are insufficient for assessing the safety of embodied agents, especially under real-time constraints. Decision latency—how long an agent takes to reason—can itself be a critical source of physical risk when the world changes during inference and execution. RT-SAFE fills a key evaluation gap by offering a dynamic, urban navigation benchmark where safety and latency are central. The results show that current VLM-based agents are far from safe in such settings, but that methods like offline RL can leverage RT-SAFE to improve safety without sacrificing task performance. The benchmark is positioned as a tool for the community to systematically measure, understand, and mitigate real-time embodied safety risks.

title: Training Advisors for LLM Agents from Task Outcomes
summary: Large language model agents tackle multi-step tasks by interleaving reasoning and tool calls with observations from the environment. Prior work has shown that natural-language feedback can help these agents revise their decisions during task execution. We introduce Caddie, a method for training critics to provide natural-language analysis and advice as agents work through a task. Unlike approaches that rely on step-level labels or reference critiques, Caddie learns from whether the agent ultimately succeeds after receiving the critic's feedback. We optimize the critic through reinforcement learning while keeping the base model frozen. Trained on multi-hop question answering with a single base model, our Qwen3-4B critic improves success rates across four base models of different scales and architectures, including three not used during critic training. On the MuSiQue benchmark, the trained critic improves Qwen3-4B's success rate by more than 25 percentage points, surpassing the performance of Kimi K3 without a critic. The same critic also yields gains on out-of-domain interactive benchmarks, including $τ^3$ and DeepDive, with no additional training. Our results show that agents can decide when to seek help from a critic at inference time and that outcome-based critic training can produce guidance that transfers across base models and task domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Caddie, a reinforcement-learned natural-language critic that gives feedback to tool-using LLM agents, improving their success on multi-step tasks without needing step-level labels.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents benefit from natural-language feedback, but training such critics usually requires costly step-level supervision or reference critiques and often fails to generalize across models and tasks. The authors want a scalable way to train a critic that can help many different agents and tasks using only outcome signals (success/failure).
AI.method: They introduce Caddie, a critic model trained via reinforcement learning while keeping the underlying agent (base model) frozen. During multi-step, tool-using reasoning (e.g., multi-hop QA), the critic observes the agent’s intermediate work and provides natural-language analysis and advice. The training signal is whether the agent ultimately succeeds after incorporating the critic's feedback, not explicit step-level labels. The critic is instantiated as a Qwen3-4B model and trained on multi-hop QA, and agents are allowed to decide at inference time when to consult the critic.
AI.result: A single Qwen3-4B-based critic, trained on multi-hop QA with outcome-based RL, significantly improves task success for four different base models of varying size and architecture, including three never seen in critic training. On the MuSiQue benchmark, the critic boosts Qwen3-4B’s success by over 25 percentage points, exceeding Kimi K3’s performance without a critic. The same critic also improves results on out-of-domain interactive benchmarks (τ^3 and DeepDive) without extra training.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-based RL can train a natural-language critic that generalizes across base models and domains, enabling agents to selectively query the critic at inference time and substantially improve performance on complex, multi-step tasks. This suggests a scalable path to reusable, language-based guidance modules for LLM agents without expensive fine-grained supervision.

title: The AI Evaluation Ecosystem
summary: AI evaluation shapes the decisions of model providers, users, funders, and regulators. We argue that designing valid benchmarks requires contextualizing design choices in the dynamics of this ecosystem of actors. We develop a simulation architecture that combines rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors, building on advances in Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM). We model benchmarks, consumer needs, and provider capabilities as vectors over a six-dimensional capability space (reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, agentic), with structural information partitions across actors. As a case study, we apply this stylized simulation to explore benchmark holdout design. We find that moving from public benchmarks to private holdout benchmarks shrinks the gap between benchmark scores and user satisfaction on most benchmarks but widens it on a few, depending on where holdout weights shift scoring credit. We stress-test our findings at both the instrument and case-study level, drawing on the V&V framework of Sargent (2013) and GABM-specific evidence criteria. Beyond holdout design, our simulation is a hypothesis-generating sandbox for studying how evaluator and policy choices, in turn, reshape the ecosystem.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a generative agent-based simulation to study how AI evaluation benchmarks influence behavior of model providers, users, funders, and regulators, with a focus on public vs private holdout benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current AI benchmarks strongly influence decisions in the AI ecosystem but are often treated as static, context-free metrics. The authors believe benchmark design choices should be understood within a broader strategic ecosystem of actors (providers, users, funders, regulators), because these actors respond strategically to evaluations. There is limited tooling to explore how different evaluation and policy designs affect this ecosystem over time, especially in a way that captures both market dynamics and the strategic reasoning of AI actors.
AI.method: They build a simulation architecture using Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM). Agents (providers, consumers, evaluators, etc.) are partly rule-based and partly controlled by large language models to capture strategic reasoning. Benchmarks, user needs, and model capabilities are all represented as vectors in a six-dimensional capability space: reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, and agentic behavior. Different actors see different parts of this capability space (structural information partitions). They then instantiate a specific case study: varying benchmark holdout design (public vs private benchmarks, and how holdout weights are distributed across capabilities) and observing effects on ecosystem outcomes. They use Sargent’s V&V framework plus GABM-specific criteria to validate and verify the instrument and the particular case study.
AI.result: In the case study, shifting from fully public benchmarks to private holdout benchmarks generally makes benchmark scores more predictive of actual user satisfaction, reducing the gap between the two for most benchmark designs. However, for some benchmarks this gap actually grows, depending on how the private holdout reweights different capabilities in the scoring function. Thus, holdout design can unintentionally overemphasize or underemphasize certain capabilities relative to user needs. The simulation also demonstrates that policy and evaluation choices can substantially reshape strategic behavior in the ecosystem.
AI.conclusion: Valid benchmark design cannot be separated from the strategic and market context in which benchmarks are used. Their GABM-based simulation serves as a hypothesis-generating sandbox to explore how different evaluation schemes (like holdout design) and policy levers propagate through an AI ecosystem of interacting, strategic actors. The paper concludes that moving to private holdout benchmarks often but not always improves alignment between benchmark scores and user satisfaction, and that careful, context-aware design and stress-testing of benchmarks is essential. More broadly, they argue for using such simulations to inform benchmark and policy design, while recognizing they generate hypotheses rather than definitive predictions.

title: Itgan at NADI 2026 shared task: Parameter-Efficient Whisper Adaptation for Robust, Mixed-Dialect and Code-Switched Arabic ASR
summary: We describe the Itgan systems for the three ASR subtasks of NADI 2026, namely robust country-level ASR (1.1), mixed-dialect ASR (1.2), and Tunisian code-switched ASR (1.3). All three share one recipe, Whisper adapted with LoRA on consumer GPUs, and each was carried by a different addition to it. On 1.1, where the dialect label is given at test time, per-dialect specialists continued from a pooled adapter gave the largest gain, and the submitted system reached 57.1% country-average WER. A post-evaluation linear probe on frozen encoder features routes utterances without the label and recovers 44% of what oracle routing gives. On 1.2 the choice of base model mattered more than adapter capacity, and system combination helped only once we added a decorrelated member, reaching 46.7% WER. On 1.3 our system placed second at 14.49% WER with the lowest CER among the leading submissions, 5.38%. Its last 0.60 WER points came without further training, mostly from an exact weight-space average of independently trained runs, with ROVER voting adding the remainder. Every comparison carries a paired-bootstrap test, and we report eight directions that did not work.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Itgan ASR systems for three NADI 2026 Arabic speech recognition subtasks, all built by adapting Whisper with LoRA and augmented with task-specific strategies, achieving competitive WERs and thoroughly evaluated with paired-bootstrap tests while also documenting negative results.
AI.motivation: To develop strong, resource-efficient ASR systems for challenging Arabic settings in the NADI 2026 shared task: robust country-level ASR, mixed-dialect ASR, and Tunisian code-switched ASR, and to understand which adaptations and training strategies most effectively improve Whisper-based models under these varied conditions.
AI.method: Use a unified recipe based on Whisper adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on consumer GPUs, then add task-specific components: (1) for country-level ASR with known dialect labels, train pooled adapters followed by per-dialect specialist adapters and explore routing via a linear probe on frozen encoder features when labels are unknown; (2) for mixed-dialect ASR, systematically compare different Whisper base models, adapter capacities, and system combination strategies including decorrelated ensemble members; (3) for Tunisian code-switched ASR, train multiple independent runs and combine them via exact weight-space averaging and ROVER voting, with all comparisons validated using paired-bootstrap tests and with explicit reporting of approaches that did not work.
AI.result: For task 1.1, per-dialect specialist adapters stemming from a pooled adapter yield the largest improvements, leading to a submitted system with 57.1% country-average WER, and a post-evaluation linear probe routing mechanism can recover 44% of the oracle routing gains without dialect labels. For task 1.2, performance depends more on the choice of Whisper base model than on adapter capacity, and system combination becomes beneficial only when adding a decorrelated ensemble member, achieving 46.7% WER. For task 1.3, the system ranks second with 14.49% WER and the lowest CER (5.38%) among top submissions; an additional 0.60 absolute WER improvement is obtained without extra training via exact weight-space averaging of independently trained models plus a small further gain from ROVER voting. All comparisons are statistically tested using paired-bootstrap, and eight unsuccessful directions are identified.
AI.conclusion: Adapting Whisper with LoRA provides a strong, GPU-efficient foundation for diverse Arabic ASR tasks, but task-specific strategies are crucial: per-dialect specialists help when labels are available, careful base-model selection and decorrelated ensembles matter in mixed-dialect settings, and weight-space averaging plus ROVER can yield non-trivial gains without extra training. Rigorous paired-bootstrap evaluation and explicit reporting of negative results deepen understanding of what works and what does not for Arabic ASR in the NADI 2026 benchmarks.

title: SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models
summary: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

AI.tldr: SearchWorld is a world-model-based framework that lets UAVs perform more effective object search in complex urban environments by planning prospectively in a spatial memory space rather than reacting to past observations.
AI.motivation: Autonomous UAV object search in urban settings is difficult due to partial observability, large areas with narrow egocentric views, complex 3D obstacles, and open-world instructions requiring selection of a specific target among distractors. Existing approaches use maps or memory but remain mainly reactive and fail to explicitly anticipate future states, while typical image-generating world models are too slow and latent world models struggle to support spatial planning. The paper aims to build a world model that is both fast and explicitly spatial to enable prospective planning for UAV search.
AI.method: The authors introduce SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that tightly couples explicit top-down (BEV) spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains bird’s-eye-view exploration and obstacle maps, and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer that represents where it is promising to search. A cognition-action network consumes this spatial value prior and performs imagined rollouts to refine the UAV’s policy, avoiding the need for a separate scalar critic. Training is staged: first learning the world model, then imitating an expert, and finally refining the policy via imagination-based exploration guided by the learned spatial value maps.
AI.result: On the UAV-ON benchmark, SearchWorld achieves a success rate of 23.8%, outperforming the strongest published baseline at 19.5%, and improves oracle success to 35.5%. It also generalizes reasonably to unseen urban scenes, maintaining a 19.9% success rate, indicating robustness and transfer beyond the training environments.
AI.conclusion: By grounding imagination in explicit, bird’s-eye spatial representations and integrating them with a recurrent state-space world model, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than acting reactively on past observations. This design improves search success, oracle performance, and generalization in challenging, partially observable urban object search tasks, suggesting that spatially grounded world models are a powerful approach for real-world autonomous UAV planning.

title: EASE: Entropy-Adaptive Distribution Shaping for Evading AI-generated Text Detectors
summary: AI-generated text (AIGT) detection can be sensitive to the decoding choices of the source large language model (LLM). We observe that perturbing next-token logits or adjusting sampling temperature can reduce detection performance, providing a clear signal of detector vulnerability to decoding-time distribution changes. Building on this observation, we propose EASE (Entropy-Adaptive Distribution Shaping for Evasion), a training-free and detector-agnostic framework for evading AIGT detectors. EASE computes predictive entropy directly from the source LLM's next-token distribution and uses it to adapt both logit perturbation and sampling temperature, without detector feedback or model fine-tuning. Experiments across three source LLMs and multiple detectors demonstrate consistent reductions in detection performance, with negligible degradation in text quality and negligible inference overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that small changes in how large language models sample text (logit perturbations, temperature changes) can significantly weaken AI-generated text detectors, and proposes EASE, a simple, training-free method that adaptively modifies sampling to evade detectors with little quality or speed cost.
AI.motivation: Current AI-generated text detectors are usually evaluated under fixed decoding settings, but in practice an attacker can easily change decoding parameters (like temperature or add small noise to logits) at generation time. The authors observe that these simple changes already harm detector performance, revealing a structural vulnerability: detectors are brittle to shifts in the generation-time token distribution. This motivates a more systematic, controlled way to shape the source LLM’s output distribution so that it remains high-quality for humans while becoming harder for detectors to identify as machine-generated, all without relying on detector access or extra training.
AI.method: The paper first empirically analyzes how modifying decoding-time distributions—via next-token logit perturbations and temperature changes—affects AI-generated text detector performance. Based on these insights, it introduces EASE (Entropy-Adaptive Distribution Shaping for Evasion), a training-free, detector-agnostic framework that operates directly on the source LLM’s next-token probability distribution. At each generation step, EASE computes the predictive entropy of the next-token distribution and uses this entropy to adapt two mechanisms: (1) logit perturbation that reshapes token probabilities, and (2) temperature adjustment that controls sampling sharpness. These adaptations are driven solely by the internal uncertainty (entropy) of the source model, require no gradient updates or fine-tuning, and do not rely on any feedback from the detector. The procedure is lightweight and can be plugged into standard decoding loops as a drop-in replacement for conventional sampling.
AI.result: Across three different source LLMs and multiple AI-generated text detectors, the authors show that applying EASE consistently reduces detector performance compared with standard decoding and with naive perturbation/temperature baselines. The reductions are observed in standard metrics such as detection accuracy and related scores, indicating that detectors become significantly less reliable in distinguishing EASE-generated text from human-written text. At the same time, automatic and (where available) human-centric quality measures demonstrate negligible degradation in perceived text quality, and runtime benchmarks show that EASE adds only minimal inference overhead relative to standard sampling.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current AI-generated text detectors are systematically vulnerable to reasonable, low-cost changes in LLM decoding, and that entropy-guided distribution shaping provides an effective practical pathway for evasion. EASE demonstrates that a training-free, detector-agnostic method can substantially degrade detector performance while preserving text quality and generation efficiency. This suggests that robust AIGT detection will require methods that are less sensitive to generation-time distribution shifts, and that detection frameworks must anticipate adaptive, entropy-aware evasion strategies like EASE in real-world deployments.

title: Relevance Is Not Sufficiency: What Actually Closes the Evidence Gap in Long-Term Memory QA
summary:
LLM agents that interact with a user across many sessions accumulate histories that exceed their context window, so they store past interactions in an external memory and answer each question from a small set of retrieved records. Existing memory systems rank records by lexical or embedding relevance, yet the top-ranked memories can each be relevant while jointly omitting a complementary fact that the answer requires, especially for multi-session and temporal questions.
  Drawing on the distinction between relevance and sufficiency in legal evidence scholarship, we recast memory retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set.
  To operationalize this view, we introduce a blinded LLM judgment over the retrieved set, together with Gold Hit and Turn Hit as evidence-coverage proxies. We then propose Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR), which builds sufficient sets over a fixed flat memory store in two stages. Specifically, we first apply Formal Concept Analysis for Memory Selection (FCA-MS) to decompose the question into information requirements and select a compact candidate subset that jointly covers them. Then, we repeatedly acquire unseen records through deeper text search or complementary entity and session views, stopping when the budget is exhausted.
  Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that BFR outperforms same-store adaptations of recent agent-memory systems in both answer quality and evidence coverage. Specifically, on LongMemEval-S it raises judged accuracy from 72.4% to 82.2% and Turn Hit to 91.4%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new memory retrieval framework for long-lived LLM agents that constructs a minimally sufficient set of memories instead of just the most relevant individual records, significantly improving answer quality and evidence coverage on long-context benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents that interact over many sessions quickly accumulate conversation histories that exceed their context window. To cope, systems use external memory and retrieve a few top-ranked records per query, based on lexical or embedding similarity. However, this "top-k relevance" paradigm fails when each retrieved memory is individually relevant but, as a set, they miss complementary information needed to answer complex, multi-session, or temporal questions. The authors are motivated by this gap: existing retrieval doesn’t reason about sufficiency of the memory set, which leads to missing evidence and degraded performance, especially in realistic long-term interaction scenarios.
AI.method: The authors reframe memory retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set, inspired by the legal distinction between relevance and sufficiency of evidence. They introduce a blinded LLM judge that evaluates whether a retrieved set is sufficient, and propose Gold Hit and Turn Hit as metrics that proxy evidence coverage. Their main algorithm, Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR), operates over a fixed flat memory store in two stages: (1) Formal Concept Analysis for Memory Selection (FCA-MS) decomposes the query into information requirements (concepts) and selects a compact candidate subset of records that jointly cover these requirements; (2) an iterative expansion phase acquires additional, previously unseen records via deeper text search and alternate memory views (e.g., entity-based, session-based), adding them until a retrieval budget is reached, aiming to make the final set collectively sufficient rather than just individually relevant.
AI.result: On two benchmarks for long-term and multi-session memory—LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S—the proposed BFR method is compared against recent agent-memory systems adapted to the same underlying memory store. BFR consistently improves both answer quality and how well the retrieved evidence covers ground-truth support. On LongMemEval-S in particular, BFR increases judged answer accuracy from 72.4% to 82.2% and boosts Turn Hit (their evidence coverage metric) to 91.4%, demonstrating that modeling sufficiency at the set level leads to more complete retrieval and better downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that long-lived LLM agents require memory retrieval mechanisms that reason about sufficiency of evidence, not just per-record relevance. By formalizing retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set and instantiating this with the BFR framework—combining FCA-based requirement decomposition with budgeted multi-view expansion—the authors achieve substantially better evidence coverage and answer accuracy on long-context benchmarks. This suggests that future agent-memory systems should incorporate set-level reasoning and coverage-aware metrics rather than relying solely on top-k similarity-based retrieval.

title: The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 8th International Conference on Cognitive Machine Intelligence (IEEE CogMI 2026). 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/obadaKraishan/anchored-minds
summary: Reasoning models allocate extra computation at inference time and present their answers as the product of deliberate thought. If this deliberation works the way dual-process accounts of human cognition suggest, longer thinking should weaken the classic decision biases that fast, intuitive judgment produces. Using 30 vignettes covering six biases (anchoring, framing, loss aversion, escalation of commitment, availability, confirmation) from an established benchmark, we run a dose-response study across four model families, pairing each reasoning model with a matched non-reasoning sibling and requesting thinking ceilings of 0, 1,024, 4,096, and 8,192 tokens, for 12,350 API calls. Because a requested ceiling is not the same as realized deliberation, we use the reasoning tokens each call consumed as the dose. First, reasoning models are not less biased than their siblings; the point estimate leans the other way in every family, but the item-level pooled contrast is not reliable (Delta = +0.031, t(29) = 1.45, p = .157). Second, bias magnitude does not reliably fall as realized deliberation grows: no slope is significantly negative, and where anything moves it is the signed score drifting further from the human direction. Third, anchoring is the only bias in the human direction (d = 1.89). Four of the other five lean the opposite way in all seven models; with five items per bias, that reversal is reliable for framing and directional for escalation of commitment, confirmation, and loss aversion, while availability is absent. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor before answering lowered anchoring on all five anchoring items, which no amount of additional thinking did, although the effect does not reach significance (p = .057). The results argue against treating test-time reasoning as a rationality guarantee and for auditing deployed models bias by bias.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLM ‘reasoning modes’ and longer test-time thinking reduce classic decision biases, and finds they generally do not.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-augmented LLMs are marketed as more reliable and less biased because they ‘think step by step.’ Psychological dual-process theories would predict that slower, more deliberate cognition should attenuate intuitive decision biases. The authors want to empirically test whether giving LLMs more inference-time computation and explicit reasoning actually makes their decisions more human-rational and less biased.
AI.method: Using 30 classic vignette items spanning six well-known cognitive biases (anchoring, framing, loss aversion, escalation of commitment, availability, confirmation), the authors compare four reasoning-oriented model families to closely matched non-reasoning siblings. They perform a dose–response study by varying the maximum allowed ‘thinking tokens’ (0, 1,024, 4,096, 8,192) across 12,350 API calls, then using the realized number of reasoning tokens consumed as the dose. They analyze bias magnitudes, how these change with increased deliberation, and the direction of model biases relative to human benchmarks. They also test a simple debiasing prompt for anchoring (restating the anchor).
AI.result: 1) Across model families, reasoning variants are not less biased than their non-reasoning siblings; if anything, the average effect slightly increases bias (Δ ≈ +0.031), but not significantly. 2) Increasing realized deliberation (more reasoning tokens) does not reliably reduce bias; no bias–dose slope is significantly negative, and some trends move away from human-like responses. 3) Only anchoring appears in the human direction (large effect, d ≈ 1.89). For four other biases, most models show effects opposite to human bias directions; framing and some others show reliable reversals, and availability bias is essentially absent. 4) A minimal prompt intervention—asking the model to restate the anchor—reduces anchoring across items more effectively than extra thinking, though the effect is marginally non-significant (p ≈ .057).
AI.conclusion: Inference-time ‘reasoning’ in LLMs should not be assumed to function like human System 2 or to guarantee more rational or less biased decisions. Simply allowing more tokens of chain-of-thought does not systematically reduce classic decision biases and can shift model behavior away from human patterns. Targeted, bias-specific interventions (e.g., explicit instructions) may be more effective than generic encouragement to think longer. Deployed models should be audited for each bias separately rather than trusted on the basis of having a reasoning mode.

title: TopoGraphRAG-Bench: Evaluating Multimodal GraphRAG on Layout-Grounded Evidence Reasoning
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Real-world documents distribute evidence across text, tables, figures, and captions within complex page layouts. Answering complex questions over such documents therefore requires more than retrieving relevant passages: systems must recover the evidence topology that connects heterogeneous evidence units. Existing GraphRAG evaluations remain largely text-centered, while multimodal document RAG benchmarks assess cross-modal retrieval and generation without directly evaluating recovery of the intended evidence topology. We introduce TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH, a layout-grounded benchmark for multimodal evidence reasoning in GraphRAG, comprising 2,024 questions over 201 long, visually rich documents. Questions are constructed bottom-up from text, figure, and table evidence units under three controlled topologies: single-hop retrieval, bridge-chain reasoning, and multi-source synthesis. To ensure that questions preserve their intended structure, we apply counterfactual validation for shortcut resistance, modality necessity, and evidence necessity. We evaluate text-only GraphRAG, page-level visual retrieval, and multimodal GraphRAG systems using retrieval, generation, and topology-aware reasoning metrics. Multimodal GraphRAG systems achieve the strongest overall performance, but still fail when visual-textual evidence alignment or multi-unit composition is incomplete. Text-only GraphRAG struggles when key dependencies are grounded in figures or tables, while page-level visual retrieval lacks the fine-grained structure needed for topology recovery. These findings motivate GraphRAG systems that move beyond text-derived entity relation graphs to explicitly model document layouts, cross-modal evidence alignment, and the reasoning roles of evidence units. Code and data are available at https://richardlrc.github.io/TopoGraphRAG-Bench/.

AI.tldr: TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH is a benchmark for evaluating how well GraphRAG systems recover and reason over the true evidence structure across text, tables, and figures in complex documents.
AI.motivation: Real-world documents are multimodal and laid out across pages, with evidence spread over text, tables, figures, and captions. Existing GraphRAG and multimodal RAG benchmarks mainly focus on text or cross-modal retrieval/generation quality, but they do not directly test whether systems can reconstruct the underlying evidence topology (how multiple heterogeneous evidence pieces connect to answer a question). A dedicated benchmark is needed to study and improve topology-aware multimodal reasoning.
AI.method: The authors build TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH, a layout-grounded benchmark with 2,024 questions over 201 long, visually rich documents. They decompose documents into evidence units from text, figures, and tables and design questions bottom-up to follow three controlled evidence topologies: (1) single-hop retrieval, (2) bridge-chain reasoning (multi-step dependency), and (3) multi-source synthesis (aggregating multiple evidence units). They enforce that each question truly depends on its intended structure through counterfactual validation targeting shortcut resistance, modality necessity (visual vs text), and evidence necessity. They then evaluate different systems: text-only GraphRAG, page-level visual retrieval, and multimodal GraphRAG, using metrics for retrieval, answer generation quality, and topology-aware reasoning accuracy.
AI.result: Multimodal GraphRAG systems outperform text-only GraphRAG and page-level visual retrieval overall on this benchmark, especially when evidence spans modalities. However, they still fail in cases where alignment between visual and textual evidence is imperfect or when reasoning requires composing multiple evidence units. Text-only GraphRAG underperforms when the crucial dependencies reside in figures or tables. Page-level visual retrieval misses the fine-grained structure needed to reconstruct evidence topologies, limiting its reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that current GraphRAG methods and multimodal RAG approaches are not yet sufficient for robust topology-aware multimodal reasoning. Good performance requires explicit modeling of document layout, fine-grained cross-modal evidence alignment, and different reasoning roles of evidence units rather than relying solely on text-derived entity-relation graphs or coarse page-level retrieval. TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH provides a benchmark to drive and measure progress on these challenges.

title: Cache the Encoder Within:Compact, Reusable Memory across LLM Queries
summary: Repeated queries over shared documents incur redundant encoding, while caching model states introduces persistent storage costs. Building on CoMem's intermediate-state interface, EncBank treats a pretrained LLM's lower layers as a reusable document encoder and compactly stores their outputs for an adapted upper-layer reader. A self-distilled suffix adapter is shared across storage precisions within each backbone, without quantization-specific retraining. Across five benchmark suites on three Qwen backbones spanning different sizes and full-attention and hybrid architectures, 4-bit storage keeps each reported benchmark aggregate within one score point of native-precision EncBank. In a fixed Qwen3-8B workload, it retains 28.1% of the native-precision persistent GPU store. Separate native-precision controls yield a 1.40x selected-pack prefill speedup over same-evidence, same-adapter text replay, at a 3.12-point RULER accuracy cost. A native-precision Qwen3.8-27B configuration also passes 70 of 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks. EncBank thus combines reusable computation with compact memory, while task fidelity and end-to-end benefits remain dependent on the workload, preparation costs, and reuse frequency.

AI.tldr: EncBank reuses lower-layer LLM computations as a compact, cacheable document encoder, enabling faster repeated querying with small memory overhead via quantized stored states and a shared adapter.
AI.motivation: When users repeatedly query the same documents with LLMs, the model redundantly re-encodes those documents each time, wasting computation. A naive alternative—caching full model states—demands large, persistent GPU memory, which is expensive and limits scalability. There is a need for a method that both avoids repeated encoding work and keeps persistent storage small, while preserving task accuracy across different model sizes and architectures.
AI.method: EncBank builds on CoMem’s intermediate-state interface and splits a pretrained LLM into two parts: lower layers that act as a reusable document encoder, and upper layers that serve as an adapted reader. It runs the lower layers once per document to produce intermediate representations, which are compactly stored, including in low-precision (e.g., 4-bit) formats. A single self-distilled suffix adapter is trained per backbone model and shared across storage precisions, so no quantization-specific retraining is needed. At query time, the system retrieves the stored intermediate states, feeds them into the upper layers plus adapter, and measures accuracy, memory use, and speed across multiple benchmarks and Qwen backbones of different sizes and attention architectures. It compares native-precision EncBank, low-bit EncBank, and text replay baselines.
AI.result: Using 4-bit storage for the cached encoder outputs keeps performance within about one score point of the native-precision EncBank across five benchmark suites and three Qwen backbones. In a fixed Qwen3-8B scenario, the quantized EncBank configuration uses only 28.1% of the persistent GPU memory required by native-precision storage. Relative to replaying the original texts with the same evidence and adapter, a native-precision EncBank configuration achieves a 1.40x prefill speedup but with a 3.12-point drop in RULER accuracy. A larger Qwen3.8-27B EncBank setup successfully completes 70 out of 89 tasks in Terminal-Bench 2.1, indicating strong task coverage.
AI.conclusion: EncBank provides an effective trade-off between reusing LLM computation and keeping persistent memory small by caching intermediate encoder states in low precision and using a shared suffix adapter. It demonstrates that substantial speed and memory gains are possible with modest accuracy degradation, and that performance scales to larger models and diverse benchmarks. However, its practical benefits still depend on the specific workload, the up-front cost of preparing and storing encodings, and how frequently those encodings are reused.

title: DUDA-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Multimodal Data-Driven Urban Diagnosis
summary: Urban diagnosis integrates heterogeneous observations to identify urban problems, localize affected areas, and investigate contributing factors, informing evidence-based urban planning and management. However, its reliance on labor-intensive, case-specific expert workflows limits scalability and reuse, motivating the exploration of agent-based execution. To evaluate this capability, we introduce DUDA-Bench, a hierarchical and interactive benchmark that formalizes data-driven urban diagnosis as a multi-stage agent workflow. It comprises 86 atomic and 22 workflow tasks spanning four analytical stages, grounded in multimodal data from 12 cities covering five urban problem types. Evaluations of seven backbone models and five agent systems reveal a substantial gap between isolated analytical competence and end-to-end diagnosis, with system benefits varying across backbones. Trajectory analysis shows that unresolved evidence gaps propagate across stages, while successful recovery involves revising assumptions and actions using feedback. These findings highlight limitations in coordinating analytical capabilities across stages, particularly adaptive planning, evidence integration, and verification. More broadly, DUDA-Bench provides a framework for translating expert analytical workflows into hierarchical agent tasks and process-aware evaluation, supporting systematic assessment of end-to-end analytical capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DUDA-Bench, a benchmark that models urban diagnosis as a multi-stage agent workflow to evaluate and improve AI agents’ ability to perform end-to-end, evidence-based urban analysis.
AI.motivation: Urban diagnosis currently depends on labor-intensive, expert-designed workflows that are case-specific and hard to scale or reuse. With the rise of AI agents, there is a need to systematically evaluate whether they can replace or assist experts in performing complex, multi-step, data-driven urban diagnosis tasks across cities and problem types.
AI.method: The authors formalize data-driven urban diagnosis as a hierarchical, multi-stage agent workflow and build DUDA-Bench, comprising 86 atomic tasks and 22 full workflow tasks. The benchmark spans four analytical stages and uses multimodal data from 12 cities and five types of urban problems. They then evaluate seven backbone language/vision models and five different agent systems on these tasks and analyze performance trajectories across stages.
AI.result: Experiments show a large gap between models’ performance on isolated analytical subtasks and their performance on full end-to-end diagnosis workflows. Agent-based systems provide varying benefits depending on the backbone model. Trajectory analysis reveals that missing or unresolved evidence in early stages tends to propagate and harm later stages, whereas successful systems are able to recover by revising assumptions and actions based on feedback.
AI.conclusion: The study finds that current agent systems struggle to coordinate analytical capabilities across multiple stages, particularly in adaptive planning, evidence integration, and verification. DUDA-Bench offers a generalizable framework for translating expert urban diagnosis workflows into hierarchical agent tasks and for process-aware evaluation, enabling more systematic assessment and future improvement of end-to-end analytical AI agents.

title: ExperienceIndex: Artifact-Grounded Memory
summary: Knowledge-intensive tasks require answering many questions by reasoning about a shared corpus of artifacts (e.g., court cases, or scientific literature). As humans interact with these corpora, they naturally accumulate experiential knowledge about artifacts, enabling them to quickly identify the complete set of relevant artifacts for each new task. However, existing AI agents lack appropriate memory solutions to build or reuse such artifact-grounded experience, leading to lower answer quality and higher online cost. Existing memory solutions extract and reuse information from prior task-solving traces, but they primarily focus on user preferences, factual attributes, or abstract reasoning patterns rather than persistent artifact-specific knowledge. We introduce ExperienceIndex, a novel experience layer for AI agents that captures and reuses knowledge about artifacts based on prior reasoning traces. ExperienceIndex stores two complementary forms of experience: (i) single-artifact experiences that summarize an artifact's contribution to prior tasks and (ii) artifact-pair experiences that encode structural relationships discovered during past reasoning. Integrated as lightweight middleware, ExperienceIndex uses an experience retrieval mechanism to guide agents toward the complete set of relevant artifacts for new tasks, improving both answer quality and efficiency. Across diverse corpora and agentic solutions with different search frameworks, ExperienceIndex delivers consistent gains, raising answer quality by up to 11.0 points and reducing online dollar cost by up to 50.5%. We further demonstrate two benefits: (i) cross-task generalization, where experiences accumulated from text-to-SQL tasks transfer to factoid QA tasks over the same artifact corpus, and (ii) teacher-student learning, where experiences from a stronger model enable a weaker model to reach comparable performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ExperienceIndex, a memory layer for AI agents that stores and reuses artifact-specific experiences to improve retrieval, answer quality, and efficiency on knowledge-intensive tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing AI agents repeatedly search large corpora (e.g., case law, scientific papers) from scratch for each task. Humans instead accumulate experiential knowledge about artifacts, quickly recalling which items are relevant for new problems. Current agent memory mechanisms mainly capture user preferences, factual snippets, or abstract reasoning patterns, but do not systematically store persistent, artifact-specific knowledge extracted from past reasoning traces. This gap leads to incomplete retrieval, lower answer quality, and higher online cost for knowledge-intensive tasks. The paper is motivated by the need for a memory solution that lets agents build, maintain, and reuse structured knowledge about artifacts themselves, akin to human experiential familiarity with documents or cases.
AI.method: The authors design ExperienceIndex, a middleware experience layer for agentic systems. From agents' past reasoning traces, it builds two forms of artifact-grounded experience: (1) single-artifact experiences, which summarize how a specific artifact has contributed to prior tasks, and (2) artifact-pair experiences, which capture structural or relational knowledge between artifacts discovered during reasoning (e.g., which documents tend to co-occur or support each other). At inference time, ExperienceIndex performs experience-based retrieval over this index to suggest a more complete and focused set of artifacts for the agent to consider on a new task. The system is integrated in a model-agnostic way across different search frameworks and corpora, serving as a lightweight middleware that guides upstream retrieval or selection processes without changing the core models.
AI.result: On multiple knowledge-intensive benchmarks spanning diverse corpora and agent architectures, ExperienceIndex consistently improves performance. It increases answer quality by up to 11.0 points (presumably in task-specific metrics such as accuracy or F1) and reduces online dollar cost by up to 50.5% by cutting redundant or inefficient retrieval and reasoning steps. The authors also run transfer-style experiments: (1) cross-task generalization, where experiences gained from text-to-SQL tasks over a corpus are successfully reused to improve factoid QA over the same corpus; and (2) teacher-student experiments, where experiences derived from a stronger model allow a weaker model to reach comparable performance, demonstrating the reusability and model-agnostic nature of the stored experiences.
AI.conclusion: ExperienceIndex is an effective, reusable experience layer that operationalizes artifact-specific experiential knowledge for AI agents. By storing both per-artifact summaries and inter-artifact relational experiences from past reasoning traces, it helps agents more reliably identify the full set of relevant artifacts for new tasks, yielding higher answer quality and significantly lower costs. Its benefits generalize across corpora, task formats, and model strengths, and it supports cross-task transfer and teacher-student knowledge sharing. This suggests that experience-centric, artifact-grounded memory architectures are a promising direction for scaling knowledge-intensive AI systems beyond traditional retrieval and preference-based memory approaches.

title: From Plausible Hierarchies to Useful Taxonomies: Evaluating Agentic Harnesses on Customer Feedback
summary: Taxonomies are the symbolic representations through which AI systems organize evidence, aggregate patterns, and answer questions over large document collections. Over customer feedback, the category tree decides how every record is counted and routed, which problems get seen, and which team owns them. Agentic harnesses now make it easy to generate a plausible-looking hierarchy, and such trees are checked today with generic, individually scoped checks: each name fits its description, sits under the right parent, and stays distinct from its siblings. We ask a more operational question: when is a generated hierarchy actually useful as a production taxonomy? We build six taxonomies over two proprietary feedback corpora (1,940 and 5,000 records): for each corpus, a production reference and two repeated runs of the same harness under identical inputs. All six pass every generic naming and structure check, and a deeper product-coverage check even prefers the generated trees. Yet in every generated tree at least 97.7% of leaf names merely restate an ancestor's name (13.9% and 2.9% in the references), and in one, three of every four records fall under multiple top-level categories. We introduce two families of whole-tree metrics: structural discriminators test whether a tree's shape was learned from the data or imposed by its generator; team partitionability tests whether branches split feedback into groups teams can own. Trees the generic checks rate as equally correct differ by 27 percentage points in cross-branch leakage, and only one of the two beats a random split. Surface plausibility is an insufficient measure of taxonomy quality: evaluation must measure the whole tree as well as each node.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI-generated taxonomies that look plausible at the node level can still be operationally useless, and proposes whole-tree metrics to evaluate whether a taxonomy is structurally learned from data and practically useful for organizing team ownership of feedback.
AI.motivation: Current practice in building taxonomies for organizing customer feedback and other document corpora relies on surface-level checks: ensuring category names match descriptions, fit under parents, and are distinct from siblings. With new agentic AI tools, it is easy to generate plausible hierarchies, but it is unclear when such hierarchies are actually useful in production. The authors are motivated by the gap between node-level plausibility and real-world operational value, and they want to understand and measure whether a generated taxonomy truly supports routing, counting, and team ownership of issues.
AI.method: The authors construct six taxonomies over two proprietary customer feedback datasets (one with 1,940 records and one with 5,000). For each dataset, they use a production reference taxonomy and compare it against two taxonomies generated by running the same AI harness twice with identical inputs. They subject all six taxonomies to standard generic checks (name-description fit, correct parentage, sibling distinctness) and a deeper product-coverage check. They then introduce and compute two sets of whole-tree metrics: (1) structural discriminators, which assess whether the tree structure reflects patterns in data versus being imposed by the generator, and (2) team partitionability metrics, which assess whether branches partition feedback in a way that can be cleanly owned by different teams, examining things like cross-branch leakage and overlapping categorization at high levels.
AI.result: All six taxonomies pass existing generic naming and structural checks, and the product-coverage check even favors the AI-generated taxonomies over the production references. However, analysis of the whole-tree metrics reveals severe issues in the generated taxonomies: at least 97.7% of leaf categories simply restate an ancestor’s name (compared to 13.9% and 2.9% in the reference taxonomies), and in one generated tree, 75% of records fall under multiple top-level categories, indicating poor partitioning. The newly proposed metrics show that trees rated equally correct by generic checks can differ by 27 percentage points in cross-branch leakage, and only one of the two generated trees performs better than a random split in terms of team partitionability.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that surface plausibility and standard node-level checks are inadequate for evaluating the quality of AI-generated taxonomies used in production settings. Even when a taxonomy passes all typical checks and appears well-formed, it may fail to provide meaningful structural differentiation or actionable partitions for teams. Therefore, taxonomy evaluation must incorporate whole-tree metrics that assess structural learning from data and team partitionability. Effective taxonomy quality assessment requires measuring properties of the entire hierarchy, not just local correctness at individual nodes.

title: I would rather quit NLP than read another paper like this: The rise of antithesis in NLP papers
summary: For better or worse, LLMs are by now used routinely for scientific writing.\footnote{This paper is no exception; we did use AI to assist with writing some of the sections (see Acknowledgments).} Many have noticed that recent models fill papers with unnecessary antithesis, stating over and over what the work does not do, in ways that do not contribute to its precision or quality of expression and annoy reviewers \emph{rather than impressing them}. We study the construction \emph{rather than} in ACL papers from 2019, ACL-style arXiv papers from 2026, and papers written by GPT models from the same titles and abstracts. Its rate in 2026 is seven times the 2019 rate, and higher still in the GPT papers. Two annotators, blind to the source, find almost no 2019 use \emph{annoying} and about one in ten 2026 uses; they seldom agree on which, yet about half of 2026 papers contain a use that annoys each of them. \emph{Annoying} uses present the rejected alternative less favorably than legitimate uses. Raters of preference data and open reward models favor the construction, and an instruction to be honest promotes it. We conjecture that it is a side effect of post-training on pairwise preferences, which credit a disavowal in a single response and cannot register its cost across a text.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes overuse and annoyance of the phrase “rather than” in scientific writing, especially in LLM-assisted texts, arguing it is a side effect of preference-based post-training.
AI.motivation: Large language models are widely used for scientific writing and seem to increasingly produce repetitive, defensive contrasts like “rather than …” that many reviewers find stylistically annoying and unhelpful. The authors want to empirically test whether this construction has become more frequent and more irritating, and to understand why modern models overproduce it.
AI.method: They compile three corpora: ACL 2019 papers, ACL-style arXiv papers from 2026, and papers generated by GPT models using the same titles and abstracts as the 2026 set. They measure the frequency of the construction “rather than” across these corpora. Two human annotators, blind to document source, label occurrences as “annoying” or not and characterize how the alternative is presented. They also examine preference data and open reward models to see how they score uses of this construction, and test instructions such as telling the model to be honest.
AI.result: The “rather than” construction appears seven times more often in 2026 ACL-style papers than in 2019 ACL papers, and even more frequently in GPT-generated papers. Human annotators find almost no 2019 instances annoying, but about 10% of 2026 instances are labeled annoying, with low inter-annotator agreement on which ones. Nonetheless, about half of 2026 papers contain at least one instance that each annotator finds annoying. Annoying uses tend to frame the rejected alternative less fairly than legitimate uses. Preference raters and open reward models generally favor the presence of such “rather than” disavowals, and prompting for honesty further increases their use.
AI.conclusion: The overuse and often annoying deployment of “rather than” in modern scientific and LLM-generated writing appears linked to how models are post-trained using pairwise preference optimization. These methods reward explicit disavowals and contrasts within single responses but cannot properly account for the cumulative cost of repetitive or needlessly contrastive phrasing across an entire text. The authors conjecture that this training setup unintentionally encourages formulaic, defensive stylistic patterns like frequent “rather than” statements.

title: Let the Library Speak: Self-Advertised Method Selection for Formal Proving
summary: LLM-based formal provers can retrieve relevant lemmas and prior proofs, but relevance alone does not say whether a mathematical method can be used on the current theorem. A method has prerequisites, a target, an intended action, and obligations that its use leaves to prove. Methods that look equally related to a theorem may therefore differ substantially in whether they offer a plausible next step. We formulate this as an applicability-aware method-selection problem and introduce self-advertisement: before candidates are ranked, a model generates a problem-specific proposal for each one, stating what part of the goal it targets, what action it would take, and what conditions that action requires. We organize 82 reusable methods from Putnam 2000-2014 as Method Contracts, which pair applicability descriptions with Mathlib anchors, a checked example or scaffold, and expected proof obligations. A single batched call elicits proposals across the library; vague or unsupported proposals are demoted, yielding a ranked shortlist accompanied by inspectable claims about each candidate's use. We analyze when similarity-based representations cannot distinguish methods with different applicability, how errors in applicability estimates affect shortlist quality, and what a checked scaffold guarantees under its stated assumptions. Against lexical, embedding, and embedding-plus-LLM reranking baselines, self-advertisement achieves 95.0% hit@5 on Putnam 2015-2025, compared with 84.2% for the strongest reranker. On IMO ProofBench, it achieves 91.7% compared with 88.3%. These results indicate improved coverage of annotated methods in the retrieved shortlists, particularly on Putnam.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method called self-advertisement to choose which proof methods an LLM-based theorem prover should try, by having each method describe how it would apply to the current goal and then ranking these proposals.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based formal provers can retrieve lemmas and proofs by similarity, but relevance does not guarantee that a method is actually applicable to the current theorem. Methods have precise prerequisites, targets, actions, and resulting obligations, and methods that appear similarly related by embeddings can differ drastically in whether they yield a promising next step. There is a need for an applicability-aware way to select proof methods so that theorem provers prioritize candidates that can genuinely move the proof forward.
AI.method: The authors formalize method selection as an applicability-aware problem and propose self-advertisement: for each candidate method, the model generates a goal-specific proposal that explains (i) what part of the current goal the method aims at, (ii) what action it would perform, and (iii) what preconditions are required. They encode 82 reusable Putnam (2000–2014) methods as Method Contracts, which pair natural-language applicability descriptions with concrete Mathlib anchors (checked examples or scaffolds) and expected proof obligations. Using a single batched LLM call, they elicit self-advertisement proposals for all methods, then down-rank vague or unsupported proposals to form a shortlist, along with interpretable claims about how each method would be used. They further analyze representation limits of similarity-based retrieval for distinguishing applicability, the impact of applicability-estimation errors on shortlist quality, and what guarantees a checked scaffold offers under its assumptions.
AI.result: On Putnam 2015–2025 problems, self-advertisement reaches 95.0% hit@5 for annotated methods, outperforming strong lexical, embedding, and embedding-plus-LLM reranking baselines, whose best score is 84.2%. On IMO ProofBench, self-advertisement attains 91.7% hit@5 versus 88.3% for the strongest baseline. The improvement is especially marked for Putnam problems, indicating better coverage of the relevant annotated methods in the retrieved shortlists.
AI.conclusion: Self-advertisement, combined with Method Contracts anchored in Mathlib, yields more applicability-aware method selection for LLM-based formal provers. By having each method generate a problem-specific proposal, the system can better distinguish between superficially similar but differently applicable methods, producing higher-quality, interpretable shortlists that cover the right proof techniques more reliably than similarity-based retrieval and reranking.

title: Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models Part 1.1: From Hybrid Attention to Hybrid Position
summary: The architectural design of Large Language Models (LLMs) is shifting from traditional full-attention-only models to hybrid models, which combine different attention modules to improve long-context efficiency and performance in length extrapolation and context extension. To explain why hybrid models work and how to design them better, we propose Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models. As Part 1.1 of this series, we begin with hybrids of full attention and either sliding-window attention (SWA) or gated variants of linear attention (LA), represented by GLA and GDN. We first observe a Seesaw Effect in Context Extension: LA hybrids benefit more from long-context continual pretraining, whereas SWA hybrids perform better under length extrapolation. We attribute this behavior to differences in the positional inductive biases induced by these attention mechanisms. We find that SWA hybrids suffer from a Short-Context Learning Trap, Short-Window Weariness, and Long-Window Laziness, and require extended windows to enhance performance in continual long-context pretraining. For LA hybrids, we summarize the Matthew Effect of Hybrid Position Extrapolation and propose Sliding-Window Linear Attention, achieving 16$\times$ training-free length extrapolation while maintaining 100\% accuracy on NIAH-SK1 in 64k context length.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why hybrid long-context LLM architectures (combining full attention with sliding-window or linear attention variants) work, characterizes their behaviors, and proposes an improved linear-attention-based hybrid for strong training-free length extrapolation.
AI.motivation: As LLMs move to long-context use cases, purely full-attention models become inefficient and hard to scale. Hybrid attention models have shown promise but lack a clear theoretical and empirical explanation of why different hybrids behave differently, and how to design them systematically for length extrapolation and context extension. The authors aim to build a principled understanding (“mechanics”) of such hybrids to guide better architecture design.
AI.method: The authors study hybrid architectures that combine standard full attention with either sliding-window attention (SWA) or gated linear attention variants (GLA, GDN). They empirically probe their behavior under two regimes: (1) length extrapolation (testing on much longer contexts than trained on) and (2) continual long-context pretraining (context extension). They analyze positional inductive biases of each attention mechanism and introduce new phenomena such as the Seesaw Effect, Short-Context Learning Trap, Short-Window Weariness, Long-Window Laziness, and the Matthew Effect of Hybrid Position Extrapolation. Based on these insights, they design a new attention variant, Sliding-Window Linear Attention.
AI.result: They discover a Seesaw Effect: LA-based hybrids improve more from continual long-context pretraining, while SWA-based hybrids perform better at zero-shot length extrapolation. They diagnose failure modes for SWA hybrids (short-context learning trap, short-window weariness, long-window laziness) that explain why they need larger windows during continual pretraining. For LA hybrids, they formalize a Matthew Effect of position extrapolation and propose Sliding-Window Linear Attention, which achieves up to 16× training-free length extrapolation and maintains 100% accuracy on the NIAH-SK1 benchmark at 64k context length.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid attention models exhibit distinct positional inductive biases that lead to complementary strengths: SWA hybrids favor length extrapolation while LA hybrids adapt better under long-context continual pretraining. Understanding these mechanics reveals pitfalls such as traps and weariness in SWA and a Matthew Effect in LA-based hybrids. Leveraging these insights, the proposed Sliding-Window Linear Attention provides strong, training-free long-context extrapolation, offering a more principled path to designing efficient long-context LLM architectures.

title: Efficient Reasoning with Flow Language Models
summary: Flow Language Models (FLMs) have emerged as a continuous-state alternative to discrete diffusion language models, yet the role of their continuous representations in reasoning remains unclear. We investigate this question by comparing the reasoning efficiency of FLMs and discrete diffusion models, measured by solution accuracy under matched denoising steps. Unlike discrete diffusion, which passes categorical states between denoising steps, FLMs evolve a continuous sequence representation throughout denoising and decodes it into discrete tokens only at the end. Our theoretical analysis shows, from a superposition perspective, how information retained in these continuous states can benefit reasoning. Intermediate-state interventions provide further empirical support for this theoretical account, showing that removing information about alternative candidates reduces subsequent solution recovery. Together, these findings show that FLMs allow evidence for multiple candidates to persist and inform subsequent reasoning before a discrete answer is produced. Furthermore, our experiments on maze planning and Sudoku tasks show that FLMs achieve greater reasoning efficiency in the few-step regime: FLMs achieves higher sequence accuracy than discrete diffusion baselines at matched model sizes and small denoising steps. On maze planning tasks, FLMs can also achieve comparable accuracy with smaller models. For example, on Maze15, FLM reaches the 95\% accuracy target at 64 denoising steps with 36.5\% fewer parameters than MDLM. These findings point to continuous state spaces as a promising foundation for reasoning models that require fewer refinement steps.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how Flow Language Models (FLMs), which operate in continuous state spaces, support reasoning compared to discrete diffusion language models, showing that FLMs can reason more efficiently with fewer denoising steps.
AI.motivation: While FLMs have been proposed as a continuous-state alternative to discrete diffusion language models, it is unclear how their continuous intermediate representations contribute to reasoning performance and efficiency. The authors aim to clarify whether and why continuous state spaces help with multi-step reasoning, especially under constraints on the number of refinement (denoising) steps.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze FLMs from a superposition perspective, explaining how their continuous hidden states can preserve information about multiple candidate solutions during denoising. They conduct empirical evaluations on maze planning and Sudoku reasoning tasks, comparing FLMs and discrete diffusion language models under matched model sizes and fixed (small) numbers of denoising steps. They also perform intermediate-state interventions, selectively removing information about some candidate solutions in the continuous representations to observe the impact on final solution recovery.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis indicates that continuous FLM states can maintain superposed evidence for multiple candidate solutions throughout the denoising process, which can benefit reasoning before final discrete decoding. Intervention experiments show that disrupting information about alternative candidates in intermediate continuous states reduces the model’s ability to recover correct solutions later, supporting the theory. Empirically, FLMs achieve higher sequence accuracy than discrete diffusion baselines in maze planning and Sudoku tasks in the few-step denoising regime, and on Maze15 can reach 95% accuracy at 64 steps with 36.5% fewer parameters than a discrete MDLM baseline.
AI.conclusion: Continuous-state FLMs support more efficient reasoning than discrete diffusion language models when the number of denoising steps is limited, because their continuous representations allow evidence for multiple candidate solutions to persist and shape subsequent updates before a final discrete answer is generated. This suggests that continuous state spaces are a promising direction for building reasoning models that achieve strong performance with fewer refinement steps and potentially smaller model sizes.

title: LLM4Impact: Integrating Heterogeneous Information for Scientific Impact Prediction
summary: Predicting the future impact of a newly published paper is challenging because it must be inferred from heterogeneous evidence available at publication time. Existing approaches often rely on a single source of information or combine multiple sources without accounting for their different predictive roles. In this paper, we present LLM4Impact, an evidence-aware method for scientific impact prediction that learns to represent, integrate, and calibrate heterogeneous information. LLM4Impact combines semantic, graph, LLM, and temporal representations, and injects graph information into a frozen LLM through continuous prefix tokens. A context aware gating mechanism adaptively weights different evidence, while a separate calibration module accounts for domain and temporal variation in citation scales. We further construct a large-scale benchmark dataset with 2 million papers, leakage-safe point-in-time heterogeneous ego graphs, temporal splits, and both year-level and month-level citation targets. Experiments show that LLM4Impact consistently outperforms strong semantic, graph, and LLM based baselines, with a 10.13% reduction in year RMSE on the in distribution test set and a 6.87% reduction under out-of-domain distribution. Our results reveal that the value of such evidence is context dependent: different papers benefit from different sources, while domain and publication time affect how evidence translates into citations. This finding motivates adaptive evidence selection and context-conditioned calibration rather than simply richer representations. We will release our code, benchmark, and an interactive web demonstration upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LLM4Impact, a model that predicts citation impact of new papers by integrating multiple heterogeneous evidence sources in an evidence-aware, calibrated way, outperforming strong baselines on a new 2M-paper benchmark.
AI.motivation: Predicting the future citation impact of a newly published paper is difficult because only partial, heterogeneous information is available at publication time (text content, early citation graph, timing, etc.). Existing methods typically use only one type of signal (e.g., text or graph) or combine them naively, without modeling their differing predictive roles or how their usefulness varies across domains and time. There is also a need for a realistic, large-scale benchmark with proper temporal splits and leakage-safe graphs to fairly evaluate impact prediction models.
AI.method: The authors propose LLM4Impact, an evidence-aware impact prediction framework that: (1) constructs multiple representations of each paper, including semantic (textual), graph-based, large-language-model (LLM) derived, and temporal features; (2) injects graph information into a frozen LLM via continuous prefix tokens, enabling the LLM to condition on graph context without full fine-tuning; (3) employs a context-aware gating mechanism that adaptively weights different evidence sources for each paper, allowing the model to emphasize the most relevant signals; and (4) uses a separate calibration module that adjusts predictions to account for domain-specific and temporal variation in citation scales. They also build a large-scale benchmark with 2M papers, point-in-time heterogeneous ego graphs that avoid future information leakage, temporal train/test splits, and year-level and month-level citation prediction targets.
AI.result: On the new 2M-paper benchmark, LLM4Impact consistently outperforms strong baselines based on semantics only, graphs only, and generic LLM approaches. Quantitatively, it achieves a 10.13% reduction in RMSE for yearly citation prediction on the in-distribution test set, and a 6.87% RMSE reduction under out-of-domain distribution shifts. Analysis shows that no single evidence source is universally best; instead, the benefit of semantic, graph, LLM, or temporal signals is context-dependent across individual papers, domains, and publication times.
AI.conclusion: LLM4Impact demonstrates that explicitly modeling heterogeneous evidence, with adaptive weighting and context-conditioned calibration, yields more accurate and robust scientific impact prediction than simply enriching representations. The study underscores that the predictive value of different signals varies with paper context, domain, and time, motivating systems that dynamically select and calibrate evidence. The authors plan to release their code, benchmark dataset, and an interactive web demo to facilitate future research in impact prediction and related areas.

title: RSI-Forge: From Research Papers to Environments for Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Environments are the foundation of recursive self-improvement: they provide the problems agents work on and the feedback used to evaluate progress. Yet constructing challenging research environments with reliable evaluation still depends on domain experts, limiting their scale and disciplinary coverage. We introduce RSI-Forge, a multi-agent pipeline that turns published papers into executable environments for self-improvement. Three agents coordinate construction, reproduction, and review to produce tasks with automated evaluators; each paper's method is independently reimplemented to establish a baseline score. We present 210 environments across 18 fields, including 90 reviewed by independent human domain experts. Both experts and agent judges give high ratings to the potential for improving the provided starting solutions and the evaluators' ability to distinguish solution quality, whereas experts are more critical of shortcut resistance, faithfulness to the source paper, and whether a single idea can exhaust a task. To validate their use for repeated improvement, we evaluate four models over 3 successive attempts on 120 environments, with each attempt inheriting prior code and notes while model weights remain fixed. At least one model improves after the first attempt in 84% of environments. Models also outperform the reproduced paper methods in 68 of the 120 environments, demonstrating room for gains beyond these baselines. Transcript analysis identifies work beyond parameter tuning in 95% of these successful attempts. Analysis of the resulting trajectories shows that models scoring lower on these tasks explore less, more often accept gains smaller than the reported standard error, and rely more heavily on tuning to the development set.
