RSI-Forge provides a scalable approach to constructing research environments for training and evaluating self-improving agents.

AI.tldr: The paper presents RSI-Forge, a multi-agent system that converts research papers into executable benchmark environments for studying and training recursively self-improving AI agents, demonstrating scalability across many fields and evidence that fixed-weight models can iteratively improve their own solutions.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement in AI requires rich, well-structured environments that present non-trivial research problems and provide reliable automatic feedback. Current benchmark and environment construction heavily depends on human domain experts, which limits scalability, breadth of disciplines covered, and update speed. The authors aim to automate the creation of such research environments from existing scientific literature so that self-improving agents can be evaluated and trained on realistic, diverse, and challenging tasks without continuous expert curation.
AI.method: The authors design RSI-Forge, a coordinated multi-agent pipeline that ingests published papers and turns them into executable environments with automatic evaluators. Three specialized agents handle: (1) construction of the task and evaluator based on the paper; (2) reproduction of the paper’s core method to produce a baseline implementation and performance; and (3) review and quality control of the resulting environment. Each environment includes a starting solution derived from a reimplementation of the paper’s method and an automated scoring function that measures solution quality. They then systematically apply this pipeline to create 210 environments spanning 18 research domains and collect expert and model-based evaluations of environment quality. Finally, they run four fixed-weight models through three iterative improvement attempts on a subset of 120 environments, where each attempt can build on previous code and notes, and analyze the behavioral trajectories.
AI.result: RSI-Forge successfully produces 210 executable research environments across 18 fields, with 90 of them reviewed by independent human domain experts. Both human experts and agent-based judges rate the environments highly for their potential to allow improvement over the provided baseline solutions and for the evaluators’ ability to distinguish between solution qualities. However, experts are more skeptical about aspects such as robustness to shortcuts, fidelity to the original paper, and whether the task can be substantially solved by a single key idea. In iterative improvement experiments with four models on 120 environments, at least one model improves its score after the first attempt in 84% of environments. Across environments, the models surpass the reimplemented paper baseline in 68 of 120 cases. Transcript and trajectory analyses show that in 95% of successful runs, improvements involve more than just simple hyperparameter tuning. Models that perform worse tend to explore less, accept marginal improvements within the noise range of the evaluation, and depend more heavily on tuning to the development set.
AI.conclusion: RSI-Forge demonstrates that a multi-agent pipeline can automatically transform scientific papers into scalable, executable research environments suitable for training and evaluating self-improving AI systems. The generated environments offer meaningful headroom beyond reproduced baselines, and fixed-weight models can iteratively refine their own solutions through code and strategy updates. Nonetheless, expert feedback highlights remaining challenges around shortcut resistance, faithfulness to the source work, and task exhaustibility. Overall, the framework provides a promising path toward large-scale, literature-grounded benchmarks for studying recursive self-improvement in AI.

title: InterView-C: A Synchronized Multimodal Corpus of VR Avatar-Mediated Survey Interviews
summary: We present InterView-C, a German multimodal corpus of 27 survey interviews conducted entirely in virtual reality, with both interlocutors represented by avatars. The corpus aligns spoken interaction with synchronized behavioral data, including gaze, head and body movement, facial behavior, hand and finger tracking. Its reference transcripts and linguistic annotations provide a reliable interface between this multimodal spoken interaction and predominantly text-based NLP methods. This interface is important because automatically transcribing speech can distort linguistically relevant information, while downstream models trained on existing resources may additionally face transfer challenges when applied to transcribed spoken data. InterView-C therefore provides word-timed and manually post-edited verbatim transcripts for all 54 recordings, interview-item timings, questionnaire responses and negation cue and scope annotations for 1,422 sentences, 1,398 of them doubly annotated (α=0.87 for cues; α=0.81 for scopes). We demonstrate both challenges empirically: nine open-weight ASR systems disproportionately misrecognize short closed answers and number words, while negation models trained on existing corpora show lower and highly variable performance on our transcribed interviews than a model trained on the InterView-C annotations. InterView-C thus enables linguistic analyses of spoken interaction while retaining their alignment with rich multimodal behavior.

AI.tldr: InterView-C is a German multimodal VR interview corpus that tightly aligns high-quality verbatim transcripts with rich behavioral signals to better support NLP on spoken interaction, particularly for negation.
AI.motivation: Existing spoken-language resources either lack rich multimodal alignment or rely on automatic speech recognition, which distorts linguistically relevant information (e.g., short answers, numbers) and causes transfer problems for downstream NLP models trained on text corpora. There is a need for a controlled, high-quality, multimodal corpus that preserves the properties of spoken interaction while remaining compatible with text-based NLP workflows, especially for nuanced phenomena like negation.
AI.method: The authors conducted 27 German survey interviews in virtual reality, with both participants represented by avatars, and recorded 54 audio/video tracks plus detailed behavioral data (gaze, head and body movement, facial behavior, hand and finger tracking). They created word-timed, manually post-edited verbatim transcripts, aligned them with interview-item timings and questionnaire responses, and annotated negation cues and scopes for 1,422 sentences, with double annotation for most and high inter-annotator agreement. They then benchmarked multiple open-weight ASR systems on the corpus and evaluated negation detection models trained on existing corpora versus models trained directly on InterView-C.
AI.result: The resulting InterView-C corpus offers synchronized multimodal behavioral data and high-quality linguistic annotations, including negation cue and scope labels with strong inter-annotator reliability (α=0.87 for cues, α=0.81 for scopes). Experiments show that nine open-weight ASR systems systematically misrecognize short closed-form answers and number words in this setting, and that negation models trained only on existing text-based resources exhibit lower and highly variable performance on the transcribed interview data compared with a model trained on InterView-C’s own annotations.
AI.conclusion: InterView-C provides a reliable bridge between multimodal spoken interaction and text-based NLP, enabling fine-grained linguistic and behavioral analyses without losing alignment between modalities. The empirical findings highlight that naïvely relying on off-the-shelf ASR and on negation models trained on traditional corpora is insufficient for this type of data, underscoring the value of a dedicated, carefully annotated multimodal corpus for robust modeling of phenomena like negation in spoken interviews.

title: LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys how large language models (LLMs) can be integrated as a semantic orchestration layer in UAV dispatch systems, proposing a taxonomy of dispatch paradigms and analyzing LLM roles, benefits, and open challenges.
AI.motivation: Existing UAV dispatch work mostly focuses on isolated path planning or optimization, lacking a unified, system-level view of how LLMs can coordinate between human intent, algorithmic solvers, and physical UAV control. As LLM-based interfaces and reasoning become more common, there is a need to systematically understand design patterns, capabilities, and limitations of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems, especially for safety-critical applications.
AI.method: The authors conduct a survey of the literature on UAV dispatch systems that incorporate LLMs or semantic reasoning. They define a conceptual framework where LLMs function as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer. They categorize existing work into four paradigms—pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch—and, for each, analyze decision logic, architecture, control flow, representative methods, and LLM roles (e.g., semantic parsing, planning, solver orchestration, explanation). They also synthesize implications for system properties and derive open research challenges.
AI.result: The survey yields a system-level taxonomy of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch organized around four dispatch paradigms and maps typical roles that LLMs play in these systems (semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver coordination, multi-agent reasoning, safety assessment, explanations). It articulates how different architectures impact scalability, robustness, coordination load, and verification complexity, and compiles a structured set of technical challenges such as latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility, edge deployment, privacy, and distributed consistency.
AI.conclusion: LLMs should be viewed not as isolated add-ons but as an integrated semantic orchestration layer that connects human intent, symbolic decision components, and low-level UAV control. The proposed taxonomy and analysis offer a design lens for building scalable and verifiable LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems and highlight key open problems—particularly around grounding, safety, real-time performance, and distributed operation—that must be addressed for deployment in safety-critical scenarios.

title: HySPE: Positional Encoding via Symplectic Dual Shears
summary: We introduce Hyperbolic Symplectic Positional Encoding (HySPE), grounding positional attention in non-compact symplectic transformations. While canonical Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) parameterizes the compact, elliptic branch of $\Sp(2,\R)$ via rotations, HySPE operationalizes its hyperbolic branch via a damped symmetric composition of dual shears, yielding a conformally symplectic contraction with two spectral decay rates per channel pair. To eliminate the exponential representation drift inherent to naive absolute factorizations, we diagonalize the operator in its invariant eigenbasis and introduce blockwise coordinate rebasing with adaptive centered execution. This guarantees length-independent numerical bounds while matching cached RoPE forward latency (7.21\,ms on an RTX 4090). On TinyShakespeare, HySPE-UltraLong maintains an invariant perplexity of 4.810 up to $16\times$ zero-shot extrapolation ($L=4096$), whereas RoPE degrades to 131.198. Scaled to a 51M-parameter subword Transformer on WikiText-103 ($L_{\text{train}}=512$), HySPE closely matches RoPE in-domain while robustly extrapolating to length 8192, reducing tail perplexity by 83.9\% over RoPE. While these controlled experiments establish HySPE's extrapolation robustness and numerical stability, evaluating its scaling behavior on large-scale foundation models remains an important direction for future investigation.

AI.tldr: HySPE is a new hyperbolic symplectic positional encoding that improves long-context extrapolation and numerical stability over RoPE while keeping similar speed.
AI.motivation: RoPE and related positional encodings degrade badly when extrapolating to much longer sequence lengths than those seen in training, partly due to their compact (elliptic) structure and numerical issues such as exponential drift. There is a need for positional encodings that are both theoretically grounded and robust for ultra-long contexts without sacrificing efficiency.
AI.method: Model positional attention as elements of the symplectic group Sp(2,R) and move from the usual compact rotational (elliptic) parameterization used by RoPE to a non-compact hyperbolic branch. Implement this via a damped symmetric composition of dual shears, realizing a conformally symplectic contraction with two decay rates per channel pair. To avoid exponential representation drift that arises from naive absolute factorizations, diagonalize the operator in its invariant eigenbasis and introduce blockwise coordinate rebasing with adaptive centered execution, which keeps numerical behavior bounded and efficient.
AI.result: In small- to mid-scale experiments, HySPE shows strong extrapolation performance and numerical stability. On TinyShakespeare, a HySPE-UltraLong configuration keeps perplexity nearly constant (4.810) up to 16x longer sequences than training length (L=4096), whereas RoPE’s perplexity explodes to 131.198. On a 51M-parameter Transformer trained on WikiText-103 with L_train=512, HySPE matches RoPE on in-domain lengths but extrapolates effectively to length 8192, reducing tail perplexity by 83.9% relative to RoPE, all while matching RoPE’s forward-pass latency on GPU.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic symplectic positional encoding provides a theoretically motivated and practically efficient way to achieve robust long-context extrapolation in Transformers. It outperforms RoPE on ultra-long sequences without harming in-domain performance or computational speed, and maintains numerically stable behavior. Further work is needed to validate these advantages in large-scale foundation models.

title: MIMESIS: Learning User Simulators as Training Environments for Interactive Agents
summary: Training and evaluating interactive language agents typically requires rich user interactions, yet collecting human feedback is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulated users offer a scalable alternative, but they must both resemble real user behavior and provide useful learning experiences for agents. In contrast, most agent-training frameworks rely on off-the-shelf assistant LLMs, whose helpfulness can make them overly cooperative, explicit, and behaviorally homogeneous compared with real users. We introduce MIMESIS, a purpose-built user simulator trained on human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns derived from real user interactions. Empirically, our 9B model achieves a SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing the strongest frontier model. Compared with Claude-Opus-5, the strongest baseline on RealUserSim and SimulatorArena, MIMESIS improves behavioral fidelity by 13.4 points and reduces Turing distance by 3.6 points, respectively. We then freeze the simulator and train an agent by interacting with the frozen simulator using multi-turn reinforcement learning. Across eight environments, training with MIMESIS yields better agent performance than training with GPT-5.5 under all nine unseen user simulators, demonstrating stronger generalization to new user simulators. Moreover, we propose Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation (CSD), which leverages simulator-generated private reasoning traces and subsequent utterances as feedback on how well the agent addresses user needs. A coach converts this information into concise coaching notes that describe how the agent can better anticipate user needs and adapt its behavior over the course of an interaction. CSD turns this feedback into dense, token-level supervision beyond sparse task rewards, yielding further gains across all nine evaluation user models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MIMESIS, a purpose-built user simulator for training interactive language agents, along with a new self-distillation method (CSD) that uses simulator feedback to improve agent performance and generalization.
AI.motivation: Human feedback for training interactive language agents is expensive and not scalable, and existing simulated users (assistant-style LLMs) are too cooperative, explicit, and homogeneous compared to real users. This gap limits the realism and effectiveness of agent training and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors design MIMESIS, a 9B-parameter user simulator trained on real human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 empirically derived behavioral patterns that mimic realistic user behavior. They evaluate it using metrics such as SOUL-Index, behavioral fidelity, and Turing distance, and compare it with frontier assistant models. They then freeze MIMESIS and train an agent via multi-turn reinforcement learning by interacting with the frozen simulator. Additionally, they introduce Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation (CSD), where the simulator’s private reasoning traces and utterances are processed by a coach model into concise coaching notes that provide dense token-level supervision on how to better address and anticipate user needs.
AI.result: MIMESIS, the 9B simulator, reaches a SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing the strongest frontier model and outperforming Claude-Opus-5 in behavioral fidelity (+13.4 points) and Turing distance (−3.6 points) on RealUserSim and SimulatorArena. Agents trained via multi-turn RL with MIMESIS outperform those trained with GPT-5.5 across eight environments when evaluated against nine unseen user simulators, showing better generalization. Incorporating CSD further improves performance across all nine evaluation user models.
AI.conclusion: Purpose-built, behaviorally realistic user simulators like MIMESIS provide more effective training signals than generic assistant LLMs, leading to agents that generalize better to new user behaviors. Enriching RL training with Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation, which translates simulator reasoning into dense coaching feedback, yields additional gains beyond sparse task rewards, suggesting that structured simulator feedback is a powerful complement to traditional reward-based training.

title: Beyond Outcome Rewards: Constructing and Assigning Retrieval Credit for Search Agents
summary: Search agents enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively retrieve and use information for complex multi-hop questions. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) offers a promising approach for post-training such agents, but its reliance on sparse, outcome-based supervision can make credit assignment difficult and limit learning efficiency. In this paper, we systematically investigate how intermediate supervision can improve reinforcement learning for search agents. We study a range of reward-shaping and credit-assignment strategies that provide learning signals from intermediate retrieval steps. Building on these insights, we develop a training framework that combines intermediate signals with final outcome rewards to improve learning from multi-step search trajectories. Experiments across multiple benchmarks under matched training conditions demonstrate improvements in aggregate search-agent performance and show that both the choice of intermediate signal and where its credit is assigned affect training behaviour. These findings show that reward design and credit assignment are important design dimensions for training effective search agents.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how adding intermediate supervision signals improves reinforcement learning for search agents that use LLMs, focusing on reward shaping and credit assignment along multi-step search trajectories.
AI.motivation: Search agents powered by LLMs need to perform multi-step information retrieval for complex questions. Existing RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) trains these agents mainly using sparse, final outcome-based rewards, which leads to inefficient learning and difficult credit assignment across long trajectories. There is a need to better understand and design intermediate supervision to make training more effective and sample-efficient.
AI.method: The authors systematically explore different forms of intermediate supervision for LLM-based search agents during reinforcement learning. They investigate multiple reward-shaping and credit-assignment strategies that leverage intermediate retrieval steps, and then propose a unified training framework that combines these intermediate signals with standard final outcome rewards. This framework is evaluated under matched training conditions on several benchmarks to isolate the impact of these design choices.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that the proposed framework with intermediate supervision improves overall search-agent performance compared to using only outcome-based RLVR. The results further indicate that both the type of intermediate signal used and how its credit is propagated through the trajectory significantly influence training dynamics and effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Reward design and credit assignment at intermediate steps are crucial design levers for effectively training LLM-based search agents with reinforcement learning. Incorporating well-chosen intermediate signals alongside final outcome rewards leads to more efficient learning and better performance on multi-step search tasks.

title: The Attribution Blind Spot: Layerwise Trajectory Diagnostics for Source Reliance in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
summary: A retrieval-augmented model can match a document without relying on it. Controlled knowledge conflicts make source choice observable and let us ask a second question that prediction alone cannot answer: which internal-state properties define useful intervention directions? We study paired hidden-state changes with Latent Trajectory Shift (LTS), a signed projection onto a training-fitted first principal component (PC1), and keep verified training exposure separate from behavioral source choice. Across the evaluated conflicts, state-change magnitude is often the stronger predictor, whereas signed PC1 is the stronger selective controller: equal-norm interventions change source preference while better preserving non-target behavior, and the frozen direction transfers across the tested datasets and aligned model pairs. A same-system OLMo study further combines positive choice and control results with inconclusive exposure detection at the achieved power. The central result is a separation: representations that diagnose what a model will choose need not be the representations that best control that choice.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to understand and control which knowledge source a retrieval-augmented model uses, showing that the representations that best predict its source choice are different from those that best control it.
AI.motivation: In retrieval-augmented models, the model can answer either from its internal parametric knowledge or from retrieved documents, and sometimes it ignores retrieval even when it should not. Existing work focuses on predicting the model’s behavior (which source it will choose) or on detecting whether it has seen information in training, but there is limited understanding of how to directly and selectively intervene on the model’s internal states to change its source choice without harming other behaviors.
AI.method: The authors construct controlled knowledge conflicts between a model’s internal knowledge and retrieved documents so that the model must choose a source. They then analyze and intervene on pairs of hidden states using Latent Trajectory Shift (LTS), defined as a signed projection of hidden-state changes onto a first principal component (PC1) fitted from training data. They keep training exposure verification separate from behavioral source-choice analysis, and compare two kinds of internal-state properties: the overall magnitude of state change and the signed PC1 value. They test interventions that adjust hidden states along these directions to see which better predicts and controls source choice across datasets and model pairs, including same-system experiments with OLMo.
AI.result: They find that the magnitude of the hidden-state change is generally a stronger predictor of which source the model will choose, while the signed PC1 direction is a stronger controller for selectively changing that choice. Interventions with equal norm but different sign along PC1 can flip the model’s source preference while mostly preserving non-target behavior. The PC1 direction found on one setup generalizes across several datasets and aligned model pairs. In their OLMo experiments, they replicate the choice and control effects, but fail to obtain conclusive evidence about training exposure with the available statistical power.
AI.conclusion: The paper’s main conclusion is that internal representations optimized for diagnosing or predicting a model’s source choice are not the same as those that best control or intervene on that choice. This separation implies that to steer retrieval-augmented models effectively, we should learn specialized control directions (like the PC1-based LTS) rather than relying on the features that are most predictive of behavior, and that source-choice control can generalize across settings even when exposure detection remains hard.

title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $ρ= 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper compares nine automated methods for measuring how persuasive large language models (LLMs) are and finds that these methods disagree substantially on which models are most persuasive.
AI.motivation: LLMs can be highly persuasive, which is useful in domains like education and health but risky for manipulation and misinformation. Developers and regulators therefore need reliable ways to evaluate LLM persuasiveness. Existing evaluations are fragmented: they define and test persuasion differently, and broad claims about model persuasiveness often rely on narrow, context-specific tests. Automated methods – especially those that include high-risk manipulative scenarios unsuitable for human experiments – could provide scalable, comparable assessments, but it is unclear whether different methods actually agree on which models are more persuasive and why.
AI.method: The authors collect nine previously published automated persuasion evaluation methods and adapt them to a unified experimental setup. They then apply all nine methods to the same set of fifteen LLMs. Using the resulting persuasion scores, they analyze the agreement between methods via rank correlations (e.g., Spearman’s ρ) and investigate what drives disagreements, focusing on (1) models’ varying tendencies to refuse certain tasks, especially manipulative ones, and (2) the relationship between persuasion scores and general model capability. They distinguish between rational, non-manipulative persuasion tasks and manipulative persuasion tasks.
AI.result: The nine automated methods show only weak agreement in how they rank the persuasiveness of the fifteen LLMs, with an average Spearman rank correlation of about 0.25. The authors identify two main contributors to this low agreement. First, models often refuse to perform some tasks (particularly manipulation tasks) while accepting others; this heterogeneity in refusal behavior reduces rank agreement by roughly a quarter. Second, general model capability has asymmetric effects: most rational persuasion metrics covary with capability, while most manipulation metrics do not, meaning high-capability models are not consistently more manipulative in these tests. Overall, task type (what is being asked) appears to matter more for cross-method agreement than the specific scoring rule a method uses.
AI.conclusion: Automated persuasion evaluations of LLMs are far from interchangeable: different methods produce notably different rankings of which models are most persuasive. This discrepancy stems largely from variation in task types and in models’ willingness to comply, rather than from differences in how persuasion is scored. Persuasion scores therefore conflate a model’s ability to persuade with its willingness to engage in persuasive behavior, especially for manipulative tasks. As a result, a single persuasion score is meaningful only within its specific task and setup and should not be overgeneralized as a model’s overall persuasiveness across contexts. Future evaluation frameworks should explicitly separate capability from willingness and carefully consider task design when assessing persuasive risk.

title: Cognitive Schemas, Laws and Tasks
summary:
This paper asks how explicit representations can support reusable cognitive schemas in knowledge-based problem solving. We develop a structural framework in which schemas are organized by the information and relations required for their use, rather than introduced as unrelated primitives. The framework also distinguishes context-dependent relations from more stable structures that can be reused across different representations.
  Tasks are described through the information available, the unknowns to be determined, and the constraints that admissible solutions must satisfy. This makes it possible to separate limitations of the representation from limitations of the solving procedure. In particular, we distinguish inconsistency, underdetermination, and contextual insufficiency, where the current representation lacks distinctions or relations required by the external task meaning. We also show formally when a reduction of representation preserves the task-relevant solution structure.
  The resulting task--schema interface offers a structured way to describe representational conditions relevant to problem solving. It supports the reuse and stabilization of derived knowledge while remaining independent of the particular mechanism used to generate candidate solutions. This may provide a useful component for future solver architectures that combine structured knowledge, verification, and learned proposal mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formal framework that links problem representations (“tasks”) to reusable cognitive schemas, clarifying when and how schemas can be stably reused across different representations.
AI.motivation: In knowledge-based problem solving, we want cognitive schemas that can be reused across tasks and representations, but current approaches often treat schemas as ad hoc primitives and conflate limits of representation with limits of solving procedures. The authors aim to systematically organize schemas by the information and relations they require, so that we can reason about when schemas are applicable, reusable, and robust to changes in representation.
AI.method: They construct a structural, formal framework that: (1) characterizes tasks via available information, unknowns, and admissible-solution constraints; (2) organizes schemas by the information and relations they depend on; (3) distinguishes context-dependent relations from more stable structures; (4) formally defines types of representational failure (inconsistency, underdetermination, contextual insufficiency); and (5) proves conditions under which representational reductions preserve the task’s solution structure. This yields a principled “task–schema interface.”
AI.result: The framework yields formal criteria for: (a) when a given representation is too weak, contradictory, or contextually impoverished for a task; (b) when schemas can be safely reused across different representational choices; and (c) when simplifications of a representation still preserve the solution-relevant structure. The authors demonstrate that schemas can be organized and reused based on structural requirements, independent of any specific solving algorithm.
AI.conclusion: By providing a structured task–schema interface, the paper shows how to separate representational adequacy from algorithmic performance and how to support stable, reusable schemas over changing representations. This framework can serve as a component in future problem-solving architectures that combine structured knowledge, formal verification, and learned proposal mechanisms, enabling more reliable reuse and integration of derived knowledge.

title: Nobody Truly Agrees on Sentiment: Humans, Bespoke Tools, and LLMs Struggle with Social Media Texts
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables, accepted for publication at TPDL 2026
summary: Social media is a rich source of real-time public sentiment, but widely used sentiment analysis tools are often applied without understanding their limitations. In this study, we evaluate the inter-rater reliability of three bespoke sentiment analysis tools (TextBlob, VADER, and Twitter-roBERTa-base) and three large language models (LLMs: Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B) against six human raters across 100 tweets. We measured agreement using two statistical measures: Cohen's kappa for pairwise comparisons and Fleiss' kappa for multiple raters. Even among the human raters, our results showed only fair agreement, highlighting the subjectivity of sentiment analysis. Higher agreement was observed under the binary sentiment classification (negative vs. non-negative and positive vs. non-positive) than under the three-class classification across both humans and automated tools. The Twitter-roBERTa-base model showed the strongest alignment with human ratings, outperforming both bespoke sentiment tools and LLMs, particularly in distinguishing negative versus non-negative sentiment. LLMs showed substantial agreement among themselves and moderate to substantial alignment with humans, performing better in positive vs. non-positive classifications. Our findings underscore that domain-specific fine-tuning remains crucial for reliable social media sentiment analysis, and human-centered evaluation remains essential for establishing gold-standard labels.

AI.tldr: The paper compares traditional sentiment tools and modern LLMs against human annotators on tweet sentiment, showing only fair human agreement, better performance with binary labels, and best human alignment from a domain-specific Twitter RoBERTa model.
AI.motivation: Sentiment analysis on social media is widely used, but tools are often applied as black boxes without understanding how well they agree with humans or with each other. The study aims to clarify the reliability and limitations of both classic sentiment tools and new LLMs when used for tweet sentiment classification, and to quantify how subjective sentiment labeling is even among humans.
AI.method: The authors collected 100 tweets and obtained sentiment labels from six human raters. They then applied three traditional sentiment tools (TextBlob, VADER, Twitter-roBERTa-base) and three LLMs (Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B) to the same tweets. Agreement was quantified using Cohen’s kappa for pairwise human–tool and tool–tool comparisons, and Fleiss’ kappa for multiple-rater agreement. They evaluated both a three-class scheme (negative/neutral/positive) and binary recastings (negative vs. non-negative and positive vs. non-positive).
AI.result: Human raters themselves only reached fair agreement, showing that tweet sentiment is inherently subjective. Both humans and automated tools achieved higher agreement in binary setups than in three-way classification. Among automated methods, Twitter-roBERTa-base aligned best with human judgments and was especially strong on negative vs. non-negative discrimination. LLMs agreed strongly with each other and had moderate to substantial agreement with humans, with relatively better performance on positive vs. non-positive distinctions.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that sentiment analysis, particularly on social media, is fundamentally subjective and that even humans do not provide highly consistent labels. Binary sentiment formulations yield more reliable agreement than three-class schemes. Domain-specific, fine-tuned models like Twitter-roBERTa-base currently provide the closest match to human annotations, outperforming both generic lexicon-based tools and general-purpose LLMs. Nonetheless, human-centered evaluation and gold-standard labeling remain essential, and practitioners should not treat off-the-shelf tools or LLMs as universally reliable sentiment annotators without domain adaptation and validation.

title: Ream: Unfolding Mutual Awareness in Human-Agent Workspaces
summary: As AI agents work alongside humans in shared workspaces, a mutual awareness challenge arises: agents act at speeds that outpace human monitoring, and users' evolving interests are not always expressed in chat. This challenge is especially pressing in literature review, where both parties retrieve, read, and synthesize a growing body of papers. We present Ream, a literature review workspace that supports mutual awareness through structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking, and localized visualizations. Users can see each party's activity within these documents, and agents can retrieve the same history to guide their work. In studies with eighteen researchers, participants used these traces to inspect evidence, steer agents, communicate through annotations, and reflect on their research focus. Shared histories also helped agents build on earlier work. These findings inform how engagement traces within shared documents can support transparency, personalized assistance, and coordination in human-agent knowledge work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ream, a shared literature review workspace that improves mutual awareness between human researchers and AI agents through shared histories, structured artifacts, engagement tracking, and visualizations.
AI.motivation: In collaborative literature review, AI agents can work much faster than humans and users’ evolving interests are not fully captured in chat, leading to a mutual awareness gap where neither side fully understands what the other has done or currently focuses on. This lack of transparency and coordination can hinder effective human–AI collaboration in knowledge-intensive tasks.
AI.method: The authors design and implement Ream, a literature review workspace that records and structures both human and agent activities in shared documents. Ream supports structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking (for both human and AI), and localized visualizations within documents. They run user studies with eighteen researchers, having them use Ream in literature review tasks, and qualitatively analyze how participants use activity traces to collaborate with agents and manage their research process.
AI.result: Researchers used the shared traces to inspect and verify evidence, steer AI agents’ work, communicate via annotations, and reflect on and adjust their research focus. The shared histories also enabled AI agents to build on past work more effectively. Overall, these features improved transparency and coordination in human–AI literature review workflows.
AI.conclusion: Embedding engagement traces and shared histories directly into the documents used for human–AI collaboration can significantly enhance mutual awareness, transparency, personalized assistance, and coordination in knowledge work. Systems like Ream demonstrate that structured, visible records of both human and agent activity can make AI collaborators more intelligible and more effectively steerable by human users.

title: Learning to Act with Task Progress: Distilling Small Agents from Compact Teacher Supervision
summary: Learning from large-model demonstrations offers a way to train small agents that can complete recurring tasks without calling a large model at every step. A central design choice is what to retain from teacher trajectories that contain reasoning, actions, and information about task progress. We introduce Task-Progress Distillation (TPD), an offline approach that pairs each demonstrated action with a short label describing the current task stage. The student learns these compact targets and selects actions by jointly scoring admissible stage--action pairs, which a deterministic harness executes in the environment. On ALFWorld, a 1.7B student trained with 404 demonstrations achieves 72.4\% mean unseen task success with either TPD or action-only supervision, compared with 48.3\% for a reasoning-trained student using constrained action selection. Explicit stages provide an additional benefit at 200 demonstrations, improving success from 48.0\% to 67.7\% over action-only supervision. With more demonstrations, the action-only student closes the gap, and both approaches reach 76.9\% at 808 demonstrations. Shared-history analyses link part of TPD's local advantage to better decisions when moving between subgoals, particularly from object acquisition to processing. These results show that compact supervision can train effective small task agents, while explicit task progress provides additional guidance at an intermediate demonstration budget.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Task-Progress Distillation (TPD), which augments action demonstrations from a large model with compact stage labels, enabling smaller agents to learn task progress and choose actions more effectively, especially with limited demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Using large models at inference time for every decision in interactive environments is costly and slow. There is a need for smaller agents that can reliably execute complex, multi-step tasks using only offline demonstrations from large models, and to understand which parts of the teacher trajectories (reasoning, actions, or task progress) are most valuable for distillation.
AI.method: The authors introduce Task-Progress Distillation (TPD), an offline distillation method where each teacher action is paired with a short label representing the current task stage. A student model is trained to predict over stage–action pairs, and at inference it selects actions by jointly scoring admissible stage–action options, which are then executed by a deterministic harness in the environment. They compare TPD to action-only supervision and to a baseline that distills chain-of-thought reasoning with constrained action selection, using the ALFWorld benchmark and varying the number of demonstrations.
AI.result: On ALFWorld, a 1.7B-parameter student trained with 404 demonstrations achieves 72.4% mean unseen task success using either TPD or action-only supervision, significantly outperforming a reasoning-distilled baseline at 48.3%. At a lower data regime (200 demonstrations), TPD outperforms action-only supervision (67.7% vs. 48.0%). As the number of demonstrations increases, the performance gap narrows, and with 808 demonstrations both TPD and action-only supervision reach 76.9% success. Shared-history analyses indicate TPD especially improves decisions at subgoal transitions, such as moving from obtaining an object to processing it.
AI.conclusion: Compact supervision in the form of task-stage labels is sufficient to train effective small task agents, achieving strong performance without full reasoning traces at inference. Explicit modeling of task progress (via TPD) offers clear benefits in intermediate data regimes by guiding the agent through subgoal transitions, while with enough demonstrations action-only supervision can eventually match its performance.

title: Reliability of LLM Judges for Evaluating Entity Alignment
summary: Entity Alignment (EA) identifies equivalent entities across knowledge graphs and is critical for knowledge base integration and ontology merging. Evaluating EA systems at scale requires expensive expert annotation, making systematic assessment across diverse domains practically infeasible. LLM-as-judge evaluation offers a potentially scalable alternative, yet its reliability for structured prediction tasks like EA remains unstudied. We present the first systematic benchmarking study across three frontier models, three datasets, and four EA systems, using perturbation bias diagnostics, meta-evaluation across all dataset-judge-prompt combinations, and counterfactual label-flip tests. We identify anchor bias, a failure mode in which judges invert discrimination when the system's decision label is visible. Label exposure causally collapses judge discrimination (J-ROC-AUC 0.12-0.87), while a label-free protocol recovers near-ceiling capability on distinctive-name datasets (0.93-1.00) and significant recovery on biomedical pairs (0.93-0.95). Counterfactual experiments confirm causality (FSR 53-99%) and reveal a frontier model paradox: stronger judges exhibit greater label sensitivity, not less. A blinded two-annotator human evaluation (102 pairs, Cohen's kappa=0.902) confirms this mechanism directly. We release the first biomedical EA benchmark (MeSH-SNOMED CT, 15K pairs) and a reproducible auditing framework for LLM judge reliability in EA. Code and data are available at https://github.com/vaibhavalakshmiravideshik/llm-as-a-judge-entity-alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks the reliability of using large language models (LLMs) as judges for entity alignment systems and uncovers a strong bias when LLMs can see model predictions.
AI.motivation: Entity alignment across knowledge graphs is key for integrating and merging knowledge bases, but evaluating EA models requires costly expert annotations, especially in specialized domains like biomedicine. LLM-as-a-judge has emerged as a scalable evaluation alternative, but its trustworthiness for structured prediction tasks like EA has not been systematically tested. The authors aim to rigorously assess whether and when LLMs can be reliable judges for EA, and to uncover potential failure modes.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic benchmarking study involving three frontier LLMs, three datasets (including a new biomedical EA dataset), and four EA systems. They design a comprehensive evaluation framework composed of perturbation bias diagnostics, meta-evaluation over all combinations of datasets, judges, and prompts, and counterfactual label-flip experiments to test causal effects of label exposure. They compare settings where the EA system's predicted label is visible to the judge versus hidden, and they also run a blinded human two-annotator evaluation to validate their findings.
AI.result: They discover an "anchor bias" failure mode: when the EA system's predicted label is shown to the LLM judge, the judge's discriminative ability degrades and can even invert, as reflected in large drops in J-ROC-AUC (down to 0.12 in some settings). With labels hidden (label-free protocol), LLM judges achieve near-perfect discrimination on datasets with distinctive entity names (0.93-1.00 J-ROC-AUC) and strong performance on biomedical entity pairs (0.93-0.95). Counterfactual label-flip experiments yield high false sign rates (53-99%), confirming that exposed labels causally drive misjudgment, and paradoxically, more capable frontier models are more sensitive to these labels. Human evaluation with high inter-annotator agreement supports the proposed mechanism. The authors also produce a 15K-pair MeSH–SNOMED CT biomedical benchmark and an open auditing toolkit.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can be highly capable judges for entity alignment, but only under carefully designed, label-blinded protocols. Exposing system prediction labels induces strong anchor bias that severely harms or even reverses judge discrimination, with stronger LLMs surprisingly more label-sensitive. The work provides both a new biomedical EA benchmark and a reproducible auditing framework, and it argues that any deployment of LLM-as-judge for structured prediction must explicitly guard against label exposure and related biases.

title: Document-Level Text Simplification in Estonian Using Large Language Models
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Published at LREC 2026
summary: Document-level text simplification involves transformations that go beyond sentence-internal edits, addressing discourse coherence, anaphora resolution, and cross-paragraph consistency. Despite advances in sentence-level simplification for high-resource languages, document-level simplification in morphologically rich, low-resource languages such as Estonian remains largely unexplored. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of five state-of-the-art multilingual large language models (LLMs) for document-level simplification in Estonian. Three prompting strategies are examined: single-pass generation, pipeline-based modular agents, and guideline-augmented pipelines. The evaluation framework integrates automatic metrics assessing readability, semantic preservation, and discourse coherence, alongside a structured manual annotation protocol. The findings indicate that Gemini-2.0 and LLaMA-3.3 produce outputs with near-native fluency and strong meaning preservation, whereas other models display notable grammatical and semantic limitations. This work contributes novel document-level coherence metrics, evidence-based prompting strategies, and publicly available resources for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates five multilingual large language models for document-level text simplification in Estonian, comparing prompting strategies and proposing new coherence metrics and resources.
AI.motivation: Document-level simplification, which must maintain discourse coherence and cross-paragraph consistency, is underexplored for morphologically rich, low-resource languages like Estonian. Existing work mostly focuses on sentence-level simplification in high-resource languages.
AI.method: The authors test five state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs on Estonian document-level simplification, using three prompting strategies: (1) single-pass generation, (2) pipeline-based modular agents, and (3) guideline-augmented pipelines. They evaluate outputs with automatic metrics for readability, semantic preservation, and discourse coherence, and apply a structured manual annotation protocol. They also introduce novel document-level coherence metrics.
AI.result: Gemini-2.0 and LLaMA-3.3 achieve near-native fluency and strong meaning preservation, while the other evaluated models show significant grammatical and semantic issues. The proposed prompting strategies and metrics reveal differences in model behavior and output quality across systems.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs can perform high-quality document-level simplification in a low-resource, morphologically rich language like Estonian, especially when using well-designed prompting strategies. The paper offers new coherence evaluation metrics, empirically grounded prompting guidelines, and releases resources to support future, reproducible research in this area.

title: DrugTargetWorld: A Synthetic Biobank for Training and Benchmarking AI Scientists
comment: 34 pages main text, 92 pages supplementary material; 6 main figures. Project: https://DrugTargetWorld.vercel.app. Code: https://github.com/sammargolis/DrugTargetWorld. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sammargolis/DrugTargetWorld-assets
summary: Drug target discovery requires distinguishing molecules that causally drive disease from those that are merely associated with it. Training and evaluating AI agents to perform this workflow end-to-end is difficult because real world biobanks lack known causal ground truth and participant-level data is access controlled. We introduce DrugTargetWorld, a framework that procedurally generates simulated biobanks, or "worlds," with known but concealed causal structure. Each world contains genotypes, proteins, health records, outcomes, and synthetic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for 54,000 participants. Agents must construct a disease phenotype, identify causal driver proteins, infer the beneficial direction of modulation, and optionally conduct virtual 'wet lab' experiments. We evaluated nine agents in 540 episodes across 20 cardiovascular worlds and three experimental budgets. Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol achieved the highest mean composite scores, 39.98 and 35.38 of 100, respectively, and both recovered 64% of causal drivers on average. However, no agent reliably distinguished misleading non-causal proteins, and performance remained limited by the integrative judgments required to connect phenotype construction, causal evidence, and intervention decisions. By making each world's causal structure known to the evaluator but hidden from the agent, DrugTargetWorld turns end-to-end drug target discovery into a scalable training and evaluation problem with verifiable reward.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DrugTargetWorld, a simulated biobank framework with hidden but known causal ground truth for benchmarking AI agents in end-to-end drug target discovery.
AI.motivation: Real-world biobanks have limited accessibility and lack explicit causal ground truth, making it hard to train and rigorously evaluate AI systems that must go from raw multimodal data to actionable drug targets. The authors want a scalable, controllable environment where an agent’s full drug-target-discovery workflow can be tested with verifiable rewards.
AI.method: The authors procedurally generate many synthetic biobanks (“worlds”), each with 54,000 simulated participants and multimodal data (genotypes, proteins, health records, outcomes, and synthetic MRI). Every world is built from an underlying, fully specified causal structure that is hidden from agents but available to evaluators. Agents are tasked with: (1) constructing a disease phenotype, (2) identifying causal driver proteins, (3) inferring whether up- or down-modulation would be beneficial, and (4) optionally running virtual wet-lab experiments. They benchmark nine AI agents across 540 episodes spanning 20 cardiovascular-disease worlds and three different experimental budgets, computing composite scores based on target-discovery performance.
AI.result: Among nine evaluated agents, Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol obtained the highest mean composite scores (39.98 and 35.38 out of 100). Both recovered, on average, 64% of the truly causal driver proteins. Nevertheless, none of the agents consistently filtered out misleading non-causal proteins, and overall task performance remained modest, especially on steps requiring integration of phenotype design, causal reasoning, and intervention planning.
AI.conclusion: DrugTargetWorld provides a scalable, controllable testbed where the true causal structure is known to evaluators but hidden from agents, enabling principled training and benchmarking of end-to-end drug-target-discovery agents with verifiable rewards. Current leading AI agents can identify a substantial fraction of causal drivers but still struggle to avoid non-causal distractors and to perform the complex integrative reasoning necessary for reliable target selection, highlighting significant room for improvement in causal and decision-making capabilities.

title: CoTrace: Data Recipes for Training Terminal Agents with Harness-Model Co-Evolution
summary: Terminal-agent capability depends jointly on model weights and the runtime harness that formats prompts, binds tools, and handles error recovery. Existing harness-model co-evolution approaches improve both components, yet often treat trajectories produced during harness search as an undifferentiated replay buffer. This practice overlooks that a trajectory's value for model training depends on the harness under which it was generated. To systematically analyze this interface, we establish an alternating co-evolution framework that decouples harness search and policy training through component-wise promotion decisions. Within this framework, we introduce CoTrace, a harness-aware data recipe that explicitly governs trajectory routing, provenance matching, and curriculum refresh. Under CoTrace, recurring execution failures guide harness synthesis, while policy training is strictly conditioned on verified rollouts matched to the adopted runtime for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or fresh online interactions for reinforcement learning (RL). On the Tmax promotion split, CoTrace advances Qwen3.5-9B from 78 to 88 solved tasks under supervised fine-tuning while an online reinforcement variant reaches 90. Specifically, a compact harness-matched corpus produces steady model gains at substantially lower compute than much larger corpora pooled across sibling harnesses. Furthermore, evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench Lite show that out-of-distribution transfer depends fundamentally on harness compatibility, where maintaining consistency between training and evaluation runtimes prevents procedural execution breakdowns observed under foreign scaffolds.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoTrace, a harness-aware framework for co-evolving terminal agents and their runtime harnesses, showing that accounting for which harness generated a trajectory significantly improves data efficiency, task success, and out-of-distribution transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing terminal-agent systems depend both on model weights and the runtime harness (prompt formatting, tool binding, error handling). Current co-evolution methods often pool trajectories from different harnesses into a single replay buffer, ignoring that data usefulness is conditional on the harness that produced it. This creates inefficiencies, mixing incompatible rollouts and obscuring how harness design affects learning and transfer, especially when moving across different runtimes or benchmarks.
AI.method: They formalize an alternating co-evolution framework that separates harness search from policy training and introduces component-wise promotion: harnesses and models are promoted independently based on their performance. Within this, they propose CoTrace, a harness-aware data pipeline that (1) routes trajectories according to their harness of origin, (2) enforces provenance matching so that SFT only uses rollouts generated under the current harness, and RL uses fresh online interactions, and (3) periodically refreshes the training curriculum using failure-driven harness synthesis. Recurrent execution failures are used to design or select better harnesses, and the model is then trained exclusively on verified, harness-compatible traces.
AI.result: On the Tmax promotion split, CoTrace improves Qwen3.5-9B from 78 to 88 solved tasks with supervised fine-tuning, and an online RL variant reaches 90 solved tasks. A relatively small corpus of trajectories that are strictly matched to their harness yields steady model improvements and is more compute-efficient than much larger mixed-harness datasets. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench Lite, they find that transfer performance depends strongly on maintaining compatibility between training and evaluation harnesses; mismatched ("foreign") scaffolds lead to procedural execution failures even when underlying model capabilities are strong.
AI.conclusion: Harness-model co-evolution should be explicitly harness-aware: trajectories must be handled with respect to the runtime that generated them, and training/evaluation harness consistency is critical. CoTrace operationalizes this by structuring data routing, provenance matching, and curriculum refresh around the harness, leading to higher task success, better data efficiency, and more reliable out-of-distribution transfer for terminal agents.

title: World Potential Model: Pretrained World Knowledge as Progress Potentials
summary: Long-horizon language agents often receive supervision only from terminal task outcomes, leaving little signal for distinguishing productive intermediate behavior from stagnation or even regression. Rather than learning a separate value function or process reward model for every task, we ask whether pretrained models can recognize task progress from their existing world knowledge. We formalize this capability with a World Potential Model (WPM), a goal-conditioned evaluator of task-relative realized progress in agent contexts. In ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, off-the-shelf pretrained models substantially outperform chance at recovering realized-progress structure without task-specific evaluator fine-tuning. We further anchor these progress judgments to task-specific milestones to obtain scalar world potentials, whose temporal differences provide process-sensitive step-level credit for policy optimization. Under matched comparisons, WPM-guided optimization improves success over outcome-only GRPO across all evaluated configurations. Together, these results provide initial evidence that pretrained world knowledge can support reusable realized-progress evaluation and provide useful supervision for long-horizon agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using pretrained language models to evaluate task progress for long-horizon agents, turning their world knowledge into a reusable signal for step-level credit assignment and improving policy optimization compared to outcome-only training.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon language agents typically get feedback only at the end of tasks, making it hard to distinguish productive intermediate steps from unhelpful ones, which hurts learning efficiency and stability. Training a separate value or reward model for each task is expensive and not easily reusable. The authors are motivated to exploit the rich world knowledge in pretrained models to recognize and score incremental task progress in a general, goal-conditioned way, so that a single mechanism can supervise many tasks and provide dense, process-aware feedback.
AI.method: They introduce the World Potential Model (WPM), a goal-conditioned evaluator that judges realized task progress from agent trajectories. Using off-the-shelf pretrained models, they assess whether these models can recover the structure of progress in environments like ALFWorld and ScienceWorld without task-specific fine-tuning. They map qualitative progress judgments onto task milestones to produce scalar “world potentials”; temporal differences of these potentials serve as process-sensitive rewards for policy optimization. They then compare WPM-guided optimization against outcome-only GRPO under controlled, matched conditions.
AI.result: In both ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, pretrained language models can detect realized progress significantly better than chance, even without specialized training for each task. The induced scalar world potentials correlate meaningfully with actual task advancement, enabling temporal-difference style rewards. When used to guide optimization, WPM-based signals consistently improve agent success rates over outcome-only GRPO across all tested setups.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained language models contain enough structured world knowledge to provide goal-conditioned evaluations of task progress, without per-task reward model training. The proposed World Potential Model framework turns these evaluations into scalar potentials whose differences yield rich, step-level supervision. This leads to better performance for long-horizon agents than relying solely on terminal outcomes, suggesting a promising, reusable approach to process-level credit assignment in complex language-based environments.

title: PHRBench: A Behavioral Evaluation of Post-Hallucination Reasoning in LLMs
summary: Hallucinated information can propagate through multi-stage LLM systems and become part of the context for subsequent reasoning. Existing studies of post-hallucination reasoning (PHR) mainly characterize changes in final outcomes and aggregate reasoning dynamics, leaving how models resolve hallucinated premises at the response level insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce PHRBench, a controlled benchmark for behaviorally structured PHR across four domains and 18 large language models. PHRBench characterizes each reasoning trajectory independently of final-answer correctness through Hallucination Compliance, Hallucination Avoidance, and Heuristic Correction, and defines an insightful trajectory as successful correction that ultimately reaches the correct answer. Across 4820 controlled instances, we find that successful recovery remains relatively rare and is associated with more frequent belief updates along the reasoning trajectory. We further find that properties of the hallucinated prompt contain substantial predictive signal for successful recovery, with a lightweight predictor achieving an AUROC of 0.847. These findings provide a behavioral view of post-hallucination reasoning, characterizing how LLMs resolve erroneous context and when successful recovery is likely to occur.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PHRBench, a benchmark to analyze how LLMs behave after being given hallucinated (false) information, focusing on detailed reasoning trajectories rather than just final accuracy.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations in one stage of an LLM pipeline can contaminate the context of later stages, but prior work mainly measures whether final answers are right or wrong, not how models behaviorally deal with incorrect premises step by step. There is a need for a structured, controlled way to study post-hallucination reasoning (PHR) at the trajectory level across models and domains.
AI.method: The authors construct PHRBench, a controlled benchmark with hallucinated premises across four domains and evaluate 18 LLMs. They annotate and categorize each reasoning trajectory using three behavioral dimensions: Hallucination Compliance (following the false premise), Hallucination Avoidance (ignoring or rejecting it), and Heuristic Correction (overwriting the hallucination via heuristics). They define “insightful trajectories” as those that successfully correct the hallucination and yield the correct final answer. They then perform large-scale analysis (4,820 instances) of trajectories, belief updates, and prompt-level features, and train a lightweight predictor to estimate the probability of successful recovery from hallucinations.
AI.result: Across 4,820 controlled instances, they observe that genuine successful recovery from hallucinated context is relatively rare among current LLMs. Successful cases show more frequent belief updates within the reasoning chain, indicating more dynamic internal revision. They further find that measurable properties of the hallucinated prompt (e.g., structure, strength or salience of the false premise) are predictive of whether recovery will succeed, enabling a simple predictive model to achieve an AUROC of 0.847 for forecasting successful PHR.
AI.conclusion: PHRBench offers a behavior-level lens on how LLMs handle erroneous context, revealing that correcting hallucinated premises during reasoning is infrequent but associated with active belief revision. Characteristics of the hallucinated input itself provide strong signal for predicting recoverability. The benchmark and findings can guide future work on designing models and pipelines that are more robust to upstream hallucinations and better at revising false premises during reasoning.

title: Dual- versus Single-Suggestion AI Support for Radiographic Interpretation in Residents: Randomized Multireader Study
summary:
Purpose: To compare dual- and single-suggestion AI support for radiographic interpretation by residents, particularly when the shared AI suggestion was incorrect.
  Materials and Methods: This prospective, multicenter, randomized three-arm reader study was conducted at three hospitals in China from July to September 2026 (ChiCTR2600129243). After specialty stratification, 132 residents with fewer than 3 years of clinical experience were randomized 1:1:1 to GPT-5.4 alone (group A), GPT-5.4 plus Kimi-K2.6 (group B), or GPT-5.4 plus Gemini-3.6 Flash (group C); 123 were analyzed. Participants interpreted 60 radiographs before and after AI support. The primary outcome was accuracy change. Welch ANOVA and Holm-adjusted t tests compared support conditions; HC3 linear models assessed specialty interaction.
  Results: Among 123 residents (mean age, 24.1 years +/- 1.4; 65 women), radiology residents showed greater accuracy improvement with dual- than single-suggestion support (B-A, 6.69 percentage points [95% CI, 0.97-12.40]; C-A, 7.87 percentage points [95% CI, 1.64-14.11]; Holm-adjusted P = .030 for both), whereas accuracy change did not differ in non-radiology residents (P = .20). When GPT-5.4 was incorrect, AI-assisted accuracy was higher with dual- than single-suggestion support in radiology residents (40.1% and 40.4% vs 20.0%) and non-radiology residents (31.3% and 31.0% vs 12.1%) (all Holm-adjusted P < .001). The dual-suggestion effect differed by specialty (interaction difference, 10.44 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.36-16.52; P < .001).
  Conclusion: Dual-suggestion support may mitigate the influence of erroneous AI suggestions, with greater accuracy improvement observed in radiology but not non-radiology residents.

AI.tldr: The paper prospectively compares single- vs dual-AI suggestions for residents reading radiographs, showing that providing two independent AI opinions improves diagnostic accuracy and buffers against following a wrong AI output, especially among radiology residents.
AI.motivation: AI tools can improve radiology interpretation but also risk propagating errors when the AI suggestion is wrong and clinicians over-rely on it. Most current workflows present a single AI recommendation. The authors aim to test whether offering two independent AI suggestions (dual support) can reduce susceptibility to erroneous AI outputs and differentially benefit residents with and without radiology training.
AI.method: Prospective, multicenter, randomized three-arm reader study at three hospitals. 132 residents (<3 years experience) stratified by specialty and randomized to: (A) single-suggestion GPT-5.4, (B) dual-suggestion GPT-5.4 + Kimi-K2.6, (C) dual-suggestion GPT-5.4 + Gemini-3.6 Flash. 123 residents analyzed. Each interpreted 60 radiographs before and after AI support. Primary endpoint: change in diagnostic accuracy with AI vs without. Statistical analysis used Welch ANOVA with Holm-adjusted pairwise t tests to compare support modes and HC3-robust linear models to assess interaction with specialty (radiology vs non-radiology). Special attention was paid to cases where the shared AI (GPT-5.4) was wrong, to see whether dual suggestions mitigated AI-induced errors.
AI.result: Radiology residents had significantly greater accuracy gains with dual AI suggestions compared with single suggestion (improvements of about 6.7–7.9 percentage points over GPT-5.4 alone, with 95% CIs excluding 0 and Holm-adjusted P = .030). Non-radiology residents showed no significant difference in accuracy change between single and dual suggestions (P = .20). In cases where GPT-5.4 was incorrect, both radiology and non-radiology residents had much higher AI-assisted accuracy under dual-suggestion conditions (~40% vs 20% for radiology; ~31% vs 12% for non-radiology; all Holm-adjusted P < .001). The beneficial effect of dual suggestions differed significantly by specialty (interaction of about 10.4 percentage points; P < .001).
AI.conclusion: Presenting two independent AI suggestions for radiograph interpretation reduces the negative impact of an erroneous AI recommendation compared with a single AI suggestion. Dual-suggestion support delivers larger accuracy improvements for radiology residents than for non-radiology residents, indicating that domain training modulates how effectively clinicians use multiple AI opinions. Implementing multi-model AI support in radiology workflows could enhance both overall accuracy and robustness to AI errors, particularly among radiology trainees.

title: Your Prompt Should Do More: Effects of Retrieval Instructions in Embedding Models
summary: Prompted embedding models have recently received increasing attention, particularly for retrieval, where detailed retrieval instructions are provided as part of the retrieval prompt. Several new datasets and studies have examined this setting, showing that the current embedding models often struggle to follow such instructions reliably. In this paper, we study the mechanism of how instructions actually affect the representations of retrieval queries in asymmetric retrieval tasks. We show that models can fail to follow even simple task instructions when query-side distractors are included in the evaluation. We hypothesize that this behavior is driven by the training setup of current embedding models and their evaluation, and show that fine-tuning with added query-side distractors leads to substantial improvements, with minimal effect on other tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why prompted embedding models often fail to follow retrieval instructions and demonstrates that fine-tuning with query-side distractors significantly improves instruction following in asymmetric retrieval, without harming other tasks.
AI.motivation: Prompted embedding models are widely used for retrieval with explicit natural-language instructions, but recent benchmarks show that they often ignore or only partially follow these instructions, especially in asymmetric retrieval tasks where queries and documents differ in form. There is limited understanding of the internal mechanism by which instructions affect query representations and why models break down when distractive content is present in the query. This gap hinders reliable deployment of instruction-based retrieval systems.
AI.method: The authors empirically study how natural-language retrieval instructions change the learned representations of queries in asymmetric retrieval tasks. They design evaluations that inject query-side distractors—irrelevant but salient information in the query—to probe when and how models fail to follow instructions. Based on the hypothesis that current training and evaluation setups encourage models to over-focus on surface query content rather than instruction semantics, they perform fine-tuning where such query-side distractors are systematically included in the training data and then measure downstream performance across retrieval and non-retrieval tasks.
AI.result: They find that even simple task instructions are frequently ignored when distractive information is present on the query side, leading to significant retrieval failures. After fine-tuning embedding models with training data that includes query-side distractors, models become substantially more robust to such distractors and follow instructions more faithfully. Importantly, this improvement in instruction following has minimal negative impact on other tasks, suggesting that the gains are not due to overfitting or harmful trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Instruction failures in prompted embedding retrieval models largely stem from the way models are trained and evaluated, rather than from an inherent inability to understand instructions. Introducing query-side distractors during fine-tuning teaches models to properly prioritize task instructions over irrelevant query content, leading to substantial robustness gains in asymmetric retrieval with little or no performance degradation elsewhere.

title: Learning Situation-Conditioned Thinking Policies for Long-Term LLM Agents
summary: Long-running autonomous agents must reuse accumulated reasoning experience without allowing explicit historical memory and LLM context to grow indefinitely. However, existing memory mechanisms mainly retrieve, summarize, or compress past content and do not directly learn when particular kinds of thinking should be activated or discover new thinking knowledge from temporally dispersed experiences. This paper proposes a situation-conditioned thinking memory framework that transforms historical reasoning experience into a lightweight policy for predicting what should be thought about in the current situation, while leaving detailed reasoning to a large language model. Situations may represent temporal or spatiotemporal evolution rather than only current states.
