AI.result: Across all three evaluated models and the diverse question set, responses produced under truth-directed prompts systematically used fewer reasoning tokens than responses under lie-directed or truth-indifferent prompts. This effect appears at the group level and is robust across reasoning domains (analytic, descriptive, normative; moral and non-moral). The token-count differences align with the hypothesis that untruthful or truth-indifferent behaviors involve greater reasoning-token expenditure than truthful behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a very low-bandwidth, content-independent metric—reasoning-token count—can reliably distinguish, at the group level, between explicitly truthful and explicitly untruthful response policies in current LLMs. While this does not yet support instance-level deception detection or cover spontaneous deception, learned deceptive strategies, or adversarial scenarios, it serves as a proof of concept. Reasoning-token count is proposed as a promising, simple candidate signal for honesty monitoring when detailed chain-of-thought content is inaccessible or unreliable, motivating further research on generalization, robustness, and integration with other safety tools.

title: NL2Hull: A Natural Language-Driven Constrained Ship Design Decision Framework
summary: Ship-form design combines smooth geometric representation, local shape editing, and constraints on the resulting hull. We present the Natural-Language-to-Hull Framework (NL2Hull Framework), which formulates ship-form editing as a typed discrete decision problem and connects language decisions to numerical geometry. Its Constrained Free-Form Deformation Engine (CFFD Engine) represents hull waterlines with non-uniform rational B-splines (NURBS), applies free-form deformation (FFD) to their control points, reconstructs the hull, and checks geometric constraints. We construct the Ship Design Decision Dataset (SDD Dataset) with 134,558 cleaned records and evaluate compared models on its subset Ship Design Decision Benchmark (SDDBench), containing 5,000 records and 43,496 typed questions. We propose Chip, a constrained ship-design decision model for processing natural-language requests. Chip reaches 95.90\% question accuracy and 99.32\% FFD exact match, with a negative log-likelihood of 0.0951, an expected calibration error of 0.0032, and a Brier score of 0.0551. The NL2Hull Framework provides a reproducible interface for evaluating language-based ship-form decisions while identifying the geometry and continuous-control components that require further development. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/wenhuahuo/NL2Hull.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NL2Hull, a framework that converts natural-language ship design requests into constrained geometric hull edits via free-form deformation and NURBS, and provides a large dataset and benchmark plus a strong model (Chip) that achieves high accuracy and calibration.
AI.motivation: Ship hull design requires smooth, editable geometry under strict hydrodynamic and structural constraints, but existing workflows are expert-driven and not easily controllable by natural language. There is a need for a reproducible way to map textual design decisions to detailed geometric changes, and to rigorously evaluate models that perform this mapping. Additionally, datasets and benchmarks specific to language-driven ship-form design decisions have been lacking.
AI.method: The authors formulate ship-form editing as a typed discrete decision problem that links natural-language instructions to numerical geometry operations. They build the NL2Hull Framework whose CFFD Engine uses NURBS to represent hull waterlines, then applies free-form deformation (FFD) on NURBS control points while enforcing geometric constraints. They construct a large Ship Design Decision Dataset (SDD) and a benchmark subset (SDDBench) containing typed questions about design decisions. On top of this, they propose a model called Chip tailored to constrained ship-design decision making from natural language and evaluate it on SDDBench using accuracy, FFD exact match, negative log-likelihood, calibration error, and Brier score.
AI.result: The SDD Dataset contains 134,558 cleaned records, and the SDDBench subset has 5,000 records with 43,496 typed questions. The Chip model achieves 95.90% question accuracy and 99.32% exact match on FFD operations, along with strong probabilistic performance: negative log-likelihood of 0.0951, expected calibration error of 0.0032, and Brier score of 0.0551. These results indicate that Chip can reliably interpret natural-language ship-design requests and convert them into correct, constrained geometric edits.
AI.conclusion: The NL2Hull Framework offers a reproducible interface for studying and evaluating language-based ship hull design decisions by tightly coupling natural-language instructions with constrained geometric modeling via NURBS and FFD. The strong performance of Chip on SDDBench demonstrates that the decision formulation is effective, though the paper highlights that some geometric and continuous control aspects still require further research. By releasing code and data, the work establishes a foundation for future improvements in language-driven computer-aided ship design.

title: RunningTab: Direct Workspace Interaction with Environment-Side Tabs
summary: Much knowledge work produces new deliverables from files a workspace already holds, and LLM agents are beginning to take such work over. Through direct corpus interaction, an agent can search and read any of those files from a terminal with no indexing, and producing a deliverable from many of them in this way is what we call direct workspace interaction (DWI). Reaching the files, however, is only half the task: nothing keeps track of what the task asks for, what has been read, and what was listed but never opened, all of which slip through the context window without leaving a trace, so an agent may extract a figure and still deliver a report without it. To address this, we present RunningTab, a framework that equips direct workspace interaction with an environment-side tab: a per-task record of what the task still owes, kept by the environment alongside the agent. Specifically, the agent adds its requirements, while the environment records every file read as an excerpt with its provenance and every listed but unopened file as a candidate; the agent can then see each requirement beside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates, resolve it against matching content or set it aside with a reason, and, should it try to finish with requirements still open, receive them in a finish check. We validate RunningTab on three benchmarks with three LLMs, where it consistently outperforms plain DWI and baselines that keep the record in the model, while its tab usually holds the values a deliverable needs once seen.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RunningTab, a framework that augments LLM-based direct workspace interaction (DWI) with an environment-maintained, per-task tab that tracks requirements, read files, and unopened candidates to improve completeness and reliability of generated deliverables.
AI.motivation: In direct workspace interaction, LLM agents can read and search files directly from a terminal without indexing, but there is no persistent tracking of task requirements, what has been read, or what was considered but not opened. This lack of explicit, persistent memory causes agents to miss important items (e.g., a specific figure) when producing final deliverables because intermediate steps fall out of the context window. The authors want a way to systematically track and surface this information so the agent can reliably satisfy all task requirements.
AI.method: The authors propose RunningTab, a framework that lives on the environment side and maintains a per-task tab. The agent explicitly logs its task requirements to this tab, while the environment automatically records (1) every file the agent reads as an excerpt plus its provenance and (2) every listed-but-unopened file as a candidate. The interface then shows each requirement alongside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates. The agent can resolve each requirement against this surfaced content or mark it as set aside with a reason. Before finishing, a “finish check” step reminds the agent of any unresolved requirements, reducing omissions. They evaluate RunningTab on three benchmarks with three different LLMs and compare against plain DWI and variants where tracking is kept inside the model’s context instead of in the environment.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks and three LLMs, RunningTab consistently outperforms plain direct workspace interaction and baselines where the record of progress and requirements is kept in-model. Empirically, the tab entries (excerpts and candidates) tend to contain the necessary information for the final deliverable once the relevant files have been seen, indicating that the framework successfully captures key content. This leads to more complete and accurate deliverables with fewer missed requested elements.
AI.conclusion: RunningTab demonstrates that moving task and file-tracking from the model’s transient context into an environment-maintained, structured tab significantly improves LLM agents’ ability to perform direct workspace interaction tasks. By explicitly tracking requirements, read evidence, and potential sources, and enforcing a final requirement check, the framework reduces omissions and increases deliverable quality. This suggests that environment-side scaffolding and memory structures are an effective way to augment LLM agents for complex knowledge work over existing file corpora.

title: Where Can a Decision Model Diagnose HVAC Faults? Reasoning Demand, Physical Representation, and Robustness Under Shift
comment: 58 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Submitted to Energy and Buildings
summary: Artificial intelligence supports building operations in several forms, each with its own barrier. Expert rules must be tuned for every system, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text that requires human-in-the-loop checking, since their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer kind of pretrained model, here called a decision model, returns a probability for every allowed answer, so one model could serve many decisions without training. This study answers three open questions for fault diagnosis in heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems: which decisions such a model can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities hold when conditions change. On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data given raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model face nine tests that change season, control configuration, or building. Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence one feature carries, but not faults that need operating context. Under shift they kept their accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still needed correction, and detection was weak. The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of work in which code computes the physics and the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a new type of pretrained "decision model" for HVAC fault diagnosis, comparing it to language models and supervised models, and finds it can generalize across buildings and conditions when given physical features, but still needs probability calibration and struggles with context-intensive faults.
AI.motivation: Current AI approaches for building operations each have key limitations: rule-based systems need extensive tuning, supervised learning requires labeled data that buildings rarely have, and language models produce free text with unreliable self-reported confidence, requiring humans in the loop. A newer class of pretrained models that output calibrated probabilities over discrete choices might alleviate these issues by reusing a single model across many decision tasks. The paper is motivated by the need to understand if such a decision model can effectively diagnose HVAC faults, what inputs it needs, and whether its probabilistic outputs remain valid when real-world conditions change.
AI.method: The authors define and use a pretrained decision model called Jev that outputs probabilities over a fixed set of fault labels. They construct a benchmark of 128 fault days from four public real-equipment HVAC datasets and grade faults by the reasoning complexity required for diagnosis. Inputs to the models are varied across three representations: raw time series data, derived physical features, and physical features augmented with Brick topology information. Jev, several open language models, and a supervised model are subjected to nine test scenarios that change season, control configuration, or building to simulate distribution shifts. Performance is measured in terms of accuracy, macro-F1, calibration of probability estimates, and robustness under shift, with special analysis of which fault types each method can or cannot diagnose given different input representations.
AI.result: With physical feature inputs, Jev and a larger open language model successfully diagnose faults where evidence is largely contained in a single feature, but fail on faults requiring richer operating context. Under distribution shifts across season, control strategy, or building, Jev and the large language model maintain both accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model suffers a macro-F1 drop of about 0.33 yet remains the best or tied within a specific building domain. All models, including Jev, need probability calibration corrections, and overall fault detection performance remains weak, indicating that none of the evaluated approaches is fully satisfactory for robust automated fault detection and diagnosis. The study also empirically characterizes the mapping between fault types, their input requirements, and model capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Decision models like Jev can act as reusable probabilistic decision engines for HVAC fault diagnosis when supplied with well-designed physical features, performing competitively across varying conditions and generalizing better than a supervised model under domain shift. However, they are limited to relatively simple faults whose evidence appears in individual features and do not yet handle context-intensive reasoning tasks or strong detection. Their probability outputs, although more structured than free-text from language models, still require calibration. The findings support a hybrid workflow in which conventional code encodes domain physics to generate candidate faults, while the decision model ranks these candidates for human operators, rather than fully automating the end-to-end diagnosis process.

title: Validity Without Ground Truth: What Stated-Preference Economics Offers the Evaluation of Language Models
summary: Many of the questions now put to large language models have no correct answer to score against: what a policy is worth, which option a user should choose, how to weigh competing values. Stated-preference economics has faced this problem for decades. It judges survey responses without knowing the true value, through a framework of validity and related concepts: content, construct, and criterion validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, and consequentiality. We argue that this framework is a general method for evaluating language models, and we set out what each concept means for LLM evaluation. We demonstrate the approach using a published water-quality stated preference economic valuation survey (Vossler et al. 2023) administered to six models. In this economic application, the validity tests take the form of predictions from economic theory: demand should slope down, and willingness to pay should respond to the scope of the good and to income. The tests separate the models sharply. Two older models fail the most basic test at a household income level of \$75,000, and the two newest pass every test of theoretical validity we can score, but diverge on convergent validity. Passing validity tests shows that a model's answers are coherent, not that they are correct.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using validity concepts from stated-preference economics to evaluate large language models on questions without objectively correct answers, illustrating the method with an economic valuation survey on water quality given to several models.
AI.motivation: Many LLM queries involve value judgments or preferences where no ground-truth label exists, making traditional accuracy-based evaluation impossible. Stated-preference economics has long faced a similar challenge—evaluating survey answers about hypothetical choices without knowing the true underlying values. The authors aim to adapt that mature validity framework to systematically assess LLM outputs in such contexts.
AI.method: The authors map key concepts from stated-preference survey evaluation—content, construct, and criterion validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, and consequentiality—onto the domain of LLM evaluation, clarifying what each means for assessing model behavior. They then run an existing stated-preference survey on water-quality valuation (Vossler et al. 2023) through six LLMs, treating the models as survey respondents. Using economic theory, they specify testable implications (e.g., downward-sloping demand, willingness to pay rising with income and the scope of the good) and check whether each model’s responses satisfy these validity criteria, including convergent validity across models.
AI.result: The economic-theory-based validity tests sharply differentiate the models. Two older models fail even the most basic validity condition at a representative household income of $75,000, indicating incoherent or theory-inconsistent responses. The two newest models satisfy all the specified theoretical validity tests, meaning their behavior is consistent with core economic predictions, but they differ in terms of convergent validity, i.e., their answers do not fully align with each other despite both passing the theory-based checks.
AI.conclusion: Validity concepts from stated-preference economics can be repurposed as a general evaluation framework for LLMs answering questions without objective ground truth. Applying this to an economic valuation survey shows that such tests can distinguish between models and reveal both improvements and remaining divergences. However, satisfying validity tests only demonstrates internal coherence and theory-consistency of the model’s responses; it does not establish that those responses are factually correct or normatively right.

title: AgentTime: Can Agents Estimate and Control Their Own Runtime?
summary: An essential control of AI agents is their ability to manage runtime. This ability requires a sense of time-awareness, to predict and estimate wall-clock time and to control their own actions. Prior work has focused on time-awareness, but duration-following and control in native agent harnesses remain unexplored. We present AgentTime, a benchmark for testing whether agents can work for a requested duration, predict their runtime, and estimate elapsed time afterward. It comprises 222 tasks from 18 sources spanning coding, computer use, agentic work, and automated research. Duration-following experiments append a single instruction specifying how long to work, with requests ranging from about a minute to multiple days. Accuracy on these instructions varies substantially: Fable 5.1 in Claude Code deviates from requested runtimes by a typical factor of 2.9$\times$, compared with only 1.2$\times$ for GPT-6 Astra in Codex. However, matching the requested runtime does not, by itself, establish continued work on the task. Among 158 reviewed Astra runs with classifiable transcripts, 14 explicitly slept after appearing to finish. In forecasting experiments, predictions tend to overestimate natural runtimes. In retrospective experiments, removing temporal information more than doubles deviation for Sol and Astra and nearly doubles it for Fable. An agent's ability to complete a task does not guarantee that it can control its own time or work for the whole requested duration. For agents to run reliably, safely, and autonomously over long horizons, we require the evaluation of both.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AgentTime, a benchmark to test whether AI agents can understand and control wall‑clock time: working for specified durations, predicting runtime, and retrospectively estimating elapsed time.
AI.motivation: Although AI agents are increasingly used for long‑running tasks, their ability to manage real-world time—beyond just being ‘time‑aware’—is poorly understood. Prior work studies temporal awareness conceptually, but not whether agents can actually follow duration instructions, forecast how long they will take, or accurately recall elapsed time in realistic agent harnesses. Reliable, safe long‑horizon autonomy demands that agents not only solve tasks but also control how long they run.
AI.method: The authors build AgentTime, a benchmark of 222 tasks from 18 sources (coding, computer use, agentic workflows, automated research). They run agents in native harnesses under three experimental settings: (1) duration‑following, by appending a single instruction specifying a target runtime (from ~1 minute to multiple days) and measuring deviation from the requested duration; (2) forecasting, by asking agents to predict their own runtime beforehand and comparing to actual wall‑clock time; and (3) retrospective estimation, by asking agents to estimate elapsed time after task completion, including a variant where temporal information is removed to test reliance on external cues. They also qualitatively analyze transcripts to distinguish genuine work from idling or sleeping.
AI.result: On duration‑following, agents show large variance in accuracy: Fable 5.1 in Claude Code deviates from requested runtimes by a typical factor of 2.9×, while GPT‑6 Astra in Codex deviates by about 1.2×. Transcript review reveals behavior where agents appear to finish early and then explicitly sleep instead of continuing meaningful work—14 such cases among 158 classifiable Astra runs—showing that matching overall runtime does not guarantee sustained engagement with the task. In forecasting, agents generally overestimate their natural runtimes. In retrospective estimation, removing temporal cues more than doubles time‑estimation error for Sol and Astra and nearly doubles it for Fable, indicating heavy dependence on external time signals. Across conditions, agents that can complete tasks still frequently fail to control or accurately reason about their own runtime.
AI.conclusion: Task competence alone is insufficient for reliable long‑horizon autonomy: agents must also be able to follow duration constraints, accurately predict runtimes, and retrospectively estimate elapsed time. Current agents show substantial weaknesses in these capabilities, sometimes stretching or filling time without genuine work. The AgentTime benchmark exposes these gaps and underscores that robust evaluation of both task performance and temporal control is necessary before deploying agents for long, autonomous, and safety‑critical operations.

title: Successive Training Stages and Large Language Model Persuasion: Effects of Misalignment, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Preference Optimization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be tuned to influence human attitudes, yet the respective contributions of successive post-training stages remain un-clear. This study examines how three successive training stages affect LLM persuasiveness: (1) misalignment through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on conspiracy data, (2) additional persuasive SFT on argumentative data, and (3) Identity Preference Optimization (IPO), a preference-optimization method. A total of 835 participants recruited on Prolific were randomly assigned to five between-subject conditions (neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, and GPT-4) and were exposed to texts on 10 divisive political issues, personalized from their individual profiles in all model conditions. Attitude change was measured as the difference between pre- and post-exposure positions on continuous Likert scales and analyzed with an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). A significant condition x baseline-attitude interaction, F (4, 825) = 5.33, p < .001, indicated that training effects depended on participants' initial attitudes. Persuasive SFT produced greater attitude change than conspiracy training alone, d = 0.30, whereas IPO provided no additional benefit, d = 0.03, and GPT-4 did not differ from neutral text, d = --0.01. These results show that targeted supervised training on persuasive data increases LLM persuasiveness, whereas preference optimization yields no significant gains beyond it.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how different post-training stages affect the ability of large language models to change human attitudes and finds that supervised fine-tuning on persuasive data increases persuasiveness, while additional preference optimization does not.
AI.motivation: To understand which components of modern LLM post-training pipelines actually contribute to their power to influence human political attitudes, and to separate the effects of simple exposure to biased content from explicit persuasive training and preference-optimization techniques.
AI.method: The authors sequentially applied three training stages to an LLM: (1) SFT on conspiracy-related data to misalign the model, (2) further SFT on explicitly persuasive argumentative data, and (3) Identity Preference Optimization (IPO). They then ran a between-subjects experiment with 835 Prolific participants randomly assigned to one of five conditions (neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, GPT-4). Participants read model-generated texts on 10 divisive political issues, personalized to their profiles. Attitudes were measured before and after exposure using Likert scales, and effects were analyzed via ANCOVA, focusing on condition by baseline-attitude interactions and standardized differences (Cohen’s d).
AI.result: There was a significant interaction between experimental condition and participants’ initial attitudes, indicating that training effects varied with baseline positions. Models with persuasive SFT produced more attitude change than conspiracy-only SFT (d = 0.30). Adding Identity Preference Optimization yielded negligible additional gains (d = 0.03). GPT-4’s impact on attitudes was statistically indistinguishable from that of neutral text (d = -0.01).
AI.conclusion: Explicit supervised fine-tuning on persuasive, argumentative data meaningfully increases the capacity of LLMs to shift human attitudes beyond what is achieved by exposure to biased or conspiratorial content alone. However, further preference-optimization using Identity Preference Optimization does not significantly enhance persuasiveness beyond persuasive SFT. Current general-purpose models like GPT-4, when used as in this study, do not produce more attitude change than neutral text controls.

title: From Expected Harmfulness to Likelihood: A Probabilistic Reformulation of Jailbreaking LLM Agents
summary: When the harmfulness of an LLM agent's output can be quantified, a natural jailbreaking objective is to maximize expected harmfulness over admissible input modifications. An alternative approach constructs or selects harmful target outputs and modifies the input to increase their likelihood. We establish a precise connection between these two approaches through a probabilistic reformulation. Specifically, we show that the gradient of the logarithm of expected harmfulness with respect to the input equals the expected input gradient of the model's log-likelihood under a harmfulness reweighted output distribution. This identity provides a unified interpretation of expected harmfulness and target likelihood optimization. Building on this connection, we propose OPUR, a sampling distribution designed to generate highly harmful target outputs and use the resulting samples to guide likelihood-based input optimization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the resulting method in jailbreaking LLM agents.

AI.tldr: The paper studies theoretical connections between two jailbreak optimization strategies for LLM agents—maximizing expected harmfulness vs. maximizing likelihood of harmful target outputs—and proposes a practical algorithm (OPUR) that exploits this link to construct stronger jailbreak attacks.
AI.motivation: Different jailbreak strategies for large language model (LLM) agents often appear distinct: some directly optimize prompts to increase expected harmfulness of outputs, while others search for or craft specific harmful target outputs and then tune prompts to make those outputs more likely. The authors aim to unify these perspectives mathematically, to better understand their relationship and to design more effective attacks by leveraging this connection. This is practically relevant for both red-teamers (to stress-test systems) and defenders (to understand failure modes).
AI.method: The authors reformulate jailbreak optimization in probabilistic terms: they quantify harmfulness as a function over model outputs and consider its expectation under the model’s output distribution. They then derive an identity showing that the gradient of the log expected harmfulness with respect to the input is equal to an expectation of input gradients of the model’s log-likelihood, but under a reweighted output distribution where each output is weighted by its harmfulness. Using this, they design OPUR, a sampling distribution tailored to draw highly harmful outputs. Samples from OPUR are then used as target outputs in a likelihood-based optimization loop over inputs/prompts, effectively approximating the derived gradient identity in a practical algorithm.
AI.result: Theoretically, the paper provides a gradient identity that rigorously connects optimizing expected harmfulness and optimizing the likelihood of harmful targets. Empirically, experiments show that the OPUR-based method can reliably generate highly harmful target outputs and that the resulting likelihood-guided input optimization is effective at jailbreaking LLM agents, outperforming competing jailbreak strategies in their benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing prompts for expected harmfulness and optimizing for the likelihood of specific harmful targets are not fundamentally different problems; they are tightly linked via a probabilistic gradient identity. Exploiting this link enables the construction of OPUR, a practical sampling-based jailbreak method that empirically strengthens jailbreak attacks. This unified view can inform both the design of stronger red-teaming tools and the development of more robust defense mechanisms for LLM agents.

title: What the Sleeve Feels: Explainable Machine Learning for Textile Pressure-Based Postural Screening
summary: Pressure-sensing smart textiles convert body-surface contact into a dense, image-like signal closely tied to posture and movement, making them a promising low-cost route to wearable posture screening. Realizing that promise, however, requires more than classification accuracy: a deployable system must generalize to wearers unseen during training, expose the physical evidence behind its decisions, and tolerate the small donning offsets that occur whenever a garment is removed and re-worn. This paper addresses these three requirements jointly using a knitted piezoresistive sleeve worn on the forearm as a testbed. We regroup fine-grained everyday activities into three coarser screening categories (neutral, potentially undesirable, and functional or transitional), engineer 29 interpretable pressure-distribution features spanning global intensity, spatial center of pressure, quadrant asymmetry, distribution complexity, and short-horizon temporal change, and evaluate under a strict subject-wise split. A tuned XGBoost classifier reaches 0.818 accuracy, 0.788 balanced accuracy, and 0.801 macro F1 on unseen test subjects, with tight frame-level bootstrap 95% intervals of about plus-minus 0.01 and a subject-to-subject standard deviation near 0.06 under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. A simple 2D-CNN baseline trained on raw frames achieves broadly similar performance, showing that hand-engineered features are not left behind by a learned spatial representation on this task. SHAP-based explanation, a feature-group ablation, per-activity error analysis inside the pooled undesirable class, class-mapping sensitivity, and a simulated donning-rotation stress test together locate what the model relies on, where it degrades, and why, directly targeting the generalization, interpretability, and robustness gaps that determine whether such a system is deployable.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates an interpretable, robust, and generalizable posture-screening system using pressure-sensing smart textiles on the forearm.
AI.motivation: Smart textile wearables can capture detailed pressure maps related to posture and movement, but practical deployment requires models that not only classify well but also generalize to new users, are interpretable, and are robust to garment repositioning. Existing work often focuses mainly on accuracy without adequately addressing these deployment-oriented requirements.
AI.method: Using a knitted piezoresistive sleeve on the forearm, the authors group many everyday activities into three screening categories (neutral, potentially undesirable, functional/transitional). They design 29 physically interpretable features describing global pressure level, spatial center of pressure, quadrant asymmetry, distribution complexity, and short-term temporal change. They train an XGBoost classifier under a strict subject-wise split and compare it to a simple 2D-CNN trained on raw sensor frames. They further use SHAP explanations, feature-group ablations, detailed error analysis, class-mapping sensitivity tests, and simulated donning-rotation perturbations to probe generalization, interpretability, and robustness.
AI.result: The tuned XGBoost model achieves 0.818 accuracy, 0.788 balanced accuracy, and 0.801 macro F1 on test subjects unseen during training, with narrow frame-level 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (about ±0.01) and subject-level performance variability of about 0.06 under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. The 2D-CNN baseline on raw frames performs similarly, indicating that the hand-engineered, interpretable features are competitive with learned spatial representations for this problem.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a pressure-sensing smart sleeve, combined with carefully engineered interpretable features and a tree-based classifier, can deliver accurate, user-generalizable, and relatively robust posture screening. The similar performance of the CNN and feature-based model, together with SHAP and ablation analyses, clarifies which aspects of the pressure distribution the system relies on and where it fails, directly addressing key barriers to deployment such as generalization to new users, interpretability of decisions, and sensitivity to donning misalignments.

title: Learning to Accumulate Knowledge with Mutual Information
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve their performance by reusing knowledge distilled from past interactions. However, curating new experiences into a knowledge bank that becomes more useful as it grows remains challenging. Effective knowledge accumulation should limit redundant overlap among entries and ensure that new knowledge contributes beyond what the bank already provides. Yet training a curator with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on standalone task success can reinforce general guidance even when it duplicates existing knowledge. Therefore, we propose Knowledge Weaver, a reinforcement learning framework that trains a language model to curate reusable knowledge from agent trajectories. We couple feedback inspired by token-wise mutual information (MI) with marginal success rewards to guide knowledge accumulation. Together, these signals encourage the curator to preserve distinct information from experience and produce entries that improve task success when added to existing knowledge. Standalone success rewards also favor entries that are useful on their own. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Knowledge Weaver achieves mean success rates of 54.0\% and 42.0\% with k=10 retrieved entries, exceeding GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points, respectively. Its knowledge banks also outperform the evaluated prompt-based and established banks, including human-written banks, in overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score with the executor frozen. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/LaoKuiZe/Knowledge-Weaver.

AI.tldr: Knowledge Weaver is an RL framework that trains an LLM curator to build a non-redundant, high-utility knowledge bank from past agent trajectories, outperforming prior and even human-written knowledge banks on ALFWorld and WebShop.
AI.motivation: LLM agents benefit from reusing knowledge from past interactions, but existing methods struggle to build knowledge banks that become more useful as they grow. Simple success-based training can lead to redundant, generic guidance that duplicates existing entries rather than adding new, complementary knowledge. There is a need for a principled way to accumulate distinct, reusable knowledge that measurably improves downstream performance when combined with what is already known.
AI.method: The paper introduces Knowledge Weaver, a reinforcement learning framework for training a language model to curate knowledge from agent trajectories. Instead of optimizing only for standalone task success (as in GRPO), the curator is optimized with two main reward components: (1) a token-wise mutual-information-inspired signal that rewards preserving distinct, informative content from the trajectory relative to existing knowledge, and (2) marginal success rewards that measure how much adding a new entry to the current bank improves task performance when retrieved alongside existing entries. Standalone success rewards are also used so that entries are individually useful. The system retrieves the top-k entries from the bank at inference time to assist an executor agent on tasks such as ALFWorld and WebShop.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, Knowledge Weaver with k=10 retrieved entries attains mean success rates of 54.0% and 42.0%, improving over GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points, respectively. When the executor is frozen, knowledge banks curated by Knowledge Weaver outperform several baselines, including prompt-based banks and established human-written knowledge banks, in terms of overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge Weaver demonstrates that explicitly rewarding distinctiveness and marginal utility of knowledge entries leads to higher-quality, more reusable knowledge banks for LLM agents. By combining MI-inspired token-level signals with marginal success rewards, the framework avoids redundancy, accumulates complementary knowledge over time, and yields significant performance gains over GRPO-curated and human-written banks on interactive benchmarks. This suggests that careful RL-based curation of experiences can be a powerful way to continuously improve LLM agents via knowledge reuse.

title: Loud Failures, Quiet Failures: Fault Detection and Recovery in Tool-Using Language Model Agents
summary: Tool-using agents are usually scored on whether they finish a task while the tools work. Deployments are less forgiving: services time out, endpoints disappear, parameter names change, and results come back well formed but wrong. Prior work has shown that language models over-trust tool outputs that fail silently; we ask how that over-trust plays out across the stages of failure handling in multi-turn agents. Wrapping the executable environments of an established function-calling benchmark in a fault-injection layer, we inject one of four typed faults at a controlled point in the trajectory and record whether the agent notices, changes plan, recovers the task, or repeats itself. Six models from three families, half of them reasoning variants, ran 1,920 trials over 24 multi-step tasks. Agents treat a failure as a problem in 91.3% of trials when the tool returns an explicit error, but in 58.8% of trials when it returns a plausible wrong value, against a 26.8% rate of reporting problems when nothing was wrong. Reasoning models are not better placed: paired against instruct siblings, they notice less (-9.3 points, p < .001) and change plan more (+10.4 points, p < .001), and recovery is unchanged (p = .512). Because agents are stochastic, two fault-free runs of the same task end in the same state only 63.3% of the time; against that baseline, only a missing tool clearly lowers recovery (39.9%), while timeouts, schema drift, and corruption stay within run-to-run variation. After a fault, agents return to the same tool three or more times in a row in up to 22.2% of trials, though strictly identical repeats are rare. A prompt line asking the agent to check each result did not move detection. Agents respond to the error channel rather than to the content of what a tool returns, so failures that stay inside the expected format pass through.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how LLM-based tool-using agents handle different types of tool failures, finding they mainly react to explicit errors and often miss realistic, silent faults, with reasoning variants not improving recovery.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations for tool-using language-model agents usually assume tools behave correctly, while real-world deployments involve timeouts, API changes, and silent corruption. Prior work shows LLMs over-trust tools that fail silently, but it is unclear how this manifests across the full sequence of detecting, reacting to, and recovering from failures in multi-turn settings. The authors want to systematically test how agents behave under realistic, injected faults and whether advanced "reasoning" model variants improve robustness.
AI.method: The authors modify an established function-calling benchmark by wrapping each executable environment in a fault-injection layer. In controlled positions of multi-step task trajectories, they inject one of four fault types: missing tools, timeouts, schema drift (API changes), and plausible-but-wrong outputs. They then observe whether agents detect problems, change plans, recover the task, or get stuck in repetition. Six LLMs from three families (including reasoning and instruction-tuned variants) are evaluated over 1,920 runs on 24 multi-step tasks, and behavior is quantified and statistically compared between model types and fault conditions.
AI.result: Agents notice failures much more when tools surface explicit errors (91.3% of trials) than when tools return plausible but incorrect values (58.8%), and they also sometimes falsely report problems even when nothing is wrong (26.8%). Reasoning-oriented models are actually worse at noticing faults (by 9.3 percentage points) and more likely to change their plans (by 10.4 points), without improving ultimate recovery rates. Due to stochasticity, two clean runs of the same task match final states only 63.3% of the time; relative to this baseline, only missing-tool faults clearly reduce recovery (to 39.9%), while timeouts, schema drift, and silent corruption leave recovery within normal variability. After faults, agents can re-call the same tool three or more times in up to 22.2% of trials, though exact duplicate calls are uncommon. Adding a prompt instruction to "check each result" did not significantly enhance detection.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based tool-using agents mostly key off explicit error signals from tools instead of critically evaluating the semantic content of tool outputs. As a result, realistic silent faults that return well-formed but wrong data often evade detection, and more advanced reasoning variants do not fix this problem. Robust deployment of such agents will require architectural or tooling changes—such as explicit error channels, monitoring, or verification steps—rather than relying on model reasoning alone or simple prompt reminders to double-check tool results.

title: HGP:An on-device personalized agent memory via hybrid graph storage
summary: LLM-based agents face challenges in personalized interactive tasks due to heterogeneous, multi-typed, and implicitly constrained long-term traces. Existing memory mechanisms struggle with accurate routing and retrieval, especially on-device where personalization is critical. Most methods use single-vector representations, blurring type distinctions and relational structure. We propose HGP, a hybrid graph memory framework. HGP employs a lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing and constructs episodic, semantic, and procedural memories as graphs. It also extracts working memory as a state trajectory to capture current state and implicit constraints, ensuring reliable decision-making. The classifier reduces large-model calls, enabling on-device deployment, while graph storage enables accurate retrieval and incremental user profile refinement. Experiments on two benchmarks show that on PAL-Set solution selection, HGP achieves an S-score of 35.58, nearly 7 points above the strongest baseline. Code and data are at https://github.com/Ouan6/HGP-.git.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HGP, a hybrid graph-based memory framework that improves personalized decision-making for LLM agents by better routing and retrieving heterogeneous long-term user traces.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents must handle personalized, long-horizon interactions, often on-device, where user history is heterogeneous (different types, formats) and includes implicit constraints. Existing memory methods mostly compress all history into single vectors, losing type distinctions and relations, leading to poor routing, retrieval, and personalization, especially under resource constraints. The paper aims to design a memory mechanism that can accurately route, store, and retrieve diverse user traces while being lightweight enough for on-device deployment.
AI.method: HGP introduces a hybrid graph memory architecture with three graph-structured memory types: episodic, semantic, and procedural. A lightweight self-enhancement classifier first routes new interaction data to appropriate memory types, reducing heavy LLM calls. Each memory type is represented as a graph to preserve entities, relations, and structure instead of single-vector embeddings. Additionally, HGP maintains a working memory modeled as a state trajectory to capture the current interaction context and implicit constraints. This combination enables personalized, structure-aware retrieval and continual refinement of the user profile.
AI.result: On two benchmarks, including PAL-Set solution selection, HGP outperforms existing memory mechanisms. In particular, on PAL-Set, it reaches an S-score of 35.58, about 7 points higher than the strongest baseline, demonstrating better decision-making quality and more accurate solution selection in personalized settings.
AI.conclusion: HGP’s hybrid graph memory combined with a lightweight routing classifier and trajectory-based working memory improves personalized interactive performance of LLM agents, particularly in on-device scenarios. Graph-structured episodic, semantic, and procedural memories enable more precise retrieval and incremental user modeling than single-vector approaches, while the classifier reduces dependence on large models. The empirical gains on benchmarks suggest HGP is an effective and practical memory solution for personalized LLM agents.

title: RewardWeaver: Long-Horizon Interactive Learning for Language Agents via Self-Evolving Reward Adaptation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has driven substantial progress in domains where task outcomes can be reliably evaluated, but long-horizon interaction remains challenging due to sparse terminal feedback and difficult credit assignment. Process rewards provide denser supervision, yet the capabilities most relevant for training can change as the policy evolves: a behavior that is easy to evaluate or frequently deficient need not be the bottleneck currently limiting task success. We introduce RewardWeaver, a self-evolving reward adaptation framework for language agents in long-horizon interaction. RewardWeaver maintains a validated capability space in which the semantics of admitted Rubrics remain fixed, and closes the loop between policy optimization, task evaluation, failure attribution, and reward adaptation. After each training stage, it performs outcome-grounded backward attribution on low-outcome trajectories, aggregates recurrent and policy-controlled capability bottlenecks, and dynamically selects the corresponding process rewards for the next stage. Recurrent failures not covered by the existing capability space trigger a separate, controlled expansion procedure. We evaluate REWARDWEAVER on SOTOPIA, Amazon?HistoryPrice, and a newly constructed Sales Benchmark. Across social interaction, bilateral bargaining, and domain-specific sales, REWARDWEAVER establishes new state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. Ablations further demonstrate the importance of dynamic reward allocation, failure-grounded attribution, and stable semantics for admitted capabilities.

AI.tldr: RewardWeaver is a self-evolving reward adaptation framework that automatically discovers and focuses on the most critical capabilities to train language agents in long-horizon tasks, leading to state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon reinforcement learning for language agents, rewards are often sparse and only available at the end of an episode, making credit assignment difficult. Process rewards can provide denser feedback, but which intermediate behaviors matter most can change as the policy improves. Existing methods lack a mechanism to continually re-identify and emphasize the capabilities that are actually limiting task success, and to do so while keeping reward semantics stable and verifiable.
AI.method: RewardWeaver maintains a validated capability space, where each capability is described by a fixed-semantics rubric and associated process reward. Training proceeds in stages. After each stage, the system analyzes low-outcome trajectories via outcome-grounded backward attribution to determine which capabilities (or missing capabilities) most contributed to failure. It then aggregates recurrent, policy-controlled bottlenecks and dynamically selects the corresponding process rewards to emphasize in the next training stage. If failures arise that existing capabilities cannot explain, RewardWeaver invokes a controlled expansion procedure to extend the capability space with new, validated rubrics, while preserving stable semantics for previously admitted ones.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—SOTOPIA (social interaction), Amazon?HistoryPrice (bilateral bargaining), and a new Sales Benchmark (domain-specific sales)—RewardWeaver achieves new state-of-the-art performance for long-horizon language interaction tasks. Ablation studies show that removing or weakening components such as dynamic reward allocation, failure-grounded attribution, or the constraint of stable capability semantics leads to degraded performance, underscoring their importance.
AI.conclusion: A closed-loop, self-evolving reward adaptation framework that operates over a stable, validated capability space can substantially improve long-horizon reinforcement learning for language agents. By continuously attributing failures to specific capabilities and reallocating process rewards accordingly—while carefully expanding the capability space when needed—RewardWeaver overcomes sparse terminal feedback and shifting training bottlenecks, yielding superior performance across diverse interactive tasks.

title: UniSkill: Learning Actor-Aligned Skill Proposals for an Evolving Policy
summary: Large language model agents can improve across tasks by retaining reusable skills distilled from prior interactions. Recent work jointly optimizes task execution and skill extraction, enabling the policy and skillbank to co-evolve. However, as the actor continues learning, rewarding skill proposals through their reuse in subsequent training steps may conflate skill benefits with actor improvement, while directly testing each proposed skill requires costly additional actor rollouts. In this paper, we introduce UniSkill, which uses a shared policy to interact with the environment and propose skillbank edits (Add, Update, or No Edit) from the resulting trajectories. Specifically, the actor learns from environment rewards, while contrastive action feedback guides skill proposal learning. This feedback provides an actor-alignment signal by measuring how replacing the retrieved skill with a proposed skill changes the current actor's action log-likelihood gap between previously collected successful and failed trajectories from the same task, thereby avoiding new rollouts for each proposal. Since proposal-level feedback may suppress an otherwise appropriate edit operation when the proposed skill content scores poorly, we further apply skill-edit support regularization to preserve exploration. Empirically, UniSkill achieves strong performance, reaching 98.4% success on ALFWorld and 84.7% on WebShop while maintaining stable joint training. Further ALFWorld experiments show that UniSkill remains effective when the shared policy uses a smaller backbone. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LimOkii/UniSKill.

AI.tldr: UniSkill is a method for training LLM agents that jointly optimizes a shared policy and a skill library using contrastive feedback, avoiding expensive rollouts for each new skill and achieving strong performance on ALFWorld and WebShop.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent methods that learn reusable skills suffer from a credit assignment problem: as the underlying policy improves, it becomes hard to disentangle whether a skill is genuinely useful or merely appears so because the actor has become better overall. Naively evaluating each proposed skill also requires many extra environment rollouts, which is computationally expensive and unstable. The authors aim to create a more sample-efficient and stable way to co-train a policy and a skillbank without conflating policy improvement with skill quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce UniSkill, which uses a single shared policy both to act in the environment and to propose edits to a skillbank. The skillbank can be modified via three operations: Add, Update, or No Edit. The actor is trained using standard environment rewards. Skill proposal learning, however, is driven by contrastive action feedback: they measure how substituting the retrieved skill with a proposed skill changes the log-likelihood gap between successful and failed trajectories on the same task under the current actor. This serves as an alignment signal for the skill proposals that does not require new rollouts for each candidate skill. To prevent overly conservative editing due to noisy skill content quality at the proposal level, they introduce skill-edit support regularization, which encourages exploration of skill edits even if some proposals initially appear suboptimal.
AI.result: UniSkill achieves 98.4% success on ALFWorld and 84.7% on WebShop, demonstrating that it can effectively learn reusable skills while maintaining stable joint training of the actor and the skillbank. Additional experiments on ALFWorld show that UniSkill remains effective even when the shared policy uses a smaller model backbone, indicating robustness and efficiency in lower-capacity settings.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that UniSkill provides an efficient and stable framework for jointly training language model agents and their skill libraries. By leveraging contrastive action feedback over existing successful and failed trajectories, it disentangles skill quality from general policy improvement and avoids the need for per-skill rollouts. Skill-edit support regularization further balances stability with exploration. The strong empirical results on ALFWorld and WebShop suggest UniSkill is a practical approach for scalable skill acquisition in LLM-based agents.

title: Agentic AI-Assisted Modeling for Production Scheduling: Assessment in Constraint Programming
summary: Developing optimization models for production scheduling requires substantial expert effort. Research on large language models (LLMs) has followed two directions: specialized approaches for automated modeling, mostly for mixed-integer linear programming, which often rely on dedicated training or problem-specific architectures that limit industrial deployment; and agentic artificial intelligence for operational decision support, which generally assumes that the optimization model already exists. This study bridges both directions by assessing whether general-purpose LLMs, orchestrated as agents without task-specific training, can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural-language problem descriptions. Singleagent and multi-agent architectures are integrated with a Model Context Protocol server that provides context-aware retrieval of solver documentation to mitigate hallucinations during implementation. Both are compared with a direct LLM baseline on six industry-oriented problems covering flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop and resource-constrained warehouse scheduling, using three LLMs and assessing modeling accuracy, execution success, latency and token consumption. Formulation proves largely within reach of current LLMs, whereas implementation is the main barrier. The multi-agent workflow raises the share of scripts that run correctly as generated from 14.8% with a direct LLM call to 59.3%, reaching 80.6% on the four less complex problems, while tightly coupled intralogistics models remain an open challenge.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether general-purpose LLM agents can automatically formulate and implement constraint programming scheduling models from natural language, showing multi-agent setups drastically improve executable code generation but complex intralogistics remain difficult.
AI.motivation: Building optimization models for production scheduling is expert- and time-intensive. Existing LLM work either focuses on narrowly trained, problem-specific modeling systems (mainly MILP) that don’t generalize well to industry, or on agentic decision-support that assumes a model already exists. There is a gap: can off-the-shelf, general LLMs, without special training, directly turn natural-language industrial scheduling problems into working constraint programming models?
AI.method: The authors design single-agent and multi-agent LLM architectures that generate constraint programming models from textual problem descriptions. These agents are connected to a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that retrieves relevant solver documentation to reduce hallucinations during code implementation. They benchmark these architectures against a simple direct LLM prompting baseline on six realistic scheduling problems (flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop, and warehouse/resource-constrained cases), using three different LLMs. They then measure modeling correctness, code execution success, runtime latency, and token usage.
AI.result: LLMs can generally capture the mathematical formulation of scheduling problems, but reliably implementing these formulations as correct, executable constraint programming scripts is challenging. The direct LLM baseline yields only 14.8% of scripts that run successfully. The proposed multi-agent workflow increases this to 59.3% overall and up to 80.6% on the four simpler problem classes, while performance on tightly coupled intralogistics/warehouse models remains poor.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose LLMs, when orchestrated as agents with access to solver documentation, can already automate a substantial part of formulating and coding constraint programming models for many industrial scheduling problems. However, implementation reliability is still a bottleneck, especially for complex, tightly integrated intralogistics settings. Multi-agent designs significantly improve executable code generation over a single direct call, but future research is needed to handle more complex models and close the gap to industrial robustness.

title: OOM-RL II: Reality Is an Oracle, Not a Debugger Provenance-Constrained Diagnosis in Continually Evolving Agent-Engineered Systems
comment: 38 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Supplementary Dataset S1: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23215521. Follow-up to arXiv:2604.11477
summary: Reality may establish that an outcome occurred without identifying which evolving procedure produced it or why. This distinction matters in production ML systems whose code, configuration, and artifacts change while external feedback accumulates. We examine it in a human-directed, agent-engineered quantitative trading system, using oracle to mean an external source of realized outcomes rather than a complete correctness specification. Across one year, the account gained and outperformed a broad market index, while annual alpha was not statistically distinguishable from zero under the main retrospective specification. Retrospectively selected subperiods include adverse relative performance and conditional candidate-level weakness under declared approximate references. Engineering records document changes during the episode, and complete recommendation-to-runtime binding is unavailable. The archive does not establish a common frozen instance or a unique cause. The case motivates an outcome--diagnosis gap: outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation support distinct claims. We distinguish frozen instances, pre-specified adaptive procedures, and ad-hoc development; organize archive-relative claim identifiability and an evidence hierarchy; and propose a prospective production-binding protocol. An illustrative compatible-history example shows how factual binding can resolve a recommendation's referent without supplying its counterfactual effect. The protocol is proposed rather than prospectively validated. External feedback constrains outcome claims, while provenance and additional identification structure determine the resolution of diagnosis.

AI.tldr: Case study of a production ML-based trading system showing that good realized performance does not, by itself, identify which evolving system produced it or why, and proposing a protocol to better bind recommendations to concrete system instances for future diagnosis.
AI.motivation: In real-world ML systems, especially in finance, code, configs, models, and data pipelines evolve while outcomes (profits, losses, feedback) are realized. After the fact, it can be unclear which exact system instance produced which outcome, or whether performance is due to skill, luck, or ad-hoc changes. This undermines claims about model quality, causal attribution, and scientific validity. The paper is motivated by this practical and epistemic gap between observing outcomes and being able to diagnose what they say about a system.
AI.method: The authors analyze a one-year deployment of a human-directed, agent-based quantitative trading system. They treat the market as an oracle providing realized outcomes (profits/returns). They evaluate performance versus a broad market index and estimate alpha under retrospective specifications. They inspect subperiods for adverse performance and conditional weaknesses. They use engineering records to reconstruct how the system changed over time and assess how well recommendations can be bound to specific code/config/model instances. On this basis they develop a conceptual framework distinguishing frozen instances, pre-specified adaptive procedures, and ad-hoc development; they define an evidence hierarchy and archive-relative identifiability of claims; and they design a prospective production-binding protocol. They include an illustrative “compatible-history” example showing how factual binding can identify which instance made a recommendation without establishing its counterfactual impact.
AI.result: Empirically, over the year the account gained and beat a broad market index, but the estimated annual alpha is not statistically distinguishable from zero under the main retrospective model. Certain retrospectively chosen subperiods show underperformance and conditional weaknesses relative to approximate reference strategies. Reconstruction of engineering records reveals numerous changes and incomplete binding between recommendations and the exact runtime configurations that produced them. The archive is insufficient to pin realized outcomes to a single frozen system instance or unique cause. Conceptually, they produce a taxonomy of system-evolution modes (frozen, pre-specified adaptive, ad-hoc), an associated evidence hierarchy, and a protocol for prospectively binding production recommendations to concrete instances while separating factual identification from counterfactual effect estimation.
AI.conclusion: The case study demonstrates an outcome–diagnosis gap in evolving ML production systems: even when external feedback (like trading performance) is available and positive, it may not support strong claims about which system instance was responsible or why it succeeded. Outcome evidence, identity of the evaluated object, and causal explanation are distinct and require different kinds of support. To improve scientific and operational rigor, systems should implement prospective production-binding protocols and richer provenance tracking so that each recommendation can be unambiguously tied to a frozen instance or well-specified adaptive procedure. External feedback constrains what we can say about outcomes, but robust provenance and identification structure are needed to meaningfully diagnose and interpret system behavior.

title: Stale, Misattributed, or Late: Where Personal Memory Fails Before Generation
summary: Personal memory for language agents is usually judged by whether the final an- swer is correct. That score hides errors that arise before generation: the memory block may contain an obsolete value, a fact about the wrong person, or no use- ful fact before the serving deadline. We measure these failures directly. Using Personal Fact Memory (PFM) as a reference layer, we find that temporal validity is primarily a property of memory construction in our setting. On a controlled revision benchmark, serving only the active value of each correctly keyed slot eliminates observed stale exposure; without update resolution, 70.3% of prompts expose a superseded value. Once retrievers share the same active store and par- ticipant information, participant-aware BM25 is equivalent to the reference ranker within a prespecified 0.02 margin. The harder problem is assigning revisions to the right slot. Missed merges leave stale values active, whereas false merges silently remove current values; four LLM key assigners achieve higher key re- call than a rule extractor yet produce lower clean-retrieval rates, and open-domain merge recall on LongMemEval never exceeds 0.062. Misattribution survives va- lidity filtering: an entity posterior reduces same-name exposure on controlled data but cannot distinguish identically named speakers in LoCoMo. Two frozen lan- guage models reproduce prompt errors in generated text. Retrieval latency varies across rankers, but prompt prefill dominates turn-level latency on our hardware. These results argue for evaluating agent memory before generation, separating stored-state validity, identity resolution, abstention, and serving latency.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes failure modes in personal memory systems for language agents, showing that many errors arise before answer generation, especially from stale or misattributed facts, and argues for evaluating memory components separately from generation.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of personal memory for language agents typically look only at whether the final answer is correct, which hides distinct upstream problems such as storing obsolete facts, mixing up people with similar attributes, or failing to retrieve in time. The authors want to expose and quantify these hidden memory-specific failure modes, understand where they originate (construction vs. retrieval), and provide guidance on how to better design and evaluate agent memory systems.
AI.method: They introduce Personal Fact Memory (PFM) as a reference memory layer and run controlled benchmarks focusing on temporal revisions, key assignment, and identity resolution. They compare different retrieval strategies (e.g., participant-aware BM25 vs. a reference ranker), manipulate whether only active (non-stale) values are served, and examine the impact of update resolution. They evaluate multiple LLM-based key assigners against a rule-based extractor on clean-retrieval rates and key recall, and measure open-domain merge performance on LongMemEval. They also test entity posteriors for disambiguating same-name individuals, evaluate misattribution persistence, and show that frozen language models reproduce retrieval-induced prompt errors in generated text. Finally, they profile latency contributions of retrieval vs. prompt prefill.
AI.result: On a revision benchmark, if each correctly keyed slot only serves its active value, stale exposure disappears; without proper update resolution, 70.3% of prompts reveal superseded information. Once all retrievers use the same active store and participant data, a participant-aware BM25 retriever matches the reference ranker within 0.02 performance margin, indicating retrieval ranking is not the main bottleneck under these conditions. The more difficult challenge is keying and merging: incorrect merges can either leave obsolete values active or drop current ones. Although four different LLM-based key assigners achieve higher key recall than a rule-based extractor, they yield worse clean-retrieval rates. Open-domain merge recall on LongMemEval stays very low (≤0.062). Even with validity filtering, misattribution persists: entity posteriors reduce same-name collisions on controlled datasets but fail on realistic multi-speaker settings like LoCoMo. Two frozen LMs replicate prompt-level memory errors in their outputs. Latency analysis shows ranker choice matters less than the dominant cost of prompt prefill on the tested hardware.
AI.conclusion: Many errors in agent “personal memory” stem from how facts are stored, keyed, merged, and attributed, not just from retrieval ranking or generation. Temporal validity is mainly a memory-construction issue; identity resolution and merge decisions are major sources of stale or missing information. Because frozen LMs propagate prompt memory errors and retrieval latency is often overshadowed by prompt prefill, the authors argue that memory components should be evaluated independently of answer generation, with explicit metrics for stored-state validity, identity resolution quality, abstention behavior, and serving latency.

title: AI Safety Considerations for Agents With Limited Time to Act
summary: In the wake of the increasingly public discussion about AI alignment, recent work has tried to propose specific AI architectures that behave safely. However, the proposed arguments that seemingly demonstrate proved alignment mostly neglect the environment the agent needs to act in. We discuss theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees in environments that can only be partially observed and within which an action is required within limited time. We introduce two realistic scenarios, one with an infinite state space and one with signal mixture. In these scenarios, we prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behaviour. It will be argued that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions need to be specifically considered together with the agent.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that in partially observable, time-constrained environments, it is impossible to provide agent-agnostic, fully proved safety guarantees for AI; safety must be reasoned about jointly over agent and environment.
AI.motivation: Existing work on AI alignment often claims to prove that certain AI architectures are safe or aligned, but typically abstracts away from the complexity and uncertainty of real-world environments. The authors want to challenge the idea that you can have environment-independent, fully formal safety guarantees and highlight fundamental limits on such guarantees when agents must act under partial observability and time pressure.
AI.method: The authors study AI safety in a formal decision-theoretic setting where agents operate in partially observable environments with limited time to choose actions. They define two illustrative, realistic scenarios: one with an infinite state space and another where observable signals are mixtures of multiple underlying factors. For these two scenarios, they provide theoretical analysis and proofs showing that, even for an idealized, perfect agent, one cannot guarantee safe behavior in all cases when the environment is only partially observed and decisions must be timely.
AI.result: For both the infinite state space scenario and the signal mixture scenario, the authors prove impossibility-type results: even a perfect decision-making agent cannot ensure guaranteed safe behavior under the given constraints. These bounds show that there are environments where, irrespective of how well-designed or aligned the agent is, unavoidable uncertainty and time limits can force potentially unsafe actions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that any rigorous proof of AI safety or alignment must explicitly model the environment and what constitutes safe actions within that environment; environment-agnostic, purely agent-internal proofs of safety are insufficient. Safety guarantees, if they exist at all, are inherently joint properties of the agent-environment system, and in some realistic partially observable, time-constrained settings, full safety guarantees are provably impossible.

title: The Handover Problem: Governing Autonomy Transitions in Human-AI Collaboration
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Human-Machine Systems
summary:
Human-machine systems rarely operate at a fixed level of AI autonomy. As operators and AI systems collaborate over time, control must shift: the AI can take on more responsibility when collaboration is stable, maintain its current role when evidence is ambiguous, or return control to the human when conditions deteriorate. Existing work on adaptive automation, supervisory control, trust in automation, and deskilling explains parts of this problem, but provides no auditable, multi-signal criterion for governing when autonomy should change across multi-cycle workflows.
  We formalise this challenge as the Handover Problem: deciding, at each operational cycle, whether to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy while keeping the process reversible, recoverable, and auditable. We introduce the Handover Readiness Score (HRS), a transparent composite measure that integrates four signal dimensions: operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, and operational performance. It is combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy that requires sustained positive evidence before increasing autonomy but reverts promptly when conditions worsen.
  Across software engineering and manufacturing domains, the HRS and hard safety guards address complementary failure regimes: guards enforce immediate corrective action when a single indicator breaches a critical threshold, while the HRS detects the slow, multi-signal erosion of operator readiness that no individual guard can observe. The framework establishes autonomy handover as a governance problem requiring explicit, composite, and auditable criteria. This provides a conceptual and formal foundation that adaptive automation research has not previously provided.

AI.tldr: The paper defines the ‘Handover Problem’ of deciding when and how to shift AI autonomy in human‑machine systems, proposes a composite Handover Readiness Score (HRS) built from four signal dimensions plus safety guards, and offers a formal, auditable framework for autonomy governance across operational cycles.
AI.motivation: In real human‑AI collaborations, autonomy cannot stay fixed: sometimes AI should assume more control, sometimes it must hand control back to humans. Existing research on adaptive automation, trust, and supervisory control addresses aspects of this but lacks a unified, auditable, multi-signal criterion for deciding *when* to change autonomy levels in ongoing, multi-cycle workflows. This gap makes autonomy shifts ad hoc, opaque, and potentially unsafe or irreversible.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize the decision of escalating, maintaining, or reverting AI autonomy at each operational cycle as the ‘Handover Problem’; (2) define a Handover Readiness Score (HRS) that aggregates four types of signals—operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, and operational performance—into a transparent metric; and (3) specify a hysteresis-based transition policy that raises autonomy only after sustained positive evidence but lowers it rapidly when conditions degrade. They apply this framework conceptually to domains such as software engineering and manufacturing, and discuss how it interacts with hard safety guards.
AI.result: The result is a governance framework rather than a single algorithmic performance number: a structured, multi-signal HRS metric and associated transition policy that distinguish fast, single-signal failures (handled by hard guards) from slow, multi-signal degradation (captured by the HRS). The framework shows how to maintain reversibility, recoverability, and auditability for autonomy shifts over time and clarifies complementary roles of safety thresholds and composite readiness scores.
AI.conclusion: Autonomy handover should be treated as a governance problem with explicit, composite, and auditable criteria, not as ad hoc tuning of automation levels. The HRS plus hysteresis policy provide a conceptual and formal foundation for safely managing dynamic AI autonomy, filling a gap in prior adaptive automation work and illuminating how to better coordinate humans and AI across repeated operational cycles.

title: Open-MMUnlearning: Unifying Methods and Evaluation for MLLM Unlearning
summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become more capable and widely deployed, concerns about privacy and safety have become increasingly pressing.
