Machine unlearning offers one approach to addressing these concerns by removing designated information from trained models while preserving unrelated capabilities. However, fragmented implementations and evaluation protocols, incomplete robustness testing, and limited understanding of metric reliability make progress in MLLM unlearning difficult to assess systematically. We introduce Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source, extensible framework that integrates target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation through shared interfaces and structured configurations. The framework supports five benchmarks spanning privacy, safety, and copyright, eight MLLMs from four model families, and twelve unlearning methods. Its evaluation suite jointly assesses forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to model interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. Using a common evaluation protocol, we compare ten representative unlearning methods. In this comparison, GD and MIP-Editor tie for the highest overall score: GD achieves the highest Forget Quality, while MIP-Editor preserves more Model Utility. We further introduce a metric meta-evaluation protocol that tests faithfulness using models with controlled exposure to target knowledge and robustness under quantization and relearning. Among the thirteen evaluated metrics, BLEU achieves the highest aggregate reliability score. KS-Test attains the highest faithfulness AUC but performs less well on robustness. Together, the framework and these findings support reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source framework to standardize and evaluate machine unlearning methods for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), along with a meta-evaluation of unlearning metrics.
AI.motivation: As MLLMs become more powerful and widely deployed, there are growing privacy, safety, and copyright concerns about specific data they may memorize. Existing unlearning work is fragmented, uses inconsistent setups, lacks robustness testing, and offers limited understanding of how reliable different evaluation metrics are, making it hard to compare or trust unlearning methods. The authors aim to provide a unified, reproducible way to benchmark both unlearning methods and the metrics used to evaluate them.
AI.method: The authors build Open-MMUnlearning, an extensible framework that standardizes the pipeline for MLLM unlearning: target-model preparation, multimodal data handling, execution of different unlearning algorithms, and evaluation through shared interfaces and configuration files. They integrate 5 benchmarks (privacy, safety, copyright), 8 MLLMs from 4 families, and 12 unlearning methods. They design an evaluation suite measuring forgetting effectiveness, retained model utility, and robustness against model interventions, adversarial prompts, and membership inference attacks. They then run a common evaluation protocol to compare 10 unlearning methods. Additionally, they propose a metric meta-evaluation protocol that constructs models with controlled exposure to target knowledge and tests metrics under quantization and relearning to study metric faithfulness and robustness.
AI.result: In their empirical comparison, GD and MIP-Editor obtain the best overall unlearning performance: GD yields the strongest forgetting (highest Forget Quality), whereas MIP-Editor better preserves general model utility. In the metric meta-evaluation over 13 metrics, BLEU has the best overall reliability score, while KS-Test shows the highest faithfulness AUC but is less robust to conditions like quantization and relearning.
AI.conclusion: Open-MMUnlearning provides a unified, open-source framework for reproducible and systematic assessment of MLLM unlearning methods, accounting for effectiveness, utility retention, and robustness. Their extensive benchmarking clarifies trade-offs between leading unlearning techniques and shows that common metrics vary substantially in reliability, with BLEU performing best overall. The framework and meta-evaluation protocol together offer a foundation for more principled development and comparison of future unlearning approaches and evaluation metrics for MLLMs.

title: SOTA: Stock Options Trading Agents Guided by Option-Implied Return Distributions
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Agenthon Workshop
summary: As option markets grow and AI advances, agentic systems for option trading are gaining increasing attention. Language-model-based agents can reason over contextual information such as news, but option trading presents a particularly challenging decision problem: a single stock can have thousands of contracts, and the agent must decide both which contracts to trade and how to combine them. Existing approaches often sidestep this complexity by restricting the policy to a fixed strategy structure, such as a straddle, limiting their ability to switch strategies as market conditions change. We present SOTA (Stock Options Trading Agents), an agentic trading framework for structured option-strategy selection. SOTA abstracts the large option universe into strategy-level decisions while deterministic resolvers handle portfolio implementation. We develop SOTA by post-training Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. SOTA is evaluated on options on nine large-cap U.S. equities and SPY against rule-based and machine-learning strategy selectors in the same trading environment. Over a six-month out-of-sample period, SOTA earns an 18.3% total return with a Sharpe ratio of 1.60 and a maximum drawdown of 8.96%. We also document an asymmetric role of news: news improves frontier-teacher trajectories, but retaining news during reinforcement learning reduces out-of-sample return from 18.3% to -2.7%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SOTA, an agentic options-trading framework that lets an LLM pick among structured option strategies rather than individual contracts, achieving strong returns and Sharpe on U.S. equities but revealing that including news during RL hurts performance.
AI.motivation: Options markets are complex because each underlying stock has thousands of contracts and many possible multi-leg strategies. Existing LLM-based trading agents usually constrain themselves to a fixed pattern (e.g., straddles), which prevents dynamic adaptation to market conditions. The authors want a scalable, flexible LLM-based system that can select among a rich set of option strategies while handling the combinatorial explosion of contracts and understanding contextual signals such as news.
AI.method: They design SOTA, a two-layer framework: (1) an LLM (Qwen3.8-27B) makes high-level strategy decisions over an abstracted strategy space, and (2) deterministic resolvers translate chosen strategies into concrete portfolios over the large universe of option contracts. The LLM is post-trained via supervised fine-tuning and then reinforcement learning. They also conduct an ablation on the role of news by comparing models trained and run with vs. without news inputs during RL.
AI.result: On options for nine large-cap U.S. stocks and SPY over a six‑month out‑of‑sample period, SOTA achieves an 18.3% total return, a Sharpe ratio of 1.60, and a maximum drawdown of 8.96%, outperforming rule-based and machine-learning strategy selectors in the same simulated trading environment. When news information is kept during RL, out‑of‑sample performance drops sharply, with total return falling from 18.3% to -2.7%.
AI.conclusion: Abstraction to strategy-level decisions enables LLM-based agents to handle the combinatorial complexity of options while maintaining flexibility across strategies, yielding strong risk-adjusted returns in backtests. However, the impact of news is asymmetric: it helps generate better supervised trajectories but degrades performance when retained during RL, suggesting that naive integration of high-dimensional contextual data into RL for trading can be harmful. The framework highlights both the promise and fragility of agentic LLMs for complex financial decision-making.

title: Before They Can Solve: Predicting Post-Training Coding-Agent Performance from Base Models
summary: How can we predict which base checkpoint is worth an expensive round of agentic post-training? End-to-end pass@$K$ tests whether successful behavior already appears in a base model's distribution, but it is a poor fit for agentic coding: many base checkpoints cannot reliably produce the well-formed tool invocation required to complete a task end-to-end. Single-shot or short-horizon tasks avoid these tool-calling failures by collapsing a multi-step interaction into a fixed prompt and a single patch, but they sidestep the core capability we care about: maintaining coherent state over many tool-using steps as the repository evolves. To bridge this gap, we treat successful post-trained agent trajectories as a lookahead signal of base-model potential. Replaying each trajectory and rerunning tests after every code-changing step identifies the decisive step: the first step whose cumulative patch flips the repository from failing to passing, certifying that the recorded action solves the task given the prior context. Motivated by a coverage principle for agentic traces, we build three screens at this step that do not require a base checkpoint to drive the harness from a cold start: (i) Decisive-Action BPB (bits per byte) measures the probability mass on the certified action, (ii) Patch MCQ tests the checkpoint's choice between that action and alternatives rejected by the same verifier, and (iii) prefix-conditioned pass@$K$ evaluates support for functionally-correct generations and credits any continuation that the tests accept. Across ten pairs of public base and post-trained models, all three screens rank the cohort in close agreement with post-trained SWE-bench Verified pass@$1$. As our methods need only a benchmark's successful trajectories and its verifier, they can be applied to turn future agentic coding benchmarks into base-model evaluations.

AI.tldr: They propose new ways to evaluate which base language models are worth expensive agentic post-training for coding, by using successful post-trained trajectories as a signal of base-model potential instead of standard pass@K.
AI.motivation: Standard end-to-end pass@K is a bad predictor for agentic coding because many base models fail at tool invocation and multi-step interactions, even if they might have the underlying capability when guided. Short-horizon or single-shot tasks avoid tool-calling issues but also avoid testing the long-horizon, multi-step, stateful behavior that matters for agentic coding. There is a need for a better screening method that predicts how well a base checkpoint will respond to post-training for agentic coding, without having to run full cold-start agentic evaluations for every candidate model.
AI.method: The authors use successful trajectories from post-trained agentic coding agents as a lookahead signal for assessing base models. For each successful trajectory, they replay it step by step, re-running the benchmark’s verifier after each code-changing action to find the decisive step at which the cumulative patch flips the repository from failing to passing. This decisive step defines an action that is certified to solve the task in its current context. Around this decisive step they design three model-agnostic screening metrics that do not require the base model to run the full agentic process from scratch: (i) Decisive-Action BPB, which computes the log-probability (bits per byte) that the base model assigns to the decisive action; (ii) Patch MCQ, a multiple-choice test where the base model must choose between the certified decisive action and alternative patches that were rejected by the benchmark’s verifier; and (iii) prefix-conditioned pass@K, where they condition on the trajectory prefix up to the decisive step and then sample continuations, counting a success whenever the verifier accepts the resulting repository.
AI.result: On ten pairs of public base and post-trained models evaluated on SWE-bench Verified, these three screening methods all produce rankings of base checkpoints that closely match the ranking obtained from the post-trained agents’ pass@1 scores. This indicates that the proposed metrics are good predictors of how beneficial agentic post-training will be for each base model. The approaches succeed without needing to run full agentic evaluations from a cold start for each candidate base model.
AI.conclusion: Using successful post-trained agent trajectories as a coverage-guided lookahead signal enables practical, verifier-based screening metrics for base models aimed at agentic coding. The three proposed screens—Decisive-Action BPB, Patch MCQ, and prefix-conditioned pass@K—provide reliable proxies for eventual post-trained performance, using only benchmark trajectories and verifiers. This framework can turn future agentic coding benchmarks, which typically focus on post-trained agents, into useful tools for evaluating and selecting base checkpoints before investing in expensive agentic post-training.

title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
summary: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.

AI.tldr: EmbodiedRSI is a self-evolving agentic harness that efficiently improves robot foundation models by actively selecting informative real-world experiments and co-evolving code, skills, and memory, achieving large performance gains and strong zero-shot transfer to real robots.
AI.motivation: Robot foundation models are powerful but brittle: their performance drops when object layouts or task instructions change, and improving them typically requires expensive post-training on large amounts of robot data collected via teleoperation. Existing self-evolving agentic harnesses can adapt without retraining the base model but use physical robot trials inefficiently, lacking principled methods for deciding which behaviors, code changes, or skill updates to try next. There is a need for a system that can autonomously and efficiently explore, turning limited physical interaction into targeted, high-value updates to policies and supporting code.
AI.method: The paper proposes EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that wraps around robot foundation models. It uses a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture. The Fast System maintains a Hypothesis Graph of competing code and skill variants and applies Value-of-Information Experiment Selection to choose real-world robot experiments that best distinguish between hypotheses. Outcomes of these experiments drive Code-Skill Co-Evolution, updating both procedural code and learned skills. The Slow System constructs a Hierarchical Memory of experiences, abstractions, and prior improvements. Reward-Grounded Memory Learning evaluates memory elements based on their contribution to downstream Fast-System improvement and retains those that are most useful, creating a feedback loop between memory, exploration, and policy/code refinement.
AI.result: On the RoboCasa365 benchmark, EmbodiedRSI achieves 77.0% overall success and 71.3% success on the challenging Composite-Unseen split, substantially outperforming the best baseline at 40.1%. On the LIBERO-Pro benchmark, it reaches 86.8% overall success. The method also demonstrates strong sim-to-real capabilities: when transferred zero-shot to a physical robot on multiple difficult tasks, EmbodiedRSI attains 71.3% overall success without task-specific real-world fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: EmbodiedRSI shows that an agentic, self-evolving harness with principled experiment selection, hypothesis-driven code/skill evolution, and reward-grounded hierarchical memory can dramatically improve the data efficiency and robustness of robot foundation models. By autonomously deciding what to try next and reusing structured memory to guide exploration and updates, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmarks and demonstrates robust zero-shot transfer to real robots. This suggests a promising direction for scalable, low-supervision adaptation of general robot policies in dynamic and previously unseen environments.

title: RECAST: Learning to Compute the Right Context through Adaptive Evidence Routing
summary: Large language models are increasingly applied to tasks grounded in long, heterogeneous information sources. Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) relies on fixed similarity-based retrieval, while agentic variants adapt queries and tool use but remain largely retrieval-centric. However, in many tasks, the evidence required for a solution is not explicitly present in any single source item. Instead, it must be derived through filtering, aggregation, or computation across multiple source items. In this work, we introduce RECAST (Routing Evidence through Computation, Access, and Synthesized Tools), a learned framework that formulates evidence construction as a sequential decision process over heterogeneous retrieval and computation operations, allowing evidence to be actively derived rather than merely retrieved. A lightweight RouterLM iteratively selects and formulates primitive operations or specifies customized operations for a frozen CompilerLM to translate into executable code. Once it judges the evidence sufficient, RouterLM passes the accepted evidence to a frozen AnswerLM to produce the final solution. We train RouterLM with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by group relative policy optimization (GRPO). Across six heterogeneous benchmark families, RECAST achieves a mean success rate of 75.6%, outperforming the strongest large-model baseline by 15.9%. Moreover, training enables the Qwen3.5-9B RouterLM to outperform a training-free Gemini 3.5 Flash RouterLM by 5.0%. On three held-out benchmarks, RECAST improves over the strongest baseline by 15.0% on average, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization across tasks and heterogeneous source representations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RECAST, a framework that treats evidence construction for RAG as a sequential decision process involving retrieval and computation, significantly improving success rates over strong baselines on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems focus on retrieving relevant documents using fixed similarity-based methods or more adaptive agentic querying, but they assume that necessary evidence is explicitly contained within individual retrieved items. Many real tasks require combining, filtering, and computing over multiple heterogeneous sources to construct evidence that is not directly stated in any single document. There is a need for a method that can actively derive such evidence, not just retrieve it, especially across diverse tasks and source formats.
AI.method: The authors introduce RECAST (Routing Evidence through Computation, Access, and Synthesized Tools), which frames evidence construction as a sequential decision process. A lightweight RouterLM iteratively chooses operations, including primitive retrieval/computation steps and requests for custom tools. When custom tools are needed, RouterLM specifies them and a frozen CompilerLM converts these specifications into executable code. RouterLM also decides when sufficient evidence has been gathered and then passes this curated evidence set to a frozen AnswerLM that produces the final answer. RouterLM is trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to learn effective routing strategies.
AI.result: On six heterogeneous benchmark families, RECAST achieves a mean success rate of 75.6%, beating the strongest large-model baseline by 15.9%. A trained Qwen3.5-9B-based RouterLM within RECAST surpasses a training-free Gemini 3.5 Flash RouterLM by 5.0%. On three additional held-out benchmarks, RECAST still outperforms the best baseline by an average of 15.0%, indicating strong zero-shot generalization to new tasks and varied source representations.
AI.conclusion: Modeling evidence construction as a learned sequence of retrieval and computation operations enables large gains over traditional and agentic RAG approaches. RECAST shows that a trained router controlling both access to information and program synthesis for computation can generalize well across heterogeneous tasks, actively deriving evidence rather than relying on direct retrieval alone.

title: SciExam for ENSO: Can AI Agents Build Climate Models?
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out open-ended scientific research, yet their results are usually graded against a known answer, a rubric, or a language-model reviewer, none of which can tell whether a new scientific model is valid. The AI Science Exam for El Nino-Southern Oscillation (SciExam for ENSO) is a benchmark in which agents build low-order stochastic models of ENSO, the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, from real observations. Within a six-hour budget, agents process the observations, write their own diagnostics, which are then frozen, and develop a model using only these diagnostics as feedback. Hidden graders then test whether the model reproduces ENSO's statistics, recovers unobserved variables, and forecasts held-out years, and score a published model in the same way. Across twelve agent systems, six produce models that score higher than the published model, mainly through better reconstruction and forecasting. The simplified forms of the stronger models are each compatible with one of the two competing explanations of ENSO's warm-cold asymmetry, an open debate that the task never mentions. Controlled runs of the top system under varied information suggest that its scores do not come from recalling the dated observational record and that the information it receives shapes how it builds its model. SciExam for ENSO can thus evaluate agent research where no answer is known, and the results suggest that agents can already build competitive models whose structures bear on questions that scientists still debate.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SciExam for ENSO, a benchmark where language-model agents must build and evaluate their own stochastic models of El Niño-Southern Oscillation from real data, without access to ground-truth solutions, demonstrating that some agents can produce models that outperform a published baseline and relate to active scientific debates.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of language-model agents in science rely on known answers, rubrics, or LLM-based grading, which cannot validate genuinely new scientific models. The authors want a way to test whether agents can conduct original, open-ended scientific modeling that has no predefined correct solution, in a domain (ENSO) that is scientifically important and still actively debated.
AI.method: The authors design the AI Science Exam for ENSO, where agents are given real observational climate data and six hours to: (1) preprocess the observations; (2) write and then freeze their own diagnostic code; and (3) use only those self-written diagnostics as feedback to iteratively build a low-order stochastic model of ENSO. Hidden graders, unseen by the agents, then objectively evaluate the produced models by checking how well they reproduce ENSO statistics, reconstruct unobserved variables, and forecast held-out years, using the same scoring on a known published model for comparison. They run twelve different agent systems under this protocol and perform controlled information-variation experiments on the best system to probe for data memorization versus genuine modeling.
AI.result: Six out of twelve agent systems construct models that outperform a published baseline ENSO model, especially in reconstructing hidden variables and forecasting unseen years. The top-performing agent models, when simplified, align structurally with one or the other of two leading scientific theories explaining ENSO's warm–cold asymmetry—despite these theories never being described in the task. Additional controlled runs show that the best system’s performance is not due to memorizing the historical observational record and that modifying the information provided meaningfully changes the models it builds.
AI.conclusion: SciExam for ENSO provides a concrete way to evaluate language-model agents on open-ended scientific modeling tasks where no unique ground-truth answer exists. The benchmark reveals that current agents can already develop competitive ENSO models whose simplified structures engage with ongoing scientific debates, implying that LLM-based agents may contribute insightfully—though not infallibly—to unresolved research questions. The setup also suggests that agent behavior and model quality are sensitive to the information they receive, supporting the view that they perform real modeling rather than simple retrieval.

title: RoboJEPA: Scaling Robotic Latent World Models
summary: Latent world models have shown a remarkable ability to predict future states and to plan in the real world. In practice, however, we lack a principled way to estimate how their capabilities scale with model size, data, and compute, an open problem that slows progress in the field. In this work we present RoboJEPA, a world model based on the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) and trained on a large-scale dataset spanning 12 robotic embodiments. We show that RoboJEPA's imagination error, the error of its latent rollouts, follows a second-order power law in compute, allowing us to predict model quality well beyond the scale at which the law is fit. We further show that downstream robotic planning performance improves predictably with compute, and that imagination error is strongly correlated with it, making it a reliable proxy for real-robot evaluation. Finally, we demonstrate that latent world models can be deployed zero-shot as robotic agents, planning toward a single goal image to solve tasks requiring long-horizon planning on real hardware. We release all model checkpoints together with our training and robot deployment code. To our knowledge, this is the first work to establish scaling laws for multi-embodiment robotic world models trained on real robot data, and RoboJEPA, at 8B parameters, is the largest JEPA predictor model trained to date.

AI.tldr: RoboJEPA is a large latent world model for robotics that demonstrates predictable scaling laws in imagination error and planning performance across multiple robot embodiments.
AI.motivation: There is no principled understanding of how robotic latent world models improve with increases in model size, data, and compute, which makes it hard to predict returns on scaling and slows practical progress in model-based robot learning.
AI.method: The authors build RoboJEPA, a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture-based latent world model trained on large-scale real-world data from 12 different robot embodiments. They measure the model’s latent rollout (imagination) error and downstream planning performance as they scale compute, then fit and analyze scaling laws—specifically a second-order power law—for imagination error and its relationship to planning success. They also deploy the model zero-shot as a planner that optimizes actions to reach a single goal image on real robot hardware.
AI.result: RoboJEPA’s imagination error follows a second-order power law in compute, enabling accurate extrapolation of model quality beyond the scales used to fit the law. Downstream planning performance on robotic tasks improves in a predictable manner with increased compute, and imagination error is strongly correlated with real-robot planning success. The authors successfully deploy the model zero-shot for long-horizon planning on physical robots and train an 8B-parameter JEPA predictor, claimed to be the largest of its kind.
AI.conclusion: Scaling laws analogous to those in language and vision also hold for multi-embodiment robotic latent world models trained on real robot data. Imagination error serves as a practical proxy for real-robot performance, and large JEPA-based world models like RoboJEPA can be used directly as zero-shot planners for long-horizon tasks. The work provides both empirical guidance for scaling robotic world models and open-source resources for further research.
